## Commentary on the Book of Ones
## In the Aṅguttara Nikāya
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One
## Introduction to the Text
I pay homage to the Buddha, who has a heart cooled by great compassion, who has dispelled the darkness of delusion with the lamp-light of the wisdom of the path of Arahatship, the wisdom of teaching, and the wisdom of unimpeded knowledge, who is the teacher of the world of beings including devas and humans, and who is liberated from the five destinations of rebirth.

I pay homage to those ten supreme Dhamma, which the Buddha attained by developing and realizing the state of Buddhahood, which are free from the defilements of kileasā, and than which there is no higher Dhamma.

I pay homage with my head to that Noble Saṅgha, the group of eight individuals, who are the breast-born sons of the Buddha and who destroy the army of Māra.

By the power of the merit gained from paying homage to the Triple Gem with a mind of faith in this way, may all obstacles be well dispelled.

For the purpose of explaining the meaning of the noble Aṅguttara collection, which is adorned with the Book of Ones, the Book of Twos, and so forth, and which generates the varied analytical insight of the most excellent Dhamma-preachers;

That commentary which was first recited by the five hundred Arahant Elders led by the Venerable Mahākassapa at the time of the First Council, and was subsequently recited again (by the Arahant Elders led by Venerable Yasa and Venerable Moggaliputtatissa) during the Second and Third Councils;

After being thus recited at the three councils, it was brought to the island of Sri Lanka by the Venerable Mahāmahinda, who was endowed with mastery, and was established in the Sinhala language for the benefit of the island dwellers.
2:
I shall discard the Sinhala language from that ancient commentary and present it in the Magadhan language, which is pleasing to the heart, faultless, and in accordance with the method of the Pali texts.

I shall do so without contradicting the views of the Elders of the Mahāvihāra tradition, who possess very subtle judgment and who illuminate the lineage of the Elders.

Omitting the meanings that have appeared repeatedly, I shall explain the meaning for the delight of good people and for the long-lasting endurance of the Dispensation.

Descriptions of cities such as Sāvatthī have already been provided by me while explaining the meanings of the Dīgha Nikāya and Majjhima Nikāya.

Therefore, I will not provide a detailed account of the stories that were already extensively told in those commentaries here again.

However, for those Suttas whose meaning is not clear without the background stories, I will provide the stories for the purpose of clarifying them.

Discourse on virtue (sīla), the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), all subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), the details of the meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti) along with the conduct (cariyā),

All the higher knowledges (abhiññā), the decisions regarding the section on wisdom, the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), faculties (indriya), and the four Noble Truths,

The teaching of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) which has a very pure and subtle method, and the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā) which is not divorced from the path of the Pali texts—

Since all these have been very clearly explained by me in the Visuddhimagga, I will not examine them again in detail here.

This Visuddhimagga stands in the middle of the four Nikāyas and will clarify the meanings as they were spoken in those Nikāyas.

Therefore, taking that Visuddhimagga together with this commentary, understand the meaning belonging to the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

In the statement 'I shall explain the meaning of that Aṅguttara Nikāya', the Aṅguttara Nikāya consists of eleven books (nipātas): the Book of Ones, the Book of Twos, the Book of Threes, the Book of Fours, the Book of Fives, the Book of Sixes, the Book of Sevens, the Book of Eights, the Book of Nines, the Book of Tens, and the Book of Elevens. In terms of the number of discourses, there are nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven (9,557) suttas in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
3:
## 1. Commentary on the Chapter on Forms, etc.
## Brief Account
In that Aṅguttara collection, there are eleven books: the Book of Ones, the Book of Twos, the Book of Threes, the Book of Fours, the Book of Fives, the Book of Sixes, the Book of Sevens, the Book of Eights, the Book of Nines, the Book of Tens, and the Book of Elevens. Regarding the number of suttas:

'There are nine thousand suttas, five hundred suttas, and fifty-seven suttas in the Aṅguttara collection.'

Among those books, the Book of Ones is the first, and among the suttas, the Cittapariyādāna Sutta is the first. The introduction to that sutta, beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' (Thus have I heard), was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council. That First Great Council has been explained in detail at the beginning of the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya; therefore, it should be understood in the same way as it was detailed there.

## Commentary on the Introduction
In the introduction beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ', 'evaṃ' is an indeclinable (nipāta), and 'me' and so forth are nouns (nāma). In the phrase 'Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati', 'vi' is a prefix (upasagga) and 'harati' is a verb (ākhyāta); in this way, the division of words should first be understood.

As for the meaning, the word 'evaṃ' has many different meanings such as simile (upamā), instruction (upadesa), appreciation (sampahaṃsana), blame (garahaṇa), acceptance of words (vacanasampaṭiggaha), manner (ākāra), indication (nidassana), and emphasis (avadhāraṇa).

Indeed, it appears in the sense of simile (upamā) in such passages as: 'Just as (evaṃ) from a heap of flowers many a garland may be made, so should many good deeds be done by one born a mortal.' It appears in the sense of instruction (upadesa) in: 'Thus (evaṃ) you should advance, thus you should retreat.' It appears in the sense of appreciation (sampahaṃsana) in: 'So it is (evam-etaṃ), Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.' It appears in the sense of blame (garahaṇa) in: 'In this very way (evam-evaṃ) this outcaste woman speaks the praise of that shaveling ascetic wherever she may be.' It appears in the sense of acceptance of words (vacanasampaṭiggaha) in: '"Yes, Bhante (Evaṃ bhante)," those monks replied to the Blessed One.' It appears in the sense of manner (ākāra) in: 'Bhante, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a manner (evaṃ).' It appears in: 'Come, young man, go to where the ascetic Ānanda is; having approached...'
4:
In my name, ask the monk Ānanda whether he is free from illness, free from affliction, active, strong, and living in comfort: 'The youth Subha, son of the brahmin Todeyya, asks the Venerable Ānanda whether he is free from illness... [as before] ...and living in comfort.' Speak also thus: 'It would be good if the Venerable Ānanda would come to the house of the youth Subha, son of the brahmin Todeyya, out of compassion.' In such examples (DN 1.445), the word 'Evaṃ' is used in the sense of indication (nidassana).

'Kālāmas, what do you think? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?' 'Unwholesome, Bhante.' 'Are they blameworthy or blameless?' 'Blameworthy, Bhante.' 'Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?' 'Censured by the wise, Bhante.' 'When undertaken and followed, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? How does it seem to you?' 'When undertaken and followed, they lead to harm and suffering; so it seems to us.' In such examples (AN 3.66), it is used in the sense of ascertainment (avadhāraṇa). Here, the word 'Evaṃ' should be understood in the senses of manner (ākāra), indication (nidassana), and ascertainment (avadhāraṇa).

Among those meanings, by the word 'Evaṃ' in the sense of manner (ākāra), this meaning is shown: Who is able to fully understand in every way the words of that Blessed One, which are subtle through various methods, arising from many dispositions, perfect in meaning and phrasing, possessing various miracles, profound in the penetration of the Dhamma, the meaning, the teaching, and the realization, and reaching the ear-path of all beings according to their respective languages? However, even while generating the desire to hear with all one's might, it means: 'Thus have I heard; I too have heard in this one manner.'

By the sense of indication (nidassana), freeing himself [from the claim of being self-enlightened] by saying, 'I am not self-enlightened (Sayam-bhū), I have not realized this myself,' he indicates the entire Sutta to be spoken now by saying, 'Thus have I heard; I too have heard it thus.'

By the sense of ascertainment (avadhāraṇa), in accordance with being praised by the Blessed One as 'Monks, among my monk disciples who are very learned, Ānanda is the foremost; among those who have mindfulness, who have good behavior, who have resolution, and who are attendants, Ānanda is the foremost' (AN 1.219, 223), and by the General of the Dhamma [Venerable Sāriputta] as 'Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, skilled in the linguistics, and skilled in the sequence' (AN 5.169), he shows his own power of retention and generates the desire to hear in beings, saying: 'Thus have I heard; and that which was heard is neither less nor more in meaning or phrasing; it is exactly so, and should not be understood otherwise.'
5:
The word 'Me' is found in three senses. This is true. In passages such as 'Food obtained by chanting verses is not to be eaten by me' (gāthābhi-gītaṃ me abhojjaneyyaṃ), it has the sense of 'mayā' (by me). In passages such as 'It would be good for me, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief' (sādhu me bhante bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṃ desetu), it has the sense of 'mayhaṃ' (to/for me). In passages such as 'Monks, be heirs of my Dhamma' (dhammadāyādā me bhikkhave bhavatha), it has the sense of 'mama' (of me/my). Here, however, both meanings 'It was heard by me' (mayā sutaṃ) and 'My hearing' (mama sutaṃ) are appropriate.

This word 'Suta', whether with a prefix or without, has many different meanings such as going, famous, wet, accumulated, devoted, cognized by ear-consciousness, and cognized following the ear-door. This is true. In passages such as 'devoted to the army' (senāya pasuto), it means 'going'. In 'one who sees the famous Dhamma' (sutadhammassa passato), it means 'famous'. In 'the wet for the wet' (avassutā avassutassa), it means 'wet'. In 'much merit has been accumulated by you' (tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ), it means 'accumulated'. In 'those wise ones devoted to meditation' (ye jhānappasutā dhīrā), it means 'devoted'. In 'seen, heard, sensed' (diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ), it means 'that which is cognized by ear-consciousness'. In 'one who remembers what is heard, a storer of what is heard' (sutadharo sutasannicayo), it means 'one who remembers what is cognized following the ear-door'.

Here, the word 'Suta' means 'that which is noted following the ear-door' or 'the act of noting'. If the word 'Me' is in the sense of 'mayā' (by me), it is appropriate as 'Thus by me it was noted following the ear-door'. If it is in the sense of 'mama' (my), it is appropriate as 'Thus my noting following the ear-door occurred'.

Thus, among these three words: 'Evaṃ' indicates the function of consciousness such as ear-consciousness. 'Me' indicates the person endowed with the aforementioned consciousness. 'Sutaṃ' indicates the reception that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor distorted, by rejecting the state of not hearing. Furthermore, 'Evaṃ' expresses the occurrence of that cognitive process (vīthi) following the ear-door upon the object in various manners. 'Me' expresses oneself. 'Sutaṃ' expresses the Dhamma. The summary here is: 'With the cognitive process occurring upon the object in various manners, I did nothing else; I only performed this act of hearing; this Dhamma was heard.'

Furthermore, 'Evaṃ' expresses the thing to be indicated. 'Me' expresses the person. 'Sutaṃ' expresses the function of the person. The meaning is: 'The Sutta which I shall indicate, that Sutta was heard by me thus.'
6:
Furthermore, the word 'Evaṃ' indicates the various modes of the mental continuum, through which various meanings and syllables are grasped. Indeed, this designation 'Evaṃ' is a designation of mode (ākārapaññatti). The word 'Me' is an indication of the agent (kattuniddesa). The word 'Sutaṃ' is an indication of the object (visayaniddesa). By this extent of the phrase 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ', the grasping and determination of the object by the agent, who possesses a mental continuum occurring in various modes, is accomplished.

Alternatively, the word 'Evaṃ' is an indication of the person's function. The word 'Sutaṃ' is an indication of the consciousness's function. The word 'Me' is an indication of the person endowed with both functions. In brief, the meaning of 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is: 'I, a person endowed with the consciousness that has the function of hearing, and who has acquired the conventional term "hearing-function" (savana-kicca) by the power of consciousness, have heard.'

In that phrase 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ', the designations 'Evaṃ' and 'Me' are 'designations of the non-existent' (avijjamānapaññatti) in terms of ultimate reality (paramattha). For what is there in this context that exists ultimately which could receive the designation 'Evaṃ' or 'Me'? However, the designation 'Sutaṃ' is a 'designation of the existent' (vijjamānapaññatti). For that which is perceived here by the ear exists in the ultimate sense. Furthermore, the words 'Evaṃ' and 'Me' are 'derivative designations' (upādāpaññatti) because they are spoken in dependence on various modes. The designation 'Sutaṃ' is a 'comparative designation' (upanidhāpaññatti) because it is spoken in comparison to seeing (diṭṭha) and so forth.

Here, by the word 'Evaṃ', non-delusion (asammoha) is shown. For one who is deluded is not capable of penetrating various modes. By the word 'Sutaṃ', non-forgetfulness (asammosa) of what was heard is shown. For one who has forgotten what was heard cannot later claim, 'I have heard.' Thus, for that Venerable Ānanda, wisdom is perfected through non-delusion, and mindfulness is perfected through non-forgetfulness. Among these two, through mindfulness preceded by wisdom, there is the ability to retain the syllables; through wisdom preceded by mindfulness, there is the ability to penetrate the meaning. By being endowed with both abilities, the status of 'Treasurer of the Dhamma' (Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika) is accomplished, as he is capable of preserving the treasury of the Dhamma, which is complete in meaning and syllable.

Another method: By the word 'Evaṃ', wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is shown, for one who attends unwisely lacks the penetration of various modes. By the word 'Sutaṃ', non-distraction (avikkhepa) is shown, for one with a distracted mind does not hear. Indeed, a person with a distracted mind, even when spoken to with all perfection, says, 'I did not hear; please say it again.' Here, through wise attention, right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi) and the state of having performed merit in the past (pubbe ca katapuññatā) are achieved. For these do not exist in one who is wrongly directed or who has not performed merit in the past. Likewise, through non-distraction, the hearing of the True Dhamma (saddhammassavana) is achieved.
7:
It also accomplishes reliance on good persons (sappurisūpanissaya). For a person with a distracted mind is unable to listen to the Dhamma, and for one who does not rely on good persons, there is no hearing of the Dhamma.

Another method: Since it was said, 'Evaṃ refers to the indication of the various modes of the mental continuum which grasps various meanings and syllables,' such a good mode is not possible for one who is wrongly self-directed or who has not performed merit in the past. Therefore, by this good mode 'Evaṃ', he shows his own endowment with the latter two wheels (cakka). By the word 'Sutaṃ', through the application of hearing, he shows his endowment with the former two wheels. Indeed, for one living in an unsuitable locality or one devoid of reliance on good persons, there is no hearing of the Dhamma. Thus, for that Venerable Ānanda, through the accomplishment of the latter two wheels, purity of intention (āsayasuddhi) is accomplished; through the accomplishment of the former two wheels, purity of effort (payogasuddhi) is accomplished. Through that purity of intention, the clarity of attainment (adhigama) is accomplished, and through purity of effort, the clarity of scripture (āgama) is accomplished. Thus, the words of one who is pure in effort and intention and endowed with scripture and attainment—just as the dawn is the precursor to the rising sun, and wise attention is the precursor to wholesome kamma—are worthy of being the precursor to the words of the Blessed One. Desiring to establish the introduction (nidāna) in its proper place, he said, 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ,' and so forth.

Another method: By the word 'Evaṃ', which shows penetration of various modes, he shows his own possession of the analytical insight of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) and the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā). By the word 'Sutaṃ', which shows penetration of the various things to be heard, he shows his own possession of the analytical insight of Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā) and the analytical insight of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā). Alternatively, by uttering this word 'Evaṃ' which shows wise attention, he shows: 'These teachings have been reflected upon by me with the mind and well-penetrated by wisdom.' By uttering this word 'Sutaṃ' which shows the application of hearing, he shows: 'Many teachings have been heard by me, retained, and mastered by speech.' By both words, the Elder, showing the completeness of meaning and syllable, inspires respect in hearing the Dhamma. Indeed, one who does not respectfully listen to the Dhamma that is complete in meaning and syllable remains outside of great benefit. Therefore, having inspired respect, the Dhamma should be listened to with care.

By this entire phrase 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ', the Venerable Ānanda, not claiming the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the level of the ignoble and, acknowledging his state as a disciple, enters the level of the virtuous. Furthermore, he raises his mind from the false Dhamma and establishes it in the True Dhamma. Showing that 'This was merely heard by me; it is the word of the Blessed One himself,' he [humbles] himself...
8:
He frees himself from blame, he points to the Teacher, he attributes the words to the Buddha, and he establishes the Guide of the Dhamma (Dhammanetti).

Furthermore, by saying "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" (Thus have I heard), he does not claim that he originated it himself, but explains the previous words, saying: "I received this in the presence of the Blessed One, who is confident with the four kinds of fearlessness, who possesses the ten powers, who stands in the place of the bull (āsabha), who roars the lion's roar, who is the supreme among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma, the Lamp of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma, the Turner of the noble Wheel of the True Dhamma, the Fully Enlightened One. In this matter, there should be no doubt or hesitation regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, the word, or the phrasing." Thus, he dispels the lack of faith of all devas and humans in this Dhamma and produces the perfection of faith. Therefore, it is said:

"The disciple of Gotama, speaking thus: 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ,' destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Dispensation."

"Ekaṃ" refers to a numerical designation. "Samayaṃ" refers to a designated time. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" indicates an indefinite time. In that context, the word samaya is seen in the senses of:

"Concordance (samavāya), occasion (khaṇa), time (kāla), assembly (samūha), cause (hetu), view (diṭṭhi), attainment (paṭilābha), abandonment (pahāna), and penetration (paṭivedha)."

Indeed, the sense of concordance (samavāya) is found in passages such as: "Perhaps we might approach tomorrow, depending on the time and the concordance." The sense of occasion (khaṇa) is found in: "Monks, there is only one occasion and time for living the holy life." The sense of time (kāla) is found in: "The hot time, the sweltering time." The sense of assembly (samūha) is found in: "A great assembly (Mahāsamaya) gathered in the forest." The sense of cause (hetu) is found in: "Bhaddāli, you did not penetrate the cause (samaya) for fulfilling the training... Bhaddāli, you did not penetrate this cause (samaya) either." The sense of view (diṭṭhi) is found in: "At that time, the wanderer Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta... was staying in Queen Mallikā’s park... where views were discussed (samayappavādaka)."
9:
The sense of attainment (paṭilābha) is intended in passages such as: "The benefit in the present life and the benefit in the future life; because of the attainment of these two benefits (atthābhisamaya), the steadfast one is called wise."

The sense of abandonment (pahāna) is intended in: "By the right abandonment of conceit (mānābhisamaya), he made an end of suffering."

The sense of penetration (paṭivedha) is intended in: "The sense of oppression of suffering, the sense of being conditioned, the sense of burning, the sense of change, and the sense of penetration (abhisamaya)."

In this context, however, the meaning of the word samaya is time (kāla). By this word samaya meaning time, it indicates one occasion among the various divisions of time such as year, season, month, fortnight, night, day, morning, midday, evening, the first, middle, or last watch, or a moment (muhutta), as "Ekaṃ samayaṃ."

Among those times such as years, etc., whatever sutta was spoken in whatever year, season, month, fortnight, part of the night, or part of the day, all that was well known and well determined by the Elder [Ānanda] through his wisdom. However, if he had said, "Thus have I heard in such a year, such a season, such a month, such a fortnight, such a part of the night, or such a part of the day," it would not be easy to remember, to recite, or to teach, and much would have to be said. Therefore, he combined that meaning into a single phrase and said, "Ekaṃ samayaṃ."

Alternatively, among the many divisions of time that are very well known among devas and humans regarding the Blessed One—such as the time of conception, the time of birth, the time of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), the time of the great renunciation, the time of practicing austerities, the time of the victory over Māra, the time of the supreme enlightenment, the time of dwelling in happiness in this very life, the time of teaching, and the time of the final Nibbāna—he indicates one occasion known as the time of teaching (desanāsamaya). It also refers to one occasion among the times of the work of wisdom and the work of compassion, specifically the time of the work of compassion; among the times of practice for one's own benefit and for the benefit of others, the time of practice for the benefit of others; among the two duties of those assembled, the time of Dhamma talk; and among the times of teaching and practice, the time of teaching.

But why is it designated here with the accusative case as "Ekaṃ samayaṃ," instead of the locative case as in the Abhidhamma, "Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ" (at which time [it is] of the sense sphere), and in other sutta passages, "Monks, at which time (yasmiṃ samaye) a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures..."; or the instrumental case as in the Vinaya, "At that time (tena samayena) the Blessed One..."?
10:
In the Abhidhamma and in other Suttas besides this one, the reference is made using the locative case as 'yasmiṃ samaye'. In the Vinaya, it is referred to using the instrumental case as 'tena samayena Buddho Bhagavā'. Why is it referred to here in the accusative case as 'ekam samayam' instead of those? It is because in the Abhidhamma and other Suttas, that specific meaning exists, whereas here, a different kind of meaning is possible. In the Abhidhamma and other Suttas, the sense of location (adhikaraṇattha) and the sense of marking one action by another (bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇattha) are possible. Indeed, 'samaya' meaning time or group is the locus for the states such as contact (phassa) mentioned in those contexts. Furthermore, by the occurrence of 'samaya'—defined as the moment (khaṇa), coincidence (samavāya), or cause (hetu)—the occurrence of those states like contact is marked. Therefore, to clarify those meanings, the reference is made in those texts using the locative case.

In the Vinaya Piṭaka, however, the sense of cause (hetuattha) and the sense of instrument (karaṇattha) are possible. The time of the prescription of training rules (sikkhāpada), which is difficult to know even for venerable ones like Sāriputta, was the cause and the instrument. While prescribing the training rules and considering the reason for their prescription, the Blessed One dwelt in various places. Therefore, to clarify that meaning, the reference is made in the Vinaya using the instrumental case.

In this Sutta and others of this nature, the sense of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga) is possible. For however long the Blessed One taught this Sutta or another, for that entire duration, he continuously dwelt in the 'abiding of compassion' (karuṇāvihāra). Therefore, to clarify that meaning, the reference is made here using the accusative case. Thus, the teachers said:
'Considering various meanings, the word samaya is spoken in other texts with the locative and instrumental cases; but in this Sutta, it is spoken with the accusative case.'

Ancient commentators, however, explain that 'tasmiṃ samaye', 'tena samayena', or 'ekam samayam' are merely differences in expression, and in all instances, the meaning is only that of the locative. Therefore, even when 'ekam samayam' is said, it should be understood as having the meaning 'ekasmiṃ samaye'.

Bhagavā means a teacher (garu) who is highly esteemed. In the world, a teacher who is highly esteemed is called 'Bhagavā'. And this Blessed One, because of his excellence in all qualities, is the teacher of all beings; therefore, he should be known as 'Bhagavā'. Ancient teachers also said:
'The word Bhagavā is the most excellent; the word Bhagavā is supreme. He is the teacher endowed with reverence; therefore, he is called Bhagavā.'
11:
Furthermore:
'He is Bhagavā because he possesses fortune (bhāgyavā), has broken the defilements (bhaggavā), is endowed [with qualities] (yutto), is a possessor of analyzed [dhamma] (vibhattavā), has frequented [attainments] (bhattavā), and has vomited out the journey through existences (vantagamano).'
Through the power of this verse, the meaning of the word 'Bhagavā' should be understood in detail. That detail has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussatiniddesa).

By the words 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' (Thus have I heard), showing the Dhamma exactly as it was heard, the Dhamma-body (dhammasarīra) of the Blessed One is made manifest. By such manifestation, he comforts the people who are distressed by not seeing the Teacher, [implying]: 'This teaching is not one whose teacher has passed away; this Dhamma itself is your teacher.' By the words 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ Bhagavā', wishing to show that the Blessed One was no longer present at that time, he establishes the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the form-body (rūpakāya). By showing the Parinibbāna of the form-body, he causes a sense of urgency (saṃvega) in those intoxicated with life, [thinking]: 'Even that Blessed One, who taught the Noble Dhamma of such nature, who possessed the Ten Powers, and whose body was like a mass of diamonds, has passed away; who else should generate desire for life?' and he inspires them to strive in the True Dhamma. By saying 'Evaṃ', he indicates the perfection of the teaching (desanāsampatti). By 'Me sutaṃ', the perfection of the disciple (sāvakasampatti). By 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ', the perfection of time (kālasampatti). By 'Bhagavā', the perfection of the teacher (desakasampatti).

'Sāvatthiyaṃ' means in the city of that name. This is a word in the locative case in the sense of proximity. 'Viharati' (dwells) is a term generally indicating being endowed with one of the abidings (vihāra) such as the abiding in postures (iriyāpatha), the divine abiding (dibba), the brahma abiding, or the noble abiding (ariya). In this context, however, it is a term indicating being engaged in one of the postures among standing, walking, sitting, and lying down. Because of this indication, whether the Blessed One was standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, he should be understood simply as 'viharati' (dwelling). Indeed, the Blessed One carries on and maintains the physical body without letting it fall by relieving the fatigue caused by one posture with another posture; therefore, it is said 'viharati'.

'Jetavane' means in the grove of Prince Jeta. Indeed, that grove was planted, nurtured, and protected by Prince Jeta, and he was its owner; therefore, it acquired the name 'Jetavana'. In that Jetavana monastery [he dwelt]. 'Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme' means in the monastery which acquired the name 'Anāthapiṇḍika's Park' because it was offered to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, who sacrificed fifty-four crores of wealth...
12:
In the monastery (he was staying). What has been stated here is only a brief explanation in this Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya. The detailed explanation has been given in the commentary on the Sabbāsava Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī.

In that (sentence), there is a point to be considered: If the Blessed One was staying in Sāvatthī, it should not be said "in Jeta’s Grove." If he was staying in that (Jeta’s Grove), it should not be said "in Sāvatthī." This is because it is impossible to stay in both places at the same time. However, it should not be viewed in this way. Have we not already said that "the locative case is used in the sense of proximity"? Therefore, just as herds of cattle grazing near the Ganges or Yamunā rivers are said to be "grazing in the Ganges" or "grazing in the Yamunā," so too here, the Blessed One, while staying in this Jeta’s Grove which is near Sāvatthī, is said to be "staying in Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove." In fact, the word "Sāvatthī" is mentioned to indicate the village for alms-resort, and the remaining word (Jetavana) is mentioned to indicate a dwelling place suitable for those who have gone forth.

Among those words, by the word "Sāvatthī," the Venerable Ānanda shows the Blessed One’s favor toward householders; by mentioning "Jetavana" and so on, he shows the favor toward those who have gone forth. Similarly, by the former word (Sāvatthī), he shows the avoidance of the practice of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) due to the acceptance of the four requisites; by the latter word (Jetavana), he shows the means of avoiding the practice of devotion to sensual pleasures (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) due to the abandonment of the objects of sensual desire. By the former word, he shows the devotion to teaching the Dhamma; by the latter word, the inclination toward seclusion. By the former word, he shows the approach (to beings) through compassion; by the latter word, the withdrawal (from defilements) through wisdom. By the former word, he shows the desire to fulfill the welfare and happiness of beings; by the latter word, the absence of being tainted (by craving) while performing the welfare and happiness of others. By the former word, he shows the pleasant dwelling due to not abandoning the happiness consistent with the Dhamma; by the latter word, the reason for the devotion to the higher human states (uttarimanussadhamma). By the former word, he shows the great benefit to humans; by the latter word, to the devas. By the former word, he shows the growth in the world of the Blessed One who was born in the world; by the latter word, the state of being untainted by the (worldly) dhammas. By the former word, in accordance with the saying, "Bhikkhus, there is one person who, when arising in the world, arises for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. Who is that one person? It is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One," he shows the fulfillment of the purpose for which the Blessed One arose; by the latter word, he shows the dwelling suitable for the place where he arose. Indeed, the Blessed One arose only in the forest, first in the Lumbinī Sal grove and secondly at the Bodhimaṇḍa, through these mundane and supramundane arisings. Therefore, he shows his dwelling only in the forest—in this way and so forth, the connection of the meaning here should be understood.

The word "tatra" (there) indicates the place and time. This is because it shows: at that time when he was staying, (he taught the Dhamma); in that monastery where he was staying, (he taught the Dhamma).
13:
In another way, it shows the appropriate place and time for teaching. For the Blessed One does not teach the Dhamma in an inappropriate place or at an inappropriate time. In this regard, the statement beginning with "It is not yet the time for teaching, Bāhiya" (Udāna 10) serves as evidence. The word "kho" is a particle used either as a mere filler, for emphasis (avadhāraṇa), or in the sense of the beginning of a time. The word "Bhagavā" indicates being the Teacher of the world. The word "Bhikkhū" refers to persons worthy of hearing the Dhamma discourse. Furthermore, in this word "Bhikkhu", the etymological meaning should be understood in such ways as: "He is a bhikkhu because he begs; he is a bhikkhu because he has undertaken the practice of wandering for alms."

"Āmantesi" means he called, he spoke, or he addressed; this is the meaning here. In other contexts, it is also used in the sense of informing. As it is said: "Monks, I inform you; monks, I announce to you." It is also used in the sense of summoning. As it is said: "Come, monk, in my name, summon Sāriputta."

The word "Bhikkhave" is an expression of the manner of addressing. This address is used because they are endowed with qualities such as the habit of begging. For grammarians consider: one endowed with the quality of having the habit of begging is a bhikkhu; one endowed with the quality of having the nature of begging is a bhikkhu; and one endowed with the quality of performing the act of begging well is also a bhikkhu. By this word associated with qualities such as the habit of begging, he describes a livelihood practiced by both the lowly and the noble, thereby subduing pride and dejection. With this word "Bhikkhave", preceded by a glance from eyes and a heart softened by the diffusion of compassion, he makes those monks face him. By that very word, which indicates the desire to speak, he generates in them the desire to listen. By that very word in the sense of addressing, he urges them to listen well and attend carefully. For the success and fulfillment of the Dispensation (Sāsana) depend on listening well and attending carefully.

If it is asked, "Why did he address only the monks when other devas and humans were present?" The answer is: because they are the eldest, the best, the close, and the constantly present. While the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching is common to all assemblies, the monks are the "eldest" among the assembly because they were the first to arise. They are the "best" because, starting with the homeless life, they follow the Teacher’s conduct and are the recipients of the entire Dispensation. They are "close" because they were seated in the presence of the Teacher there. They are "constantly present" because they frequent the vicinity of the Teacher. Furthermore, they are like vessels for the Dhamma teaching because they practice according to the instruction. Therefore, he addressed only the monks.
14:
For what purpose does the Blessed One address the monks first when teaching the Dhamma, rather than teaching the Dhamma directly? It is for the purpose of generating mindfulness (sati). Indeed, monks might be sitting there thinking of other things, being distracted in mind, reflecting on the Dhamma they have learned, or attending to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). If the Dhamma were taught without addressing them, they might be unable to note: "What is the source of this teaching? What is its cause? Due to what specific incident was it taught?" Thus, they might grasp it wrongly or not grasp it at all. Therefore, to generate mindfulness in them, the Blessed One addresses them first and teaches the Dhamma afterwards.

"Bhadante" is a word of respect or a response given to the Teacher. Furthermore, in this context, the Blessed One addresses those monks by saying "Bhikkhave". Those monks respond to the Blessed One by saying "Bhadante". Likewise, the Blessed One speaks "Bhikkhave" at the beginning, and they reply "Bhadante". He causes them to give a response by saying "Bhikkhave", and they give the response by saying "Bhadante". "Te bhikkhū" refers to those monks whom the Blessed One addressed. "Bhagavato paccassosuṃ" means they listened attentively to the Blessed One’s address; the meaning is that they listened facing him, acknowledged it, and accepted it. "Bhagavā etadavoca" means the Blessed One spoke this entire Sutta which is now to be told. With this, the explanation of the meaning of the Introduction (Nidāna)—which was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda and adorned with the time, place, speaker, and assembly for the sake of easy comprehension of this Sutta—is completed.

## Description of Forms, etc. (Rūpādivaṇṇanā)

Now, the opportunity has arrived for the commentary on the Sutta laid down by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with: "Monks, I do not see even a single other form..." Since this commentary on the Sutta becomes clear only after examining the reason for the Sutta’s delivery (suttanikkhepa), the examination of the delivery of the Sutta should first be understood. There are four reasons for the delivery of a Sutta: (1) by one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya), (2) by the inclination of others (parajjhāsaya), (3) on account of a question (pucchāvasika), and (4) due to a specific incident (atthuppattika). Among these four, those Suttas which the Blessed One taught solely by his own inclination without being requested by others—such as the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, the Vattha Sutta, and so on—are called "delivery by one's own inclination" (attajjhāsaya-nikkhepa). However, those taught by way of the inclination of others, after observing their inclination, preference, disposition, aspiration, and their capacity for enlightenment—such as: "The things that ripen for the liberation of Rāhula have matured; what if I were to further guide Rāhula toward the destruction of the taints (āsavas)"—these are taught by the inclination of others.
15:
The Rāhulovāda Sutta, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and others are Parajjhāsaya Nikkhepa, delivered based on the inclinations of others. When various deities and humans approached the Blessed One and asked questions in various ways, the discourses delivered according to those questions, such as the Devatā Saṃyutta and Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta, are called Pucchāvasika Nikkhepa. Discourses delivered based on an arising incident, such as the Dhammadāyāda Sutta and Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta, are called Atthuppattika Nikkhepa. Among these four types of delivery, this Sutta is a Parajjhāsaya Nikkhepa. Indeed, this Sutta was delivered by the power of others' inclinations. By whose inclination was it delivered? It was delivered by the inclination of men who are preoccupied with visual forms (rūpagaruka).

In that Sutta, among the words beginning with 'Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave,' the letter 'na' expresses negation. The word 'ahaṃ' refers to the Teacher himself. By the word 'bhikkhave,' he addresses the monks. 'Aññaṃ' refers to a form other than the female form that is about to be mentioned. 'Ekarūpampi' means even a single form. In the word 'samanupassāmi,' contemplation (samanupassanā) is of two kinds: contemplation through wisdom (ñāṇa-samanupassanā) and contemplation through wrong view (diṭṭhi-samanupassanā). Therein, contemplating as 'He contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent' is called ñāṇa-samanupassanā. Contemplating as 'He contemplates form as self,' etc., is called diṭṭhi-samanupassanā. Between these two, ñāṇa-samanupassanā is intended here. This word should be understood in connection with the letter 'na.' The meaning is: 'Monks, even when I look with omniscient knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), I do not see even a single other form besides the female form.'

'Yaṃ evaṃ purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati' means that which stands having completely overwhelmed, seized, and exhausted the wholesome consciousness of the four planes (catubhūmaka-kusala-citta) of a man who is preoccupied with visual forms. In contexts such as 'having overwhelmed the entire elephant corps,' the word 'pariyādāna' means seizing. In contexts such as 'Monks, the perception of impermanence, when developed and frequently practiced, overwhelms all sensual lust,' it means exhausting. Here, both meanings are appropriate. In this context, when this female form seizes the wholesome consciousness, it is not like a man seizing a bundle of blue lotuses with his hand; nor, when it exhausts, is it like fire heating and drying up water on a tripod. It should be understood that by preventing the arising of wholesome consciousness, it both seizes and exhausts the wholesome consciousness of the four planes. Therefore, it is said: 'It stands having overwhelmed the mind of a man.'

'Yathayidaṃ' is analyzed as 'yathā idaṃ.' 'Itthirūpaṃ' is the form of a woman. In that word, the derivative meaning and the general characteristic of 'rūpa' should be understood in accordance with the Sutta: 'Monks, why do you say rūpa? Monks, it is called rūpa because it is deformed (ruppati). By what is it deformed? It is deformed by cold and it is deformed by heat,' etc.
16:
The derivative meaning and the general characteristic of the term 'rūpa' should be understood. This term 'rūpa' occurs in many senses, such as aggregate (khandha), existence (bhava), sign (nimitta), cause (paccaya), body (sarīra), color/appearance (vaṇṇa), and shape (saṇṭhāna).

Indeed, this term 'rūpa' occurs in the sense of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) in the passage: 'Whatever form, whether past, future, or present...' It occurs in the sense of form-existence (rūpabhava) in the passage: 'He develops the path (jhāna) for the sake of arising in the form-sphere.' It occurs in the sense of a kasina sign (kasina-nimitta) in the passage: 'Being percipient of the formless internally, he sees forms externally.' It occurs in the sense of cause (paccaya) in the passage: 'Monks, evil unwholesome states arise with a cause, not without a cause.' It occurs in the sense of the body (sarīra) in the passage: 'Space that is enclosed comes to be reckoned as a body.' It occurs in the sense of color/appearance (vaṇṇa) in the passage: 'Dependent on the eye and color, eye-consciousness arises.' It occurs in the sense of shape (saṇṭhāna) in the passage: 'He is measured by shape, he is pleased by shape.' By the word 'etc.' (ādi), terms such as 'dear nature,' 'pleasant nature,' and 'tasteless nature' are also included.

In this context, however, this term 'rūpa' refers to the color/appearance (vaṇṇa) known as the form-base (rūpāyatana) of a woman, which is produced by the four causes. Furthermore, whatever color/appearance is connected to the body—such as a woman's clothing, ornaments, perfumes, cosmetics, or the flowers she wears—when it becomes an object of a man's eye-consciousness, all of that should be understood as 'female form' (itthirūpa). The statement 'Monks, the female form stands having overwhelmed the mind of a man' was spoken to strengthen the meaning previously mentioned. Or, the previous statement 'Monks, just as this female form...' was spoken by way of a simile, while this statement was spoken by way of showing the power of overwhelming the mind.

In this regard, there is this story concerning the power of the female form to overwhelm the mind: King Mahādāṭhika Nāga, having built the Great Stūpa at Ambatthala on Cetiyagiri and performed the Giribhaṇḍa offering, used to go to Cetiyagiri from time to time accompanied by his harem to give great offerings to the Saṅgha of monks. In a place where many people assemble, mindfulness is not well-established in everyone. The King's chief queen, named Damila Devī, was in the prime of her youth, beautiful and graceful. Then, an elderly monk who had gone forth in his old age, named Citta Thera, looked with an unrestrained manner and took the sign of beauty in her form. He became like one insane, wandering about and crying out in every place he stood or sat, 'Aha, Damila Devī! Aha, Damila Devī!'
17:
He wandered about lamenting, "O Queen Damila Devi, O Queen Damila Devi!" From then on, the young novices called that elder by the name "Ummattakacittatthera" (the Mad Elder Citta). Soon after, the queen passed away. When the community of monks returned from visiting the cemetery to view the corpse, the young novices went to the elder and said, "Venerable Citta, for whom are you lamenting? We have just returned from the cemetery after viewing the queen's corpse." Even when told this, the elder did not believe them and spoke only the words of a madman, saying, "You must have gone to see the cemetery of just any woman; your faces are dark like smoke." In this way, the form of this woman remained, having completely overwhelmed the mind of Ummattakacittatthera.

Another story: It is said that one day King Saddhātissa came to the monastery surrounded by his harem. While a young monk was standing at the gateway of the Lohapāsāda (Brazen Palace), he looked at a woman without restraint. She also stopped her journey and looked back at the young monk. Both of them, consumed by the fire of lust that arose within them, passed away. In this way, the form of a woman remains, having completely overwhelmed the mind of a young monk.

Another story: It is said that a young monk from the Kalyāṇiya Mahāvihāra went to a monastery near the gate of Kāḷadīghavāpi village for the purpose of study. When his studies were completed, without heeding the words of his well-wishing teachers, he thought, "If the young novices in the places I visit ask me, I must be able to describe the layout and appearance of the village." While wandering for alms in the village, he took note of a sign of beauty in an unsuitable female object. Upon returning to his residence, he recognized the garment she had worn and, when asking, "Venerable sir, where did you get this?" he learned of her death. Thinking, "Such a woman has died because of me," he was consumed by the fire of lust arising from within and reached the end of his life. In this way, it should be understood that the form of a woman remains, having completely overwhelmed the mind of a man.

The second and subsequent discourses were taught according to the inclinations of those who prioritize sound and so forth. Among them, "female sound" (itthisadda) refers to the sound of speech, singing, and music produced by a woman's mind. Furthermore, the sound of a woman's clothing, the sound of her ornaments, and the sounds of the lute, conch, and drums produced by a woman's effort should also be understood as "female sound." All such sounds remain, having completely overwhelmed the mind of a man.
18:
In that context (where female sound remains having overwhelmed the mind of a man), the stories of the Golden Crab, the Golden Peacock, the young monk, and others should be understood. It is said that a large family of noble elephants lived near a mountain range. Not far from them was a large lake used by living beings, and in that lake lived a golden crab with a massive body. That golden crab would seize the legs of any creature that descended into the lake with its claws, as if with pincers, lead them to its dwelling, and kill them. The noble elephants, being wary of the danger from that golden crab, wandered about with a great bull elephant as their leader.

One day, the golden crab seized that great bull elephant. The bull elephant, endowed with strength and mindfulness, thought, "If I cry out in fear, all the elephants will flee without playing as they wish." Thus, he stood perfectly still. Then, knowing that all the elephants had emerged from the water, he trumpeted to let his wife, the female elephant, know that he had been captured, saying:

"There is a creature with horn-like claws, with long and protruding eyes, whose skin is but bone, who dwells in the water, and is hairless (the golden crab). Overwhelmed by that crab, I cry out piteously; do not abandon me, who am as dear as your own life."

Hearing that sound and knowing her husband, the elephant king, was captured, the female elephant, wishing to speak with both the bull elephant and the crab to free him from that danger, said:

"Noble elephant king, I shall not abandon you, who are sixty years old yet undiminished in strength, who trumpets like a crane and walks majestically. In this earth bounded by the four oceans, you are my most beloved.

Among the crabs that exist in the ocean, in the Ganges, and in the Yamuna, you, O water-born golden crab, are the most excellent. Please release my husband who is lamenting."

As soon as the golden crab heard the female's voice, it loosened its grip. Then the bull elephant, thinking, "This is the very opportunity to subdue this crab," kept one foot as if it were still captured, raised the second foot, and crushed the golden crab's shell to pieces. He then dragged it slightly and threw it onto the shore. Then all the elephants gathered and, saying "This is our enemy," crushed the crab to powder. In this way, first, the female sound remained, having completely overwhelmed the mind of the golden crab.
19:
The Golden Peacock King also entered the Himavanta and lived depending on a vast mountain thicket. At all times, at the hour of sunrise, he would look up at the solar disc and, desiring to provide protection for himself, would speak thus:

“There he rises, the king who sees all, the one king,
Golden-hued, illuminating the earth;
Therefore, I revere you, the golden-hued, illuminating the earth,
Guarded by you today, may we live through the day.

Those Brahmans who have reached the end of the Vedas in all dhammas,
May my homage be to them, and may they protect me;
Homage be to the Buddhas, homage be to Enlightenment,
Homage to the Liberated Ones, homage to Liberation.”

Having made this protection (paritta), the peacock wanders in search of food.

Having searched for and consumed food throughout the day, when returning to his dwelling place in the evening, he would look at the setting solar disc and also speak this verse:

“There he sets, the king who sees all, the one king,
Golden-hued, illuminating the earth;
Therefore, I revere you, the golden-hued, illuminating the earth,
Guarded by you today, may we live through the night.

Those Brahmans who have reached the end of the Vedas in all dhammas,
May my homage be to them, and may they protect me;
Homage be to the Buddhas, homage be to Enlightenment,
Homage to the Liberated Ones, homage to Liberation.”

Having made this protection, the peacock took up his residence.

Having passed seven hundred years in this manner, one day, even before performing the act of protection, he heard the cry of a peahen. Forgetting the act of protection, he fell under the power of the hunter sent by the king. Thus, the sound of a woman stands having overwhelmed the mind of the Golden Peacock King. It is said that the young monk living on Chātapabbata and the young monk living at Sudhāmuṇḍaka also reached ruin and destruction upon hearing the sound of a woman.
20:
In the third discourse, 'the scent of a woman' (itthigandha) refers to the scent-base (gandhāyatana) of a woman arising from four causes. Although the natural body odor of a woman is often unpleasant, what is intended here is the scent of external perfumes and such applied to the body. Some women have the scent of a horse, some of a goat, some of sweat, and some of blood. An extremely foolish worldling (puthujjana) is attached even to a woman with such scents. However, from the body of the woman-treasure of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), the scent of sandalwood wafts, and from her mouth, the scent of a blue lotus. This does not happen to all women; in this discourse, only external perfumes are intended. Animals such as elephants, horses, and cattle travel even one, two, three, or four leagues (yojana) following the seasonal scent of females of their own kind. Whether it is the scent produced in a woman's body or the scent of clothes, perfumes, and flowers worn by her, all should be understood simply as 'the scent of a woman' (itthigandha).

In the fourth discourse, 'the taste of a woman' (itthirasa) refers to the taste-base (rasāyatana) of a woman arising from four causes. The Elders Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga and Cūḷābhaya, however, say that 'the taste of a woman' is the taste found in hearing her voice when she asks, 'What shall I do?' and the taste found in enjoyment. Even so, the taste of saliva on a woman's lips, and the taste of gruel, rice, etc., given to her husband—all these should be understood simply as 'the taste of a woman' (itthirasa). Many beings, considering whatever is given by their own women with their own hands to be sweet, reach ruin and destruction.

In the fifth discourse, 'the touch of a woman' (itthiphoṭṭhabba) refers to the bodily contact of a woman and the touch of clothes, ornaments, flowers, etc., placed on her body. All such touches of a woman overwhelm the mind of a man. It is like the touch of a woman of the opposite sex overwhelming the mind of a young monk reciting in a group on the terrace of the Great Stūpa (Mahācetiya).

Thus, the Teacher, taking each of the objects such as forms according to the inclinations and underlying tendencies of beings, said, 'I do not see any other single object like this.' Just as for a man who values forms, the form of a woman causes the arising of thoughts to be distracted, obstructed, harassed, bound, deluded, and intensely infatuated, so other objects like sounds cannot do. And for those who value sounds and so on, sounds and so on do the same, while forms and so on cannot. For some men, only one of the five sense objects overwhelms the mind. For others, two, three, four, or all five overwhelm it. Therefore, these five discourses are taught according to the power of individuals who value the five sense objects. Although not taught by the power of the Pañcagaruka Jātaka, that Jātaka is brought as evidence. In that Jātaka, the five companions of the Bodhisatta once reached destruction due to being attached to their respective valued objects. These discourses, however, are taught solely according to the power of individuals who value the five sense objects. It is not only men who value the five sense objects.
21:
These five suttas are taught by way of those who regard the five sense objects as heavy (important), not by way of the Pañcagaruka Jātaka. However, the Pañcagaruka Jātaka should be brought in as evidence to be taught. To elaborate on that: in that Pañcagaruka Jātaka, when there was an arrangement of shops and such created by non-humans in the middle of a wilderness, among the Great Being's five companions, the one who valued visual forms was bound by visual objects and met with ruin and destruction; similarly, those who valued sounds and so forth met with ruin in the objects of sound and so forth. Thus, that Jātaka should be brought in as evidence to be taught. These five suttas, however, are taught solely by way of those who regard the five sense objects as heavy.

Since it is not only men who regard the five sense objects as heavy, but women also regard them as heavy, he taught another five suttas by way of those women. The meaning of those suttas should also be understood in the same manner as previously stated. Among the stories, in the first sutta, the story of the king's concubine who died after looking at a young monk standing at the door of the Lohapāsāda should be understood. That story has already been detailed below. 

In the second sutta, the story of the woman in Vārāṇasī who lived by her beauty should be understood. It is said that Guttila the lute player sent a thousand coins to a certain woman; she mocked him and did not wish to take them. He thought, 'I will do what needs to be done in this matter,' and at eventide, having adorned himself, he sat at the door of another house opposite her house. Having tuned the strings of the lute evenly, he sang without letting the sound of the song deviate from the sound of the strings. When that woman heard the sound of his singing, she mistook it for the door and, thinking 'I will go to him through the open casement window,' she jumped and reached the end of her life even in mid-air.

In the third sutta, this statement should be brought in: 'From the body of a Cakkavatti king, the scent of sandalwood wafts, and from his mouth, the scent of a blue lotus.' In this sutta, this story should be understood: In Sāvatthī, the husband of a certain householder's daughter, after hearing the Buddha's Dhamma teaching, thought, 'I cannot fulfill this Dhamma while being a layman,' and ordained under a certain elder who was a pindapātika (alms-collector). Then, knowing that his wife was a 'woman without a husband,' King Pasenadi of Kosala had her brought to the palace. One day, the King entered the palace carrying a bunch of blue lotuses and had one blue lotus given to each woman. While the flowers were being distributed, into that woman's hands, two flowers...
22:
...reached. She showed a sign of joy, smelled them, and then wept. The King, seeing her two-fold behavior (of joy and weeping), had her summoned and questioned her. She explained the reason for her joy and the reason for her weeping. Although she explained it up to three times, the King did not believe her. On the following day, he had all the fragrant scents such as flowers and perfumes removed from the entire royal residence. He then had seats prepared for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and gave a great offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. At the conclusion of the meal, he asked the woman, "Which one is your elder?" When she replied, "This is he," and he knew, he paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, may the Saṅgha of monks depart with you; our elder of such-and-forth name will perform the Anumodanā (thanksgiving)." The Teacher left that monk behind and went to the monastery. As soon as the elder began to speak the Anumodanā, the entire royal residence became fragrant like a perfumed chamber. The King, becoming devoted and thinking, "This woman spoke only the truth," asked the Teacher about that matter the next day. The Teacher explained, "Great King, in the past, while listening to the Dhamma, this monk listened respectfully and uttered the cry of appreciation, 'Sādhu, Sādhu.' Because of that respectful listening, Great King, he has obtained this kind of benefit."

"When the True Dhamma is being taught, for one who speaks 'Sādhu, Sādhu',
From the mouth, a fragrance arises, like a lotus in the water."

The rest is clear in all respects. In this chapter, only the cycle of suffering (vaṭṭa) is taught.

## Commentary on the Rūpādivagga

## 2. Commentary on the Nīvaraṇappahānavagga

In the first sutta of the second chapter, regarding the term "ekadhammampi," the word "Dhamma" should be understood in the sense of a nature devoid of a being (nissatta), as in "at that time, dhammas arise" and so forth. Therefore, "ekadhammampi" means a single nature that is not a being. In the term "anuppanno vā," the word "vā" should be understood in the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), as in the sentences: "For the stability of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking to be... Bhikkhus, as far as there are beings, whether footless or two-footed," and so forth.
23:
In this context, the word 'vā' should be understood in the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), as in 'bhūtānaṃ sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā, sambhavesīnaṃ vā anuggahāya' and so on, and not in the sense of alternative (vikappa). The meaning in this Pali text is: 'I do not see any other single thing, such as the sign of the beautiful (subhanimitta), by which unrisen sensual desire (kāmacchanda) arises, and arisen sensual desire tends towards further growth and abundance.'

In that passage, 'anuppanno' means not yet arisen, not well-produced, not manifested, and not well-occurred repeatedly. 'Kāmacchanda' refers to the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), which is explained in detail as 'that sensual desire, sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual craving for sense pleasures,' and so on. 'Uppajjati' means to be born or to manifest. It should be understood that this sensual desire arises having previously been unrisen, either by way of non-occurrence (asamudācāra) or by way of an unexperienced object (ananubhūtārammaṇa). This is because in the beginningless saṃsāra, there is no such thing as sensual desire that has never arisen before.

In this regard, for some, defilements do not occur repeatedly due to the fulfillment of duties (vatta); for others, they do not occur due to one of the following: study (gantha), ascetic practices (dhutanga), concentration (samādhi), insight (vipassanā), or construction work (navakamma). How? For instance, some are perfect in duties; while performing the eighty-two minor duties (khuddakavatta), the fourteen major duties (mahavatta), and the duties toward the shrine terrace, the Bodhi tree terrace, the drinking and utility water, the Uposatha hall, the duties for guests, and the duties for those departing, defilements find no opportunity to arise. However, later on, when that person abandons the duties and lives with broken observances, defilements arise due to unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and the loss of mindfulness (sativossagga). Thus, it is said that unrisen sensual desire arises by way of non-occurrence (asamudācāra).

Some are devoted to study; they learn from one to five Nikāyas. While that person is learning, reciting, teaching, preaching, and explaining the word of the Buddha—the Tipitaka—by way of meaning, text, sequence, and context, defilements find no opportunity to arise. However, later on, when that person abandons the work of study and lives lazily, defilements arise due to unwise attention and the loss of mindfulness. Thus, it is said that unrisen sensual desire arises by way of non-occurrence.

Some are practitioners of ascetic practices; they undertake and practice the thirteen dhutangas. While that person is maintaining the virtues of the dhutangas, defilements find no opportunity to arise. However, later on, when that person abandons the dhutangas and turns to living for the sake of abundance, defilements arise due to unwise attention and the loss of mindfulness. Thus, it is said that unrisen sensual desire arises by way of non-occurrence.
24:
Some are proficient in the eight attainments (samāpatti). While that person dwells by way of mastery in adverting (āvajjanavasī) and so on regarding the first jhāna and others, defilements find no opportunity to arise. However, later on, whether that person has fallen away from jhāna or has neglected jhāna, while dwelling devoted to talk and so on, defilements arise due to unwise attention and the loss of mindfulness. Thus, it is said that unrisen defilement arises by way of non-occurrence (asamudācāra).

Some are practitioners of insight (vipassanā). They dwell performing the work of insight in either the seven contemplations (anupassanā) or the eighteen great insights (mahāvipassanā). While dwelling thus, defilements find no opportunity to arise. However, later on, when that person abandons the work of insight and dwells mostly in the indulgence of bodily comfort, defilements arise due to unwise attention and the loss of mindfulness. Thus, it is said that unrisen defilement arises by way of non-occurrence.

Some are engaged in construction work (navakamma); they cause Uposatha halls, refectories, and so on to be built. While that person is thinking about the materials for those buildings, defilements find no opportunity to arise. However, later on, when the construction work is finished or abandoned, defilements arise due to unwise attention and the loss of mindfulness. Thus, it is said that unrisen defilement arises by way of non-occurrence.

Some are pure beings (suddhasatta) who have come from the Brahma world. Because they have no previous habituation, defilements find no opportunity to arise. However, later on, when that person gains habituation, defilements arise due to unwise attention and the loss of mindfulness. Thus, it is said that unrisen defilement arises by way of non-occurrence. In this way, first, the arising of unrisen defilements by way of non-occurrence should be understood.

How does it occur by way of an unexperienced object (ananubhūtārammaṇa)? Here, some person encounters a pleasant object, such as a visible form, that has never been experienced before. In that person, lust (rāga) arises due to unwise attention and the loss of mindfulness toward that object. Thus, it is said that unrisen defilement arises by way of an unexperienced object.

'Uppanno' means arisen, well-arisen, produced, fully produced, or manifested. 'Bhiyyobhāvāya' means for the sake of repeated occurrence. 'Vepullāya' means for the sake of abundance or for the sake of becoming a mass. In that context, the sensual desire that has arisen once will not cease; once...
25:
It is impossible that sensual desire (kāmacchanda) which has ceased will arise again on that very same day. Rather, even if one instance of sensual desire has ceased, sensual desire arising successively—whether in that previously experienced object or in another object—is said to lead to further growth and abundance.

Subhanimitta (the sign of beauty) refers to an object that is a basis for lust (rāga). In the passage, "Monks, evil unwholesome states arise only with a cause, not without a cause," the term 'nimitta' is a name for cause (paccaya). In the passage, "Monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind (adhicitta) should attend to five signs (nimitta) from time to time," it is a name for cause (karaṇa). In the passage, "That monk resorts to that sign, develops it," it is a name for concentration (samādhi). In the passage, "Depending on which sign, for one who attends to which sign, the destruction of taints (āsava) occurs immediately after," it is a name for insight (vipassanā). In this context, however, the nature of a pleasant object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) which is a cause for lust is intended as 'subhanimitta'. Regarding 'ayoniso manasikārototi' (by unwise attention): "In that context, what is unwise attention? Taking what is impermanent as permanent, what is suffering as happiness, what is non-self as self, and what is foul as beautiful—this is unwise attention, a wrong path of attention. Alternatively, the advertence, repeated advertence, application, and attention of the mind in a way contrary to the realization of the Truth is called unwise attention." This means for one who attends in an improper way through the power of this attention.

In the second sutta, byāpāda (ill-will) is the perversion of the mind, like the spoiling of rice, the state of abandoning its natural condition. "In that context, what is the hindrance of ill-will? The thought 'He has done me harm' arises as resentment." This is the name for the hindrance of ill-will as expanded in this way. Paṭighanimitta (the sign of repulsion) is an undesirable (aniṭṭha) object. This is a name for both anger (paṭigha) and the object of anger (paṭighārammaṇa). It is also stated in the Commentary: "Anger is called paṭighanimitta, and the state which is the object of anger is also called paṭighanimitta." The rest should be understood in the same way as stated for sensual desire. As in this sutta, so in the subsequent ones. I shall mention only the specific differences in each case.

In the third sutta, thīnamiddha (sloth and torpor) consists of sloth (thīna) and torpor (middha). Among them, the unfitness (incapacity) of the mind for work is sloth; it is a name for the state of laziness. The unfitness for work of the three mental aggregates (feeling, perception, and formations) is torpor,
26:
This name (middha) is a name for 'monkey-sleep' and drowsiness (the flickering of eyelids). The detailed explanation of both (sloth and torpor) should be understood by the method: "Among them, what is sloth? It is the sickness of the mind, unfitness for work, shrinking, and retreating. What is torpor? It is the sickness of the body (the group of mental aggregates), unfitness for work, shrouding, and enveloping," and so forth (from the Dhammasaṅgaṇī). Arati (discontent) and so forth should be understood according to the method analyzed in the Vibhaṅga. It is said: "Among them, what is arati? It is discontent, the state of being discontented, lack of delight, the state of not delighting, boredom, and anxiety in secluded dwellings or in other higher wholesome states (calm and insight). This is called arati. Among them, what is tandī (laziness)? It is laziness, the act of being lazy, the state of having a mind oppressed by laziness, indolence, the manner of being indolent, the state of being indolent. This is called tandī. Among them, what is vijambhitā (stretching/yawning)? It is the shaking of the body, repeated shaking, bending forward, bending backward, bending sideways, stretching upwards, and the state of having the affliction of defilements. This is called vijambhitā. Among them, what is bhattasammada (food-drowsiness)? It is the confusion caused by food in one who has eaten, exhaustion caused by food, feverishness caused by food, and the unfitness of the body for work. This is called bhattasammada. Among them, what is cetaso līnatta (sluggishness of mind)? It is the sickness of the mind, unfitness for work, shrinking, retreating, the state of shrinking, cowering, the manner of cowering, the state of being cowered, sloth (thīna), the act of sloth, and the state of sloth of the mind. This is called cetaso līnatta."

Here, the first four states (arati, tandī, vijambhitā, bhattasammada) assist the hindrance of sloth and torpor by way of conascence (sahajāta) and by way of strong dependence (upanissaya). Cetaso līnatta, however, is not conascent with itself; it assists only by way of strong dependence (upanissaya). In the fourth sutta, uddhaccakukkucca (restlessness and remorse) consists of both restlessness (uddhacca) and remorse (kukkucca). Among them, restlessness is the state of the mind being agitated. Remorse is the regret and worry caused by not having done good and having done evil. Cetaso avūpasamo (unrest of mind) is just another name for this restlessness and remorse. Avūpasantacittassa means for one whose mind has not been calmed by either jhāna or insight (vipassanā). This lack of calm assists restlessness and remorse by way of strong dependence (upanissaya).
27:
In the fifth sutta, 'doubt' (vicikicchā) refers to the hindrance of doubt (vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa) as explained in detail by the method starting with 'doubts about the Teacher' (in Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1167). 'Unwise attention' (ayoniso manasikāra) also possesses the characteristics already mentioned.

In the sixth sutta, the phrase 'unarisen sensual desire does not arise' means that unarisen sensual desire does not arise due to two reasons: either through non-recurrence (asamudācāra) or through an unexperienced object. In this way, it is abandoned by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna); furthermore, it finds no cause (hetu) or condition (paccaya) to arise again. In this context, non-recurrence should be understood through the fulfillment of major and minor duties (vatta). For some, while devoted to and performing duties in the manner described, defilements find no opportunity and are suppressed by the power of those duties. Such a person, having thus suppressed the defilements, turns [to insight] and attains Arahantship, like the Elder Milakkhatissa.

It is said that this venerable one was born into a family of hunters in the alms-resort of Gāmeṇḍavāla Mahāvihāra in the Rohana region. Upon reaching age, he married and, thinking 'I will support my wife and children,' he prepared a hundred snares, set a hundred traps, planted a hundred stakes, and committed much evil. One day, taking fire and salt from home, he went to the forest. Having killed a beast caught in a snare and eaten its meat roasted over embers, he became thirsty and entered Gāmeṇḍavāla Mahāvihāra. Finding not even enough water to quench his thirst in about ten water pots at the water-stand, he began to complain: 'In a place where so many monks reside, is there really not even enough water for those who come here thirsty to quench their thirst?' The Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissa, hearing his words and approaching him, saw that the ten pots at the water-stand were actually full of water. Thinking, 'This must be a living hungry ghost (peta),' he said, 'Layman, if you are thirsty, drink water,' and lifting a pot, poured it into his hands. Due to his [evil] kamma, the water he drank vanished as if poured into a red-hot cauldron; though he drank from all the pots, his thirst was not quenched. Then the Elder said, 'Layman, how terrible is the deed you have done! You have become a hungry ghost even now; what will the result be in the future?' Hearing the Elder's words, he was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He paid homage to the Elder, destroyed his snares and other equipment, and hurried home to see his wife and children...
28:
Having destroyed his weapons and released the decoy deer and birds into the forest, he approached the Elder and requested ordination. "Friend, ordination is difficult; how will you live as a monk?" (the Elder asked). "Venerable Sir, having seen such a visible cause before my eyes, how could I not become a monk?" he replied. The Elder gave him the meditation subject of the fivefold skin-group (tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him. Devoted to his duties and learning the Buddha's word, one day he heard a passage from the Devadūta Sutta: "Monks, the hell-wardens cast him again into the Great Hell." Hearing this, he said, "A being who has suffered such a mass of misery is cast again into the Great Hell! Oh, Venerable Sir, the Great Hell is truly grave." "Yes, friend, it is grave," (the Elder replied). "Venerable Sir, is it possible to see it?" he asked. "It is not possible to see it [directly], but I will show you something similar to seeing it," the Elder said. He then urged the novices to make a pile of wet wood on a flat rock. The novice did as instructed. The Elder, while remaining seated, used his psychic power to bring forth a spark of fire the size of a firefly from the Great Hell and, while the monk was watching, cast it into the woodpile. Its falling and the wet woodpile burning to ashes occurred simultaneously, without any interval between before and after.

Seeing this, the monk asked, "Venerable Sir, how many burdens (dhura) are there in this Dispensation?" "Friend, there are the burden of insight (vipassanā-dhura) and the burden of study (gantha-dhura)," (the Elder replied). "Venerable Sir, the burden of study is for those who are capable. For me, however, faith has arisen with suffering as its proximate cause. I will fulfill the burden of insight; please give me a meditation subject," he said, paying homage and sitting down. The Elder, thinking "This monk is one accomplished in duties," taught him a meditation subject based on the fulfillment of duties. Taking the meditation subject, he practiced insight and fulfilled his duties. One day he performed his duties at Cittalapabbata Mahāvihāra, another day at Gāmeṇḍavāla Mahāvihāra, and another day at Gocaragāma Mahāvihāra. When drowsiness overcame him, fearing a lapse in his duties, he would soak straw in water, place it on his head, and sit with his feet in water. One day, after performing his duties for two watches at Cittalapabbata Mahāvihāra, when he began to fall asleep in the early dawn, he sat with wet straw on his head and heard a novice on the eastern mountainside reciting the Aruṇavatiya Sutta:

"Exert yourselves, go forth,
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's Dispensation;
Crush the army of Death,
As an elephant destroys a hut of reeds.

Whoever shall dwell heedfully
In this Dhamma and Vinaya,
Abandoning the cycle of births,
Shall make an end of suffering."

Hearing this, he thought, "The Blessed One must have taught this sutta for an energetic monk like me." Filled with joy, he developed jhāna and, using that jhāna as a basis, established himself in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala). Practicing further stage by stage, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). At the time of his final passing (parinibbāna), he manifested that same attainment.
29:
"Whoever dwells diligent in this Dhamma-Vinaya, having abandoned the round of rebirths, will make an end of suffering." Hearing this Dhamma teaching, he thought, "The Blessed One must have preached this Sutta for a monk of such striving energy as myself," and he gave rise to joy and attained Jhāna. Based on that very Jhāna, he established himself in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala) and, striving further, attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (Paṭisambhidā). At the time of his final passing (Parinibbāna), wishing to show that very cause, he said:

"I walked the cankama carrying a pile of wet straw on my head. Now I have reached the third stage (Anāgāmi-phala); in this, I have no doubt."

Defilements suppressed by the power of such practice remain suppressed. For some, as mentioned, while dedicated to the scriptures—learning, reciting, teaching, preaching, and explaining the meaning—defilements find no opportunity and remain suppressed by the power of the scriptures. Based on those very suppressed defilements, such a person turns towards the Unconditioned (Nibbāna) and attains Arahantship, like the Elder Maliyadeva.

That venerable one, during his third year as a monk, was learning the Pali texts and practicing Vipassanā at the Maṇḍalārāma Mahāvihāra in Kallagāma. One day, while wandering for alms in Kallagāma, a female lay follower (upāsikā) offered a ladle of gruel. Developing a motherly affection for him as if he were her son, she invited the Elder inside her house, offered him excellent food, and asked, "Dear son, in which village do you live?" He replied, "Lay sister, I am performing scriptural duties at the Maṇḍalārāma Mahāvihāra." She said, "Then, dear son, as long as you are performing scriptural duties, please accept alms regularly at this very house." The Elder consented and regularly took alms there. After the meal, when giving the blessing (anumodanā), he would only say the two phrases, "Sukhaṃ hotu, dukkhā muccatu" (May you be happy, may you be free from suffering), and then depart.
