Throughout the three months of the rains retreat, while supporting that lay follower and using the alms-food to exhaust defilements, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā. The resident Elder said, "Friend Mahāေdeva, today a great crowd will gather at the monastery; please give the gift of Dhamma to them." The Elder consented.
30:
The young novices signaled to the lay follower, "Today your son will preach the Dhamma; go to the monastery and listen." She said, "Dear sons, not all monks know how to preach the Dhamma. All this time, when my son preached to me, he only said the two phrases, 'May you be happy, may you be free from suffering.' Do not make fun of me." They replied, "Lay sister, whether you think he knows or not, do not mind it; just go to the monastery and listen to the Dhamma." The lay follower took flowers, incense, and so on, went and made offerings, and sat at the edge of the assembly to listen. During the day, the Dhamma preachers and the reciters, knowing their own limits, stood up and left. Then Elder Maliyadeva sat on the Dhamma seat, held a decorative fan, and after giving a sequential discourse, thought, "For three months, I gave the blessing to the great lay follower with only two phrases. Today, I will explain the meaning of those very two phrases by investigating the Three Pitakas all night long." He began the Dhamma desanā and preached the whole night. At dawn, at the conclusion of the teaching, the great lay follower was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

Another Elder named Tissabhūti, while also studying the Vinaya at that same Mahāvihāra, entered the village at the time of alms-round and looked at a "disagreeable object" (the form of a woman). Greed arose in that Elder. Without moving his feet from where he stood, he poured the gruel from his bowl into the bowl of a young monk who was his attendant, and thinking, "If this sensual thought increases, it will sink me into the four woeful states," he turned back from that very village. He went to his teacher, paid respects, and standing in a suitable place, said, "A disease of defilement has arisen in me. I will return only if I can cure this disease; otherwise, I will not return. Please note my presence during the daytime and evening Pali lessons, but do not mark me present for the dawn lesson." Having said this, he went to Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita, who lived in the Malaya region. While the Elder was plastering his leaf-hut, he said without even looking at him, "Friend, put away your bowl and robes." He replied, "Venerable sir, I have a disease of defilement. If you can cure it, I will put them away." The Elder said, "Friend, you have come to one who is capable of curing the disease that has arisen. Put them away." That monk, being easy to admonish, thought, "Our teacher would not speak like this without knowing," and after putting away his bowl and robes, he performed his duties to the Elder, paid respects, and sat in a suitable place.
31: The Elder, knowing "This person is of a lustful temperament," taught him the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna). That person stood up, slung his bowl and robes over his shoulder, and paid homage to the Elder repeatedly. The Elder asked, "Friend Mahābhūti, why do you show such excessive reverence?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, if I am able to accomplish my task, such ability is good. If I am not able, this sight of you is my final sight." The Elder said, "Friend Mahābhūti, for a clansman who exerts effort in such a manner, jhāna, insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), or the fruit (phala) is not difficult to obtain." Having heard the Elder's words and shown reverence, he went to the foot of a Seppanni tree covered with leaves and branches, which he had noted upon his arrival. Sitting cross-legged, he made the meditation on foulness his basis, developed insight, and established himself in the fruit of Arahantship. At dawn, he reached the level of being able to teach the Pali texts. For such individuals, the defilements suppressed by the power of studying the scriptures remain suppressed in that manner.  For some individuals, when they undertake the ascetic practices (dhutanga) in the manner mentioned, defilements find no opportunity to arise and are suppressed by the power of the dhutanga. Such a person, having kept the defilements suppressed and turning away from the cycle of rebirth, attains Arahantship, like the Great Elder Mahāsīva who lived in a cave-dwelling near a village. It is said that Elder Mahāsīva, while residing at the Tissa Mahāvihāra in the great village of Mahāgāma, taught the three Pitakas according to both meaning and text to eighteen great groups. Based on the Elder's instruction, sixty thousand monks attained Arahantship. Among those monks, one monk, feeling joyful regarding the Dhamma he had realized, thought, "Does our teacher possess this bliss of the path and fruit?" Upon reflection, he realized the Elder was still a worldling (puthujjana) and thought, "I will arouse spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in the Elder by some means." He went from his dwelling to the Elder, paid homage, performed his duties, and sat down. Then the Elder Mahāsīva asked, "Friend Piṇḍapātika, why have you come?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, if you would grant me the opportunity, I wish to learn a single verse of the Dhamma." The Elder said, "Friend, many are learning; there will be no opportunity for you." Not getting an opportunity throughout the day and night, the monk said, "Venerable Sir, if there is no opportunity like this, how will you find the opportunity for death?" Then the Elder thought, "This monk has not come for the sake of instruction, but has come to arouse spiritual urgency in me." That monk also said, "Venerable Sir, a monk should be like me," paid homage to the Elder, and flew up into the ruby-colored sky and departed.
32: From the time that Arahant Elder departed, spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in the Elder. After teaching the Pali texts in the morning and evening, he placed his bowl and robes within arm's reach. Having taken his lesson at dawn, he descended with the monk who was also descending, taking his bowl and robes with him. Having fully undertaken the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutanga), he went to a cave-dwelling near a village, cleared the cave, and set up a couch. He made a firm resolve, "I will not stretch my back on this couch until I attain Arahantship," and began his walking meditation.  While he was striving, thinking, "Today I shall attain Arahantship, today I shall attain Arahantship," the Pavāraṇā day arrived. As Pavāraṇā approached, he thought, "I will abandon the state of a worldling and perform the pure Pavāraṇā," and he became extremely exhausted from his efforts. Being unable to produce the path or fruit on that Pavāraṇā day, he said, "Even one like me who has begun insight meditation does not obtain it; how truly difficult to obtain is Arahantship!" Continuing in that same manner, mostly standing and walking, he practiced the monk's duties for thirty years. Standing in the midst of the Great Pavāraṇā, he looked at the full moon and reflected, "Is the moon's orb pure, or is my virtue (sīla) pure?" He considered, "In the moon's orb, the sign of the rabbit is still visible. But in my virtue, from the time of my higher ordination until today, there is not even a flaw as large as a black mole or as small as a pimple." Upon reflecting thus, joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa) arose. Because his knowledge was mature, he suppressed the joy and attained Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). For such a person, the defilements suppressed by the power of the dhutanga remain thus suppressed.  For some, in the manner mentioned, because of frequently entering the first jhāna and other attainments (samāpatti), defilements find no opportunity and remain suppressed by the power of the attainments. Such a person, having kept the defilements suppressed, turns to insight and attains Arahantship like the Elder Mahātissa.  It is said that Elder Mahātissa was one who had obtained the eight attainments since he was a young monk. Because his defilements were suppressed by the attainments and did not manifest, and because of his proficiency in learning and questioning the Pali and Commentaries, he used to speak words close to the Noble Path. Even at the age of sixty rains, he did not realize he was still a worldling. Then one day, the community of monks from Tissa Mahāvihāra in Mahāgāma sent a message to Elder Dhammadinna, who resided in Talangara, saying, "May the Elder come and deliver a Dhamma talk to us." Elder Dhammadinna accepted and thought, "There is no monk more senior than I in my presence. However, Elder Mahātissa is my meditation teacher; I shall go, placing that Elder as the Sanghatthera (Senior of the Sangha)..."
33: Thinking, "I will go," and surrounded by a company of monks, he went to the Elder's monastery. Having performed the duties for the Elder at the place of day-rest, he sat in a suitable place. The Elder asked, "Friend Dhammadinna, have you come after a long time?" "Yes, Bhante, the Saṅgha from Tissamahāvihāra sent word to me. I did not want to go alone, but wished to go with you, so I have come." While speaking pleasant words, he delayed and then asked, "Bhante, when did you attain this Dhamma?" "Friend Dhammadinna, it has been sixty years," he replied. "Bhante, do you enjoy the attainments (samāpatti)?" he asked. "Yes, friend," he replied. "Bhante, can you create a pond?" he asked. "Friend, this is not difficult," he said, and created a pond right before him. "Bhante, create a cluster of lotuses in this pond," he requested again, and he created that cluster as well. "Now, show a large lotus flower in it," he requested, and the Elder showed that flower too. "Show the form of a sixteen-year-old woman in this flower," he requested, and the Elder showed the form of a sixteen-year-old woman. Then Dhammadinna Thera said, "Bhante, contemplate this woman's form as beautiful again and again." While the Elder was looking at the woman's form he had created himself, lust arose. At that moment, realizing his status as a worldling (puthujjana), he sat in a crouching position before his pupil, saying, "Good man, be my refuge." "Bhante, I have come for this very purpose," he said. Making the Elder feel light through the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā) and teaching him the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he went outside to give the Elder space. The Elder, whose formations were well-scrutinized, attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) just as he emerged from that place of day-rest. Then, Dhammadinna Thera, having placed him as the Senior of the Saṅgha, went to Tissamahāvihāra and preached the Dhamma to the Saṅgha. For such a person, defilements suppressed by the power of attainment remain suppressed in that way. For some, while performing the work of insight (vipassanā) in the manner described, defilements find no opportunity and remain suppressed by the power of insight. Such a person, based on those suppressed defilements, turns to insight and attains Arahantship, like the sixty monks who practiced insight during the time of the Buddha. It is said that those monks, having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher and entered the secluded forest to practice insight, because defilements did not manifest, they perceived, "We have realized the paths and fruits"...
34: Those monks, no longer making effort for the sake of the paths and fruits, thought, "We have realized the Dhamma; let us inform the Ten-Powered One," and came to the Teacher. Even before they arrived, the Teacher said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, the monks who are practitioners will come to see me today. Without giving them the opportunity to see me, send them away, saying, 'Go to the cemetery where there are fresh corpses and develop the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā).'" When those monks arrived, the Elder told them the message spoken by the Teacher. They thought, "The Tathāgata would not speak without knowing; there must be a reason for this." They went to the cemetery and, while looking at the fresh corpses, lust arose. Realizing, "The Fully Enlightened One must have surely seen this," they were struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and began practicing the meditation subject they had already obtained from the beginning. The Teacher, knowing they had begun insight meditation, while sitting in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), uttered this verse of radiance: "Like these gray bones, like gourds cast away in autumn, what delight is there in seeing them?" (Dhp. 149). At the end of the verse, they were established in the fruit of Arahantship. For such persons, defilements suppressed by the power of insight remain suppressed in that way. For some, while performing new construction work (navakamma) in the manner described, defilements find no opportunity and remain suppressed by the power of that work. Such a person, based on those suppressed defilements, turns to insight and attains Arahantship, like Tissa Thera of Cittalapabbata. It is said that in his eighth year, dissatisfaction (anabhirati) arose in him. Unable to dispel that dissatisfaction, he washed and dyed his robes, fired his bowl, shaved his hair, and stood after paying homage to his preceptor. Then the preceptor Elder asked him, "Friend Mahātissa, why is it that your appearance is like that of one who is unhappy?" "Yes, Bhante, dissatisfaction has arisen in me; I am unable to dispel it," he replied. The Elder, looking into Tissa's inclination and seeing the strong support for Arahantship, said out of compassion, "Friend Tissa, we are old; build a place for us to live." That monk, who had never before refused the word of his preceptor, accepted, saying, "Very well, Bhante."
35:
Then the Elder, who was the teacher, said to that monk: "Friend, while performing the new construction, do not neglect the course of recitation; attend to the meditation subject, and from time to time, perform the preliminary work for the kasina." Having agreed, saying, "I will do so, venerable sir," he paid homage to the Elder. After surveying a suitable place and deciding, "It is possible to do it here," he filled it with wood, cleared it by burning, surrounded it with bricks, and fitted the main door, air-vents, and so forth. Having completed the cave-dwelling along with the walkway ground and the preparation of the walls, and having spread out the couch and stool, he went to the Elder, paid homage, and said: "Venerable sir, the work on the cave is finished; please reside there."

The Elder said: "Friend, you have performed this work with great hardship; for this one whole day, you yourself stay there." He consented, saying, "Very well, venerable sir," paid homage, washed his feet, and entered the cave. Sitting down cross-legged, he reflected on the work he had done. While he was thinking, "I have performed the pleasing service for my preceptor," joy (pīti) arose within him. He suppressed that joy, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained the highest fruit, the fruition of Arahantship. For such a person, the defilements suppressed by the power of new construction remain truly suppressed.

Furthermore, some person is a pure being come from the Brahma world. Because of his lack of habitual indulgence, defilements do not manifest in him; they are suppressed by the power of his [previous] existence. Having made those defilements suppressed in that way, he turns to insight and attains Arahantship, like the Venerable Mahākassapa. For that venerable one, even while in the midst of the household life, did not enjoy sensual pleasures; he renounced great wealth and went forth. On the way, seeing the Teacher who had come to meet him, he paid homage and received higher ordination through the three instructions. On the dawn of the eighth day, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). For such a person, the defilements suppressed by the power of existence remain truly suppressed.

However, one who encounters an object such as a visible form never experienced before, and right there develops insight and attains Arahantship—for such a person, by the power of the unexperienced object, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is said to be unarisen as it has never arisen before.

In the phrase "the arisen sensual desire is abandoned," the word "arisen" means that which has been born, become, or manifested. "Is abandoned" means it is abandoned through the five kinds of abandoning: abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), abandoning by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna), and abandoning by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna).
36:
It means the sense of not arising again. Among those five kinds of abandoning, because insight abandons defilements by the power of substitution of opposites, insight should be known as abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna). Because meditative attainment (samāpatti) suppresses defilements, that attainment should be known as abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). The Path (magga) arises by eradicating defilements; the Fruit (phala) arises by tranquilizing defilements; Nibbāna is the escape from all defilements. These three are called abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), abandoning by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna), and abandoning by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna). The meaning is that [defilements] are abandoned by these five kinds of abandoning, both mundane and supramundane.

"The sign of foulness" (asubha-nimitta) refers to the first jhāna having as its object one of the ten kinds of foulness. Therefore, the ancient teachers said: "The foulness itself is the sign of foulness; the states having foulness as their object are also the sign of foulness." For one who attends with wise attention—meaning one who attends by way of skillful attention (upāya-manasikāra) as taught in the method beginning with "impermanent as impermanent"—unarisen sensual desire does not arise, and arisen sensual desire is abandoned through the fivefold abandoning.

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire: taking up the sign of foulness, devotion to the meditation on foulness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, good friendship, and suitable talk. For sensual desire is abandoned in one who takes up the ten signs of foulness, in one who develops them, in one who has the doors of the faculties closed, and in one who is moderate in eating by the habit of sustaining oneself by drinking water when there is still room for four or five mouthfuls of food. Thus it was said:

"Having not eaten four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water. This is sufficient for the comfortable living of a monk with a resolute mind."

Sensual desire is also abandoned in one who associates with a good friend who delights in the meditation on foulness, such as the Elder Tissa who was devoted to the practice of foulness, and by suitable talk based on the ten kinds of foulness while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it was said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire."

In the seventh sutta, "deliverance of mind through loving-kindness" (mettā-cetovimutti) is loving-kindness that pervades all beings with welfare. Because the mind associated with that loving-kindness is liberated from opposing states such as the hindrances, it is called "deliverance of mind" (cetovimutti). Specifically, it should be known as deliverance of mind because it is liberated from all obsession with ill-will (byāpāda). Therein, "loving-kindness" (mettā) means...
37:
With this much, the loving-kindness occurring in the preliminary stage is also appropriate. However, because it is called 'liberation of mind' (cetovimutti), in this context, only absorption (appanā) by way of the third and fourth jhānas is intended. 'Wise attention' (yoniso manasikāra) refers to the person who attends to that loving-kindness liberation of mind with wise attention characterized by the aforementioned means.

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of ill-will (byāpāda): learning the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the meditation on loving-kindness, reflection on the ownership of kamma, frequent reflection (on faults and benefits), good friendship, and suitable talk. For a person who learns loving-kindness by way of either specified or unspecified pervasion of the directions, ill-will is abandoned; it is also abandoned for one who develops loving-kindness by way of specified or unspecified pervasion of the directions. 

'What will you do by being angry with this person? Will you be able to destroy his virtue and so on? Have you not come by your own kamma and will go by your own kamma? Being angry with another is like wanting to strike another after picking up a flameless ember, a hot iron rod, or excrement. What will this person do by being angry with you? Will he be able to destroy your virtue and so on? He has also come by his own kamma and will go by his own kamma. Like a gift not accepted, or like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger will only fall back on his own head.' 

Thus, ill-will is abandoned for the person who reflects on the ownership of kamma for himself and others, for the person who stands in reflection after having reflected on the ownership of kamma for both, for the person who associates with good friends who delight in the meditation on loving-kindness like Elder Assagutta, and by suitable talk related to loving-kindness during standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'Six things lead to the abandoning of ill-will.' The remaining words in this sutta and in the subsequent suttas should be understood in the same manner as already stated; I shall only mention the distinctions.

In the eighth sutta, among the terms beginning with 'element of initiative' (ārambha-dhātu), the element of initiative is the first aroused energy. The 'element of exertion' (nikkama-dhātu) is stronger than that, as it has emerged from laziness. The 'element of endeavor' (parakkama-dhātu) is even stronger than that, as it advances to successive stages. In the Commentary, however, it is said: 'Initiative is for the dispelling of sensual desires from the mind; exertion is for the opening of the bolt of ignorance in the mind; endeavor is for the cutting of the mind's bonds.' Thus, it is stated: 'By these three, only supreme energy is spoken of.'
38:
'Of one with aroused energy' (āraddha-vīriyassa) refers to one with fulfilled energy and upheld energy. Herein, energy free from the four faults should be known as 'aroused.' It is neither too lax, nor too tense, neither shrunken inwardly, nor distracted outwardly. 

That energy is of two kinds: bodily (kāyika) and mental (cetasika). Among these, as it is said, 'Here, a monk purifies his mind from the hindering qualities by walking and sitting during the day,' the energy of a person who strives and exerts with the body throughout the five periods of the night and day is to be known as bodily energy.

'I will not leave this cave as long as my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging'—thus binding the mind by delimiting the location; or, 'I will not break this cross-legged posture'—thus binding the mind by delimiting the posture such as sitting; the energy of one who strives and exerts in this way is to be known as mental energy. 

In this context, both kinds of energy are appropriate. For one with aroused energy through these two kinds of energy, unarisen sloth and torpor (thina-middha) do not arise, and arisen sloth and torpor are abandoned, as in the cases of Elder Milakkhatissa, Elder Mahāsīva who dwelt in Gāmantapabbhāra, Elder Pītimallaka, and Elder Kuṭumbiyaputta Tissa. 

Among these, the first three and others of such nature were those with energy aroused through bodily energy. Elder Kuṭumbiyaputta Tissa and others were those with energy aroused through mental energy. Elder Mahānāga who dwelt in Uccāvāluka, however, was one with energy aroused through both kinds of energy. It is said that the Elder would walk for one week, stand for one week, sit for one week, and lie down for one week. For the Great Elder, there was no such thing as an unsuitable posture; in the fourth week, having developed insight, he was established in Arahantship.

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor: taking note of the sign in overeating, changing the postures, attention to the perception of light, living in the open air, good friendship, and suitable talk. 

For one who performs the recluse's duties while sitting in the night-quarters or day-quarters after eating like the gluttons known as āharahatthaka, bhuttavamitaka, tatravaṭṭaka, alaṅsāṭaka, and kākamāsaka, sloth and torpor come overwhelming him like a great elephant. However, for a monk who is moderate in eating, leaving space for four or five mouthfuls and drinking water, that does not happen. Thus, for one who takes note of the sign in overeating, sloth and torpor are abandoned. 

It is also abandoned for one who changes from the posture in which sloth and torpor descend to another posture; for one who [attends to] the light of the moon, the light of a lamp, or the light of a torch at night, and the light of the sun during the day...
39:
... For one who attends [to it], for one who lives in the open air, and for one who associates with good friends who have abandoned sloth and torpor like the Venerable Mahākassapa, sloth and torpor are abandoned. Sloth and torpor are also abandoned by suitable talk related to the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of sloth and torpor."

In the ninth sutta, "vūpasantacittassa" refers to one whose mind is calmed by either jhāna or vipassanā.

Alternatively, six things lead to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca). They are: great learning, questioning and discussion, proficiency in the Vinaya, serving the elder monks, having good friends, and suitable talk. Through great learning, for one who learns one, two, three, four, or all five Nikāyas both in terms of the Pali text and the meaning, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. For one who frequently questions and discusses what is allowable and what is not, for one who is proficient and well-versed in the Vinaya regulations, for one who approaches senior and elderly monks, and for one who associates with good friends who are masters of the Vinaya like the Venerable Upāli, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. Restlessness and remorse are also abandoned by suitable talk related to what is allowable and what is not while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse."

In the tenth sutta, "yoniso bhikkhave manasikaroto" refers to one who attends by way of skillful means, according to the method already described.

Alternatively, six things lead to the abandonment of doubt (vicikicchā). They are: great learning, questioning and discussion, proficiency in the Vinaya, abundance of decision (conviction), having good friends, and suitable talk. Through great learning, for one who learns from one to five Nikāyas by way of the Pali text and the meaning, doubt is abandoned. For one who frequently questions and discusses concerning the Three Jewels, for one who is well-versed in the Vinaya, for one who has an abundance of decision characterized by faith that is settled in the Three Jewels, and for one who associates with good friends who are eminent in faith like the Venerable Vakkali, doubt is abandoned. Doubt is also abandoned by suitable talk related to the virtues of the Three Jewels while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of doubt." In this Nīvaraṇappahāna-vagga, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) have been taught.

## Commentary on the Nīvaraṇappahāna-vagga.
40:
## 3. Akammaniyavagga-vaṇṇanā

21-22. In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'abhāvitaṃ' refers to a mind that is not developed or brought into being by way of samatha-bhāvanā and vipassanā-bhāvanā. 'Akammaniyaṃ hoti' means being incapable or unsuitable for the tasks of samatha and vipassanā meditation. In the second sutta, the meaning should be understood as the opposite of what was just said. Among these suttas, in the first sutta, 'mind' refers to the mind arisen by way of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), and in the second sutta, it refers to the mind arisen by way of the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). In this context, the distinction between the round (vaṭṭa), the basis of the round (vaṭṭapāda), the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), and the basis of the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭapāda) should be understood. The 'round' (vaṭṭa) refers to the round of existence in the three planes, and the 'basis of the round' (vaṭṭapāda) refers to the kamma that is the cause for obtaining the round. The 'cessation of the round' (vivaṭṭa) refers to the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma), and the 'basis of the cessation of the round' (vivaṭṭapāda) refers to the kamma that is the cause for obtaining the cessation of the round. Thus, in these suttas, only the round and the cessation of the round are taught.

23-24. In the third sutta, the mind should be understood as that which arises only by way of the round. 'Leads to great harm' means that although it may grant the prosperity and happiness of devas and humans, or the sovereignty of Māras and Brahmās, it repeatedly gives only the round of rebirth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, physical pain, mental grief, and despair, along with the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), and dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Thus, it is said to give only a mass of suffering. Therefore, it is said to lead to great harm. In the fourth sutta, 'mind' refers to the mind arisen only by way of the cessation of the round.

25-26. In the fifth and sixth suttas, there is this distinction: 'not developed, not manifested.' The intention in these suttas is that a mind arisen by way of the round, even if it has arisen, is considered 'not developed' and 'not manifested' because it is not developed by the power of concentration. Why? Because it is unable to enter into the jhānas, vipassanā, paths, fruitions, and Nibbāna, which are the bases of the supramundane. However, a mind arisen by way of the cessation of the round is called 'developed' and 'manifested.' Why? Because it is able to enter into those supramundane states. But the Elder Phussamitta, a resident of Kurundaka, said: "Friends, only the path-mind (magga-citta) is called 'developed' and 'manifested'."

27-28. In the seventh and eighth suttas, 'abahulīkataṃ' means not done repeatedly. The two types of mind taught in these suttas should also be understood as minds arisen by way of the round and the cessation of the round.

29. In the ninth sutta, it is called 'dukkha-adhivaha' because it brings the suffering taught by the method beginning with 'birth is suffering' (jātipi dukkhā). There is also a variant reading 'dukkha-adhivāha'. Its meaning is: because that mind is directed with difficulty and pain towards the noble states such as the jhānas which are the basis of the supramundane, it is called 'dukkha-adhivāha'. The mind taught in this ninth sutta is also only the mind arisen by way of the round. Although that mind gives the aforementioned prosperity of devas and humans, it is called 'dukkha-adhivaha' because it brings sufferings such as birth. It is also called 'dukkha-adhivāha' because it must be directed with difficulty to attain the noble states.
41:
Because it is directed with difficulty and pain toward the noble states such as jhāna, which are the basis of the supramundane, it is called 'dukkhādivāha' (difficult to direct). The mind mentioned in this ninth sutta is also a mind that arises by the power of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Indeed, although that mind provides the aforementioned fortunes of devas, humans, and so on, it is called 'dukkhādivaha' because it carries the sufferings of birth and so forth; and it is called 'dukkhādivāha' because it is directed with difficulty toward the attainment of the noble states.

In the tenth sutta, the mind is said to be the mind that arises by the power of the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). Indeed, because that mind brings about divine happiness over human happiness, jhāna happiness over divine happiness, vipassanā happiness over jhāna happiness, path happiness over vipassanā happiness, fruition happiness over path happiness, and the happiness of Nibbāna over fruition happiness, it is called 'sukhādivaha' or 'sukhādivāha' (bringing happiness). Because that mind is easily directed toward the noble states such as jhāna, which are the basis of the supramundane, and is like the released thunderbolt (vajira) of Sakka, it is also called 'sukhādivāha'. In this chapter (vagga) as well, only the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are discussed.

## Commentary on the Akammaniya Vagga.

## 4. Commentary on the Adanta Vagga

In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, 'adanta' (untamed) refers to a mind that is accompanied by the thorns of defilements and is like an untamed elephant, horse, and so on. 'Citta' (mind) refers only to the mind that arises by the power of the round of rebirth.

In the second sutta, 'danta' (tamed) refers to a mind that is free from the thorns of defilements and is like a tamed elephant, horse, and so on. In both of these suttas, only the mind that arises by the power of the round and the cessation of the round is discussed. As it is here, so it is in the subsequent suttas.

In the third sutta, 'agutta' (unguarded) refers to a mind that is not protected, is devoid of the restraint of mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), and is like an unguarded elephant, horse, and so on.

In the fourth sutta, 'gutta' (guarded) refers to a mind that is protected, possesses the restraint of mindfulness that is not released, and is like a guarded elephant, horse, and so on.

35-36. The fifth and sixth suttas are spoken according to the inclination of those who understand easily through the terms 'arakkhita' (unprotected) and 'rakkhita' (protected). The meaning here is the same as in the previous suttas.
42:
37-38. The same method applies to the seventh and eighth suttas. The simile here should be understood by way of a house with unguarded doors and so forth.

39-40. The ninth and tenth suttas are spoken by combining them with all four terms. In this Adanta Vagga as well, only the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are discussed.

## Commentary on the Adanta Vagga.

## 5. Commentary on the Paṇihita-accha Vagga

41. In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, the word "seyyathāpi" is a particle used in the sense of a simile. In illustrating that simile, the Blessed One in some suttas surrounds the meaning with a simile, as in the Vattha Sutta, the Pāricchattakopama Sutta, and the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta. In other suttas, He surrounds the simile with the meaning, as in the Loṇambila Sutta, the Suvaṇṇakāra Sutta, and the Suriyopama Sutta. In this Sālisūkopama Sutta, however, wishing to surround the simile with the meaning, He spoke the words beginning with "seyyathāpi bhikkhave."

In that passage, "sālisūkaṃ" means the spike of hill-rice. The same method applies to the spike of barley (yavasūka). The word "vā" has an alternative sense. "Micchāpaṇihitaṃ" means wrongly placed. The meaning is that it is not placed with the tip pointing upwards in a way that it could pierce. "Bheccati" means it will break or it will cut the skin. "Micchāpaṇihitena cittena" means by a wrongly directed mind. This is spoken with reference to the mind that arises by the power of the round of rebirth. "Avijjaṃ" refers to the dense and thick great ignorance (mahā-avijjā) which is non-knowledge regarding the eight points. In the phrase "vijjaṃ uppādessati," "vijjā" refers to the knowledge of the path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa). "Nibbānaṃ" refers to the Deathless (amata), so called because of the state of having exited from the forest (vāna) of craving. "Sacchikarissati" means he will realize it for himself.

42. In the second sutta, "sammapaṇihitaṃ" means well-placed with the tip pointing upwards so that it can pierce and break. In the phrase "akkantaṃ" in this sutta, it is not called "akkanta" only when trodden upon by the foot; even pressing with the hand is called "akkanta" by the power of conventional usage (ruḷhī-sadda). This is the noble parlance (ariya-vohāra) in this context. Why are the large thorns such as the sepaṇṇi thorn or the madana thorn not taken, but only the subtle and weak spikes of hill-rice and barley? It is taken to show that even a small amount of wholesome kamma is capable of escaping from the round of results (vipāka-vaṭṭa). To explain further, whether it be the subtle and weak spikes of hill-rice or barley, or the large thorns such as sepaṇṇi and madana...
43:
This analogy is given to demonstrate that even a small wholesome deed (kusala kamma) is capable of leading to liberation (vivaṭṭa). Just as a fine and weak rice-awn or barley-awn, or even large thorns such as the seppaṇṇi or madana thorns, if placed in a wrong position, cannot pierce the hand or foot or cause bleeding; but if placed correctly (pointing upwards), they can. In the same way, whether it be a small wholesome deed like giving a handful of grass or a great wholesome deed like the gift of the Brahmin Velāma, if it is placed wrongly by being based on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and wishing for worldly success (vaṭṭa-sampatti), it can only bring about the suffering of the round, not liberation (vivaṭṭa). However, if it is placed correctly by means of liberation, wishing for liberation with the thought, “May this gift of mine lead to the destruction of the taints (āsavas),” then it is indeed capable of granting the fruit of Arahantship, the knowledge of Private Buddhahood (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).

Thus it is also said:
“Analytical insights, liberations, the perfection of a disciple, Private Buddhahood, and the stage of a Buddha (Omniscience)—all this can be obtained through that (merit of giving).” (Khuddakapāṭha, 8.15). In these two suttas, the round (vaṭṭa) and liberation from the round (vivaṭṭa) are discussed.

In the third sutta, ‘paduṭṭhacitta’ means a mind corrupted by anger (dosa). ‘Cetasa cetoparicca’ means having delimited and known the mind of another with one’s own mind (the supernormal knowledge of penetrating others' minds). ‘Yathābhataṃ nikkhitto’ means as if one were brought and placed. ‘Evaṃ niraye’ means it should be said that one will likewise remain in hell. All terms such as ‘apāya’ are merely synonyms for ‘niraya’ (hell). Indeed, hell is called ‘apāya’ because it is devoid of happiness, which is called ‘aya’. It is called ‘duggati’ because it is the destination of suffering. It is called ‘vinipāta’ because evildoers fall into it helplessly and perish. It is called ‘niraya’ because of the sense of being devoid of any pleasant taste.

In the fourth sutta, ‘pasanna’ means a mind that is clear through faith (saddhā). ‘Sugati’ means the destination of happiness. ‘Saggaṃ lokaṃ’ means a world that is exceedingly excellent due to the perfection of forms and so on (the heavenly realm).

In the fifth sutta, ‘udakarahado’ means a lake. ‘Āvilo’ means unclear or turbid. ‘Luḷito’ means stirred up and not calm (due to wind). ‘Kalalībhūto’ means having become muddy. In the phrases ‘sippisambukaṃ’ and so on, ‘sippi’ and ‘sambuka’ refer to mussels and snails. ‘Sakkhara’ and ‘kaṭhala’ refer to pebbles and potsherds. A collection or shoal of fish is called ‘macchagumba’. In the phrase ‘carantampi tiṭṭhantampi’, here the pebbles and potsherds only remain stationary, while the others (mussels, snails, etc.) both move and stay still. However, just as one says of cows that are standing, sitting, or lying down in between others, “These cows are grazing (moving),” referring to the cows that are actually moving, so too, regarding the pebbles and potsherds which only remain stationary...
44:
...referring to the moving cows, the others that are standing, sitting, or lying down are also said to be 'moving'. Similarly, referring to the pebbles and potsherds which only remain stationary, the other two (mussels and snails) are also said to be 'stationary'. And referring to the other two which move, the pebbles and potsherds are also said to be 'moving'.

‘By a clouded (mind)’ (āvilena) means by a mind enveloped by the five hindrances (nīvaraṇas). In the terms ‘one’s own benefit’ (attattha) and so on, ‘attattha’ refers to the benefit pertaining to one’s own present life, which is a mixture of mundane and supramundane. ‘Parattha’ refers to the benefit pertaining to one’s own future life, which is a mixture of mundane and supramundane. That benefit is called ‘parattha’ because it occurs in the hereafter (parattha). The combination of both is called ‘ubhayattha’. Alternatively, ‘attattha’ refers to the mundane and supramundane benefit of oneself in both the present and the future; such benefit for another is called ‘parattha’; and the combination of both is called ‘ubhayattha’. In the phrase ‘superior to human Dhamma’ (uttariṃ manussadhamma), ‘human Dhamma’ refers to the ten wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha). These ten types of Dhamma are called ‘human Dhamma’ because at the end of a sword-interval age (satthantarakaappa), humans, moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), adopt them on their own without any other prompter. The states superior to that should be understood as the jhānas, insight (vipassanā), the paths (magga), and the fruits (phala). ‘Distinction of knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones’ (alamariyañāṇadassana-visesa) refers to the distinction consisting of knowledge and vision that is suitable for the noble ones (ariyas) or capable of making one a noble one. It should be understood that it is called ‘knowledge’ (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing, and ‘vision’ (dassana) in the sense of seeing. This is a designation for the divine eye, insight-knowledge, path-knowledge, fruit-knowledge, and reviewing-knowledge.

In the sixth sutta, ‘accho’ means not turbid; it is also interpreted as ‘clear’. ‘Vippasanno’ means very clear. ‘Anāvilo’ means not turbid, meaning pure; it is said to be free from foam, bubbles, shells, weeds, and water-plants. ‘By an unclouded (mind)’ (anāvilena) means by a mind liberated from the five hindrances. The rest is as explained in the fourth sutta. In these two suttas also, only the round (vaṭṭa) and liberation (vivaṭṭa) are discussed.

In the seventh sutta, ‘rukkhajātānaṃ’ is a genitive case used in the sense of the nominative, meaning ‘trees’. ‘Yadidaṃ’ is merely a particle. In the phrase ‘due to its softness’ (mudutāya), some trees are supreme in color, some in scent, some in taste, and some in hardness. But the phandana tree (black cutch) is shown to be the foremost and best due to its softness and its workability (kammaññatā). In the phrase ‘Monks, the mind that is developed and cultivated’ (cittaṃ bhāvitāṃ bahulīkataṃ), it refers to the mind that is developed and repeatedly practiced by means of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
45:
(In this sutta) the mind is intended. However, the Elder Phussamitta, who resided in Kuruṇdaka, said: "Friend, that which is called the mind that is truly soft and wieldy is only the fourth jhāna mind, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā)."

48. In the eighth sutta, 'evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ' means that which arises and vanishes thus quickly. This word 'yāvañca' is a particle in the sense of an extreme measure, and 'ati-viya na sukarā' means it is extremely difficult. 'Idaṃ' is merely a particle. Regarding the term 'cittaṃ', some teachers first said it is the "bhavaṅga-citta". Rejecting that statement, it is said: "In this context, by the Pali term 'cittaṃ', all minds are intended, down to even eye-consciousness."

On this matter, King Milinda asked the Dhamma-preacher, Elder Nāgasena: "Venerable Nāgasena, if the mental formations that occur within a single finger-snap were to have physical form, how large a heap would they be?" "Great King, indeed, fifty vāhas (half of a hundred vāhas), one vāha, seven ammaṇas, and two tumbas of rice would not even reach the number of minds occurring in a single finger-snap, nor a sixteenth part, nor even a fraction of that part," he replied.

If so, why did the Fully Enlightened One say, "It is not easy even to give a simile"? To explain—just as similes were given for the length of an aeon using a mountain of one league or a city filled with mustard seeds of one league, despite it being difficult; and just as similes were made for the suffering of hell using the analogy of being struck by a hundred spears, and for the bliss of heaven using the analogy of the prosperity of a Universal Monarch; should a simile not also be made here for the quickness of the mind? In those cases, similes were given because of questions like "Venerable Sir, is it possible to give a simile?" In this sutta, no simile was given because there was no such question. In truth, this sutta was taught at the conclusion of a Dhamma discourse. Thus, in this sutta, the multitude of minds is spoken of.

49. In the ninth sutta, 'pabhassaraṃ' means bright and pure. 'Cittaṃ' refers to the bhavaṅga-citta. If asked whether the mind has a color, the answer is no. Indeed, whether it has a color such as blue or is colorless, it is called 'pabhassara' (luminous) because of its purity. This mind is also called 'pabhassara' because it is pure, being free from defilements. 'Tañca kho' refers to that bhavaṅga-citta. 'Āgantukehi' (adventitious) refers to those states that do not arise together with it but arise later at the moment of javana (impulsion). 'Upakkilesehi' (by defilements) means it is called "defiled" because it is made dirty by defilements such as greed (rāga).

How so? Just as parents who are virtuous and accomplished in conduct, or teachers and preceptors, receive blame and ill-repute, saying "They do not threaten, train, admonish, or restrain their own children, pupils, or disciples" because of children and disciples who are immoral, ill-behaved, and fail in their duties; the completion of this simile should be understood.
46:
...saying "They do not admonish," they receive blame and ill-repute; the completion of this simile should be understood. The bhavaṅga-citta should be regarded like the parents, teachers, and preceptors who are accomplished in conduct. Just as those parents and teachers receive ill-repute due to their children and so on, the naturally pure bhavaṅga-citta is called "defiled" because of the adventitious defilements that arise through the power of minds associated with greed and so on, which have the nature of lusting, hating, and being deluded at the moment of javana.

In the tenth sutta also, 'citta' refers only to the bhavaṅga-citta. 'Vippamutta' (freed) means it is called "freed" from the adventitious defilements when it arises through the power of wholesome states such as those associated with knowledge and the three roots (tihetuka), without lusting, hating, or being deluded at the moment of javana. In this sutta also, just as parents and others receive praise and fame because of virtuous and well-behaved children, saying "These people train, admonish, and restrain their own beautiful children," so too, this bhavaṅga-citta is said to be "freed" from adventitious defilements through the power of the wholesome mind arising at the moment of javana.

## Commentary on the Panihita-accha Vagga.

## 6. Commentary on the Accharāsaṅghāta Vagga.

In the first sutta of the sixth vagga, "taṃ assutavā puthujjanā" refers to an uninstructed worldling regarding that bhavaṅga-citta. Therein, one should be known as "assutavā" (uninstructed) because of the absence of scripture (āgama) and attainment (adhigama). A person who, while investigating this sutta from the beginning according to its meaning, does not know either through scripture or through attainment that "this bhavaṅga-citta, though naturally pure, is defiled by adventitious defilements such as greed that arise at the moment of javana." For such a person, there is no scripture (āgama) that accomplishes the penetration of knowledge as it really is, because of the absence of learning, inquiry, and discernment regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, dependent origination, foundations of mindfulness, and so on. Nor is there attainment (adhigama) because the paths and fruits to be attained through practice have not been attained. Such a person is known as "uninstructed" (assutavā) due to the absence of both scripture and attainment. That worldling (puthujjana)—

"He is called a worldling (puthujjana) because of reasons such as generating many (puthu) defilements.
Because he is included in the multitude of people, and because he is separate from the Noble Ones, he is called a worldling."
48:
In the second sutta, 'learned' (sutavā) refers to a person endowed with learning. In detail, the meaning should be understood here as the opposite of the word 'unlearned' (assutavā). Regarding 'noble disciple' (ariya-sāvaka): there is one who is a Noble One (ariya) but not a disciple (sāvaka), such as the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas. There is one who is a disciple but not a Noble One, such as a layperson who has not yet reached the fruit (phala). There is one who is neither a Noble One nor a disciple, such as the many sectarians (titthiyas). There is one who is both a Noble One and a disciple, such as the monks of the Sakyan lineage who have understood the Teaching and reached the fruit. In this sutta, however, whether a layperson or a monk, one who is endowed with learning according to the meaning of 'sutavā' stated here should be understood as a 'noble disciple.'

'Knows as it really is' means knowing according to reality that 'this life-continuum mind is liberated from adventitious defilements, and it is defiled in this way.' 'Mental development exists' shows that the presence of mental stability and mental comprehension is taught as 'it exists.' In this sutta, strong insight (balava-vipassanā) is taught. Some teachers, however, say it is tender insight (taruṇa-vipassanā).

The third sutta was taught due to a specific occasion. What was that occasion? It was the occasion for the arising of the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta. It is said that at one time the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery near Sāvatthī. When the Buddhas stay anywhere, they do not abandon the five kinds of duties. The five duties of the Buddha are: the duty before the meal, the duty after the meal, the duty in the first watch, the duty in the middle watch, and the duty in the last watch.

Among those five duties, the duty before the meal is as follows: The Blessed One, having risen early in the morning, performs personal duties such as washing the face for the benefit of the attendant monks and for his own physical comfort. He spends the time in a secluded seat until the time for alms-round. At the time for alms-round, he dresses in the lower robe, fastens the girdle, puts on the upper robe, and taking the bowl, enters a village or town for alms, sometimes alone and sometimes accompanied by the community of monks. Sometimes he enters in the ordinary way, and sometimes accompanied by many miracles. These miracles are as follows: as the Lord of the World enters for alms, gentle winds go before him and clean the ground. Clouds release drops of water to settle the dust on the path and then stand above like a canopy. Other winds bring flowers and scatter them on the path.
49:
High places of the earth sink down, and low places rise up. At the moment He sets His foot down, the ground becomes perfectly level. Lotus flowers, pleasant to the touch, also rise to receive His feet. As soon as He places His right foot inside the threshold, six-colored rays of light emanate from His body, adorning the pinnacles and gabled chambers of palaces like molten gold or like being draped in exquisite variegated cloth, darting here and there. Even animals such as elephants, horses, and birds, remaining in their respective places, make sweet sounds. Likewise, musical instruments such as drums and lutes, as well as the ornaments worn on the bodies of people, produce melodious sounds. By these signs, people know, "Today the Blessed One has entered here for alms." Those people, properly dressed and robed, take perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, leave their houses, enter the main street, and respectfully honor the Blessed One with perfumes and flowers. After paying homage, they request, "Venerable Sir, please give us ten monks, twenty, fifty... a hundred," and taking the Blessed One's bowl, they prepare seats and respectfully serve Him with alms-food. When the Blessed One has finished His meal, He surveys the latent tendencies and mental dispositions of those people and teaches the Dhamma in such a way that some are established in the Refuges, some in the Five Precepts, some in one of the fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, or Non-returning, and some, having gone forth, are established in the highest fruit, Arahatship. Having thus benefited the great multitude, He rises from His seat and returns to the monastery. Upon reaching the monastery, He sits on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the circular pavilion perfumed with various scents, awaiting the conclusion of the monks' meal. Then, when the monks have finished their meal, the attendant monk informs the Blessed One. Thereupon, the Blessed One enters the Gandhakuṭi. This constitutes the morning duties (purebhattakicca).

Then the Blessed One, having thus performed the morning duties, sits near the Gandhakuṭi, washes His feet, and standing on the footstool, exhorts the assembly of monks: "Bhikkhus, strive with diligence. Rare is the appearance of a Buddha in the world; rare is the attainment of human birth; rare is the opportune moment; rare is the going forth; rare is the hearing of the True Dhamma." Then, some monks ask the Blessed One for meditation subjects. The Blessed One gives them meditation subjects suitable to their temperaments. Thereafter, all the monks pay homage to the Blessed One and depart to their respective night quarters and day quarters. Some go to the forest, some to the root of a tree, some to a certain place such as a mountain, and some go to the realm of the Four Great Kings... and some
50:
to the realm of the Vasavatti devas. Then the Blessed One enters the Gandhakuṭi and, if He so desires, mindful and clearly comprehending, He rests for a moment in the lion’s posture on His right side. Then, when His body is refreshed, He rises and surveys the world during the second part of the day. In the third part, the great multitude in the village or market town near which He dwells, having given alms before the meal, gather at the monastery after the meal, properly dressed and robed, bringing perfumes, flowers, and so forth. Then the Blessed One, proceeding with psychic power suitable for the assembled audience, sits on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma hall and teaches the Dhamma appropriate to the time and occasion. Then, knowing the time is right, He dismisses the assembly; the people pay homage to the Blessed One and depart. This constitutes the afternoon duties (pacchābhattakicca).

Having thus finished the afternoon duties, if He wishes to bathe His body, He rises from the Buddha-seat, enters the bathhouse, and refreshes His body with water prepared by the attendant monk. The attendant monk also brings the Buddha-seat and prepares it in the precinct of the Gandhakuṭi. The Blessed One, dressing in a well-dyed double-layered robe, fastens the waistband, places the upper robe over His left shoulder, and coming to that place, sits alone for a moment in seclusion. Then, monks come from various places to attend upon the Blessed One. Among them, some ask questions, some request meditation subjects, and some request to hear the Dhamma. The Blessed One, fulfilling their desires, spends the first watch of the night (purimayāma). This constitutes the duties of the first watch (purimayāmakicca).

At the conclusion of the duties of the first watch, when the monks have paid homage to the Blessed One and departed, the deities of the entire ten thousand world systems, obtaining the opportunity, approach the Blessed One and ask questions they have prepared, even those as short as four syllables. The Blessed One, answering the questions of those deities, spends the middle watch (majjhimayāma). This constitutes the duties of the middle watch (majjhimayāmakicca).

The last watch (pacchimayāma) He divides into three parts. To relieve the physical fatigue caused by sitting since the morning, He spends one part in walking meditation. In the second part, He enters the Gandhakuṭi and, mindful and clearly comprehending, rests in the lion’s posture on His right side. In the third part, He rises and sits, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye (buddhacakkhu) to see those individuals who have performed meritorious deeds such as generosity and virtue in the presence of former Buddhas. This constitutes the duties of the last watch (pacchimayāmakicca).
51:
On that day too, the Blessed One, remaining in the duties to be performed during the last watch of the night, surveyed the world of sentient beings and saw this: "While I am wandering in the Kosala country, when a certain sutta is preached using the simile of a mass of fire, sixty monks will attain Arahantship, hot blood will vomit from the mouths of about sixty monks, and about sixty monks will return to the lay life." Among those monks, those who were to attain Arahantship would do so simply by hearing any Dhamma discourse. However, desiring to wander for the sake of supporting the remaining monks, he said, "Ānanda, inform the monks."

Elder Ānanda went to every precinct and said, "Friends, the Teacher desires to wander for the sake of supporting the great multitude; let those who wish to go come forth." The monks, with joyful hearts as if they had received a great gain, thought, "We shall indeed obtain the rare opportunity to behold the golden-hued body of the Blessed One as he preaches the Dhamma to the great multitude, and to hear his sweet Dhamma talk." Thus, they shaved off their long hair, baked their stained bowls, washed their soiled robes, and made themselves ready for the journey. The Blessed One, surrounded by an indefinite number of the Saṅgha of monks, set out for the Kosala country. While traveling through villages and towns in succession, covering a distance of one gāvuta, half a league (yojana), three gāvutas, or at most one league per day, he saw in a certain place a large hollow tree burning with fire. Thinking, "I shall preach a Dhamma discourse using this burning tree as the subject, adorned with seven factors," he halted his journey, approached the foot of a certain tree, and indicated his desire to sit. Elder Ānanda, knowing the Teacher's intention, reflected, "Surely there must be a reason; the Tathāgatas do not halt their journey and sit without a cause," and he spread out the four-fold outer robe (saṅghāṭi). After the Blessed One had sat down, he addressed the monks, saying, "Monks, do you see that great mass of fire over there?" and he preached the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta (AN 7.72).

While this prose exposition (veyyākaraṇa) was being preached, hot blood vomited from the mouths of about sixty monks; about sixty monks renounced the training and returned to the lower life of a layman; and the minds of about sixty monks were liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging. Indeed, upon hearing that exposition, the mental bodies (nāmakāya) of about sixty monks became heated; when the mental body was heated, the physical body (karajakāya) became heated; and when the physical body was heated, hot blood from the internal repository (the heart) vomited from their mouths. About sixty monks, reflecting, "It is indeed difficult to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) perfectly and purely for as long as life lasts in the Buddha's Dispensation," renounced the training and returned to the lay life.
52:
About sixty monks, directing their knowledge toward the Teacher's discourse, attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

Among those monks, those from whose mouths hot blood vomited had committed Pārājika offenses. Those who returned to the lay life had been wandering about trampling upon minor and lesser training rules. Those who attained Arahantship were those of pure virtue. The Teacher's Dhamma discourse became fruitful for all these three types of persons. Let it be that it was fruitful for those who attained Arahantship; but how was it fruitful for the others—those who vomited blood and those who disrobed? Indeed, if they had not heard this Dhamma discourse, they would have remained heedless and unable to give up their status (as monks). Consequently, their evil unwholesome deeds would have increased and caused them to sink only into the states of deprivation (apāya). However, having heard this discourse, they were struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and gave up their status. Remaining in the stage of a novice (sāmaṇera), they fulfilled the ten precepts and, being devoted to wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), some became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmi), some Non-returners (Anāgāmi), and some were reborn in the celestial realms. Thus, it was fruitful even for those who had committed Pārājika offenses. As for the others who returned to lay life, if they had not heard this discourse, as time went by, they would have eventually committed Saṅghādisesa and Pārājika offenses, and being reborn only in the states of deprivation, they would have experienced great suffering. Having heard this discourse, they thought, "Oh, how the Buddha's Dispensation is one of effacement (sallekhita)! We are unable to fulfill this practice for as long as life lasts. Let us renounce the training, fulfill the Dhamma of lay followers (upāsaka), and be liberated from suffering," and so they returned to the lay life. Established in the Three Refuges and observing the five precepts, they fulfilled the Dhamma of lay followers; consequently, some became Stream-enterers, some Once-returners, some Non-returners, and some were reborn in the celestial realms. Thus, for them too, it was indeed fruitful.

Upon hearing this Dhamma discourse of the Teacher, the hosts of devas—both those who heard it and those who did not—went about informing all others. The monks, hearing it successively, thought, "Friends, it is indeed difficult to lead the holy life perfectly and purely for as long as life lasts in the Dispensation of the Buddhas," and in a single moment, ten, twenty, sixty, a hundred, or even a thousand monks became laymen. The Teacher, having wandered as he pleased, returned again to the Jetavana monastery and addressed the monks: "Monks, while the Tathāgata was wandering, he lived for a long time crowded (with people). Monks, I wish to go into solitary retreat (paṭisallāna) for half a month. No one should approach me, except for the one monk who brings the alms-food."
53:
Having spent half a month in solitude, upon emerging from his seclusion, the Blessed One was wandering through the monastery with the Venerable Ānanda. Seeing the community of monks had become sparse in every place he looked, he asked the Elder, though he already knew: “Ānanda, at other times when the Tathāgata returns to Jetavana after wandering for alms, the entire monastery is bright with the glow of the monks' robes and filled with the breeze caused by their movements. But now, the community of monks appears sparse, and for the most part, the monks look pale, like the color of a withered leaf. Why is this?”

“Venerable Sir, from the time the Blessed One preached the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta, the monks have been struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, ‘We are unable to fulfill this Dhamma in all its aspects; it is not proper for those who do not practice well to consume the requisites donated through the faith of the people.’ Thus, they have returned to the lay life,” Ānanda replied.

At that moment, spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose in the Blessed One. Then he said to the Elder: “While I was staying in seclusion, no one spoke a word of consolation to my sons. Just as there are many landing places to descend into the ocean, so too are there many grounds for consolation in this Dispensation (Sāsana). Go, Ānanda, prepare the Buddha’s seat in the precinct of the Gandhakuṭi and assemble the community of monks.” The Elder did as he was told. The Teacher, having sat upon the noble Buddha’s seat, addressed the monks: “Monks, that which is the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (mettā) is neither absorption (appanā) nor access concentration (upacāra); it is merely the pervading of welfare for beings.” Having said this, he preached this Cūḷa-accharāsaṅghāta Sutta based on this occasion.

In that Sutta, “accharāsaṅghātamattaṃ” means for the duration of a single finger-snap, just the time it takes to make a sound by snapping two fingers. “Mettācittaṃ” means a mind wishing to pervade all beings with welfare. In the word “āsevati” (cultivates/practices), how does one cultivate? One cultivates by reflecting, by knowing, by seeing, by reviewing, by resolving the mind, by being convinced through faith, by exerting energy, by establishing mindfulness, by concentrating the mind, by understanding with wisdom, by directly knowing what should be directly known, by fully understanding what should be fully understood, by abandoning what should be abandoned, by developing what should be developed, and by realizing what should be realized. In this context, however, it should be understood that one cultivates merely by pervading welfare in the preliminary stage of mettā-jhāna.
54:
“Arittajjhāno” means one whose meditation is not empty, or one who has not abandoned meditation. “Viharati” means to exist, proceed, maintain, sustain, or carry on the body through postures such as standing and sitting. Therefore, it is said “viharati” (dwells). By this word, the dwelling through postures of a monk who practices loving-kindness is described. “Satthusāsanakaro” means one who follows the Teacher’s instruction. “Ovādapatikaro” means one who acts according to the advice.

In this context, a single instance of instruction is called “ovāda,” while repeated instruction is called “anusāsanī.” Instruction given in one's presence is “ovāda,” while instruction sent through another in one's absence is “anusāsanī.” Instruction given when a specific matter arises is “ovāda,” while instruction given to establish the scriptural tradition regardless of whether a matter has arisen is “anusāsanī.” Thus, the distinction between ovāda and anusāsanī should be understood. In the ultimate sense, however, whether it is called ovāda or anusāsanī, both are the same, identical in meaning, equal, of the same nature, and the very same thing. In this Sutta, the statement, “Monks, if a monk practices a mind of loving-kindness even for the duration of a finger-snap,” is itself the Teacher’s instruction (sāsana) and advice (ovāda). Because he follows that instruction, this monk is known as “sāsanakaro ovādapatikaro.”

“Amoghaṃ” means not in vain. “Raṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ” refers to the alms-food received from the houses of others by one who has gone forth, relying on the country after abandoning his circle of kin; thus it is called raṭṭhapiṇḍa (alms-food of the country). In the word “pribhuñjati” (consumes), there are four types of usage (paribhoga): usage as a thief (theyyaparibhoga), usage as a debt (iṇaparibhoga), usage as an inheritance (dāyajjaparibhoga), and usage as an owner (sāmiparibhoga).

Among these, the usage by one who lacks virtue is called usage as a thief. The usage by one who has virtue but does not reflect (on the purpose of the requisites) is called usage as a debt. The usage by the seven types of learners (sekha) is called usage as an inheritance. The usage by an Arahant (khīṇāsava) is called usage as an owner. Among these, this monk’s consumption of the country’s alms-food is not in vain for two reasons. A monk who practices a mind of loving-kindness even for the duration of a finger-snap consumes the country’s alms-food as an owner, as one free from debt, and as an heir; thus his consumption of the country’s alms-food is not in vain.

Furthermore, the gift given to a monk who practices loving-kindness even for the duration of a finger-snap is of great merit, great fruit, great advantage, great splendor, and great pervasion; thus his consumption of the country’s alms-food is not in vain. What then need be said of those who practice this mind of loving-kindness frequently, develop it, and do it repeatedly? They certainly consume the country’s alms-food not in vain. Indeed, monks of such nature consume the country’s alms-food as owners, as those free from debt, and as heirs.
55: 54-55. In the fourth sutta, 'bhāveti' means he produces, he increases. In the fifth sutta, 'manasi karoti' means he does in the mind (he attends). In both these suttas, the remaining terms should be understood in the same way as stated in the third sutta. He who frequents, he indeed develops; he indeed attends. With whatever mind he frequents, with that very mind he develops; with that very mind he attends. The Blessed One, because of his thorough penetration of the element of Dhamma (dhammadhātu), attained the splendor of teaching. Due to that thorough penetration of the element of Dhamma, and relying on his own splendor of teaching, his mastery of the Dhamma, his proficiency in the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and his unimpeded omniscient knowledge, he showed by analyzing a single mind arising in a single moment into three portions (repetition, development, and attention). In the sixth sutta, the phrase 'ye keci' (whatever...) is an indefinite expression. The word 'akusalā' (unwholesome) is the word that defines those indefinite things. By this much phrasing, all unwholesome states are included without remainder. The names 'akusalabhāgiyā' (partaking of the unwholesome) and 'akusalapakkhikā' (siding with the unwholesome) are names for the unwholesome states themselves. Indeed, some unwholesome states associate with the unwholesome by way of co-nascence (sahajāta), and some by way of strong dependence (upanissaya), and they are also the partisans of those states. Therefore, they are called 'partaking of the unwholesome and siding with the unwholesome'. In the phrase 'sabbe te manopubbaṅgamā' (all those have mind as their precursor), they are called 'manopubbaṅgama' because the mind arises before those unwholesome mental factors. Indeed, although those unwholesome mental factors have the same arising, the same cessation, the same physical base, and the same object as the mind, the mind is called 'manopubbaṅgama' because it is their producer, maker, generator, originator, and bringer-into-existence. In the phrase 'paṭhamaṃ uppajjati' (arises first), for example, when it is said, "The King has departed," there is no reason to ask, "Did only the King depart, or did the rest of the royal army depart or not?" for it is understood that all have departed. In the same way, from the time it is said that the mind has arisen, there is no reason to ask whether the remaining co-nascent, conjoined, and associated mental factors have arisen or not; it is understood that they have all arisen. Based on this meaning, although the mind has the same arising and same cessation as those mental factors with which it is conjoined and associated, it is said that the mind arises first before those states. 'Anvadeva' means following immediately, simultaneously, or together. However, one should not take the shadow of the expression 'paṭhamaṃ uppajjati' to mean that the mind arises first and the mental factors arise later. For the meaning is...
56: ...the meaning alone is the refuge, not the letter. This is the same method in the verse: "Mind is the precursor of all states, mind is chief, they are mind-made." (Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā). In the seventh sutta, 'kusalā' (wholesome) refers to the wholesome states belonging to the four planes. The rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the sixth sutta. In the eighth sutta, in the phrase "yathayidaṃ bhikkhave pamādo", "bhikkhave" is an address. The meaning is "just as this negligence (pamāda)". Negligence is the mode of being negligent. For it has been said: "Therein, what is negligence? It is the letting loose of the mind, the repeated letting loose of the mind, in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, or mental misconduct, or in the five cords of sensual pleasure; lack of respect, lack of constancy, lack of steadfastness, shrinking, giving up of desire, laying down the burden, lack of resolution, lack of application, lack of frequenting, lack of development, and lack of repeated practice in the development of wholesome states. Such negligence, the mode of being negligent, the state of being negligent, is called negligence." (Vibhaṅga, 846). "Wholesome states that have arisen decline"—this is said by way of jhāna and insight (vipassanā). As for the Paths and Fruits, once they have arisen, there is no such thing as declining again. In the ninth sutta, 'appamāda' (diligence) should be understood in detail by way of the opposite of negligence. In the tenth sutta, 'kosajja' means laziness. The rest is just as the method already stated. ## Commentary on the Accharāsaṅghāta Vagga. ## 7. Commentary on the Vīriyārambhādi Vagga In the first sutta of the seventh chapter, 'vīriyārambha' (arousal of energy) means the arousal of Right Effort (sammappadhāna) which has four functions; it means the state of having aroused, upheld, and fulfilled energy.
57: In the second sutta, mahisicchatā means great greed. Regarding this mahisicchatā, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "Among these (great desire and fewness of wishes), what is mahisicchatā? It is the state of wanting more, being dissatisfied with the requisites—whether inferior or superior—of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal supports for the sick, or with the five cords of sensual pleasure. Such desire, the arrival at desire, great desire, lust, intense lust, and the intense lust of the mind is called mahisicchatā." In the third sutta, appicchatā means non-greed (alobha). Appiccha refers to the state of one who is without desire. In this term appicchatā, although the syllable seems to imply a remainder, the meaning is complete without remainder. One is not called appiccha merely because of having a small amount of desire; rather, one is called appiccha because of the absence of desire and because of the nature of non-greed that has been repeatedly cultivated. Furthermore, in this context, four distinctions should be understood: atricchatā, pāpicchatā, mahisicchatā, and appicchatā. Among these four, atricchatā is the longing for the gains of others while being dissatisfied with one's own gains. To one possessed of this atricchatā, even if a cake is baked in the same pot, the cake that falls into his own bowl appears as if it is not well-cooked or as if it is small. However, that same cake placed in another's bowl appears as if it is well-cooked and large. Pāpicchatā is the pretending to have virtues that one does not possess and not knowing the measure in receiving requisites. This pāpicchatā is as mentioned in the Abhidhamma: "Here, a certain person, though lacking faith, wishes, 'May people know me as one who has faith,'" and so on. A person possessed of this pāpicchatā stands in hypocrisy (kohañña). Mahisicchatā is the displaying of virtues that one actually possesses and not knowing the measure in receiving requisites. This mahisicchatā also appears in the following way: "Here, a certain person, though possessing faith, wishes, 'May people know me as one who has faith'; though possessing virtue, wishes, 'May people know me as one who is virtuous.'" A person possessed of this mahisicchatā is difficult for others to satisfy. Even his own mother who gave birth to him cannot satisfy his mind. Therefore, the teachers have said: "A great mass of fire, the ocean, and a person of great desire—these three are insatiable, even if requisites are given by the cartload."
58:
The concealing of virtues that one actually possesses and knowing the measure in receiving requisites is called fewness of wishes (appicchatā). A person possessed of this fewness of wishes, because of the desire to hide the virtues present in himself, does not wish, "May people know me as one who has faith," even though he has faith. Even if he is virtuous, secluded, learned, energetic, possessed of concentration, wise, or an Arahant, he does not wish, "May people know me as an Arahant," just like the Elder Majjhantika.

That Elder was indeed a great Arahant, yet his bowl and robes were worth only about a quarter (of a coin). He was the Sangha Elder on the day of King Asoka's great monastery festival. Then, seeing his very ragged appearance, people said, "Venerable sir, please step outside for a moment." The Elder thought, "If an Arahant like me does not support the King, who else will?" and diving into the earth, he emerged while receiving the almsfood offered to the Sangha Elder. Thus, even though he was an Arahant, he did not wish, "May people know me as an Arahant." A monk who is thus few in wishes brings about gains that have not yet arisen, makes stable the gains that have arisen, and pleases the minds of the donors. Indeed, the more that monk takes only a little due to his fewness of wishes, the more the people, being inspired by his conduct, give abundantly.

There are also four other kinds of fewness of wishes: fewness of wishes regarding requisites (paccaya-appicchatā), fewness of wishes regarding ascetic practices (dhutaṅga-appicchatā), fewness of wishes regarding learning (pariyatti-appicchatā), and fewness of wishes regarding attainments (adhigama-appicchatā). Among these four, one who is few in wishes regarding the four requisites is called paccaya-appiccha. He knows the wish of the donor, he knows the measure of the gift, and he knows his own capacity. If the gift is abundant but the donor wishes to give only a little, he takes only a little according to the donor's wish. If the gift is small but the donor wishes to give much, he takes only a little according to the measure of the gift. If the gift is abundant and the donor also wishes to give much, he knows his own capacity and takes only a moderate amount.

One who does not want others to know that he has undertaken ascetic practices is called dhutaṅga-appiccha. To illustrate this point, there are these stories: The Elder Mahā-Kumāra, a cemetery-dweller, lived in a cemetery for sixty years, yet not even another single monk knew of it. Therefore, it is said:

"I lived in the cemetery for sixty years. I did not want even a second person to know me as a noble cemetery-dweller," he declared.
59:
