“For sixty years I have lived in the cemetery, unmingled with people. Let no second person know me; oh, he is the most excellent among those who observe the cemetery-dweller's practice,” he said. Two brother elders lived on Cetiyapabbata. The younger elder took a piece of sugarcane sent by a supporter and went to the elder brother, saying, “Venerable sir, please consume this.” At that time, the elder had finished his meal and it was time to wash his mouth. The elder said, “Enough, friend.” When asked, “Venerable sir, how is it? Are you observing the practice of the one-sessioner (ekāsanika-dhutaṅga)?” the elder, although he had been a one-sessioner for fifty years, wished to conceal his ascetic practice and said, “Friend, bring the piece of sugarcane.” After consuming it and washing his mouth, he re-undertook the ascetic practice and departed.

One who, like Elder Tissa of Sāketa, does not want others to know of his vast learning is called 'one of few wishes regarding scriptural learning' (pariyatti-appiccha). It is said that when this elder was urged by his disciples, who said, “Venerable sir, if you remain without giving an opportunity for instruction and inquiry, saying ‘there is no time,’ when will you find the opportunity for death?” he left the group and went to the Kaṇikāravālika Samudda Vihāra. There, during the three months of the rainy season, he was of service to the senior, middle, and junior monks, and on the day of the Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā), he stirred the entire district with a Dhamma talk and then departed. One who, being one of the noble ones such as a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), does not want others to know of his attainment of stream-entry and so on, is called 'one of few wishes regarding attainment' (adhigama-appiccha). This is like the three noble sons and Ghaṭīkāra the potter. In this context, both a trainee (sekha) and a worldling (puthujjana) who are endowed with powerful non-greed acquired through practice should be understood as 'one of few wishes' (appiccha).

In the fourth sutta, 'discontentment' (asantuṭṭhitā) refers to greed, known as lack of contentment, which arises in one who associates with, frequents, and attends upon discontented persons.

In the fifth sutta, 'contentment' (santuṭṭhitā) refers to non-greed, known as contentment (santuṭṭhi), which arises in one who associates with, frequents, and attends upon contented persons. 'Of one who is contented' (santuṭṭhassa) refers to a person endowed with contentment with whatever requisites are obtained. That contentment is of twelve kinds. How? There are three kinds regarding robes: contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābha-santuṭṭhi), contentment according to one's strength (yathābala-santuṭṭhi), and contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi). Regarding alms-food and so on, it is the same, making a total of twelve kinds. I shall further explain the divisions of these twelve kinds of contentment—in this Dispensation, a monk receives a robe, whether it be of good or poor quality. That monk is satisfied with only that robe he has received; he does not long for another, and even if he receives another, he does not take it. This is called 'contentment with whatever is obtained' regarding robes. Another monk is naturally weak or oppressed by illness and old age; if he has to wear a heavy robe, he becomes exhausted. Even if that monk exchanges that heavy robe with a compatible monk and is satisfied with a light robe, he is still one who is contented. This is called 'contentment according to one's strength' regarding robes. Another monk is one who receives excellent requisites. When he receives expensive robes such as silk robes or many robes, he gives them away, thinking, “This robe is suitable for senior elders of long standing, this robe is suitable for those of vast learning, let this robe be for the sick, or let this robe be for those who receive few gains.” Then, by wearing their old robes or by picking up rags from dust heaps and the like to make a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi), he is still one who is contented. This is called 'contentment with what is appropriate'.
60:
Contentment (santuṭṭhi) is of twelve kinds. They are: contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābha-santuṭṭhi), contentment according to one's strength (yathābala-santuṭṭhi), and contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi) regarding robes—thus there are three kinds. Similarly, there are three kinds each regarding alms-food and so on.

To explain the divisions of that contentment—in this Dispensation, a monk receives a robe, whether it be good or bad. That monk is satisfied with only that robe he has received; he does not long for another, and even if he receives another, he does not take it. This is his 'contentment with whatever is obtained' (yathālābha-santuṭṭhi) regarding robes. Furthermore, a monk who is naturally weak or oppressed by illness and old age finds it exhausting to wear a heavy robe. Even if that monk exchanges that heavy robe with a compatible monk and is satisfied with a light robe, he is still one who is contented. This is his 'contentment according to one's strength' (yathābala-santuṭṭhi) regarding robes. Another monk is one who receives excellent requisites. He receives an expensive robe such as a silk robe or many robes and gives them away, saying, “This robe is suitable for senior elders of long standing, this robe is suitable for those of vast learning, this robe is suitable for the sick, let this robe be for monks who receive few gains.” By wearing their old robes or by picking up rags from dust heaps and the like to make a double-layered robe and wearing it, he is still one who is contented. This is his 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi) regarding robes.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives alms-food, whether it be coarse or fine. That monk is satisfied with only that alms-food he has received; he does not long for another, and even if he receives another, he does not take it. This is his 'contentment with whatever is obtained' (yathālābha-santuṭṭhi) regarding alms-food. A monk who receives alms-food that is unsuitable for his natural constitution or unsuitable for his illness, such that he would be uncomfortable if he consumed it, gives that food to a compatible monk and, by eating suitable food from that monk's hand and performing the recluse's duties, he is still one who is contented. This is his 'contentment according to one's strength' (yathābala-santuṭṭhi) regarding alms-food. Another monk receives much fine alms-food. Just as with the robes, he gives that food to senior elders, those of long standing, those of vast learning, those who receive few gains, and the sick, and by eating their leftovers or by wandering for alms and eating mixed food, he is still one who is contented. This is his 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi) regarding alms-food.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives a lodging, whether it be pleasant or unpleasant. That monk does not give rise to either joy or displeasure because of that place; even with at least a grass mat...
61:
This is called contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi) regarding robes for that bhikkhu. (Nipāta 7, Vīriyāradivagga-vaṇṇanā). A bhikkhu who consumes leftovers or mixed food obtained by wandering for alms is also contented. This is called contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi) regarding almsfood for that bhikkhu.

Regarding lodging (senāsana): In this Dispensation, a bhikkhu obtains a lodging that is either pleasant or unpleasant. He does not feel joy because of it, nor does he feel displeasure; he is satisfied and contented even with a mere spread of grass. This is called contentment with what is obtained (yathālābha-santuṭṭhi) regarding lodging for that bhikkhu. A bhikkhu who obtains a lodging that is unsuitable for him, either by nature or due to illness, where living is uncomfortable. He gives that lodging to a compatible bhikkhu and stays in a suitable lodging belonging to that bhikkhu, yet he remains contented. This is called contentment according to strength (yathābala-santuṭṭhi) regarding lodging for that bhikkhu.

Another bhikkhu of great merit obtains many excellent lodgings such as caves, pavilions, or gabled houses. Like with robes, he gives them to senior elders, those long ordained, the learned, those who receive little, or the sick, and stays anywhere at all, yet he remains contented. This is called contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi) regarding lodging for that bhikkhu. Also, a bhikkhu who reflects: 'An excellent lodging is a ground for negligence; sitting there, sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) overcome one; when one wakes up after being overcome by sleep, unwholesome thoughts (akusala-vitakka) manifest.' Reflecting thus, even if he reaches such an excellent lodging, he does not accept it but rejects it and stays in the open air or at the foot of a tree, yet he remains contented. This also is called contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi) regarding lodging for that bhikkhu.

Regarding medicinal requisites (bhesajja): In this Dispensation, a bhikkhu obtains medicine, whether coarse or excellent. He is contented with whatever he obtains, does not desire anything else, and even if he receives more, he does not take it. This is called contentment with what is obtained (yathālābha-santuṭṭhi) regarding medicinal requisites for that bhikkhu. A bhikkhu who, needing oil, obtains molasses. He gives that molasses to a compatible bhikkhu and, taking oil from that bhikkhu's hand or seeking other oil, makes medicine, yet he remains contented. This is called contentment according to strength (yathābala-santuṭṭhi) regarding medicinal requisites for that bhikkhu.

Another bhikkhu of great merit obtains many excellent medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses. Like with robes, he gives them to senior elders, those long ordained, the learned, those who receive little, or the sick, and sustains himself with whatever simple medicine they bring, yet he remains contented. A bhikkhu who, when offered yellow myrobalan steeped in cow's urine in one vessel and the four sweets (catumadhura) in another, with the words 'Venerable sir, take whichever you wish,' thinks: 'If the disease can be cured by either of these, then the yellow myrobalan steeped in cow's urine is praised by the Buddhas and others.' Rejecting the four sweets, he makes medicine with the yellow myrobalan, yet he is supremely contented. This is called contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi) regarding medicinal requisites for that bhikkhu. Among these three types of contentment for each requisite, contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi) is the most excellent.

In the sixth and seventh suttas, unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) have the characteristics already mentioned below. The remaining words in these suttas have clear meanings.

68. In the eighth sutta, lack of clear comprehension (asampajañña) means not knowing well and thoroughly. This is a name for delusion (moha). 'For one who lacks clear comprehension' (asampajānassa) means for a person who does not know, who is greatly confused.

69. In the ninth sutta, clear comprehension (sampajañña) means knowing well and thoroughly.
62:
66-67. In the sixth and seventh suttas, unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) have the characteristics already mentioned below. The remaining words in these suttas have very clear meanings.

68. In the eighth sutta, lack of clear comprehension (asampajañña) means not knowing well and thoroughly, and is a name for delusion (moha). 'For one who lacks clear comprehension' (asampajānassa) means for a person who does not know, who is greatly confused.

69. In the ninth sutta, clear comprehension (sampajañña) means knowing well and thoroughly, and is a name for wisdom (paññā). 'For one who has clear comprehension' (sampajānassa) means for a person who knows thoroughly.

70. In the tenth sutta, bad friendship (pāpamittatā) means a person who has evil, low friends is called a 'bad friend' (pāpamitta). The state of being a bad friend is 'bad friendship' (pāpamittatā). This is simply a name for the four mental aggregates that arise through the mode of delighting in such bad friends. It is also said: 'Therein, what is bad friendship? Those persons who are faithless, immoral, of little learning, stingy, and unwise. The following of such persons, associating with them, frequenting them, being devoted to them, being strongly devoted to them, being loyal to them, being strongly loyal to them, and being inclined towards them—this is called bad friendship' (as found in the Vibhaṅga).

## Commentary on the Chapter beginning with Arousal of Energy (Vīriyārambhādivagga-vaṇṇanā).

## 8. Commentary on the Chapter beginning with Good Friendship (Kalyāṇamittatādivagga-vaṇṇanā)

71. In the first sutta of the eighth chapter, good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā) means a person who has good friends is called a 'good friend' (kalyāṇamitta). The state of being a good friend is 'good friendship' (kalyāṇamittatā). The remaining words should be understood by the method opposite to what was said (in the tenth sutta).

72-73. In the second sutta, devotion (anuyoga) means effort or application. Lack of devotion (ananuyoga) means lack of effort or lack of application. 'By devotion' (anuyogā) and 'by lack of devotion' (ananuyogā) have these meanings. 'Of wholesome states' (kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ) means of wholesome states belonging to the four planes. The third sutta has a very clear meaning.

74. In the fourth sutta, factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgā) means the seven states that are the components (or causes) for a being who will realize the Four Noble Truths. Or, they are the collection of states by which that person realizes (the Four Noble Truths), or wakes up from the sleep of defilements...
63:
Or one realizes the Four Noble Truths. They are called 'Factors of Enlightenment' (Bojjhaṅga) because they are constituent parts of that enlightenment. In this term 'Bojjhaṅga', for what reason are they called Bojjhaṅga? They are called Bojjhaṅga because they know; they are called Bojjhaṅga because they know appropriately; they are called Bojjhaṅga because they know directly; they are called Bojjhaṅga because they know well; they are called Bojjhaṅga because they lead to the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths. In this way, this term 'Bojjhaṅga' is analyzed.

75. In the fifth sutta, by the phrase "reaching the fulfillment of development" (bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchanti), the plane which is the true function of the Factors of Enlightenment is spoken of. That plane is of four kinds: insight (vipassanā), jhāna as a basis for insight, the path (magga), and the fruition (phala). Among these four, at the time when insight arises, the Factors of Enlightenment are of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara); at the time when jhāna as a basis for insight arises, they are of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara); at the time when they arise in the path and fruition, they are supramundane (lokuttara). Therefore, in this fifth sutta, the Factors of Enlightenment occurring in the four planes are spoken of.

76. The beginning of the sixth sutta is an introduction based on an occasion (atthuppatti). Indeed, this sixth sutta was delivered because of an occasion that arose. To elaborate, many monks were sitting together in the Dhamma Hall. In the midst of those monks, a conversation arose concerning Bandhula, the Mallian general: "Friends, such and such a family formerly had many relatives and many followers. Now, it has few relatives and few followers." Then the Blessed One, knowing the inclination of those monks' minds and realizing, "If I go, there will be a great teaching," came out from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma Hall, and said, "Monks, for what conversation are you sitting together now?"

The monks replied, "Venerable Sir, there is no other talk concerning villages or market towns, etc. We are sitting here saying that such and such a family formerly had many relatives and many followers, but now it has few relatives and few followers." Because this occasion had arisen, the Teacher began to teach this sutta: "Monks, this loss is a minor one (appamattikā esā bhikkhave parihāni)."

In that sutta, "appamattikā" means small or of a small measure. Indeed, by this loss of relatives, there is no such thing as falling away from heaven or from the path. He said this is merely a loss of welfare in the present life. "Etāṃ paṭikiṭṭhaṃ" means this is the lowest, this is the meanest. "Yadidaṃ paññāparihāni" means whatever loss there is in my Dispensation (Sāsana) regarding the wisdom of ownership of deeds (kammassakata-paññā), the wisdom of jhāna, the wisdom of insight, the wisdom of the path, and the wisdom of fruition—this loss of wisdom is the lowest, the meanest, and should be discarded.
64:
The seventh sutta was also spoken because of an occasion that arose. It is heard that while the monks were sitting in the Dhamma Hall, some monks said, "Such and such a family formerly had few relatives and few followers; now that family has many relatives and many followers." To whom were they referring when they spoke thus? They were referring to the lay devotee Visākhā and the Licchavīs in the city of Vesālī. The Teacher, knowing the inclination of those monks' minds, came just as in the previous manner, sat on the Dhamma seat, and asked, "Monks, for what conversation are you sitting together now?" Those monks reported the matter as it truly was. The Teacher began this sutta because of this occasion. In that sutta, "appamattikā" (minor) refers to something very small (insignificant) because there is no one who reaches heaven or the path by depending on that prosperity (of relatives). "Yadidaṃ paññāvuddhi" refers to the increase of the wisdom of ownership of deeds, etc. "Tasmā" (therefore) is used because the increase of relatives is merely for the present life and is very small, as that increase of relatives is unable to make one reach heaven or the path. "Paññāvuddhiyā" means because of the increase of the wisdom of ownership of deeds, etc.

The eighth sutta was also spoken because of an occasion that arose. It is heard that many monks were sitting together in the Dhamma Hall and spoke concerning the son of Mahādhana the merchant: "Such and such a family formerly had great wealth, much gold and silver; now that family has little wealth." The Teacher came just as in the previous manner, heard the words of those monks, and began this sutta.

The ninth sutta was also spoken because of an occasion that arose. It is heard that the monks sitting in the Dhamma Hall spoke concerning the merchant Kāka-valiya and the merchant Puṇṇa: "Such and such a family formerly had little wealth; now that family has great wealth." The Teacher came just as in the previous manner, heard their words, and began this sutta. The remaining words in both of these suttas should be understood in the same manner as stated below.

The tenth sutta was also spoken because of an occasion that arose. It is heard that the monks in the Dhamma Hall spoke concerning the Great King of Kosala: "Such and such a family formerly had great fame and a great retinue; now it has little fame and a little retinue." The Blessed One came just as in the previous manner, heard their words, and began this Dhamma teaching. The remaining words should be understood in the same manner as already stated.

## Commentary on the Chapter beginning with Good Friendship (Kalyāṇamittatādivagga).
65:
## 9. Pamādādivaggavaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the ninth chapter as well, only the occasion of its origin is mentioned. It is said that while many monks were sitting in the Dhamma Hall, they spoke concerning Kumbhaghosaka, saying: "This particular family was formerly of little wealth and few followers, but now it has become of great wealth and many followers." The Teacher, having arrived in the manner previously described and hearing the words of those monks, began teaching this sutta. The meaning of this sutta should be understood in the same way as stated below.

In the second sutta and others, "mahato anatthāya" means for the sake of great harm. The remaining words here are quite clear.

## Pamādādivaggavaṇṇanā.

## 10. Dutiyapamādādivaggavaṇṇanā
In the tenth chapter, "ajjhattikaṃ" refers to a state that is internal, by way of occurring within one's own continuum. "Aṅgaṃ" means a cause. "Iti karitvā" means having done so (having made this a cause). This is what is meant: Monks, I do not see even one other cause that arises internally within one's own continuum like this.

110-114. "Bāhiraṃ" means existing outside of the internal continuum. "Saddhammassa" means of the pure Dhamma or of the Dispensation (Sāsana). "Sammosāya" means for the sake of destruction. "Antaradhānāya" means for the sake of disappearance (not being evident).

"Ṭhitiyā" means for the sake of long endurance. The terms "asammosāya anantaradhānāya" should be understood by the method of being the opposites of the meanings already stated. The remaining words here are in the same manner as stated in the four-fold (catukka-koṭika) sutta.

In the suttas starting with "adhammaṃ dhammoti dīpenti" which follow this sutta, according to the Suttanta method, first, the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) are called Dhamma, and the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapatha) are called non-Dhamma (adhamma). Likewise, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma)—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the noble eightfold path (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga)—are called Dhamma. The three foundations of mindfulness...
66:
...the three right efforts, the three bases of power, the six faculties, the six powers, the eight factors of enlightenment, and the ninefold path; as well as the four types of clinging (upādāna), the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa), the seven latent tendencies (anusaya), and the eight wrong states (micchatta)—these are called non-Dhamma (adhamma).

Among those two, Dhamma and non-Dhamma, if one takes an unspecified portion of non-Dhamma and thinks, "We will make this non-Dhamma into Dhamma; by doing so, our teacher's lineage will be one that leads out of suffering, and we shall become famous in the world," and while speaking of that non-Dhamma, they say, "This is Dhamma," they are said to explain non-Dhamma as Dhamma. Similarly, if they take one of the portions of Dhamma and say, "This is non-Dhamma," they are said to explain Dhamma as non-Dhamma. According to the Vinaya method, however, a legal act (kamma) that is performed after charging and reminding with a true cause, and in accordance with a confession, is called Dhamma. A legal act that is performed without charging with a true cause, without reminding, and without a confession, is called non-Dhamma.

According to the Suttanta method, the removal of lust (rāga), the removal of hatred (dosa), the removal of delusion (moha), restraint, abandonment, and reflection—this is called Discipline (vinaya). The non-removal of lust, etc., non-restraint, non-abandonment, and non-reflection—this is called non-Discipline (avinaya). According to the Vinaya method, the perfection of the basis (vatthu), the perfection of the motion (ñatti), the perfection of the proclamation (anussāvana), the perfection of the boundary (sīmā), and the perfection of the assembly (parisa)—this is called Discipline. The failure (vipatti) of the basis, the failure of the motion, the failure of the proclamation, the failure of the boundary, and the failure of the assembly—this is called non-Discipline.

According to the Suttanta method, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts ...pe... the noble eightfold path—this teaching was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata. The three foundations of mindfulness, the three right efforts, the three bases of power, the six faculties, the six powers, the eight factors of enlightenment, and the ninefold path—this teaching was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata. According to the Vinaya method, the four pārājikas, the thirteen saṅghādisesas, the two aniyatas, and the thirty nissaggiya pācittiyas—this teaching was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata. The three pārājikas, the fourteen saṅghādisesas, the three aniyatas, and the thirty-one nissaggiya pācittiyas—this teaching was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata.

According to the Suttanta method, the daily practice of entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), entering the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇāsamāpatti), surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, teaching the Suttanta according to the occasion, and telling Jātaka stories—this practice was habitually cultivated. The daily practice of not entering the attainment of fruition ...pe... not telling Jātaka stories—this practice was not habitually cultivated.
67:
According to the method of the Vinaya teaching, the practice of departing for a journey after residing for the three months of the Rains Retreat upon being invited, departing for a journey after performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, and first performing the duties of hospitality towards guests—this nature is called 'practiced' (āciṇṇa). Not performing that practiced habit is called 'unpracticed' (anāciṇṇa).

According to the method of the Suttanta teaching, from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the Eightfold Path, this nature is called 'prescribed' (paññatta). From the three foundations of mindfulness up to the ninefold path, this nature is called 'unprescribed' (apaññatta). According to the method of the Vinaya teaching, from the four Pārājikas up to the thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiyas, this nature is called 'prescribed'. From the three Pārājikas up to the thirty-one Nissaggiya Pācittiyas, this nature is called 'unprescribed'.

In the statement 'They cause this True Dhamma to disappear,' spoken at the end of all Suttas, there are five kinds of disappearance (antaradhāna). They are: the disappearance of attainment (adhigama-antaradhāna), the disappearance of practice (paṭipatti-antaradhāna), the disappearance of learning (pariyatti-antaradhāna), the disappearance of the outward signs (liṅga-antaradhāna), and the disappearance of the relics (dhātu-antaradhāna). Among these five, 'attainment' (adhigama) refers to the four paths, the four fruits, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the three true knowledges (vijjā), and the six higher powers (abhiññā). When these attainments decline, they decline starting from the analytical insights. Indeed, for only one thousand years after the Parinibbāna of the Buddhas are they able to produce the analytical insights. After that thousand years, they are able to produce the six higher powers. After that, being unable to produce those higher powers, they produce the three true knowledges. As time goes on, being unable to produce even those true knowledges, they become only dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka). In this same manner, there are Non-returners, Once-returners, and Stream-enters. As long as these Non-returners, Once-returners, and Stream-enters exist, attainment is said to have not yet disappeared. Only with the end of the life of the last Stream-enterer is attainment said to have disappeared. This is called the disappearance of attainment (adhigama-antaradhāna).

The disappearance of practice (paṭipatti-antaradhāna) means that, being unable to produce jhāna, insight, the path, and the fruit, they protect only the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). As time goes on, they reach a state of decline, thinking, 'We shall protect virtue to fulfillment and we shall apply ourselves to the practice, yet we are unable to realize the path or the fruit; now there is no longer the penetration of the Noble Dhamma.' Being full of indolence, they do not admonish or remind one another, and they live heedlessly. From then on, they trample upon (violate) the minor and very minor training rules. As time goes on, they fall into Pācittiya and Thullaccaya offenses. After that, they fall into Saṅghādisesa offenses. Only the Pārājikas remain. As long as monks who protect the four Pārājikas exist, even by the hundreds or thousands, practice is said to have not yet disappeared. Only with the breach of virtue or the end of the life of the last monk is practice said to have disappeared. This is called the disappearance of practice (paṭipatti-antaradhāna). Learning (pariyatti) refers to the Word of the Buddha, the Tipitaka together with its commentaries. As long as that Pali text together with its commentaries exists, the fulfillment of learning and inquiry (pariyatti-paripucchā) is said to still exist. As time goes on, kings and viceroys become unrighteous. When those kings are unrighteous, the king's ministers and so forth also become unrighteous. From then on, the people of the country and districts also become unrighteous.
68:
The disappearance of practice (paṭipatti-antaradhāna) occurs through the breach of virtue or the end of life (of the last monk).

Learning (pariyatti) is the Pali text of the Word of the Buddha, the Tipitaka together with its commentaries. As long as that learning exists, learning is said to be complete. When a long time has passed, kings and viceroys become unrighteous; when those kings are unrighteous, the king's ministers and so forth become unrighteous; from then on, the people of the country and districts also become unrighteous. Because of their unrighteousness, the rain does not fall properly; then the crops do not succeed. When the crops do not succeed, the donors of the four requisites are unable to offer the four requisites to the Saṅgha of monks. The monks, being weary for lack of the four requisites, are unable to support their students. As a long time passes, learning declines; they are no longer able to maintain it by way of the meaning, but maintain it only by way of the Pali text. From then on, as a long time passes, they are unable to maintain even the Pali text in its entirety; first, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka declines and disappears. When it declines, it declines starting from the top. First, the great treatise of the Paṭṭhāna declines; when that treatise disappears, the Yamaka, Kathāvatthu, Puggalapaññatti, Dhātukathā, Vibhaṅga, and Dhammasaṅgaṇī disappear.

When the Abhidhamma Piṭaka has thus disappeared, the Suttanta Piṭaka declines starting from the top. First, the Aṅguttara Nikāya declines; in that Nikāya also, first the Book of the Elevens, then from there the Book of the Tens... and so on, it declines down to the Book of the Ones. When the Aṅguttara Nikāya has thus disappeared, the Saṃyutta Nikāya declines starting from the top. First the Mahāvagga, then the Saḷāyatanavagga, Khandhavagga, Nidānavagga, and Sagāthāvagga disappear. When the Saṃyutta Nikāya has thus disappeared, the Majjhima Nikāya declines starting from the top. First the Uparipaṇṇāsa, then the Majjhimapaṇṇāsa, then the Mūlapaṇṇāsa disappear. When the Majjhima Nikāya has thus disappeared, the Dīgha Nikāya declines starting from the top. First the Pāthikavagga, then the Mahāvagga, then the Sīlakkhandhavagga disappear. When the Dīgha Nikāya has thus disappeared, the Suttanta Piṭaka is said to have disappeared. Together with the Vinaya Piṭaka, they maintain only the Jātakas. Only conscientious (lajjī) monks maintain the Vinaya Piṭaka; however, monks who desire gain, saying, 'Even if the Suttanta is preached, there is no one to take note of it,' maintain only the Jātakas. As a long time passes...
69:
As time passes, they will no longer be able to maintain the Jātakas. At that time, first the Vessantara Jātaka will decline and disappear. Then, in reverse order, the Puṇဏက Jātaka, the Mahānārada Jātaka, and so on, until finally the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka declines and disappears. When the Jātakas have thus disappeared, they will maintain only the Vinaya Piṭaka.

As time passes, the Vinaya Piṭaka will also decline and disappear, starting from the top. Indeed, first the Parivāra will decline. Then the Khandhaka, the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, and the Mahā Vibhaṅga will decline in order, until they maintain only the Uposathakkhandhaka. Even then, learning (pariyatti) is not yet said to have disappeared. As long as even a single four-line stanza (gāthā) remains among humans, learning has not disappeared. When a king, faithful and devoted to the Triple Gem, places a purse of a thousand pieces in a golden casket on an elephant's back and has a drum beaten throughout the city, saying, 'Let him who knows a four-line stanza spoken by the Buddhas take this thousand,' and finds no one to take it; and even after having the drum beaten three times, thinking, 'By beating it once, there may be those who hear and those who do not,' he still finds no one to take it, and the king's men return that purse of a thousand to the palace—at that time, learning is said to have disappeared. This is known as the disappearance of learning (pariyatti-antaradhāna).

As time passes, the wearing of the robe, the carrying of the bowl, the bending and stretching of limbs, and the looking ahead and aside will no longer be inspiring. Like the Nigaṇṭha ascetics who wander carrying a gourd-bowl hanging from the tip of their arm, monks too will wander carrying their bowls hanging from the tip of their arms. Even by this much, the outward sign (linga) has not yet disappeared. But as time passes, they will lower it from the tip of the arm and wander carrying it by hand or in a bag. They will not dye their robes properly but will wear them the color of a camel's back. As time passes, there will be no dyeing, no cutting of the fringe, and no sewing of the waistband; they will use them after making only a ritual smudge (kappabindu). Later, even if they sew the waistband, they will not make the ritual smudge. After that, doing neither, they will cut off the edges and wander like wandering ascetics (paribbājaka). As time passes, thinking, 'What use is this to us?' they will tie a small piece of yellow cloth to their hands or necks, or attach it to their hair. While supporting a wife and children, they will wander about making a living by plowing and sowing. At that time, donors will give gifts to them, intending them for the Saṅgha. Referring to such giving, the Blessed One said: 'Ānanda, in the future there will be clan-members with yellow robes around their necks (kāsāva-kaṇṭha), who are immoral and of evil nature. People will give gifts to those immoral ones, intending them for the Saṅgha. Even then, Ānanda, I say that a gift given to the Saṅgha...'
70:
"...is of incalculable and immeasurable fruit" (M. Ni. 3.380). Thereafter, as a long time passes, while performing various kinds of work, they will say, "What is this robe? What use is this robe to us?" and they will cut off the piece of yellow cloth and throw it into the forest. At that time, the outward sign (linga) is said to have disappeared. It is heard that from the time of the Buddha Kassapa, it became the custom of the Yonakas to wander wearing white clothes. This is known as the disappearance of the outward sign (linga-antaradhāna).

The disappearance of the relics (dhātu-antaradhāna) should be understood thus: There are three kinds of parinibbāna: the parinibbāna of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna), the parinibbāna of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna), and the parinibbāna of the relics (dhātu-parinibbāna). Among these three, the parinibbāna of defilements occurred at the seat of enlightenment (Bodhi-pallaṅka); the parinibbāna of the aggregates occurred at Kusināra; and the parinibbāna of the relics will occur in the future. How will it occur? Later, not receiving honor and respect in various places, the relics will, by the power of the Buddhas' resolution, go to places where they will receive honor and respect. As a long time passes, when honor and respect are no longer found in any place, at the time of the decline of the Dispensation, all the relics in this Island of Tambapaṇṇi will gather and go to the Mahācetiya, from there to the Rājāyatana Cetiya in Nāgadīpa, and from there to the seat of enlightenment (Bodhi-pallaṅka). From the realm of the nagas, from the deva worlds, and from the brahma worlds, the relics will go only to the Mahābodhi-pallaṅka. Not even a relic the size of a mustard seed will be lost in the interval.

All the relics will gather at the Mahābodhi-maṇဍိုင် and, taking the form of the Buddha, will display the glory of the Buddha's body seated in the cross-legged posture at the Bodhi-maṇဍိုင်. The thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor marks, and the fathom-wide radiance will all be perfectly complete. Then, they will perform a miracle like the one on the day of the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya). At that time, no human being will go to that Bodhi tree. However, all the deities in the ten thousand world-systems will assemble and lament, saying, "Today the Ten-Powered One attains parinibbāna; from today onwards there will be darkness." Then, the element of fire (tejo-dhātu) will arise from the body of relics and cause that body to reach the state beyond designation (apaṇṇattika-bhāva). The flame arising from the body of relics will ascend as far as the brahma world. As long as there is even a remaining relic the size of a mustard seed, there will be a single flame. Only when the relics are completely exhausted will it be extinguished. Having thus shown great power...
71:
The relics disappear. At that time, the assembled hosts of devas, as on the day of the Buddhas' Parinibbāna, perform offerings and honors with divine flowers, scents, musical instruments, and so forth. Having circumambulated three times and paid homage, they say, "Venerable One, we wish to see the Buddha who will arise in the future," and return to their respective abodes. This is known as the disappearance of the relics (dhātu-antaradhāna).

Among these five types of disappearance, the disappearance of the Pariyatti (the scriptures) is the root cause. Indeed, when the Pariyatti disappears, the Patipatti (practice) disappears; as long as the Pariyatti remains, the Patipatti is established. For this very reason, when the great peril of Caṇḍāla-Tissa arose in this island of Laṅkā, Sakka, the king of devas, created a great raft and had it announced to the monks: "A great peril will arise; the rain will not fall properly. The monks, being weary for lack of the four requisites, will not be able to maintain the Pariyatti. It is proper for the venerable ones to go to the other shore to preserve their lives. Venerable sirs, please board this great raft and go. For those monks for whom there is not enough seating on this raft, let them go by leaning their chests against pieces of wood; there shall be no danger for any of the monks."

Then, upon reaching the shore of the ocean, sixty monks made a pact: "We have no business going to the other side of this ocean. We shall stay right here on this island and preserve the Tipitaka." Turning back from the shore, they went to the southern Malaya district and lived by sustaining themselves on tubers, roots, and leaves. When their bodies were strong enough, they sat and recited; when they were not strong enough, they cleared and piled up sand, surrounded it, and placing their heads together in one place, they contemplated the Pariyatti. In this manner, for twelve years, they maintained the Tipitaka together with the commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) in its entirety.

When the peril had subsided, the seven hundred monks (who had gone to the other shore) returned to this island of Laṅkā, having preserved the Tipitaka with the commentaries in the places they had reached without losing even a single letter or syllable. They entered the Maṇḍalārāma monastery in the Kallagāma district. Hearing of the arrival of those elders, the sixty monks who had remained on this island went to see them, saying, "We shall see the elders." While checking the Tipitaka together with the elders, they did not find even a single letter or syllable that did not match. In that place, this discussion arose among the elders: "Is Pariyatti the root of the Sasana, or is it Patipatti?" The elders who were forest-dwellers (paṃsukūlika) said, "Patipatti is the root." The Dhamma-preachers (dhammakathika) said, "Pariyatti is the root." Then the elders said, "We do not wish to decide based merely on the words of you two parties; bring forth a Sutta spoken by the Conqueror (Jina)." Since bringing forth a Sutta was not a burden, they cited: "And these..."
72:
"Subhadda, if these monks live rightly, the world will not be empty of Arahants" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.214). "Great King, the Dispensation of the Teacher has Patipatti as its root and Patipatti as its essence. As long as Patipatti remains, the Sasana stands" (Milindapañhā 4.1.7). They brought forth these Suttas. Hearing these Suttas, the Dhamma-preachers, in order to establish their own view, brought forth these verses:

"As long as the Suttantas remain, as long as the Vinaya shines,
so long will they see the light, just as when the sun has risen.

When the Suttantas are no more, and the Vinaya is forgotten,
there will be darkness in the world, just as when the sun has set.

When the Suttanta is preserved, the Patipatti is preserved;
the wise one established in Patipatti does not fall away from Yogakkhema (Nibbāna)."

When these verses were brought forth, the Paṃsukūlika elders remained silent; only the words of the Dhammakathika elders stood at the forefront. Just as in the midst of a hundred or a thousand cows, if there is no cow to maintain the lineage, that lineage and succession cannot continue; even so, though there be a hundred or a thousand monks practicing insight (vipassanā), if there is no Pariyatti, there can be no penetration of the Noble Path (ariya-magga). And just as when letters are inscribed on a stone slab to make known the location of a treasure jar, as long as those letters remain, the treasure jar is not considered lost; even so, as long as the Pariyatti remains, the Sasana is not considered to have disappeared.

73:
## 12. Anāpattivagga-vaṇṇanā
In the twelfth chapter, the Anāpattivagga, regarding the terms 'non-offense' (anāpatti), 'offense' (āpatti), and so forth: 'Non-offense' refers to what is stated in various training rules as, 'There is no offense for one who does not know, for one who has no intention to steal, for one who has no intention to kill, for one who has no intention to speak [falsely], and for one who has no intention to release [semen].' 'Offense' refers to what is stated by the method, 'For one who knows, for one who has the intention to steal,' and so forth. The five groups of offenses are called light offenses (lahukāpatti). The two groups of offenses are called heavy offenses (garukāpatti). The two groups of offenses are called gross offenses (duṭṭhullāpatti). The five groups of offenses are called non-gross offenses (aduṭṭhullāpatti). The six groups of offenses are called curable offenses (sāvasesāpatti). The one group of Pārājika offenses is called an incurable offense (anavasesāpatti). A curable offense is indeed a remediable offense (sappaṭikammāpatti). An incurable offense is indeed an irremediable offense (appaṭikammāpatti). The remaining text is clear in all the suttas.

## Anāpattivagga-vaṇṇanā.

## 13. Ekapuggalavagga-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Ekapuggalavagga, 'Ekapuggalo' means a single person. Here, the word 'eka' (one) is a numerical limitation meaning the exclusion of a second and so forth. The word 'puggalo' (person) is conventional talk (sammuti-kathā), not ultimate talk (paramattha-kathā). Indeed, the teaching of the Blessed Buddha is of two kinds: conventional teaching (sammuti-desanā) and ultimate teaching (paramattha-desanā). Among them, the teaching that takes the form of 'person, being, woman, man, king, brahmin, deva, Māra' is called conventional teaching. The teaching that takes the form of 'impermanence, suffering, non-self, aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)' is called ultimate teaching. Between these two, the Blessed One teaches conventional teaching to those beings who, by hearing the teaching through the power of convention, are able to penetrate the meaning, abandon delusion, and attain distinction. However, he teaches ultimate teaching to those beings who, by hearing the teaching through the power of the ultimate, are able to penetrate the meaning, abandon delusion, and attain distinction.

In this regard, there is this analogy: For example, a teacher who is skilled in various dialects and can explain the meaning of the three Vedas teaches in the Tamil language (Damiḷa-bhāsā) to those youths who understand the meaning when spoken in Tamil. To those youths who understand in another language such as the Andhra language (Andha-bhāsā)...
74:
...he speaks to those youths in those respective languages. Thus, those youths, relying on a clever and competent teacher, learn the arts quickly. In this analogy, the Blessed Buddha, the knower of the Four Noble Truths, should be understood as the teacher. The three Pitakas, which stand as that which is to be taught, should be understood as the three Vedas. Skill in conventional and ultimate [teachings] should be understood as skill in dialects. The teachable beings (veneyya-satta) who are capable of penetrating [the truth] through the power of convention and the ultimate should be understood as the youths skilled in various dialects. The Blessed One's teaching through the power of convention and the ultimate should be understood as the teacher's instruction in the Tamil language and so forth. And it has been said in this regard:

'The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, declared two truths:
conventional truth and ultimate truth; a third is not found.

Symbolic speech is true because of worldly convention;
ultimate speech is true because of the actual nature of things.

Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World, who is skilled in usage,
no falsehood arises when he speaks according to convention.'

Furthermore, the Blessed One speaks of 'persons' for eight reasons: for the purpose of showing shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), for the purpose of showing the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā), for the purpose of showing individual human effort (paccatta-purisakāra), for the purpose of showing the immediate [kamma] (ānantariya), for the purpose of showing the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), for the purpose of showing the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa), for the purpose of showing the purity of offerings (dakkhiṇā-visuddhi), and for the purpose of not discarding worldly convention (loka-sammuti). Indeed, if it were said, 'Aggregates, elements, and sense bases feel shame and fear,' the general public would not understand and would fall into confusion; they might even become hostile, asking, 'What is this called aggregates, elements, and sense bases feeling shame and fear?' But if it is said, 'A woman feels shame and fear; a man, a king, a brahmin, a deva, or Māra feels shame and fear,' they understand, do not fall into confusion, and do not become hostile. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of 'persons' for the purpose of showing shame and fear.

Even if it were said, 'Aggregates have kamma as their own; elements and sense bases have kamma as their own,' it would be the same way. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of 'persons' for the purpose of showing the ownership of kamma.

Even if it were said, 'Great monasteries such as Veḷuvana were built by aggregates; they were built by elements and sense bases,' it would be the same way. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of 'persons' for the purpose of showing individual human effort.
75:
Even if it were said, "The aggregates deprive the mother of the life faculty, the father, the Arahant (of the life faculty); they perform the act of shedding the blood of a Buddha and the act of causing a schism in the Saṅgha; the elements and the sense bases (deprive the mother of the life faculty)," the method remains the same. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks the discourse on persons (puggala-kathā) for the purpose of illustrating the heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma).

Even if it were said, "The aggregates produce loving-kindness; the elements and the sense bases (produce loving-kindness)," the method remains the same. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks the discourse on persons for the purpose of illustrating the sublime abodes (brahmavihāra).

Even if it were said, "The aggregates recollect the aggregates lived in the past; the elements and the sense bases (recollect the aggregates lived in the past)," the method remains the same. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks the discourse on persons for the purpose of illustrating the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa).

If it were said, "The aggregates receive offerings; the elements and the sense bases (receive offerings)," the masses would not understand and would fall into great confusion, becoming antagonistic, thinking, "How can these aggregates, elements, and sense bases be said to receive?" However, when it is said, "Persons who are virtuous and of good character receive offerings," they understand, do not fall into great confusion, and do not become antagonistic. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks the discourse on persons for the purpose of illustrating the purity of offerings (dakkhiṇāvisuddhi).

Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not abandon worldly convention (lokasammuti); they teach the Dhamma while standing firm in worldly designations, worldly language, and worldly expressions. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks the discourse on persons also for the purpose of not discarding worldly convention.

Thus, he is 'one' and he is a 'person,' hence he is called a 'Unique Person' (ekapuggala). In what sense is he a Unique Person? He is a Unique Person in the sense of being incomparable, in the sense of being distinguished by virtues, and in the sense of being equal to the unequal (the previous Buddhas).

Indeed, that Blessed One, starting from the reflection on the sequence of the ten perfections (pāramī), is incomparable to the rest of the masses due to the virtues of the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) and the virtues of a Buddha; thus, he is a Unique Person also in the sense of being incomparable. Whatever virtues he possesses, those virtues are superior to the virtues of other beings; thus, he is a Unique Person also in the sense of being distinguished by virtues. The previous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas were unequal to all beings; this Buddha alone is equal to them in terms of the virtues of the form-body (rūpakāya) and the virtues of the mental-body (nāmakāya); thus, he is a Unique Person also in the sense of being equal to the unequal.

In the word 'world' (loka), there are three worlds: the world of beings (sattaloka), the world of space (okāsaloka), and the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). The detailed explanation of these three worlds is stated in the Visuddhimagga. Among these three, the world of beings is intended here. Even when arising in the world of beings, he does not arise in the deva world, nor in the brahma world; he arises only in the human world.
76:
Even in the human world, he does not arise in another universe (cakkavāḷa), but only in this universe. Even in this universe, he does not arise in all places.

"In the eastern direction, there is a market town named Gajaṅgala; beyond it is Mahāsālā (a large sal tree); beyond that are the border regions (paccantariṭṭha), and on this side is the Middle Country (majjhimadesa). In the south-eastern direction is the river named Sallavatī; beyond it are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country. In the southern direction is the market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond it are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country. In the western direction is the brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond it are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country. In the northern direction is the mountain named Usīraddhaja; beyond it are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country" (Mahāvagga, 259). Thus defined, he arises in the Middle Country, which is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. It is not only the Tathāgata who arises in the Middle Country; Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Elders, the Buddha's mother, the Buddha's father, Universal Monarchs, and other brahmins and householders who have reached special excellence also arise only in this Middle Country.

The phrase "uppajjamāno uppajjati" (one who is arising, arises) refers to an action that is not yet completed. Here, the meaning should be understood as: he arises for the welfare and benefit of the many, and for no other reason. Such a grammatical characteristic cannot be refuted by any other grammatical rule.

Furthermore, the distinction between 'one who is arising' (uppajjamāno), 'arises' (uppajjati), and 'has arisen' (uppanno) should be understood. Indeed, this Bodhisatta, having received the prophecy at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, searching for the qualities that make one a Buddha (budhhakāraka-dhamma), seeing the ten perfections and making the resolution, "I must fulfill these qualities," is called 'one who is arising' (uppajjamāno) even while fulfilling the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī). While fulfilling these ten perfections from the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī) up to the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī), while fulfilling the ten minor perfections (upapāramī), and while fulfilling the ten ultimate perfections (paramattha-pāramī), he is called 'one who is arising.' While sacrificing the five great renunciations (mahāpariccāga), while fulfilling the conduct for one's own benefit (attattha-cariyā), conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariyā), and conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariyā), he is called 'one who is arising.' While bringing the qualities that make one a Buddha to the summit throughout four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand cycles, he is called 'one who is arising.' As King Vessantara...
77:
Having passed away from the state of King Vessantara and taking rebirth in the Tusita heaven, even while remaining there for five hundred and seventy-six million years, he is called 'one who is arising' (uppajjamāna). When requested by the deities, having made the five great observations (pañcamahāvilokita) and taking rebirth in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā, or while dwelling in the mother's womb for exactly ten months, he is called 'one who is arising.' While living in the household life for twenty-nine years, he is called 'one who is arising.' Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefits in renunciation, and departing on the day Prince Rāhula was born, with the minister Channa as his companion, riding the noble horse Kanthaka, he is still called 'one who is arising.' Even while crossing three kingdoms or ordaining on the banks of the Anomā River, he is called 'one who is arising.' While performing the great exertion for six years, he is called 'one who is arising.' When his knowledge matured and he partook of gross food, he is still called 'one who is arising.'

On the evening of the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), having ascended the seat of the Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa), defeated the army of Māra, attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa) in the first watch, purified the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) in the middle watch, and immediately after the last watch, contemplated the twelve-linked Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in forward and reverse order and penetrated the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), he is still called 'one who is arising.' At the moments of the Fruition of Stream-entry, the Path of Once-returning, the Fruition of Once-returning, the Path of Non-returning, and the Fruition of Non-returning, he is still called 'one who is arising.' However, at the moment of the Path of Arahatship, he is said to be 'arising' (uppajjati). At the moment of the Fruition of Arahatship, he is said to have 'arisen' (uppanna). The reason is that for the Buddhas, unlike for the disciples, the knowledges such as the supernormal powers (iddhividhañāṇa) do not arise sequentially; rather, the entire mass of qualities such as Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) arrives simultaneously with the Path of Arahatship. Therefore, because those Buddhas have completed all tasks, they are called 'those who have arisen' at the moment of the Fruition of Arahatship. In this discourse as well, referring only to the moment of the Fruition of Arahatship, it should be understood as 'arising' (uppajjati); 'he has become one who has arisen' is the meaning here.

'For the welfare of many' (bahujanahitāya) means he arises for the benefit of the great multitude. 'For the happiness of many' (bahujanasukhāya) means he arises for the happiness of the great multitude. 'Out of compassion for the world' (lokānukampāya) means he arises based on compassion for the world of beings. What kind of world of beings is meant? It refers to the world of beings who, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata and drunk the beverage of the Deathless Nibbāna, penetrate the Four Noble Truths. This is because the Blessed One, after spending seven weeks at the seat of the Great Enlightenment, went from the Bodhi tree to the Deer Park and said, 'Monks, these two extremes should not be [followed] by one who has gone forth...'
78: '...should not be followed,' when this was taught in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, eighteen crores of Brahmas along with the Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña drank the beverage of the Deathless. He has arisen out of compassion for this world of beings. On the fifth day, at the conclusion of the teaching of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, the group of five elder monks were established in the Fruit of Arahatship. He has arisen out of compassion for this world of beings as well. Thereafter, he established fifty-five men, headed by the youth Yasa, in the Fruit of Arahatship. Thereafter, in the Kappāsika grove, he caused thirty Bhaddavaggiya princes to attain the three paths and the three fruits. He has arisen out of compassion for this world of beings as well. At the conclusion of the teaching of the Ādittapariyāya Sutta at Gayāsīsa, he established a thousand ascetics in the Fruit of Arahatship. In the Laṭṭhivana (Palm Grove), one hundred and ten thousand brahmins and householders, headed by King Bimbisāra, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Teacher, were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry; ten thousand beings were established in the refuges. At the conclusion of the appreciation (anumodanā) with the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, eighty-four thousand beings drank the beverage of the Deathless. At the meeting with Sumana the florist, eighty-four thousand beings; at the meeting with the Dhanapāla elephant, ten thousand beings; when the Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka was taught, eighty-four thousand beings; at the meeting with Jambuka the naked ascetic, eighty-four thousand beings; and at the meeting with the wealthy man Ananda, eighty-four thousand beings drank the beverage of the Deathless. On the day the Pārāyana Sutta was taught at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine, fourteen crores of beings drank the beverage of the Deathless. On the day he performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), twenty crores of beings; while sitting on the Pandukambala yellow stone throne in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and making the deity Santussita (who had been his mother) the witness to the mental body (nāmakāya) to receive the Dhamma teaching, when he taught the Abhidhamma consisting of seven books, eighty crores of beings; on the day he descended from the celestial realm, thirty crores of beings; and on the day the Sakkapañha Sutta was taught, eighty thousand deities drank the beverage of the Deathless. In these four instances—the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Maṅgala Sutta, the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, and the Samacittapaṭipadā Sutta—there is no limit to the beings who attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths. He has arisen out of compassion for this world of beings as well. This meaning should also be understood by way of the beings who, up to this day and in the future, rely on the Dispensation (Sāsana) and are established on the path to heaven and liberation. 'Devamanussānaṃ' means he has arisen not only for the sake of devas and humans, but also for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the remaining beings such as nagas and garudas. Of those with triple-rooted rebirth (sahaituka-paṭisandhika)...
79:
However, this was spoken (regarding devas and humans) to show those persons who are capable of realizing the Path and Fruition by the power of their rebirth with three roots (tihetu-paṭisandhi). Therefore, it should be understood that he appeared for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of even those Nāgas, Garuḷas, and so forth. 

'Who is the unique person?'—this statement is a question (pucchā). Such a question is of five kinds: a question to illuminate what is not seen (adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā), a question to compare what is seen (diṭṭhasandandanā-pucchā), a question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā-pucchā), a question for consent (anumati-pucchā), and a question from a desire to explain (kathetukamyatā-pucchā). 

The distinction among these five questions is as follows: 

What is the question to illuminate what is not seen? By nature, a characteristic is not known, not seen by wisdom, not weighed, not investigated, not manifested, and not developed. One asks a question for the purpose of knowing, seeing with wisdom, weighing, investigating, manifesting, and clearly developing that characteristic; this is called a question to illuminate what is not seen. 

What is the question to compare what is seen? By nature, a characteristic is known, seen by wisdom, weighed, investigated, manifested, and clearly developed. That person asks a question for the purpose of comparing it with other wise people; this is called a question to compare what is seen. 

What is the question to cut off doubt? By nature, one has fallen into doubt and uncertainty, being of two minds, thinking, 'Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? In what way?' That person asks a question for the purpose of cutting off doubt; this is called a question to cut off doubt. 

What is the question for consent? The Blessed One asks a question to seek the consent of the bhikkhus: 'What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?' 'Impermanent, Bhante.' 'Is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?' 'Suffering, Bhante.' 'Is it fit to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as "This is mine, this I am, this is my self"?' 'No, Bhante.' This is called a question for consent. 

What is the question from a desire to explain? The Blessed One asks a question from a desire to explain to the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four?' This is called a question from a desire to explain. 

Among those five, the first three types of questions do not exist for the Buddhas. Why? Because for the Buddhas, in the three periods of time, there is no conditioned thing (saṅkhata) or unconditioned thing (asaṅkhata) which is beyond time that is not seen, not known, not weighed, not investigated, not manifested, or not clearly developed. Therefore, the question to illuminate what is not seen does not exist for the Buddhas. Regarding the Dhamma that the Blessed One has penetrated with his own knowledge, there is no need for the task of comparing it with another recluse, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā...
80:
...there is no task of comparison (with Māra or Brahmā). Therefore, for the Blessed One, there is no question to compare what is seen (diṭṭhasandandanā-pucchā). Since this Blessed One is free from perplexity, has crossed over doubt, and has removed doubt in all dhammas, there is no question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā-pucchā) for him. However, the other two types of questions exist for the Blessed One; among them, this current question should be understood as a question from a desire to explain (kathetukamyatā-pucchā). 

Now, manifesting the 'unique person' who is the subject of that question, he said: 'The Tathāgata, the Arahat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.' In that phrase, the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata' for eight reasons: 
(1) He is called Tathāgata because he has come (āgato) in the same way (tathā) as the previous Buddhas. 
(2) He is called Tathāgata because he has gone (gato) in the same way (tathā). 
(3) He is called Tathāgata because he has arrived at the true characteristics (tatha-lakkhaṇaṃ). 
(4) He is called Tathāgata because he has awakened to the true dhammas (tatha-dhamme) as they really are. 
(5) He is called Tathāgata because of seeing truly (tatha-dassitāya). 
(6) He is called Tathāgata because of speaking truly (tatha-vāditāya). 
(7) He is called Tathāgata because of acting according to his word (tatha-kāritāya). 
(8) He is called Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming (abhibhavanaṭṭhena). 

How is the Blessed One called Tathāgata because he has come in the same way as the previous Buddhas? Just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones who were devoted to the welfare of the whole world came—such as the Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed One Kassapa. 

What is meant? In whatever way of aspiration (abhinīhāra) those Blessed Ones came, in that same way our Blessed One also came. Alternatively, just as the Blessed One Vipassī... up to... the Blessed One Kassapa, having fulfilled the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), and the perfections of virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—thus fulfilling the thirty perfections consisting of the ten perfections, the ten intermediate perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections; having sacrificed the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga) such as the sacrifice of limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, and children and wife; having fulfilled the previous efforts (pubbayoga), previous conduct (pubbacariya), the teaching of Dhamma (dhammakkhāna), acting for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariya), and so forth, and having reached the pinnacle of the conduct for enlightenment (buddhi-cariyā), they came; in that same way our Blessed One also came. And just as the Blessed One Vipassī... up to... the Blessed One Kassapa came after developing and increasing the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path; in that same way our Blessed One also came, and thus he is called 'Tathāgata'.
81:
“Just as the Buddhas such as Vipassī came to the state of omniscience in this world, so too has our Blessed One, the Sage of the Sakyans, come. Therefore, the Visionary One is called ‘Tathāgata’ (Thus-come).”

In this way, because he has come in that same manner, he is called ‘Tathāgata’.

How is he called ‘Tathāgata’ because he has gone in that same manner? Just as the Blessed One Vipassī, when newly born, went... just as the Blessed One Kassapa went (so too did our Buddha go). And how did he go? Indeed, as soon as he was born, he stood on the earth with level feet and, facing the north, went with a stride of seven steps.

The Buddha taught this: “Ānanda, as soon as the Bodhisatta is born, he stands on the earth with level feet and, facing the north, goes with a stride of seven steps. While a white umbrella is held over him, he surveys all directions and utters the noble words: ‘I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world. This is my last birth; now there is no more rebirth.’”

That going of his was true (tatha) and unerring, as it was a precursor to the attainment of many special qualities. The fact that he stood on the earth with level feet as soon as he was born was the precursor to his obtaining the four bases of power (iddhipāda). His facing the north was the precursor to his attainment of all supramundane (lokuttara) states. The stride of seven steps was the precursor to his obtaining the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). The fanning of the fly-whisks, mentioned in the phrase ‘fly-whisks with golden handles are waved,’ was the precursor to his crushing of all sectarians. The holding of the white umbrella was the precursor to his obtaining the noble and stainless white umbrella of liberation, which is the fruit of Arahantship. His surveying of all directions was the precursor to his obtaining the unimpeded knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). His uttering of the noble words was the precursor to his turning of the noble Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka), which cannot be turned back by others.

In that same manner, this Blessed One also went. And that going of his was true as a precursor to the attainment of those very special qualities. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

“Just as the Lord of the World (Gavampati), born but a moment ago,
Touch the earth with level feet,
That Gotama strode seven steps,
And the gods held the white umbrella.”
82:
“Having gone those seven steps, that Gotama
Surveyed the directions which appeared equal on all sides;
He uttered a voice endowed with eight qualities,
Like a lion standing on a mountain peak.”

In this way, because he has gone in that same manner, he is called ‘Tathāgata’.

Alternatively, just as the Blessed One Vipassī... just as the Blessed One Kassapa went, this Blessed One also went in that very same way, having abandoned sensual desire (kāmacchanda) through renunciation (nekkhamma). He went having abandoned ill will (byāpāda) through non-ill will (abyāpāda), sloth and torpor (thina-middha) through the perception of light (āloka-saññā), restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) through non-distraction, and doubt (vicikicchā) through the definition of phenomena (dhamma-vavatthāna). He went having pierced through ignorance (avijjā) with knowledge (ñāṇa), and having dispelled discontent (arati) with joy (pāmojja). He went having opened the door of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) with the first jhāna, having stilled applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) with the second jhāna, having faded away rapture (pīti) with the third jhāna, and having abandoned pleasure and pain (sukha-dukkha) with the fourth jhāna. He went having transcended the perception of form, the perception of sensory impact, and the perception of diversity through the attainment of the sphere of infinite space; having transcended the perception of the sphere of infinite space through the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness; having transcended the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness through the attainment of the sphere of nothingness; and having transcended the perception of the sphere of nothingness through the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

He went having abandoned the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), delight through the contemplation of revulsion (nibbidā), lust through the contemplation of fading away (virāga), origination through the contemplation of cessation (nirodha), grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissagga), the perception of compactness (ghana-saññā) through the contemplation of destruction (khaya), accumulation through the contemplation of vanishing (vaya), the perception of stability through the contemplation of change, the perception of a sign (nimitta) through the contemplation of the signless (animitta), longing through the contemplation of the desireless (appaṇihita), wrong adherence through the contemplation of emptiness (suññata), the adherence to a core through the contemplation of insight into phenomena with higher wisdom (adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā), the adherence to delusion through the knowledge and vision of things as they are (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana), the adherence to attachment through the contemplation of danger (ādīnava), non-reflection through the contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhā), and the adherence to fetters through the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭa). He went having broken the defilements associated with wrong view through the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), having abandoned coarse defilements through the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga), having uprooted subtle defilements through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga), and having completely cut off all defilements through the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). In this way also, because he has gone in that same manner, he is called ‘Tathāgata’.
83:
In what way is he the Tathāgata because he has arrived at the true characteristics? The characteristic of hardness of the earth element is true and unerring. The characteristic of flowing of the water element, the characteristic of heat of the fire element, the characteristic of supporting (distension) of the air element, the characteristic of non-contact of the space element, and the characteristic of cognizing of the consciousness element are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of deformation of matter (rūpa), the characteristic of experiencing the flavor of the object of feeling (vedanā), the characteristic of perceiving the object of perception (saññā), the characteristic of constructing and conditioning of mental formations (saṅkhāra), and the characteristic of cognizing the object of consciousness (viññāṇa) are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of directing associated states towards the object of initial application (vitakka), the characteristic of repeatedly examining the object of sustained application (vicāra), the characteristic of pervading the object of joy (pīti), the characteristic of making the object pleasant of happiness (sukha), the characteristic of non-distraction in the object of one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā), and the characteristic of touching the object of contact (phassa) are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of resolution towards the object of the faith faculty (saddhindriya), the characteristic of upholding associated states of the energy faculty (vīriyindriya), the characteristic of establishing presence in the object of the mindfulness faculty (satindriya), the characteristic of non-distraction in the object of the concentration faculty (samādhindriya), and the characteristic of understanding the object in various ways of the wisdom faculty (paññindriya) are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of unshakability by the unwholesome state of faithlessness of the faith power (saddhābala), the characteristic of unshakability by laziness of the energy power (vīriyabala), by forgetfulness of the mindfulness power (satibala), by agitation of the concentration power (samādhibala), and by ignorance of the wisdom power (paññābala) are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of establishing presence in the object of the mindfulness enlightenment factor (satisambojjhaṅga), the characteristic of investigating the four Noble Truths of the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga), the characteristic of upholding associated states of the energy enlightenment factor (vīriyasambojjhaṅga), the characteristic of delighting in the object of the joy enlightenment factor (pītisambojjhaṅga), the characteristic of calming the fever of body and mind of the tranquility enlightenment factor (passaddhisambojjhaṅga), the characteristic of non-distraction in the object of the concentration enlightenment factor (samādhisambojjhaṅga), and the characteristic of reflecting with equanimity without exertion of the equanimity enlightenment factor (upekkhāsambojjhaṅga) are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of seeing Nibbāna of Right View (sammādiṭṭhi), the characteristic of directing associated states towards the object of Right Thought (sammāsaṅkappa), the characteristic of embracing associated states and the listener of good speech of Right Speech (sammāvācā), the characteristic of originating good actions of Right Action (sammākammanta), the characteristic of purification of the maintenance of the life faculty of Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva), the characteristic of upholding associated states of Right Effort (sammāvāyāma), the characteristic of establishing presence in the object of Right Mindfulness (sammāsati), and the characteristic of non-distraction in the object of Right Concentration (sammāsamādhi) are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of unknowing of ignorance (avijjā), the characteristic of volition of formations (saṅkhāra), the characteristic of cognizing the object of consciousness (viññāṇa), the characteristic of bending towards the object of name (nāma), the characteristic of deformation of matter (rūpa), the characteristic of the gathering of the bases of the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), the characteristic of touching the object of contact (phassa), the characteristic of experiencing the object of feeling (vedanā), the characteristic of being the cause of the round of rebirth of craving (taṇhā), the characteristic of grasping the object of clinging (upādāna), the characteristic of striving of existence (bhava), the characteristic of arising of birth (jāti), the characteristic of decaying of aging (jarā), and the characteristic of passing away of death (maraṇa) are also true and unerring.
84:
The characteristic of emptiness from a self or a being of the elements (dhātu), the characteristic of the gathering of the bases of the sense bases (āyatana), the characteristic of establishing presence in the object of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the characteristic of upholding associated states of the right efforts (sammappadhāna), the characteristic of accomplishment of the bases of power (iddhipāda), the characteristic of predominance of the faculties (indriya), the characteristic of unshakability of the powers (bala), the characteristic of leading out from the suffering of the round of rebirth of the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga), and the characteristic of being the cause of Nibbāna of the path (magga) are true and unerring.

The characteristic of truth of the truths (sacca), the characteristic of non-distraction of calm (samatha), the characteristic of repeated contemplation of insight (vipassanā), the characteristic of having a single function, namely the non-overtaking of each other, of calm and insight (samatha-vipassanā), and the characteristic of non-overtaking of each other of the yoked calm and insight (yuganaddha) are true and unerring.
