The characteristic of guarding of the purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi), the characteristic of non-distraction of the purification of mind (cittavisuddhi), and the characteristic of seeing the cause of mind and matter of the purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi) are true and unerring.

The characteristic of the absolute cutting off of defilements of the knowledge of the path of Arahatship (arahattamagga-ñāṇa) occurring at the destruction of defilements, and the characteristic of the calming of defilements of the knowledge of the fruition of Arahatship (arahattaphala-ñāṇa) occurring at the end of the non-arising of defilements are true and unerring.

The characteristic of being the basis of desire (chanda), the characteristic of being the cause of the arising of associated states of attention (manasikāra), the characteristic of meeting of contact (phassa), the characteristic of being the convergence of associated states of feeling (vedanā), the characteristic of being the leadership of associated states of concentration (samādhi), the characteristic of being the predominance of mindfulness (sati), the characteristic of being the supremacy over those associated states of wisdom (paññā), the characteristic of being the excellence by way of attributes such as virtue of the fruition of Arahatship (arahattaphala), and the characteristic of being the consummation of Nibbāna which is plunged into the deathless are true and unerring. Thus, he has arrived at the true characteristics through the arrival of knowledge; he has reached and attained them without fail, therefore he is the "Tathāgata." Thus, because he has arrived at the true characteristics, he is the "Tathāgata."

In what way is he the Tathāgata because he has fully awakened to the true dhammas as they really are? The true dhammas are the four Noble Truths. As it was said: "Bhikkhus, these four are true, unerring, and not otherwise. Which four? 'This is suffering,' bhikkhus, this is true, this is unerring, this is not otherwise," and so on, as preached in detail. The Blessed One has fully awakened to those truths; therefore, because of his full awakening to the truths, he is called the "Tathāgata." For here, the word "gata" has the meaning of full awakening (abhisambodha).

Furthermore, the nature of the arising of aging and death due to the cause of birth is true, unerring, and not otherwise... [pe]... the nature of the arising of formations due to the cause of ignorance is true, unerring, and not otherwise. Likewise, the nature of ignorance being the cause for formations, formations being the cause for consciousness... [pe]... birth being the cause for aging and death is true, unerring, and not otherwise. The Blessed One has fully awakened to all of that.
85:
The nature of formations arising due to the cause of ignorance, and their subsequent arising according to their causes, is true, unerring, and not otherwise. Likewise, the nature of ignorance being a condition for formations, the nature of formations being a condition for consciousness, and so on, up to the nature of birth being a condition for aging and death, is true, unerring, and not otherwise. The Blessed One has penetrated and realized all these causal natures of ignorance, formations, and so forth. Because He has thus penetrated and realized these true causal natures, He is called the 'Tathāgata'. Thus, He is the Tathāgata because He has penetrated and realized the true dhammas as they truly are.

In what way is He the Tathāgata because of His seeing things as they truly are (tathadassitā)? In the world with its devas... among the multitude of humans including conventional gods (kings), the Blessed One knows and sees in every aspect whatever visible object comes into the range of the eye-door of the immeasurable beings in the immeasurable world systems. Knowing and seeing thus, whether by way of the desirable or undesirable nature of that visible object, or by way of the terms found among the 'seen, heard, sensed, and cognized', He analyzes it: 'What is that form which is the form-base? That form which, depending on the four great essentials, is possessed of color and brightness, is visible and impinging, blue, yellow, etc.' By such methods, through many names, through thirteen turns (vāra), and through fifty-two methods, that form as analyzed is exactly as it is, and not otherwise. This same principle applies to sounds and so forth that come into the range of the ear-door and other sense bases. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... in the world of beings, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and pondered by the mind, that I know; that I have fully understood. That is known to the Tathāgata, but the Tathāgata does not abide supported by it.' Thus, He is the Tathāgata because of His seeing things as they truly are. In this context, the derivation of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood in the sense of 'seeing truly' (tathadassī).

In what way is He the Tathāgata because of His speaking truly (tathavāditā)? From the night the Blessed One sat on the unconquered throne at the terrace of enlightenment and fully realized the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, having crushed the heads of the three Māras, until the night He attained final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue between the twin Sāla trees—during this interval of forty-five years, whatever the Blessed One spoke, whether Sutta, Geyya... or Vedalla, all of it is beyond reproach in both meaning and phrasing. It is neither deficient nor redundant, but perfect in every aspect. It crushes the intoxication of lust, hatred, and delusion. In that teaching, there is not even a hair's breadth of deviation. All of it is as if stamped with a single seal, as if measured with a single measure, or as if weighed with a single balance—it is exactly true and not otherwise. Therefore, He said: 'Cunda, on the night the Tathāgata fully realizes the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and on the night He attains final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue, in this interval...'
86:
(The Tathāgata) speaks, declares, and points out; all that speech is exactly so and not otherwise. Therefore, He is called the 'Tathāgata'. In this context, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'gada' (speech). Thus, He is the Tathāgata because of His speaking truly.

Furthermore, 'āgada' means 'speaking', which has the sense of 'vacana' (speech). Because the Blessed One has speech that is true and not otherwise, by changing the letter 'd' to 't', the word 'Tathāgata' is formed; thus should the derivation of the word be understood in this sense.

In what way is He the Tathāgata because of His acting according to His speech (tathākāritā)? The Blessed One's bodily actions conform to His speech, and His speech conforms to His bodily actions. Therefore, as He speaks, so He acts; as He acts, so He speaks. For the Blessed One who is thus, as His speech is, so His body 'goes' (gata), meaning it proceeds. And as His body is, so His speech 'goes'. Therefore, He is the Tathāgata. For this very reason, He said: 'Bhikkhus, as the Tathāgata speaks, so He acts; as He acts, so He speaks. Since He acts as He speaks and speaks as He acts, He is called the Tathāgata.' Thus, He is the Tathāgata because of His acting according to His speech.

In what way is He the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming (abhibhavana)? From the peak of existence above to the Avīci hell below, and across the immeasurable world systems, He overcomes all beings by virtue, by concentration, by wisdom, and by liberation. There is no one equal to Him or comparable to Him. He is peerless, immeasurable, the unsurpassed King of kings, God of gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, and the Brahmā beyond Brahmās. Therefore, He said: 'Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... in the world of beings with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the overcomer, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power. Therefore, He is called the Tathāgata.'

In that sense (of overcoming), the derivation of the word should be understood as follows: He is like 'agada' (medicine). What is it that is like medicine? It is the grace of His teaching and the abundance of His merit. With that teaching-grace and abundance of merit, which are like medicine, the Great Physician of great power overcomes all those of other views and the world with its devas, just as one overcomes snakes with divine medicine. Thus, in overcoming the entire world, He possesses the medicine (agada) of unerring teaching-grace and abundance of merit; by changing the letter 'd' to 't', He is to be known as the 'Tathāgata'. Thus, He is the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.
87:
In another way, he is called 'Tathāgata' because he has known things according to their true nature (tathā). He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has reached Nibbāna, which is unfailing (tathā). The word 'gata' means knowing, transcending, reaching, and practicing. In this term 'Tathāgata', he is called 'Tathāgata' because he has penetrated and known the entire world through the unfailing full understanding of investigation (tīraṇapariññā). He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has transcended the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca), the cause of the world, through the unfailing full understanding of abandoning (pahānapariññā). He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has reached Nibbāna, the cessation of the world, through the unfailing realization (sacchikiriyā). He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has practiced the path leading to Nibbāna, the cessation of the world, in an unfailing manner.

Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is detached from the world. Monks, the origin of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Monks, the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. Monks, the path leading to the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata. Monks, whatever in the world with its devas... all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata. Therefore, he is called 'Tathāgata'." (A. Ni. 4.23).

The meaning of the term 'Tathāgata' should be understood in this way as well. This explanation is merely a brief indication of the Tathāgata's nature as a Tathāgata. In every respect, however, only a Tathāgata could praise and explain the Tathāgata's nature as a Tathāgata.

Regarding the two terms 'Arahaṃ Sammāsambuddho': first, he should be known as 'Arahaṃ' because he is remote from defilements, because he has destroyed the enemies (defilements) and the spokes of the wheel of existence, because he is worthy of requisites and so on, and because he has no secrecy in doing evil. He is called 'Sammāsambuddho' because he has rightly and by himself awakened to all dhammas. This is a brief explanation here. In detail, these two terms have been explained in the Visuddhimagga, in the commentary on the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati).

In the second sutta, 'pātubhāvo' means arising through rebirth and attaining the state of an Ariya. 'Dullabho lokesmiṃ' (rare in the world) means extremely rare, exceedingly rare, and supremely rare in this world of beings. Why is he rare? Because one cannot become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī) just once, or twice, or ten times, or twenty times, or fifty times, or a hundred times, or a thousand times, or a hundred thousand times, or even a hundred thousand crores of times...
88:
...it is not possible to become a Buddha. Likewise, it is not possible to become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfection of generosity for one day, two days, ten days, twenty days, fifty days, a hundred days, a thousand days, a hundred thousand days, or a hundred thousand crores of days. For one month, two months... a hundred thousand crores of months. For one year, two years... a hundred thousand crores of years. For one aeon (kappa), two aeons... a hundred thousand crores of aeons. It is not possible to become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfection of generosity for one incalculable (asaṅkheyya), two incalculables, or three incalculables of aeons. The same method applies to the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī), the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī)... and the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī). At the very least, one can become a Buddha only after fulfilling the ten perfections for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. For this reason, the Blessed One is very rare in the world.

In the third sutta, 'acchariya-manusso' means a wonderful man. 'Acchariya' means something that does not happen constantly, just as a blind man's climbing of a mountain is not a regular occurrence. This is the grammatical method. According to the method of the commentaries, however, he is called 'acchariya' because he is worthy of the snapping of fingers (applause); the meaning is that he is worthy of being looked at with a snap of the fingers. Furthermore, he is called 'acchariya-manusso' because he is endowed with many wonderful and marvelous qualities, as stated: "Monks, with the manifestation of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, four wonderful and marvelous things (acchariya abbhuta dhammā) appear" (A. Ni. 4.127), and so forth. He is also called 'acchariya-manusso' because he is a person who practices uncommon virtues.

Indeed, the act of sitting at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree, having combined the eight factors that fulfill the initial resolve (abhinīhāra) and having fixed the mind in the presence of a Buddha, is not the practice of anyone else; it is the practice only of an Omniscient Bodhisatta. Likewise, after receiving the prophecy (byākaraṇa) in the presence of the Buddhas, the fulfillment of the ten perfections that make one a Buddha, by making a firm determination of energy without turning back, is not the practice of anyone else; it is the practice only of an Omniscient Bodhisatta. Likewise, while maturing the perfections and remaining in an existence such as that of King Vessantara, giving the great gift of the 'Seven Hundreds' (Sattasataka Mahādāna)—such as seven hundred elephants and seven hundred horses adorned with all ornaments—and then giving away a son like Prince Jāli, a daughter like Princess Kaṇhājinā, and a wife like Queen Maddī as gifts, and remaining there until the end of his life, and then taking rebirth in the second existence in the Tusita heaven, is not the practice of anyone else; it is the practice only of an Omniscient Bodhisatta. Remaining in the Tusita heaven until the end of his life, accepting the invitation of the devas and Brahmās to become a Buddha, and performing the five great observations (pañcamahāvilokana)...
89:
Mindful and clearly comprehending, passing away from the Tusita heaven and taking conception in a family of great wealth is not the habit of anyone else; it is the habit only of an omniscient Bodhisatta. Furthermore, the shaking of the ten thousand world systems on the day of taking conception; mindful and clearly comprehending, residing in the mother’s womb; mindful and clearly comprehending, the shaking of the ten thousand world systems on the day of being born from the mother’s womb; the newly born Bodhisatta taking seven steps; the holding of the divine white parasol; the raising of the divine yak-tail fan; looking in all directions with the gaze of a lion and, seeing no being equal to himself, uttering a bold lion’s roar: "I am the foremost in the world"; when his knowledge reached maturity, renouncing great wealth and making the Great Renunciation; while sitting on the throne at the Great Bodhi Tree, beginning with the victory over Māra, purifying the super-knowledges of the recollection of past lives and the divine eye, and at the moment of penetrating the mass of qualities of omniscient knowledge at dawn, the shaking of the ten thousand world systems; and in the first teaching, the preaching of the peerless and noble Dhammacakka with its three rounds—all such qualities are not the habit of others, but the habit only of an omniscient Buddha. Because he is practiced in such uncommon qualities, he is called a Wonderful Man (Acchariya-manussa).

In the fourth sutta, 'Kālakiriyā' (passing away) means an action that is manifest at a certain time. To elaborate: the Blessed One, having remained for forty-five years, having proclaimed the three Piṭakas, the five Nikāyas, the nine-fold Dispensation of the Teacher, and the eighty-four thousand units of Dhamma, and having made the multitude of people incline and lean towards Nibbāna, lay down between the twin Sāla trees, addressed the assembly of monks, exhorted them with the teaching of diligence (appamāda), and, being mindful and clearly comprehending, attained Parinibbāna with the Nibbāna element without remainder. This action of the Blessed One remains manifest to this day; therefore, because it is an action manifest at a certain time, it is called 'Kālakiriyā'. 'Anutappā hoti' means it causes remorse or sorrow. In this regard, the death of a Cakkavatti King causes sorrow to the devas and humans within one world system. The Parinibbāna of the Buddhas causes sorrow to the devas and humans in ten thousand world systems. Therefore, it is said: "It causes sorrow to many people."

In the fifth sutta, 'Adutiyo' means peerless because there is no second Buddha. To elaborate, there are four kinds of Buddhas: Suta-buddha, Catusacca-buddha, Pacceka-buddha, and Sabbaññu-buddha. Among these four, a monk of great learning is called a Suta-buddha. An Arahant is called a Catusacca-buddha. One who fulfills the perfections for two incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand cycles...
90:
...one who fulfills the perfections for two incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand cycles and personally penetrates the knowledge of Pacceka-enlightenment is called a Pacceka-buddha. One who fulfills the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand cycles, crushes the heads of the three Māras, and penetrates the knowledge of omniscience is called a Sabbaññu-buddha (Omniscient Buddha). Among these four types of Buddhas, only the Sabbaññu-buddha is called 'Adutiyo' (the Peerless). This is because no other omniscient Buddha arises together with that omniscient Buddha.

'Asahāyo' means he is without a companion because there is no companion equal to him, whether in terms of his physical form (attabhāva) or the Dhamma he has penetrated. However, by the method of the statement, "Indeed, that Blessed One is the companion obtained by those in training (sekhas)," those in training and those beyond training (asekhas) are called companions of the Buddhas. 'Appaṭimo' means the physical form is called 'paṭimā' (image/likeness), and since there is no other physical form equal to the physical form of that Blessed One, he is 'Appaṭima' (Incomparable). Even in the images (paṭimā) that humans make of gold, silver, etc., there is no one capable of making even a space the size of the tip of a hair equal to the physical form of the Tathāgata; thus, he is 'Appaṭima' in every way.

'Appaṭisamo' means there is no one equal to that Blessed One in terms of physical form. 'Appaṭibhāgo' means that in the teachings the Blessed One has taught, such as the "Four Foundations of Mindfulness," there is no one capable of creating a counterpart by saying, "There are not four foundations of mindfulness, but three or five." 'Appaṭipuggalo' means there is no other person capable of making the claim, "I am a Buddha." 'Asamo' means he is unequal to all beings simply because there is no person who is his match. 'Asamasamo' means the omniscient Buddhas of the past and future are called 'Asama' (the Unequalled), and because he is equal to those who are unequalled, he is 'Asamasamo' (Equal to the Unequalled).

'Dvipadānaṃ aggo' means the Fully Enlightened One is indeed the foremost among beings—whether footless, bipeds, quadrupeds, many-footed, with form, without form, with perception, without perception, or with neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Why is it said here that he is the foremost among bipeds? It is spoken by way of being the most excellent. Indeed, when a Great Being arises in this world, he does not arise among the footless, quadrupeds, or many-footed; he arises only among bipeds. Among which bipeds? He arises among humans and devas. When he arises among humans, in order to bring the hundred thousand crores of world systems under his influence...
91:
(When born among humans,) he arises as a Buddha capable of making a hundred thousand crores of world systems follow his will. When born among devas and brahmas, he arises as a Great Brahma (Mahābrahmā) capable of making ten thousand world systems follow his will. That Great Brahma becomes one who performs suitable duties or a park-keeper for that Blessed One. Thus, because he is even more noble than that Great Brahma, that Blessed One is called the supreme among bipeds (two-footed beings).

## 175-186. In the Sixth Sutta and others, "Monks, with the appearance of one person, the appearance of the Great Eye occurs" means, monks, with the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is the unique person, the appearance of the great eye of wisdom occurs. When that Blessed One appears, that eye of wisdom indeed appears; it does not appear without his appearance. Appearance (pātubhāva) means the first arising and the subsequent manifestation. What kind of eye is it? It is the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu). What is its nature? It is the eye of wisdom similar to the insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) of the Elder Sāriputta and similar to the wisdom associated with concentration (samādhi-paññā) of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. The same method applies to light (āloka) and so forth. Indeed, in this context, the light similar to the light of wisdom of the two Chief Disciples and the radiance similar to the radiance of wisdom are intended. It should be understood that these three suttas—"the Great Eye, the Great Light, the Great Radiance"—are taught as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

"Six Unsurpassable things" (channaṃ anuttariyānaṃ) refers to the appearance of the six supreme dhammas, than which there is nothing higher. Those six are: Unsurpassable Seeing (dassanānuttariya), Unsurpassable Hearing (savanānuttariya), Unsurpassable Gain (lābhānuttariya), Unsurpassable Training (sikkhānuttariya), Unsurpassable Service (pāricariyānuttariya), and Unsurpassable Recollection (anussatānuttariya). It means the appearance of these six unsurpassable things occurs. The Elder Ānanda, in the evening and morning, gets the opportunity to see the Tathāgata with eye-consciousness; this is called Unsurpassable Seeing. Other Stream-enterers, Once-returners, or Non-returners, like the Elder Ānanda, also get the opportunity to see the Tathāgata; this too is called Unsurpassable Seeing. Furthermore, another good worldling (puthujjana-kalyāṇaka), like the Elder Ānanda, gets the opportunity to see the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala), and by developing that seeing, reaches the Path of Stream-entry. This is merely called seeing (dassana), but the original seeing is called Unsurpassable Seeing.

The Elder Ānanda himself frequently gets the opportunity to hear the words of the One of Ten Powers with ear-consciousness; this is called Unsurpassable Hearing. Other Stream-enterers and so forth, like the Elder Ānanda, also get the opportunity to hear the words of the Tathāgata; this too is called Unsurpassable Hearing. Another good worldling, like the Elder Ānanda...
92:
(A good worldling) gets the opportunity to hear the words of the Blessed One, and by developing that hearing, reaches the Path of Stream-entry. Such attainment is merely called hearing (savana), but the original hearing is called Unsurpassable Hearing.

The Elder Ānanda himself obtains faith in the One of Ten Powers; this obtaining is called Unsurpassable Gain (lābhānuttariya). Other Stream-enterers and so forth, like the Elder Ānanda, also obtain faith in the One of Ten Powers; this obtaining is also called Unsurpassable Gain. Furthermore, another good worldling, like the Elder Ānanda, obtains faith in the One of Ten Powers, and by developing that gain, reaches the Path of Stream-entry; this is merely called gain (lābha), but the original gain is called Unsurpassable Gain.

The Elder Ānanda himself practices the three trainings in the Dispensation of the One of Ten Powers; this practice is called Unsurpassable Training (sikkhānuttariya). Other Stream-enterers and so forth, like the Elder Ānanda, also practice the three trainings in the Dispensation of the One of Ten Powers; this practice is also called Unsurpassable Training. Furthermore, another good worldling, like the Elder Ānanda, practices the three trainings in the Dispensation of the One of Ten Powers, and by developing those trainings, reaches the Path of Stream-entry; this is merely called training (sikkhā), but the original training is called Unsurpassable Training.

The Elder Ānanda himself constantly serves the One of Ten Powers; this service is called Unsurpassable Service (pāricariyānuttariya). Other Stream-enterers and so forth, like the Elder Ānanda, also constantly serve the One of Ten Powers; this service is also called Unsurpassable Service. Furthermore, another good worldling, like the Elder Ānanda, serves the One of Ten Powers, and by developing that service, reaches the Path of Stream-entry; this is merely called service (pāricariyā), but the original service is called Unsurpassable Service.

The Elder Ānanda himself recollects the mundane and supramundane virtues of the One of Ten Powers; this recollection is called Unsurpassable Recollection (anussatānuttariya). Other Stream-enterers and so forth, like the Elder Ānanda, also recollect the mundane and supramundane virtues of the One of Ten Powers; this recollection is also called Unsurpassable Recollection. Furthermore, another good worldling, like the Elder Ānanda, recollects the mundane and supramundane virtues of the One of Ten Powers, and by developing that recollection, reaches the Path of Stream-entry; this is merely called recollection (anussati), but the original recollection is called Unsurpassable Recollection. These six unsurpassable things appear. It should be understood that these six unsurpassable things are taught as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
93:
Regarding the phrase, "The realization of the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) occurs": there are four analytical insights—analytical insight into meanings (attha-paṭisambhidā), analytical insight into dhammas (dhamma-paṭisambhidā), analytical insight into language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and analytical insight into perspicacity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). Among these four, knowledge regarding effects is called attha-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge regarding causes is called dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge regarding the Magadhi language, which is the natural nirutti (expression) for explaining meanings and dhammas, is called nirutti-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge regarding those [previous] three analytical insights is called paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā. This is a brief explanation in this commentary. Their detailed explanation should be understood as it appears in the Abhidhamma (Vibhaṅga). The realization of these four analytical insights occurs only during the appearance of a Buddha; it cannot happen without the appearance of a Buddha. This is the meaning of "the realization of these." These four analytical insights should be understood as being taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

"Penetration of manifold elements (anekadhātupaṭivedha)" means the penetration of the eighteen elements, such as the eye-element and the form-element, occurs only during the appearance of a Buddha; it cannot happen without the appearance of a Buddha. In the phrase "penetration of various elements (nānādhātupaṭivedha)," it should be understood that these eighteen elements are called "various elements" because of their diverse natures. The penetration of these elements by way of their diversity, such as "these elements have diverse natures," is called nānādhātupaṭivedha. In the phrase "realization of the fruit of knowledge and liberation (vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyā)," "knowledge (vijjā)" refers to the knowledge in the fruit, and "liberation (vimutti)" refers to the remaining states associated with the fruit. In the phrase "realization of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyā)," "stream (sota)" refers to the first path; the fruit to be attained by that stream is the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). The fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala) and so forth are clear.

"Unsurpassed (anuttara)" means having nothing higher. "Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka)" means the noble wheel. Indeed, the word "wheel (cakka)" [is used in various senses]:

"From four dogs, eight dogs approached,
From eight dogs, sixteen approached,
From sixteen, thirty-two;
The razor-wheel approaches the person who is excessively greedy.
The wheel rotates on the head of the man overcome by desire."

In this verse, the word "wheel" appears in the sense of a razor-wheel (uracakka). In the passage, "People, having mounted the wheel of postures, wander about," it appears in the sense of the wheel of postures (iriyāpathacakka). In the passage, "Then, monks, that wheel-wright set in motion the wheel that was finished in six months," it appears in the sense of a wooden wheel (dārucakka). In the passage, "The brahmin Doṇa saw the wheel-marks with a thousand spokes on the feet of the Blessed One," it appears in the sense of the wheel-mark (lakkhaṇacakka). In the passage, "Monks, there are these four wheels, possessed of which, gods and humans..."
94:
"...the four wheels roll for gods and humans," it appears in the sense of the wheel of prosperity (sampatticakka). In the passage, "The divine wheel-treasure appears," it appears in the sense of the wheel-treasure (ratanacakka). But here [in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta], it appears in the sense of the wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka).

In the word "set in motion (pavattitaṃ)," the following distinctions should be understood: aspiring for the wheel of Dhamma (abhinīharati), having aspired (abhinīhaṭaṃ), producing (uppādeti), having produced (uppāditaṃ), setting in motion (pavatteti), and having set in motion (pavattitaṃ). From what point is it said that he "aspires for the wheel of Dhamma"? From the time when, as the brahmin Sumedha, seeing the danger in sense pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, he gave the great gift of seven-hundred-fold items, went forth as a hermit, and produced the five superknowledges and eight attainments—from that point, he is said to "aspire for the wheel of Dhamma."

From what point is it said that he "has aspired"? From the time when, having fulfilled the eight conditions, he firmly resolved at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara for the sake of the Great Bodhi-mandala, and lying down with the determination of energy, "I shall not rise until I receive the prophecy," he received the prophecy from the One of Ten Powers—from that point, he is said to "have aspired for the wheel of Dhamma."

From what point is it said that he "produces"? From the time of receiving that prophecy, while fulfilling the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), he is said to "produce the wheel of Dhamma." While fulfilling the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī)... up to... while fulfilling the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī), he is said to "produce the wheel of Dhamma." While fulfilling the ten perfections, the ten minor perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections; while making the five great sacrifices; while fulfilling the conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariyā), he is said to "produce the wheel of Dhamma." While existing in the state of King Vessantara, giving the great gift of seven-hundred-fold items, handing over his children and wife as gifts, reaching the pinnacle of perfections, being reborn in the Tusita heaven, staying there for the full lifespan, being requested by the deities and giving his consent, and making the five great observations—he is said to "produce the wheel of Dhamma." While taking conception in his mother's womb, while shaking the ten thousand world-systems at the moment of conception, while shaking the world in the same way on the day of his birth, while taking seven steps immediately after birth and uttering the lion's roar "I am the foremost," while living in the household for twenty-nine years, while making the Great Renunciation, while going forth on the banks of the Anomā river, while exerting energy in the great struggle for six years, while eating the honey-milk-rice given by Sujātā, while floating the golden bowl in the river, while going to the excellent Bodhi-mandala in the evening and sitting down facing the eastern world-system, while defeating the host of Māra's army even before the sun set, while recollecting the knowledge of past lives in the first watch, while purifying the divine eye in the middle watch, while contemplating dependent origination in the last watch, penetrating the path of stream-entry and realizing the fruit of stream-entry, while realizing the path and fruit of once-returning, the path and fruit of non-returning, and while penetrating the path of Arahatship—he is said to "produce the wheel of Dhamma."

At the moment of the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala), however, the Blessed One is said to "have produced the wheel of Dhamma." Indeed, the entire collection of mundane and supramundane qualities of the Buddhas is perfected only with the fruit of Arahatship. Therefore, at that moment of the fruit of Arahatship, he is said to "have produced the wheel of Dhamma."

At what time is he said to "set in motion"? During the period of the seven weeks (sattasattāha) at the Bodhi-mandala...
95:
While recollecting his former existences in the first watch; while purifying the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) in the middle watch; while contemplating dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) and penetrating the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) immediately after dawn; while realizing the fruition of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala); while realizing the path and fruition of once-returning (sakadāgāmi), and the path and fruition of non-returning (anāgāmi); and while penetrating the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga)—at all these times, he is said to be bringing the Wheel of Dhamma into being.

However, at the moment of the fruition of arahantship (arahatta-phala), the Wheel of Dhamma is said to have been truly brought into being by the Blessed One. This is because the entire mass of mundane and supramundane qualities of the Buddhas is perfected only along with the fruition of arahantship. Therefore, at that moment, the Wheel of Dhamma is said to have been brought into being by the Blessed One.

When is it said to be set in motion? After spending the seven weeks at the Bodhi tree, while teaching the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta at the Deer Park in Isipatana, making the Elder Aññākoṇḍañña a personal witness—at that time, he is said to be setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.

It should be understood that from the moment the Elder Aññākoṇḍañña, through the power of the Blessed One's knowledge of teaching, gained the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and attained it before all others, the Wheel of Dhamma is said to have been set in motion. This term 'Dhammacakka' (Wheel of Dhamma) is a name for both the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa). Among these, the knowledge of teaching is mundane, while the knowledge of penetration is supramundane. To whom do these knowledges of teaching and penetration belong? It should be understood that they belong to no one else but the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) alone.

'Sammadeva' means only by the proper method and cause. 'Anuppavatteti' (follows in setting in motion) means that just as one who follows behind another who goes before is said to follow him, so the Elder follows in setting in motion the Dhamma that was first set in motion by the Teacher. How? When the Teacher says, 'Monks, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?' he is said to be setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. When the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, also says, 'Friends, there are these four foundations of mindfulness,' he is said to follow in setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. The same method applies to the right efforts (sammappadhāna) and so on. This method should be applied not only to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) but also to such teachings as 'Monks, there are these four noble truths' and 'Monks, there are these four noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa).' Thus, the Perfectly Enlightened One is said to set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and the Elder is said to follow in setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma that was set in motion by the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala).

In this way, whether the Elder who follows in setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion teaches or explains the Dhamma, it is considered as having been taught and explained by the Teacher himself. Whether it be any monk, nun, lay follower (upāsaka), lay woman follower (upāsikā), deity, or Sakka...
96:
...or Māra or Brahmā who teaches or explains the Dhamma, all of it is said to be taught and explained by the Teacher himself. Other people are merely in the position of messengers carrying the King's decree. How? Just as whatever work is done by reading the royal letter given by the King—whether that work is done by someone himself or he causes another to do it—it is said to have been caused by the King. The Perfectly Enlightened One is like the Great King. The Tipitaka Buddhavacana (Word of the Buddha) is like the King's royal letter. Giving the method and guidance in the Tipitaka is like giving the royal letter. The four assemblies learning the Word of the Buddha by their own strength and teaching or explaining it to others is like reading the royal letter and performing various tasks. In that analogy, just as the work done or caused to be done by anyone after reading the letter is indeed caused by the King, so too, the Dhamma taught or explained by anyone is said to be taught and explained by the Teacher himself. The rest of the words are clear in meaning everywhere.

## Commentary on the Ekapuggalavagga

## 14. Etadaggavagga

## (14) 1. First Etadaggavagga

## Explanation of the word Etadagga

In the first sutta of the first chapter among the Etadagga chapters, 'etadaggaṃ' means 'etaṃ aggaṃ' (this is the foremost). Here, this word 'agga' is seen in the senses of beginning (ādi), tip or peak (koṭi), portion (koṭṭhāsa), and best or foremost (seṭṭha). In passages such as 'From today (ajjatagge) onwards, friend gatekeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs,' it is found in the sense of 'beginning'. In passages such as 'With that very fingertip (aṅgulagge), one should touch that fingertip; the tip of a sugarcane (ucchagga), the tip of a bamboo (veḷagga),' it is found in the sense of 'tip' or 'peak'. In passages such as 'A portion of sour taste (ambilagga), or a portion of sweet taste (madhuragga), or a portion of bitter taste (tittakagga); Monks, I allow you to distribute by the portion of the monastery (vihāragga) or by the portion of the precinct (pariveṇagga),' it is found in the sense of 'portion'. In passages such as 'Monks, as far as there are beings, whether footless... the Tathāgata is called the best (agga) among them,' it is found in the sense of 'best'. Here, this word 'agga' is suitable both in the sense of 'peak' and 'best'. For those Elders are 'agga' because they have reached the peak in their respective fields, and they are also 'agga' because they are the best. Therefore, 'etadaggaṃ' means 'this one is the peak, this one is the best.' This is the meaning here. This same method should be understood in all the suttas.
97:
This conferment of the title of 'Foremost' (Etadagga) is obtained due to four reasons: an occasion arising (atthuppatti), past aspiration (āgamana), mastery through practice (ciṇṇavasita), and excellence in qualities (guṇātireka). Among these four reasons, some elders receive the position of 'Foremost' due to one reason, some due to two, some due to three, and some, like the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, due to all four reasons. Indeed, that Venerable Sāriputta received the title of 'Foremost' in the category of great wisdom due to an occasion arising, as well as due to past aspiration and so on. 

How so? On one occasion, while the Teacher was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, he performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) at the foot of a mango tree planted by a gardener named Kaṇḍa to subdue the heretics. Then, reflecting, 'Where did the previous Buddhas spend the Rains Retreat after performing the Twin Miracle?' he realized it was in the Tāvatiṃsa Heaven. He then displayed two footsteps and, with the third step, stood in the Tāvatiṃsa Heaven. Upon seeing the Blessed One, Sakka, the king of devas, rose from the Paṇḍukambala stone throne and went with the host of devas to welcome him. The devas thought: 'Sakka, the king of devas, surrounded by the host of devas, sits and enjoys splendor on the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, which is sixty leagues in length. From the moment the Buddhas sit down, it is impossible for anyone else even to place a hand on this stone throne.' 

The Teacher, while sitting there, knew the thoughts of those devas and, like a person wearing rag-robes covering a small stool, he sat covering the entire Paṇḍukambala stone throne. In this regard, it should not be considered whether he made his body large or made the Paṇḍukambala stone throne small. For the range of a Buddha (Buddhavisaya) is unthinkable (acinteyya). While sitting thus, making the deva Santusita, who had been his mother, the chief witness, he preached the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, beginning with 'Kusalā dhammā, akusalā dhammā, abyākatā dhammā,' to the devas and Brahmas who had come from the ten thousand world systems. 

At the place where the miracle was performed, the entire assembly, spanning twelve leagues, approached the Venerable Anuruddha Thera and asked, 'Venerable Sir, where has the One of Ten Powers gone?' Venerable Anuruddha replied, 'He has gone to spend the Rains Retreat on the Paṇḍukambala stone throne in the Tāvatiṃsa Heaven to preach the Abhidhamma.' They said, 'Venerable Sir, we will not return without seeing the Teacher. Do you know when the Teacher will return?' He replied, 'Entrust this task to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera; he will go to the presence of the Buddha and bring back the news.' Was it because the Venerable Anuruddha lacked the power to go there? No, he said this because he wanted them to see the special quality of those who possess special qualities. Then the great crowd approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera...
98:
The crowd requested the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera to bring back news of the Teacher. While the great crowd was watching, the Elder dived into the earth, traveled through the interior of Mount Sineru, and after paying homage to the Teacher, said: 'Venerable Sir, the great crowd desires to see you; they wish to know the day of your arrival.' The Buddha replied, 'In that case, tell them: "You shall see me at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa at the end of three months from today."' The Elder brought the Teacher's message and told it to the great crowd. The crowd built an encampment and stayed right there for three months. Cūဠa Anāthapiṇḍika provided rice-gruel and meals to the assembly of twelve leagues for the three months. 

The Teacher, having preached the seven books of the Abhidhamma, showed his intention to descend to the world of humans. Sakka, the king of devas, summoned the deva Vissakamma and ordered him to create staircases for the Tathāgata's descent. Vissakamma created a golden staircase on one side, a silver staircase on the other, and a ruby staircase in the middle. Standing on the ruby staircase, the Teacher resolved: 'Let the great crowd see me.' By his own power, he also resolved: 'Let the great crowd see the Avīci Great Hell.' Knowing the sense of urgency (saṃvega) that arose in them upon seeing the hell, he then showed them the deva world. 

Then, as he was descending, Mahābrahmā held the white parasol, Sakka, the king of devas, carried the bowl, Suyāma, the king of devas, fanned him with a divine yak-tail fan, and the Gandhabba deva-son Pañcasikha descended in front, playing the Beluva-pandu lute, which produced fifty musical tones. When the Buddha reached the earth, the great crowd stood waiting, thinking, 'I shall be the first to pay homage, I shall be the first to pay homage.' However, as the Blessed One stepped upon the great earth, neither the great crowd nor the eighty great disciples were able to pay the first homage; only the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, succeeded in paying the first homage. 

Then the Teacher, in the midst of the assembly of twelve leagues, intended to make known the power of the Elder's wisdom and began to ask a fivefold set of questions. First, thinking that the worldly people would be able to understand, he asked questions within the scope of a worldling (puthujjana). Whichever worldlings could understand them, they answered. Secondly, going beyond the scope of worldlings, he asked questions related to the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). The worldlings remained silent, and only the Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) answered. After that...
99:
When a question was asked regarding the Path of Once-returning, which is beyond the scope of Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), the Stream-enterers remained silent, and only the Once-returners (sakadāgāmī) answered. When a question was asked regarding the Path of Non-returning, which is beyond the scope of Once-returners, the Once-returners remained silent, and only the Non-returners (anāgāmī) answered. When a question was asked regarding the Path of Arahantship, which is beyond the scope of Non-returners, the Non-returners remained silent, and only the Arahants answered. Then, starting from the lower levels, questions were asked of the well-known disciples, and those disciples answered according to their own scope of analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Then, when Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was questioned, the other disciples remained silent, and only the Elder answered. When a question was asked within the scope of Venerable Sāriputta, which is beyond the scope of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna remained silent, and only the Elder Sāriputta answered.

When a question was asked within the domain of the Buddhas, which is beyond the scope of the Elder, even the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, could not see the answer despite reflecting on it. Though he looked here and there toward the four cardinal directions—East, West, North, and South—and the four intermediate directions, he was unable to discern the origin of the question. The Blessed One, knowing that the Elder was becoming fatigued, thought, "Sāriputta is weary; I will show him a hint of the method." He said, "Wait, Sāriputta," and then informed him that it was the domain of the Buddhas, saying, "This question is not within your scope; it is the domain of the glorious Buddhas, the All-Knowing Ones." Then He said, "Sāriputta, do you see this as 'it has come to be' (bhūtamidaṃ)?" The Elder understood, "The Blessed One is telling me about the discernment of the group of materiality based on the four great elements (mahābhūta)." He then replied, "I understand, Blessed One; I understand, Sugata."

At that time, words of praise arose: "Friends, how great is the wisdom of Venerable Sāriputta! He can answer a question that no one else knows, and by standing on the method granted by the Buddhas, he can even answer a question that is within the domain of the Buddhas." Thus, the power of the Elder's wisdom pervaded all places where the fame of the Buddhas had spread. In this way, the Elder received the foremost title (etadagga) in wisdom due to this occurrence.

How did he receive the foremost title through past tradition (āgamana)? Because of this very event, the Blessed One said, "Sāriputta is not wise only now; in the past, throughout five hundred births as an ascetic, he was also a person of great wisdom." He preached: "You should worship that Sāriputta, who abandoned the delightful sensual pleasures, who lived as an ascetic for five hundred births, who is free from lust, whose faculties are well-composed, and who is quenched." While thus cultivating the state of an ascetic, in one life, he was born into a Brahmin family in Vārāṇasī. Although he studied the three Vedas, he saw no essence in them and thought, "It is proper to seek the Dhamma of Nibbāna, the liberation from defilements, by becoming an ascetic." At that time, the Bodhisatta was also born into a prominent wealthy Brahmin family in the Kāsī kingdom. Upon reaching maturity and completing his studies, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation. He left the household life, entered the Himalayan forest, practiced the kasina preliminaries, attained the five higher powers (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti), and lived in the Himalayan region, subsisting on forest roots and fruits...
100:
He who went forth for five hundred births,
Abandoning delightful sensual pleasures;
That one with lust removed, with well-composed faculties,
The quenched Sāriputta—him you should worship.

While thus praising and cultivating the state of an ascetic, in another time, he was born into a Brahmin family in Vārāṇasī. Having studied the three Vedas and seeing no essence in them, he gave rise to the thought, "It is proper to become an ascetic and seek the single Dhamma of Nibbāna, the liberation from defilements."

At that time, the Bodhisatta was also born into a prominent wealthy Brahmin family in the Kāsī kingdom. Upon reaching maturity and completing his studies, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation. He abandoned the household life, entered the Himalayan forest, practiced the kasina preliminaries, and attained the five higher powers and the eight attainments. He lived in the Himalayan region, consuming roots and fruits. That Brahmin youth also renounced the world and became an ascetic under that Bodhisatta. His retinue was large, consisting of about five hundred ascetics.

Then, the chief disciple of that Bodhisatta took some of the followers and went to human habitations to seek salt and sour food. At that time, the Bodhisatta passed away in that very Himalayan region. At the time of his passing, the disciples gathered and asked, "Has your reverence attained any distinction?" The Bodhisatta said, "There is nothing" (natthi kiñci) and, with his jhana unimpaired, was reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma realm.

Although that Bodhisatta was a gainer of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), there is no such thing as rebirth in the immaterial realm (arūpabhūmi) for Bodhisattas. Why? Because it is an unsuitable place for them. Thus, even though he was a gainer of the immaterial attainment, he was reborn only in the fine-material realm (rūpabhūmi).

The disciples thought, "The teacher said 'There is nothing'; his death was in vain," and they did not perform any honor or respect. Then, the chief disciple returned after the vassa (rainy season) and asked, "Where is the teacher?" They replied, "He has passed away." He asked, "Did you ask about the qualities the teacher attained?" They said, "Yes, we asked." "What did he say?" "He said 'There is nothing'." "We also thought there was no quality attained by the teacher, so we did not perform any honor." The chief disciple said, "You do not know the meaning of what was said; the teacher was a gainer of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana)."
101:
The disciples of the Bodhisatta also thought, "The teacher said, 'There is nothing'; his death was in vain," and they did not pay any respect to him. Then, the chief resident disciple arrived after the rainy season and asked, "Where is the teacher?" They replied, "He has passed away." He asked, "Did you ask him about the special attainment he had achieved?" They replied, "We did." When he asked, "What did he say?", they answered, "He said, 'There is nothing' (natthi kiñci). We thought there were no special qualities to be found in the teacher, so we did not pay him any respect." Then the chief disciple said, "You do not understand the meaning of those words; the teacher had attained the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana jhāna)." However, those disciples did not believe the words of the chief resident disciple. Even though he explained it repeatedly, he could not make them believe. Then, the Bodhisatta, upon reflection, thought, "The multitude is very foolish; they do not accept the words of my chief resident disciple. I shall make this matter clear." He descended from the Brahma realm and, standing in the sky above the hermitage, praised the power of the chief disciple's wisdom and uttered this verse:

"Even if more than a thousand fools gather
And lament for a hundred years,
Better is a single wise man
Who understands the meaning of what is spoken."

Having thus convinced the group of ascetics, the Bodhisatta returned to the Brahma realm. The remaining group of ascetics, having maintained their meditative absorptions without decline, passed away and were reborn in the Brahma realm. In that birth story, the Bodhisatta became the All-Enlightened Buddha, the chief resident disciple became the Elder Sāriputta, and the remaining ascetics became the Buddha's assembly. Thus, it should be understood that even in the past, Sāriputta was of great wisdom and was capable of knowing in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief.

Based on the story of these same five worldlings, He also told this Parosata Jātaka:

"Even if more than a hundred fools gather
And ponder for a hundred years,
Better is a single wise man
Who understands the meaning of what is spoken."

The meaning of this Jātaka should be understood in the same way as explained in the previous Parosahassa Jātaka.

Again, based on the story of these same five worldlings, He told this Anaṅgaṇa Jātaka:

"Those with perception are miserable, and those without perception are also miserable. Avoid both of these; that happiness of attainment is stainless (anaṅgaṇa)."

As for...
102:
He preached this Anaṅgaṇa Jātaka. In this Jātaka as well, when the teacher was asked by his disciples at the time of his death, he said, "Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). The rest should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

Again, based on the story of these same five worldlings—
He preached this Candābha Jātaka with the verse: "Candābhaṃ suriyābhañca, yodha paññāya gādhati; avitakkena jhānena, hoti ābhassarūpago." In this Jātaka too, when the teacher was asked by his disciples at the time of his death, he said, "The white kasina (odāta-kasiṇa) is called Candābha (moon-like light); the yellow kasina (pīta-kasiṇa) is called Suriyābha (sun-like light). Whoever enters into both these kasinas with wisdom, he reaches the Ābhassara realm through the second jhāna which is without initial application (avitakka). I am such a person." Intending this, he said, "Candābhaṃ suriyābhaṃ." The rest should be understood according to the previous method.

Based on the story of these same five worldlings—
A man should hope (for happiness); a wise man should not grow weary. I see myself as I desired.

A man should hope; a wise man should not grow weary. I see myself as one who has ascended from the water to the dry land.

A man should strive; a wise man should not grow weary. I see myself as I desired.

A man should strive; a wise man should not grow weary. I see myself as one who has ascended from the water to the dry land.

A wise person, even when fallen into suffering, should not cut off the hope for obtaining happiness. For there are many contacts, both harmful and beneficial; unthought-of harmful contacts come to beings.

The unthought-of thing also happens; the thought-of thing also perishes. Wealth for a woman or a man is not accomplished by mere thinking.
103:
"O Great King, you previously followed the Sarabha deer in the difficult mountain; relying on the effort of that deer who had an undaunted mind, you live.

"That Sarabha deer, having made the rock ledges suitable for a man to climb, brought you out of the difficult hellish pit where you were suffering; he released you from the mouth of death. You praise that animal who had an undaunted mind.

"O Brahmin, were you yourself present in that forest at that time? Or did someone tell you this? Are you a Buddha who has removed the veil and sees all? Or is your knowledge of a powerful nature?"

"O Great King, I was not present in that forest at that time, nor did anyone tell me this. Wise men can grasp the meaning of well-spoken verses," he said.

Thus, He also preached the Sarabha Jātaka in the Thirteenth Nipāta. These five Jātakas were preached by the Teacher solely to manifest the power of wisdom of the General of the Dhamma, Elder Sāriputta, saying, "In the past too, my son knew in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief." Because of this past cause, the Elder obtained the title of Etadagga (Foremost) in the category of those with Great Wisdom.

How did he obtain it through mastery (ciṇṇavasitoto)? It is said that when the Elder preached the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly, he preached without omitting the Four Noble Truths. Thus, preaching without omitting the Four Noble Truths was the Elder's habit. Because of such mastery, the Elder obtained the title of Etadagga in the category of those with Great Wisdom.

How did he obtain it through excellence of qualities (guṇātirekato)? Except for the Possessor of Ten Powers (the Buddha), there is no other single disciple who is equal to the General of the Dhamma in great wisdom. Thus, because of the excellence of his qualities, the Elder obtained the title of Etadagga in the category of those with Great Wisdom.

Just like Elder Sāriputta, Elder Mahāmoggallāna also obtained the title of Etadagga through these same four reasons. How? The Elder possessed great psychic power and majesty, taming dragon kings such as Nandopananda. Thus...
104:
Firstly, he attained the foremost position (etadagga) due to the occasion of the event (atthuppatti). This Venerable Moggallāna possessed great psychic power and majesty not only in the present; even in the past, while he was ordained as an ascetic for five hundred births, he possessed great psychic power and majesty.

“He who was ordained for five hundred births, having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures; worship that Moggallāna, who is free from passion, with well-restrained senses, and who is cooled (parinibbuta).”

Thus, he also attained the foremost position due to past tradition (āgamana). It was the Elder's habit to go to hell and, by his psychic power, resolve upon coolness to bring relief to the denizens of hell, create a lotus the size of a cartwheel, and sit upon the pericarp of the lotus to preach the Dhamma. He would also go to the celestial realm to let the hosts of devas know the destination of their karma and preach the Truth. Thus, he also attained the foremost position due to practiced proficiency (ciṇṇavasī). Excluding the Fully Enlightened Buddha, there is no other disciple who possesses such great psychic power and majesty as Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Thus, he also attained the foremost position due to the excellence of his qualities (guṇātireka).

Just like this Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, Venerable Mahākassapa also attained the foremost position due to these same four reasons. How? The Fully Enlightened Buddha went out to welcome the Elder for a distance of three gāvutas, ordained him with three exhortations, and exchanged robes with him. At that time, the great earth shook as far as the water's edge, and the Elder's fame spread and overwhelmed the multitude. Thus, he attained the foremost position due to the occasion of the event. This Elder was a dhuta-practitioner not only in the present; even in the past, while he was ordained as an ascetic for five hundred births, he was indeed a dhuta-practitioner.

“He who was ordained for five hundred births, having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures; worship that Mahākassapa, who is free from passion, with well-restrained senses, and who is cooled.”

Thus, he also attained the foremost position due to past tradition. It was the Elder's habit that when preaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly, he preached without abandoning the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu). Thus, he also attained the foremost position due to practiced proficiency. Excluding the Fully Enlightened Buddha, there is no other disciple equal to Venerable Mahākassapa in the thirteen dhuta qualities. Thus, he also attained the foremost position due to the excellence of his qualities.
105:
He attained [the position]. In this very manner, it is appropriate to praise the qualities of various Elders as they were attained.

Indeed, by the power of qualities, just as a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), having attained royal glory within the world-system by the power of the Wheel-treasure, does not become indifferent, thinking, “I have attained what was to be attained; what use is there now for the people's observation?” and merely enjoy royal luxury. Instead, from time to time, he sits in the place of judgment, restrains those who should be restrained, encourages those who should be encouraged, and appoints those worthy of being appointed to various positions.

In the same way, the King of Dhamma (Dhamma-rāja), who has reached the state of a King of Dhamma by the power of the Omniscient Knowledge attained at the Great Bodhi-tree, does not fall into indifference, thinking, “What use is there now for the world's observation? I shall only enjoy the incomparable bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).” Instead, sitting upon the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the midst of the fourfold assembly, he preaches the Dhamma, emitting the divine voice (brahma-sara) endowed with eight factors. When preaching thus, he restrains those with dark qualities who deserve restraint by threatening them with the fear of the lower realms, as if casting them to the foot of Mount Sineru. He encourages those with beautiful qualities who deserve encouragement, as if lifting them up and seating them at the peak of existence (bhavagga). Wishing to appoint disciples such as Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña to various positions according to their actual and essential qualities, he said: “Monks, among my disciple monks who are of long standing (rattaññū), Aññāsikoṇḍañña is the foremost.”

## The Story of Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña

In that passage, the word “etadaggaṃ” has the meaning already stated. “Rattaññūnaṃ” means among those who know the nights. Excluding the Fully Enlightened Buddha, there is no other disciple who was ordained earlier than Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña; therefore, because he has known the nights for a long time since the time of his ordination, he is called “rattaññū”. Because he was the very first to penetrate the Dhamma, and has known the nights for a long time since that realization, he is also called “rattaññū”. Furthermore, for Arahants, the distinction of nights and days is indeed clear, and since this Elder was the first Arahant, he is the first, the foremost, and the most excellent among the disciples who know the nights. Therefore, it was said: “Among those of long standing, Aññāsikoṇḍañña is the foremost (rattaññūnaṃ yadidaṃ aññāsikoṇḍañño).”
106:
In this context, 'yadidaṃ' is a particle. Its meaning, when referring to the Elder, is 'who is this'; when referring to the word 'agga' (foremost), it means 'which is this'. 'Aññāsikoṇḍañña' means Koṇḍañña who has known the Four Noble Truths, or Koṇḍañña who has penetrated the Four Noble Truths. For this very reason, (the Buddha) exclaimed: "Koṇḍañña has indeed understood, friends! Koṇḍañña has indeed understood, friends!" Thus, the Venerable Koṇḍañña came to be known only as 'Aññāsikoṇḍañña'.

Regarding all those who attained the foremost positions (etadagga), the following questions should be understood: Under which Buddha did this Elder make his initial aspiration (abhinīhāra)? When did he ordain? When did he first attain the Dhamma? When was he placed in the foremost position?

Among those questions, this is the chronological account of this Elder's story—one hundred thousand eons ago, a Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in the world. That Buddha, possessed of the penetrated Knowledge of Omniscience, rose from the Great Bodhi-throne, and as soon as He lifted His feet to step upon the earth, a magnificent lotus flower sprang up to receive His feet. The outer petals of that lotus were ninety cubits; the filaments were thirty cubits; the pericarp was twelve cubits; and the area where the foot rested was eleven cubits. The body of that Blessed One was fifty-eight cubits in height. When His right foot was placed upon the pericarp of the lotus, pollen the size of a large bushel rose up, sprinkling and descending upon His body. When He placed His left foot, a similar lotus also sprang up to receive it. From that lotus too, pollen of the aforementioned measure rose up and sprinkled His body. Overpowering that pollen, the radiance from the Blessed One's body emerged like a stream of liquid gold released from a mechanical tube, creating a solid mass of light for twelve yojanas all around. When He lifted His foot for the third time, the first lotus that had appeared vanished, and another new lotus sprang up to receive His foot. In this manner, wherever He wished to go, a great lotus would spring up. For that reason, He was named 'Padumuttara Sammāsambuddha'.

Thus, that Blessed One, having appeared in the world and being surrounded by one hundred thousand monks, arrived at the city of Haṃsavatī while wandering for alms through villages, market towns, and royal capitals for the benefit of the great multitude. Hearing of the Blessed One's arrival, His father, the Great King...
107:
(The father, King Ānanda) went out to welcome Him. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to the King. At the conclusion of the discourse, some became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), some Non-returners (Anāgāmī), and some attained Arahatship. The King invited the Possessor of Ten Powers for the next day's meal, and after announcing the time the following morning, he offered a great alms-giving (mahādāna) in his palace to the Blessed One who was surrounded by one hundred thousand monks. The Teacher, after giving the blessing (anumodanā) for the meal, returned to the monastery. In that same manner, the citizens gave alms on the next day, and the King on the day after that; thus they gave alms for a long period.

At that time, this Elder (the future Koṇḍañña) was born into a wealthy householder family (gahapati mahāsāla) in the city of Haṃsavatī. One day, at the time of the Buddha's Dhamma discourse, he saw the citizens of Haṃsavatī carrying perfumes, garlands, and such, going with their hearts inclined, leaned, and directed towards the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; he then went to the place of the discourse along with that great multitude. At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara placed a certain monk, who was the first to penetrate the Dhamma in His dispensation, in the foremost position (etadagga). That young man, hearing of this matter, thought: "Great indeed is this monk! It is said that, excluding the Buddha, there is no one else who has penetrated the Dhamma earlier than this monk. Oh, would that I too might be one capable of being the first to penetrate the Dhamma in the dispensation of a future Buddha!" After the discourse ended, he approached the Blessed One and invited Him, saying, "Please accept my alms-meal tomorrow." The Teacher accepted.

Having paid homage to the Blessed One and performed the circumambulation, he returned to his home. Throughout the night, he decorated the place where the Buddhas would sit with strings of perfumes and garlands. Having prepared excellent hard and soft food, at the end of that night, he offered to the Blessed One and the one hundred thousand monks in his home a meal of fragrant hill-paddy rice, complete with various flavored soups and curries, and accompanied by exquisite gruel and snacks. At the conclusion of the meal, he placed new cloths sufficient for the triple robes (ticīvara) at the feet of the Tathāgata and thought: "I am not practicing for the sake of a minor position; I practice aspiring for a great position. However, it is not possible to aspire for such a position by giving alms for only a single day. Therefore, I will give a great alms-giving for seven consecutive days and then make my aspiration." In that manner, he gave a great alms-giving for seven days. At the conclusion of the meal on the seventh day, he had his cloth-storehouse opened, placed supreme and delicate cloths at the feet of the Buddha, and presented (covered) the one hundred thousand monks with triple robes each.
108:
Approaching the Tathāgata, he said, "Venerable Sir, seven days ago from today, you appointed a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position (etadagga). May I also, like that bhikkhu, be ordained in the dispensation of a future Buddha and be able to penetrate the Four Noble Truths first." Having said this, he prostrated himself, placing his head at the feet of the Teacher.

The Teacher, hearing the words of that clansman, reflected, "This clansman has made a great aspiration. Will this aspiration of his be fulfilled or not?" Sending forth his knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa), he saw that it would be fulfilled. Indeed, for the Buddhas who reflect upon things past, future, or present, there is no obstruction. Whether it be the past or future within many hundreds of thousands of crores of aeons, or the present within ten thousand world systems, it is connected only with their reflection and attention. With such unimpeded knowledge, the Blessed One saw this: "In the future, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world. At that time, this clansman's aspiration will be fulfilled." Then he said to that clansman, "O clansman, in the future, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world. At the conclusion of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, his first discourse with its three rounds, you will be established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) together with eighteen crores of Brahmās, endowed with a thousand methods."

Thus, having given the prophecy to that clansman and preached eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma, the Teacher attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). After the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, his body became a single solid mass like a block of gold. They built a cetiya to enshrine his bodily relics, seven leagues (yojanas) in height. The bricks were made of gold; orpiment and realgar served as mortar, and oil served as water. While the Buddhas are alive, their bodily radiance extends for twelve leagues. But after they have attained final Nibbāna, their rays emanate and cover an area of a hundred leagues all around.

This treasurer caused a thousand pavilions made of jewels to be built surrounding the cetiya of the Buddha's relics. On the day the cetiya was established, he had a house of jewels built inside the cetiya. Having performed meritorious deeds such as great giving for a hundred thousand years, when he passed away from the human world, he was reborn in the celestial realm. While that clansman was wandering through the celestial and human realms...
109:
Ninety-nine thousand nine hundred and nine aeons passed away. After the lapse of this much time, ninety-one aeons before this present auspicious aeon (Bhadda-kappa), this clansman was reborn in a house of a householder in a village near the gate of the city of Bandhumatī. His name was Mahākāla, and his younger brother was named Cūḷakāla.

At that time, the Bodhisatta Vipassī, having passed away from the Tusita heaven, took conception in the womb of the chief queen of King Bandhuma in the city of Bandhumatī. In due course, having attained omniscience and being requested by the Great Brahmā to preach the Dhamma, he reflected, "To whom should I preach the Dhamma first?" Seeing that his younger brother, Prince Khaṇḍa, and Tissa, the son of the royal chaplain, were capable of penetrating the Dhamma first, he thought, "I will preach the Dhamma to them and also favor my father, the King." Traveling through the air from the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimanda), he descended at the Khema Deer Park. He had them summoned and preached the Dhamma to them. At the conclusion of the discourse, those two, together with eighty-four thousand living beings, were established in the fruit of Arahantship.

Afterwards, eighty-four thousand clansmen who had followed the Bodhisatta into monkhood during his time as a Bodhisatta, hearing the news of his becoming a Buddha, came to the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and were established in the fruit of Arahantship. Right there in the Deer Park, the Teacher appointed Elder Khaṇḍa to the position of Chief Disciple and Elder Tissa to the position of Second Disciple. King Bandhuma, hearing the news, went to the park thinking, "I will see my son, the Buddha." After listening to the Dhamma, he was established in the Three Refuges. He invited the Teacher for the next day's meal, paid homage respectfully, circumambulated him, and departed.

Having reached his noble palace and while sitting there, the King reflected: "My eldest son has renounced the world and become a Buddha. My second son is the Chief Disciple. The son of the royal chaplain is the Second Disciple. These remaining monks also used to wander around accompanying my son when they were laymen. These Buddhas and Arahants were my responsibility in the past and are so now. I alone will support them with the four requisites; I will not give others the opportunity to support them." From the gate of the monastery to the gate of the palace, he had a fence of catechu wood built on both sides of the road, covered with cloth. Above, he had a canopy made of various flower garlands, as large as palm trunks, hanging down and adorned with golden stars...
110:
Having had the ground below covered with exquisite carpets, and having placed flower bushes and full jars on both sides within, and having placed flowers among perfumes and perfumes among flowers to make the entire path fragrant, he had it announced to the Blessed One that it was time. The Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, entered the palace only within the enclosure of curtains, and after finishing his meal, returned to the monastery. No one else even got the chance to see him, let alone offer alms or pay homage.

The citizens thought: "It has now been over seven years and seven months since the Teacher appeared in the world, yet we have not even had the chance to see him, let alone offer alms, pay homage, or hear the Dhamma. The King, possessing him as 'My Buddha, my Dhamma, my Saṅgha,' serves him alone. When the Teacher appears, he appears for the benefit of the whole world including the devas, not for the King alone. Hell is not hot for the King alone, nor is it as cool as a forest of blue lotuses for others. Therefore, let us say this to the King: 'If you allow us to serve the Teacher, it is well. If you do not, we shall fight the King, take the Saṅgha, and perform meritorious deeds such as giving.' However, we cannot do this with just the citizens; let us also win over a leading man." They approached the General, informed him of the matter, and asked, "Lord General, will you be on our side or the King's side?" He said, "I will be on your side, but the first day must be given to me." They accepted.

He approached the King and said, "Great King, the citizens are angry with you." "Dear man, why?" he asked. "It is because you alone serve the Teacher and we do not get the chance. If they get the chance now, they will not be angry. If they do not, they wish to fight with you, O King," he replied. "Dear man, I will fight; I cannot give the community of monks," the King said. "Great King, your servants say they will fight with you; whom will you take to fight?" he asked. "Are you not the General?" the King said. "Great King, without the citizens, I am powerless," he replied. Then the King, realizing "The citizens are powerful, and even the General is on their side," said, "Let them allow me to serve the community of monks for another seven years and seven months." The citizens did not accept. The King reduced it to "six years, five years," and so on, and finally (requested) another seven days.
111:
King Bandhuma pleaded. The citizens thought, "It is not proper to be extremely antagonistic toward the King now," and they granted permission. The King prepared the offerings that were intended for over seven years and seven months within just seven days. For six days, he gave alms without letting anyone see, and on the seventh day, he summoned the citizens and asked, "Dear men, will you be able to give such an offering?" They replied, "Did this offering not arise for Your Majesty because of us? We are able." The King, wiping away tears with the back of his hand, paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, I intended to serve the six million eight hundred thousand monks with the four requisites for the rest of my life without making it a burden for others. Now the citizens do not allow me. The citizens are angry, saying 'We do not get the chance to give alms.' From tomorrow onwards, please show favor to them."

Then on the second day, the General gave a great offering. Thereafter, the citizens gave alms, performing honors and respects even more excellent than those performed by the King. In this manner, as the turn went through the whole city in order, it reached those living near the gate. The householder Mahākāla asked his younger brother Cūḷakāla, "Tomorrow it is our turn to honor the Blessed One; what kind of honor shall we perform?" Cūḷakāla said, "Only you, elder brother, know." Mahākāla said, "If you do as I wish, there are Sāli rice plants in our fields of about sixteen karīsas that have just begun to form milk. I want to split the rice husks, take the milk, and have it cooked in a manner suitable for the Buddhas." Cūḷakāla said, "If done this way, it will benefit no one, so I do not like it." Mahākāla said, "If you do not do this, I will divide my property." He split the sixteen-karīsa field in the middle, set a boundary at the eight-karīsa mark, split the rice husks, took the milk, had it cooked in undiluted milk, added the four sweet foods (catumadhura), and offered it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. Every place where the householder split and took the husks was filled back as before.
