At the time of making parched rice, he offered the first parched rice; together with the villagers, he offered the first harvest; at the time of reaping, the first of the reaping; at the time of binding sheaves, the first of the sheaves; at the time of making bundles, the first of the bundles; at the threshing floor, the first of the threshing floor; at the heap, the first of the heap; and at the granary, the first of the granary. Thus, he made the offering of first fruits nine times during a single crop. That crop also became exceptionally abundant.

Having performed good deeds in this manner as long as the Buddha and the Saṅgha remained, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the deva realm and among the devas...
112:
Wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he enjoyed prosperity for ninety-one aeons. When our Teacher appeared in the world, he was reborn into a wealthy Brahmin family (Brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla) in the Brahmin village of Doṇavatthu, not far from the city of Kapilavatthu. On the day of his naming ceremony, they named him the youth Koṇḍañña. As he grew up, he mastered the three Vedas and reached the perfection of the Vedic texts on marks (Lakkhaṇa-mantas). At that time, our Bodhisatta passed away from the Tusita heaven and was reborn in the city of Kapilavatthu. On the naming day of the Bodhisatta, one hundred and eight Brahmins were dressed in brand-new clothes and fed with sweet milk-rice (madhupāyāsa) without added water. Among them, eight Brahmins were selected and seated on the upper floor. The Bodhisatta, adorned and decorated, was placed on a white cloth cushion and brought before them to examine his marks. The Brahmin seated in the foremost seat, observing the physical perfection of the Great Man (Mahāpurisa), raised two fingers. In this manner, seven Brahmins sequentially raised two fingers each.

However, the youngest among them, the youth Koṇḍañña, observing the perfection of the Bodhisatta’s excellent marks, thought, "There is no reason for him to remain in the household life; he will certainly become a Buddha who has removed the veil of defilements." Thus, he raised only one finger. The other seven Brahmins, seeing two possible destinies, raised two fingers, saying, "If he lives the household life, he will become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti); if he renounces the world, he will become a Buddha."

This Koṇḍañña, being a being in his final existence (pacchimabhavika) who had made the necessary aspirations, surpassed the other seven Brahmins with his wisdom. Seeing only one destiny, he raised only one finger, thinking, "For one endowed with these marks, there is no reason to remain in the household life; he will undoubtedly become a Buddha."

Thereafter, the Brahmins returned to their homes and called their sons, saying, "Dear ones, we are old. We may or may not live to see the son of King Suddhodana attain Omniscience. When that prince attains Omniscience, you should ordain in his Dispensation (Sāsana)."

King Suddhodana also provided the Bodhisatta with attendants, starting with nurses, and let him grow up. When the Great Being reached maturity, he enjoyed prosperity like a deva. As his wisdom matured, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation, on the day Prince Rāhula was born, accompanied by the courtier Channa and mounting the horse Kanthaka, he departed on the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) through the gate opened by the devas. In that very night, he crossed three kingdoms, and having ordained on the banks of the Anomā River, [he took] the robes which are the banner of the Arahants brought by the Great Brahma Ghaṭīkāra...
113:
...having taken the robes which are the banner of the Arahants brought by the Great Brahma Ghaṭīkāra, he appeared with a graceful posture like an elder of sixty years' standing. He reached the city of Rājagaha, wandered for alms there, and partook of his alms-food in the shadow of Mount Paṇḍava. Although invited by King Bimbisāra of Magadha with the offer of royal splendor, he rejected it and proceeded sequentially to the forest of Uruvelā. Thinking, "Delightful indeed is this spot of ground; it is truly fit for the exertion of a clansman intent on striving," he directed his mind toward spiritual exertion and took up residence there.

At that time, the other seven Brahmins had passed away according to their kamma, but the youngest examiner of marks, the youth Koṇḍañña, was still healthy. Hearing that "The Great Man has renounced the world," he approached the sons of those Brahmins and said, "It is said that Prince Siddhattha has renounced the world. He will undoubtedly become a Buddha. If your fathers were healthy, they would have gone forth and ordained today. If you also wish, come, let us follow that Great Man and ordain." Not all of them could reach a single consensus. Three of them did not ordain, but the other four, with the Brahmin Koṇḍañña as their leader, went forth.

These five, having ordained, wandered through villages, market towns, and royal capitals for alms and came to the presence of the Bodhisatta. While the Bodhisatta was performing the great exertion for six years, they attended to him, staying nearby and thinking, "Now he will become a Buddha, now he will become a Buddha." However, when the Bodhisatta, even while passing time with a single sesame seed or a grain of rice, realized that the realization of the Noble Dhamma was not possible through the practice of austerities (dukkharacariyā) and took solid food, those five left him and went to Isipatana.

Then the Bodhisatta, having restored his skin, flesh, and blood by consuming solid food, on the full moon day of Vesākha, partook of the excellent food offered by Sujātā. Having floated the golden bowl upstream in the Nerañjarā River and made the resolution, "Today I shall become a Buddha," he was praised with hundreds of verses by the Naga King Kāla in the evening. He then ascended the Mahābodhi seat (maṇḍa), sat cross-legged on the unshakable spot facing the eastern world-system, and determined his energy endowed with four factors. Even before the sun set, he defeated the host of Māra. In the first watch of the night, he recollected his past existences; in the middle watch, he purified the divine eye; and immediately after the dawn, he applied his knowledge to Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) in forward and reverse order...
114:
While contemplating the cycle of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), and having realized the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññutañāṇa)—which is penetrated by all Buddhas and is not shared with other disciples—He spent seven days at that very seat of enlightenment (Bodhimpallaṅka) in the Attainment of Fruition (Phalasamāpatti) with Nibbāna as the object.

In this manner, having stayed for seven weeks at the Bodhimaṇḍa and partaken of the honey-ball (Madhupiṇဍika) at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, He returned to the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree. While sitting there, He reflected on the profundity of the Dhamma. As His mind inclined toward inaction (not teaching), He was entreated by Mahābrahmā. Looking upon the world with the Buddha-eye, He saw beings with varying degrees of faculties, such as those with keen faculties, and He gave His word to Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma. Thinking, 'To whom shall I first teach the Dhamma?', He realized that the ascetics Āḷāra and Udaka had passed away. Then He thought, 'The five monks (Pañcavaggiya) who attended to me while I was striving were of great help. It would be well if I were to teach the Dhamma first to the five monks.'

All such thoughts were merely the reflections of the Buddhas. In truth, apart from the Brahmin Koṇḍañña, no one else was capable of first penetrating the Dhamma. Koṇḍañña himself had performed meritorious deeds for a hundred thousand aeons for the sake of this benefit of first realizing the Dhamma. He had previously given the noble gift of the first-fruits (aggasassadāna) nine times to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha.

Then the Blessed One, taking His bowl and robes, traveled by stages to the Isipatana forest and approached the five monks. Upon seeing the Tathāgata coming, the five monks were unable to remain in their agreement. One took His bowl and robes, one prepared the seat, one set out the water for washing the feet, one washed His feet, and one stood fanning Him with a palmyra fan.

Thus, when they had performed these duties and were seated near Him, the Teacher, taking the Elder Koṇḍañña as a witness, began the peerless and noble Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta with its three rounds. Although there were only five people in the human assembly, the assembly of devas and brahmas was immeasurable. At the conclusion of the discourse, the Elder Koṇḍañña, together with eighteen crores of Mahābrahmas, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). Then the Teacher, reflecting, 'He has first understood the Dhamma that I attained with great difficulty,' addressed the Elder, saying, 'Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood! Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood!' From then on, that very name 'Aññāsikoṇḍañña' became known for him. Therefore, it was said, 'Thus...'
115:
...thus the name 'Aññāsikoṇḍañña' came to be for the Venerable Koṇḍañña.

Thus, the Elder was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry on the full moon day of Āsāḷha. On the first day of the waning moon, the Elder Bhaddiya; on the second day, the Elder Vappa; on the third day, the Elder Mahānāma; and on the fourth day of the fortnight, the Elder Assaji were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. On the fifth day of the fortnight, at the conclusion of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta discourse, all of them were established in Arahantship.

At that time, there were six Arahants in the world. From then on, the Teacher led many people into the Noble Stage (Ariyabhūmi), including the fifty-five men led by the youth Yasa, the thirty Bhaddavaggiya brothers in the Kappāsiya woodland, and the one thousand former matted-hair ascetics (Jaṭilas) on the stone plateau of Gayāsīsa. He established one hundred and ten thousand people led by King Bimbisāra in the Fruit of Stream-entry, and ten thousand in the Three Refuges. Making the Sāsana flourish throughout Jambudīpa with the flowers of higher knowledge (abhiññā) and analytical insight (paṭisambhidā) and the fruits of the Paths and Fruitions (Magga-phala), making the entire circle of Jambudīpa radiant with saffron robes and filled with the presence of sages, He arrived at the Jetavana Monastery on one occasion. While staying there, seated on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the midst of the Saṅgha and preaching the Dhamma, He appointed the Elder Koṇḍañña to the position of foremost (Etadagga) to show: 'Among my sons, the monks who first penetrated the Dhamma, Koṇḍañña is the foremost.'

The Elder, seeing the two Chief Disciples performing respectful services for him, desired to withdraw from the presence of the Buddhas. Seeing that 'the youth Puṇṇa will ordain and become the foremost Dhamma-preacher in the Sāsana,' he went to the Brahmin village of Doṇavatthu and ordained his nephew, the youth Puṇṇa. Ensuring that he would be a disciple of the Buddha, saying, 'This one shall live in the presence of the Buddhas,' he himself approached the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) and said, 'Venerable Sir, a monastery near a village is not suitable for me. I am unable to live while crowded with people. I shall go and live at Chaddanta Lake.' Having obtained permission from the Blessed One, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Teacher, and went to Chaddanta Lake. Living there for twelve years supported by the Chaddanta elephant clan, he attained Parinibbāna there with the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).
116:
## The Story of the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna

189-190. In the second and third suttas, "Mahāpaññānaṃ" means those endowed with great wisdom. "Iddhimantānaṃ" means those endowed with psychic power. Sāriputta and Moggallāna are the names of those elders.

In answering the question regarding these elders, the chronological account is as follows: More than one hundred thousand eons and one incalculable (asaṅkheyya) ago, Sāriputta was born into a wealthy Brahmin family and was known by the name Sarada the youth. Moggallāna was born into a wealthy householder family and was known by the name Sirivaḍḍhana the merchant. Both of them were childhood friends who played together in the dust. After his father passed away, Sarada the youth inherited the vast family wealth. One day, while in a secluded place, he reflected: "I know only this life, not the life hereafter. For beings who are born, death is certain. It is proper for me to renounce the world and seek the Dhamma of liberation (mokkha)."

Sarada the youth went to his friend Sirivaḍḍhana and asked, "Friend Sirivaḍḍhana, I am going to renounce the world and seek the Dhamma of liberation. Will you be able to renounce with me?" Sirivaḍḍhana replied, "Friend, I cannot. You alone should renounce." Sarada the youth thought, "When going to the next world, there is no such thing as taking along companions, relatives, or friends. Only the merit or demerit one has performed becomes one's own property." Then, he had the treasure houses opened and gave a great alms-offering to the poor, travelers, and beggars. He then entered the foot of a mountain and renounced as a hermit (isi). Following Sarada the hermit, one, two, three, and so on, eventually seventy-four thousand hermits renounced after him. Sarada the hermit attained the five superknowledges (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti), and he taught the preliminary work for kasina meditation to those hermits. All those hermits also attained the five superknowledges and the eight attainments.

At that time, the Buddha named Anomadassī appeared in the world. The royal capital was Candavatī; the father was King Yasavanta, and the mother was Queen Yasodharā. The Bodhi tree was the Ajjuna tree. The Elder Nisabha and the Elder Anoma were the two chief disciples. The Elder Varuṇa was the attendant. Sundarā and Sumanā were the two chief female disciples. The lifespan was one hundred thousand years, and his height was fifty-eight cubits. The radiance of his body spread for twelve yojanas. He had a retinue of one hundred thousand monks.
117:
Then one day at dawn, the Blessed One emerged from the Attainment of Great Compassion and, surveying the world, saw Sarada the hermit. He thought, 'Today, because of my journey to Sarada the hermit, there will be a great teaching of the Dhamma. That Sarada the hermit will also aspire for the position of Chief Disciple. His friend, Sirivaḍḍhana the merchant, will aspire for the position of Second Chief Disciple. At the conclusion of the teaching, his retinue of seventy-four thousand hermits will attain Arahantship. It is proper for me to go there.' Taking his bowl and robes, without inviting any other monk, he traveled alone like a lion king. While Sarada the hermit's disciples were away searching for various fruits, the Buddha, intending for him to recognize his Buddhahood, descended from the sky and stood on the ground while Sarada the hermit was watching. Seeing the Buddha's psychic power and the perfection of his physical form, Sarada the hermit reflected on the science of marks and realized, 'A person endowed with such marks, if he remains in the household life, will become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). If he renounces, he will become an Omniscient Buddha who has removed the roof of defilements in the world. This great man is certainly a Buddha.' He went out to welcome him, paid homage with the five-point prostration, and prepared and offered a seat. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Sarada the hermit also took a suitable seat for himself and sat in a proper place.

At that time, the seventy-four thousand hermits returned to their teacher, bringing various exquisite and nutritious fruits. Seeing the seats where the Buddha and their teacher were sitting, they said, 'Teacher, we have traveled about thinking that there is no one greater than you in this world. However, we think this great man is greater than you.' Sarada replied, 'Dear sons, what are you saying? Do you wish to make a mustard seed equal to Mount Sineru, which is one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas high? Dear sons, do not compare me with the Omniscient Buddha.' Then those hermits thought, 'If this person were an inferior being, our teacher would not have brought such a comparison. How great this man truly is!' and they all prostrated at his feet and paid homage with their heads. Then the teacher hermit said, 'Dear sons, we do not have offerings suitable for the Buddha. The Buddha has come here at the time of the alms-round. We shall offer what we can as gifts. Bring whatever exquisite fruits you have collected.' Having them brought, he washed his hands and personally [offered] into the Blessed One's bowl...
118: (Sarada the ascetic) placed the fruits in the bowl. As soon as the Teacher accepted the fruits, large and small, the deities infused them with divine essence. The ascetic himself filtered the drinking water and offered it. Then, after the meal was finished and the Teacher had washed his hands and was seated, the ascetic called all his disciples and sat near the Teacher, engaging in pleasant conversation. The Teacher thought, "Let the two chief disciples come together with the community of monks." Knowing the Teacher's thought, those chief disciples arrived accompanied by a hundred thousand Arahants, paid homage to the Teacher, and stood at a respectful distance. Then Sarada the ascetic addressed his disciples, "Friends, the seating place of the Buddhas is low, and there are no seats for the hundred thousand Arahants. Today, it is fitting for you to perform a grand offering to the Buddha. Bring flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain." Although the time taken to speak seemed long, the sphere of those with psychic power is inconceivable, and in just a moment, those ascetics brought flowers endowed with color and fragrance and prepared a flower seat for the Buddha measuring one league (yojana). For the two chief disciples, it was three gāvutas, for the remaining monks, it varied from half a league downwards, and for the new monks (navaka), it was about one usabha. When the seats were thus prepared, Sarada the ascetic stood before the Tathāgata with palms joined and said, "Venerable Sir, for my long-term welfare and happiness, please ascend and occupy this flower seat." Having collected various flowers and scents together and prepared the flower seat, he spoke these words: "O Heroic Buddha, this seat is prepared for you, befitting you. Making my heart clear and confident, please sit upon this flower seat." "The Buddha sat upon the flower seat for seven days and nights, making my heart clear and confident and gladdening the world including the devas." When the Teacher was thus seated, the two chief disciples and the remaining monks also sat in their respective appropriate seats. Sarada the ascetic took a large flower parasol and stood holding it over the Teacher's head. The Teacher, thinking, "May this offering of the matted-hair ascetics be of great fruit," entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Knowing that the Teacher had entered the attainment, the two chief disciples and the remaining monks...
119: The two chief disciples and the remaining monks also entered the attainment of cessation. While the Buddha Anomadassī sat having entered the attainment of cessation for seven days, the disciple ascetics, when it was time to seek alms, consumed forest roots and various fruits, and for the rest of the time, they stood with palms joined towards the Buddhas. Sarada the ascetic, however, did not even go to seek food; he spent the seven days in the bliss of rapture (pīti-sukha), just as he was, holding the flower parasol. The Teacher, having emerged from the attainment of cessation, addressed the chief disciple, Elder Nisabha, who was sitting on the right side, "Nisabha, deliver a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) for the flower seats to the ascetics who have made this offering." The Elder, with a joyful heart like a great warrior who had received a grand reward from a universal monarch, established himself in the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) and began the discourse of appreciation for the flower seats. At the end of that Elder's discourse, the Teacher addressed the second disciple, "You too, preach the Dhamma." Elder Anoma also reflected on the word of the Buddha known as the Tipitaka and preached the Dhamma. Through the preaching of the two chief disciples, not even a single ascetic attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths. Then the Teacher, established in the immeasurable sphere of a Buddha, began the Dhamma discourse. At the conclusion of the discourse, excluding Sarada the ascetic, all seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics attained Arahantship. The Teacher stretched out his hand and said, "Come, monks (Ehi bhikkhavo)." At that very moment, their hair and beards disappeared, and the eight requisites appeared as if worn on their bodies. Why did Sarada the ascetic not attain Arahantship? It was because his mind was distracted. It is said that from the time he began to listen to the discourse of the chief disciple, who sat in the second seat of the Buddhas and preached the Dhamma established in the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, the thought arose in him: "Oh, would that I too might obtain the post of chief disciple, just as this disciple has, in the dispensation of a Buddha to be born in the future!" Because of that thought, he was unable to penetrate the paths and fruits. That ascetic paid homage to the Teacher, stood before him, and asked, "Venerable Sir, who is this monk sitting in the seat next to you in your dispensation?" "He is the one who follows and turns the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me, who has reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, and who stands having penetrated the sixteenfold wisdom; he is the chief disciple in my dispensation, named Elder Nisabha." "Venerable Sir, by the merit of this offering made by me holding the flower parasol for seven days, I do not aspire to any other status such as that of Sakka or Brahmā. But in the future, may I become the chief disciple of a Buddha, just like this Elder Nisabha." Thus he made his aspiration.
120:
The Teacher, sending forth his knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) to see whether this man's aspiration would be fulfilled, saw that it would be fulfilled after the passing of one incalculable (asankheyya) and one hundred thousand aeons (kappas). Having seen this, he said to the ascetic Sarada: "This aspiration of yours shall not be in vain. In the future, after the passing of one incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world. His mother will be a queen named Mahāmāyā, his father a king named Suddhodana, his son will be named Rāhula, his attendant will be named Ānanda, and his second disciple will be named Moggallāna. You, however, will be his Chief Disciple, the General of the Dhamma (Dhamma-senāpati) named Sāriputta." Having thus given the prophecy to the ascetic and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, the Buddha, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, rose into the air.

The ascetic Sarada also went to the elder disciples and sent a message to his friend, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana: "Venerable sirs, please tell my friend: 'Your friend, the ascetic Sarada, at the feet of the Buddha Anomadassī, has made an aspiration for the position of Chief Disciple in the dispensation of the future Buddha Gotama; you, too, should aspire for the position of second disciple.'" Having said this, he went ahead of the elders from one side and stood at the door of Sirivaḍḍhana's house.

The householder Sirivaḍḍhana, saying, "It has been a long time since my lord has come," invited him to sit on a seat, while he himself sat on a lower seat and asked, "Venerable sir, your circle of disciples is not seen." "Yes, friend Sirivaḍḍhana, the Buddha named Anomadassī came to our hermitage, and we honored him to the best of our ability. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to all; at the end of the discourse, except for me, all the rest attained Arahantship and went forth as monks." When asked, "Why did you not go forth, venerable sirs?", he replied, "I saw the Elder Nisabha, the Chief Disciple of the Buddha, and made an aspiration for the position of Chief Disciple in the dispensation of the future Buddha named Gotama. You, too, should aspire for the position of second disciple in that Buddha's dispensation." When Sirivaḍḍhana said, "Venerable sir, I am not familiar with Buddhas," Sarada replied, "Let the responsibility of speaking with the Buddha be mine; you just prepare a great offering."
121:
The householder Sirivaḍḍhana, having heard the words of the ascetic Sarada, had an area of about eight karīsas on the main road at the door of his house leveled, scattered with sand, and strewn with flowers of five kinds including popped rice. He had a pavilion constructed with a roof of blue lotuses, arranged a seat for the Buddha and prepared seats for the remaining monks. Having prepared a grand and respectful offering, he gave a signal to the ascetic Sarada to invite the Buddhas. Upon hearing the householder's word, the ascetic brought the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to the householder's residence. Sirivaḍḍhana went out to meet them, took the alms-bowl from the hand of the Tathāgata, led them into the pavilion, and after they were seated on the prepared seats, he offered water of donation and served the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with choice food. After the meal, he offered the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha very costly garments and said, "Venerable sir, this effort is not for a small benefit; in this same manner, please show compassion to me for seven days." The Teacher consented.

The householder continued the great offering (mahādāna) in that same manner for seven days, then paid homage to the Blessed One and, standing with palms joined, said: "Venerable sir, my friend the ascetic Sarada has made an aspiration to be the Chief Disciple of whichever Teacher; I, too, wish to be the second disciple of that same Buddha."

The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, gave the prophecy: "After the passing of one incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons from now, you will become the second disciple of the Buddha Gotama." Hearing the Buddha's prophecy, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana was exceedingly joyful. The Teacher, having given the blessing after the meal, returned to the monastery with his followers. From then on, Sirivaḍḍhana performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and, in his second life, was reborn in the celestial realm of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-devaloka). The ascetic Sarada, having developed the four divine abidings (brahma-vihāra), was reborn in the Brahma world. From that time on, the intervening deeds of these two are not mentioned. Long before the birth of our Buddha, the ascetic Sarada took conception in the womb of the Brahmin lady Sārī in the village of Upatissa, not far from the city of Rājagaha. On that very same day, his friend also took conception in the womb of the Brahmin lady Moggallī in the village of Kolita, not far from Rājagaha. Those two families...
122:
These families were friends who had been continuously connected for seven generations. They provided pregnancy protection for both on the same day. When the children were born after ten months, sixty-six nurses attended to them. On the naming day, the son of the Brahmin woman Sārī was named 'Upatissa' because he was the son of the leading family in Upatissa village. The other was named 'Kolita' because he was the son of the leading family in Kolita village. As they grew up, both reached the further shore of all arts and sciences.

When the youth Upatissa went to the river, garden, or mountain for recreation, five hundred golden palanquins were his retinue. For the youth Kolita, five hundred carriages drawn by thoroughbred horses were his retinue. Both had retinues of five hundred youths each. In the city of Rājagaha, there was an annual festival called the 'Mountain Top Festival' (Giraggasamajja). A single couch was prepared for the two of them in one place. Sitting together and watching the festival, they would laugh when it was time to laugh, be moved when it was time to be moved, and give gifts when it was appropriate to give. In this manner, one day while watching the festival, because their wisdom had matured, they did not laugh at what was laughable, feel moved at what was moving, or give gifts as they had on previous days. Both of them thought: "What essence is there to behold in this festival? All these people, before a hundred years have passed, will reach a state where they can no longer be designated as living beings (death). It is proper for us to seek the one Dhamma of Liberation (Mokkhadhamma)." Thus, they sat reflecting on a single object of thought.

Then Kolita said to Upatissa: "Friend Upatissa, you are not joyful and cheerful as on other days; you seem troubled. What have you noticed?" Upatissa replied: "Friend Kolita, there is no essence in looking at these people; it is useless. I am sitting here thinking that it is proper to seek the Dhamma of Liberation for oneself." Then he asked: "And why are you troubled?" Kolita said the same. Then, knowing that their inclinations were identical, Upatissa said to him: "Both of us have thought well. For those seeking the Dhamma of Liberation, it is proper to obtain ordination. Under whom shall we ordain?"

At that time, the wanderer named Sañjaya was living in Rājagaha with a large following of wanderers. They thought: "We will ordain under this wanderer Sañjaya."
123:
They ordained under Sañjaya along with the five hundred youths. From the time they ordained, Sañjaya reached the pinnacle of gains, offerings, and fame. Within a few days, they mastered all of Sañjaya's doctrine and asked: "Teacher, is your known doctrine only this much, or is there more?" Sañjaya said: "It is only this much; you know the entire doctrine."

Hearing Sañjaya's words, they thought: "If this is so, living the holy life under this teacher is useless. We have come out to seek the Dhamma of Liberation (Mokkhadhamma), and it is impossible to attain it under this teacher. Jambudīpa is very vast; if we wander through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, we will surely find a teacher who can preach the Dhamma of Liberation." From that day on, whenever they heard that there were wise recluses or brahmins in certain places, they went there and engaged in discussions and questions. There was no one else capable of answering the questions they asked; rather, they were the ones who could answer the questions of those wise recluses and brahmins. Having thus explored the whole of Jambudīpa, they returned to their own place and made a pact: "Friend Kolita, whoever first attains the Deathless (Amata) shall inform the other."

At that time, our Teacher, the Buddha, having first realized the Four Noble Truths and set the Noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, had arrived at Rājagaha in due course. Then, when it was said that "Sixty-one Arahants have appeared in the world," the Elder Assaji, who was among the group of five (Pañcavaggiya) monks sent out to wander for the benefit of many and to manifest the virtues of the Triple Gem, returned and arrived at Rājagaha. The next morning, early, he took his bowl and robes and entered Rājagaha for alms.

At that time, the wanderer Upatissa, having finished his morning meal and going towards the wanderers' monastery, saw the Elder and thought: "I have never seen such a monk before. If there are Arahants in the world or those who have attained the Path to Arahantship, this monk must be one of them. What if I approach this monk and ask: 'Friend, on whose account have you ordained? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve of?'" Then he thought: "It is not the time to ask this monk questions; he is entering the village and wandering for alms. What if I follow closely behind this monk? Those who desire can understand the way." That Upatissa, [following] the Elder who had received alms...
124:
Seeing Elder Assaji going to a certain place and knowing his desire to sit, Upatissa spread out his own wanderer’s stool and offered it. When the meal was finished, he also gave him water from his own water-pot.

Having performed the duties toward a teacher in this way, and after exchanging pleasant greetings with the Elder who had finished his meal, he asked: “Friend, your faculties are very serene, and your complexion is pure and bright. Friend, on whose account have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve of?” The Elder replied: “Friend, there is the Great Samana, a son of the Sakyans, who went forth from the Sakyan clan. I have gone forth on account of that Blessed One. That Blessed One is my teacher, and I approve of the Dhamma of that Blessed One.” Then he asked: “What does your teacher proclaim? What does he teach?” The Elder thought: “These wanderers are opponents of the Dispensation; I will show him the depth of this Dispensation.” Showing his status as a newly ordained monk, he said: “Friend, I am newly ordained, not long gone forth, and have only recently come to this Dhamma-Vinaya. I am not yet able to teach the Dhamma to you in detail.” The wanderer thought: “I am named Upatissa. Speak little or much according to your ability; it is my responsibility alone to penetrate this teaching through a hundred or a thousand methods,” and he said:

“Speak little or much, but tell me only the essence;
I have need only of the essence; what will you do with many words and syllables?”

When this was said, the Elder recited the verse beginning with: “Ye dhammā hetuppabhavā” (Of those things that arise from a cause...). Upon hearing only the first two lines, the wanderer was established in the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), endowed with a thousand methods. The remaining two lines were completed when he became a Stream-enterer.

Having become a Stream-enterer, and noticing that higher distinctions did not yet arise, he reflected, “There must be a reason for this,” and said to the Elder: “Venerable Sir, do not further the Dhamma teaching for now; let it be just this much. Where does our Teacher dwell?” “He dwells at the Veḷuvana Monastery.” “Venerable Sir, you may proceed ahead. I have a friend. We have made a pact with each other: ‘Whoever first attains the Deathless (Amata) shall inform the other.’ I shall release myself from that promise and—”
125:
“—having taken my friend, I will come to the Teacher’s presence by the same path you have taken.” Saying this, he prostrated at the Elder’s feet with the fivefold prostration, circumambulated him three times, and after seeing the Elder off, he went toward the wanderers’ monastery.

Kolita the wanderer, seeing Upatissa coming from afar, thought: “Today the complexion of my friend’s face is not like other days; surely he must have attained the Deathless.” He then asked about the attainment of the Deathless. Upatissa acknowledged, “Yes, friend, the Deathless has been attained,” and recited the same verse. At the end of the verse, Kolita was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and asked: “Friend, where is it said the Teacher dwells?” “Friend, our teacher Elder Assaji told me he dwells at the Veḷuvana Monastery.” “In that case, friend, let us go; we shall see the Teacher.” Now, the Elder Sāriputta was one who always honored his teachers; therefore, he said to his friend, the youth Kolita: “Friend, let us also tell the Deathless Dhamma we have attained to our teacher, Sañjaya the wanderer. If he understands, he will penetrate the Truth; if he cannot penetrate it, he will follow us to the Teacher’s presence out of faith in our words. Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, he will be able to attain the Paths and Fruits.”

Then both of them went to Sañjaya and said: “Teacher, what are you doing? A Buddha has arisen in the world, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, and the Saṅgha is practicing well. Come, let us see the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala).” He asked: “What are you saying, dear ones?” and refusing them, he showed them only his own abundance of gain and following. They said: “Let such a life of being a disciple be for us forever; as for your going or not going, you decide for yourself.” Sañjaya, knowing “These people know this much and will no longer follow my words,” said: “Go, dear ones; I cannot live as a disciple in my old age.” Being unable to make the teacher understand through various reasons, they took the people who followed their advice and went to the Veḷuvana Monastery. At that time, of their five hundred disciples, two hundred and fifty turned back, and two hundred and fifty went along with them.

The Teacher, while preaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly, saw them from afar and addressed the monks: “Monks, these two friends, Kolita and Upatissa, are coming. These will be my pair of chief disciples, the excellent pair.” Then, he expanded the Dhamma teaching according to the temperaments of that assembly. Except for the two chief disciples, all those two hundred and fifty wanderers reached the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahatta-phala).
126:
(Those wanderers) attained the fruit of Arahantship. The Teacher stretched out his hand and said, "Come, monks" (Etha bhikkhavo). The hair and beards of all the monks disappeared, and robes and bowls created by psychic power appeared attached to their bodies. For the two chief disciples as well, robes and bowls created by psychic power arrived; however, the work of the three higher paths was not yet finished. Why? Because of the greatness of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa).

Then, on the seventh day after his ordination, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was dwelling near the village of Kallavāla in the Magadha country and practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, sloth and torpor (thina-middha) overcame him. Being stirred by the Teacher, he dispelled the sloth and torpor, and while listening to the meditation on the elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna) given by the Tathāgata, he completed the work of the three higher paths and reached the summit of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection. The Venerable Sāriputta, too, half a month (15 days) after his ordination, while dwelling with the Teacher near that same city of Rājagaha in the Sūkarakhata (Boar's Cave), sent forth his knowledge according to the discourse while the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being preached to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha. Like one eating food prepared for another, he reached the summit of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection. His nephew, however, was established in the fruit of stream-entry at the end of the discourse. Thus, the work of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection for both great disciples reached its summit while the Tathāgata was still residing in Rājagaha. Later, while the Teacher was residing at the Jetavana monastery, he appointed the two great disciples to their respective positions, saying, "This is the foremost among those of great wisdom, namely Sāriputta; this is the foremost among those of psychic power, namely Mahāmoggallāna."

## The Story of Mahākassapa Thera

In the fourth sutta, regarding the word "dhutavādānaṃ," one should understand dhuta, one should understand dhutavāda, one should understand the dhuta-dhammas, and one should understand the dhutaṅgas. Therein, dhuta refers to a person who has shaken off defilements or a quality (dhamma) that shakes off defilements.

In this context of dhutavāda, there is a person who is dhuta but not a dhutavāda; there is a person who is not dhuta but is a dhutavāda; there is a person who is neither dhuta nor a dhutavāda; and there is a person who is both dhuta and a dhutavāda. Among these four, the person who shakes off his own defilements through ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) but does not admonish or instruct others regarding ascetic practices, like the Venerable Bākula, is one who is dhuta but not a dhutavāda. Thus it was said: "This Venerable Bākula is dhuta but not a dhutavāda." He who...
127:
...however, does not shake off his own defilements through ascetic practices but merely admonishes and instructs others through ascetic practices, like the Venerable Upananda, is one who is not dhuta but is a dhutavāda. Thus it was said: "This Venerable Upananda is not dhuta but is a dhutavāda." He who is deficient in both, like the Venerable Lāḷudāyī, is one who is neither dhuta nor a dhutavāda. Thus it was said: "This Venerable Lāḷudāyī is neither dhuta nor a dhutavāda." He who is endowed with both, like the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera, is one who is both dhuta and a dhutavāda. Thus it was said: "This Venerable Mahākassapa is both dhuta and a dhutavāda."

Regarding "the dhuta-dhammas should be understood": fewness of wishes (appicchatā), contentment (santuṭṭhitā), effacement (sallekhatā), seclusion (pavivekatā), and desiring only what is necessary for the body (idam-aṭṭhikatā)—these five qualities, which are the attendants of the intention for ascetic practices, are called dhuta-dhammas according to the words beginning with "relying only on fewness of wishes." Among those five qualities, appicchatā and santuṭṭhitā are non-greed (alobha). Sallekhatā and pavivekatā fall within two qualities: non-greed and non-delusion (amoha). Idam-aṭṭhikatā is wisdom (ñāṇa) itself. Therein, through non-greed, one shakes off greed for objects that should be rejected. Through non-delusion, one shakes off the delusion that covers the faults in those same objects. Through non-greed, one shakes off the devotion to sensual pleasure (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) that arises by way of indulging in the four requisites that are permitted. Through non-delusion, one shakes off the devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) that arises by way of extreme effacement in ascetic practices. Therefore, these qualities should be understood as dhuta-dhammas.

Regarding "the dhutaṅgas should be understood": the thirteen ascetic practices should be understood, from the refuse-rag-robe practice (paṃsukūlika-aṅga) up to the sitter's practice (nesajjika-aṅga).

Regarding "Dhutavādānaṃ yadidaṃ mahākassapo": among all those who speak of shaking off defilements, this Venerable Mahākassapa Thera is the foremost; thus he was appointed to the foremost position. He is called "Mahākassapa" (Great Kassapa) to distinguish him as great in comparison to the junior elders such as Uruveḷa Kassapa, Nadī Kassapa, Gayā Kassapa, and Kumāra Kassapa.

This is the successive account of his aspiration: It is said that one hundred thousand aeons ago, a Teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world. While that Teacher Padumuttara was residing in the Khemā Deer Park near the city of Haṃsāvatī, a householder named Vedeha, who possessed wealth of eighty crores, ate a delicious meal early in the morning and [undertook] the factors of the Uposatha...
128:
Having undertaken the Uposatha precepts and taking perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he went to the monastery, worshipped the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place. At that moment, the Teacher appointed the third disciple named Mahānisabha Thera to the position of foremost, saying, "Monks, among my disciple monks who are speakers of dhutaṅga practices, this Nisabha is the foremost." Hearing this, the lay devotee Vedeha was inspired. When the crowd left at the end of the Dhamma talk, he worshipped the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept my alms-offering for tomorrow." The Teacher said, "Lay devotee, the community of monks is very large." He asked, "How many are there, Blessed One?" "There are six million eight hundred thousand monks," He replied. "Venerable Sir, please accept the alms-offering without leaving even a single novice in the monastery," he requested. The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent. Knowing the Teacher's acceptance, the lay devotee returned home, prepared a great offering, and the next day announced that it was time for the meal. The Teacher, taking his bowl and robes and surrounded by the community of monks, went to the lay devotee's house, sat on the prepared seat, and after the water of donation was poured, accepted the gruel and so forth, and partook of the meal. The lay devotee also sat near the Teacher.

In the meantime, Mahānisabha Thera, while wandering for alms, arrived at that very street. Seeing him, the lay devotee stood up, went to the Elder, worshipped him, and said, "Venerable Sir, please give me your bowl." The Elder gave him the bowl. "Venerable Sir, please enter this house; the Teacher is also sitting inside," he said. "Lay devotee, it is not proper for me," the Elder replied. The lay devotee took the Elder's bowl, filled it with alms-food, brought it back, and offered it. Then, after seeing the Elder off and returning, he sat near the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, although I told Mahānisabha Thera that the Teacher is in the house, he did not wish to enter. Does that Elder possess a special quality superior to your own virtues?" There is no such thing as envy of another's praise (vaṇṇamacchera) for Buddhas. Then the Teacher said, "Lay devotee, we sit in the house waiting for alms, but that monk does not wait for alms by sitting like this. We live in a monastery near a village, but that monk lives only in the forest. We live under a roof, but that monk lives only in the open air. Thus, he possesses such and such virtues," He explained, as if filling the great ocean. The lay devotee, like a lamp already burning that is then poured with oil, became even more inspired and thought, "What use is any other prosperity to me? I shall make an aspiration to become the foremost among those who practice dhutaṅga in the presence of a future Buddha."
129:
That lay devotee Vedeha invited the Teacher again and, in the same manner, gave a great alms-offering for seven days. On the seventh day, he offered triple robes to the community of monks headed by the Buddha and, prostrating at the Teacher's feet, said:

"Venerable Sir, while I have been giving alms for seven days, bodily actions associated with loving-kindness, verbal actions associated with loving-kindness, and mental actions associated with loving-kindness have been present before me. By this merit, I do not aspire for any other heavenly prosperity, nor the prosperity of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā. May this deed of mine be a realization for attaining the foremost position among the thirteen practitioners of dhutaṅga, the same position attained by this Mahānisabha Thera, in the presence of a future Buddha."

The Teacher, considering, "This man aspires for a great position; will it be fulfilled or not?" saw that it would be fulfilled and said, "Lay follower, you have aspired for a pleasing position. In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. You will be his third disciple, named Mahākassapa Thera."

Hearing those words, the lay devotee thought, "There is no such thing as two different words for Buddhas," and regarded that prosperity as if he would receive it the very next day. That lay devotee, having given various kinds of alms throughout his life, observed the precepts, and performed various good deeds, passed away from that human world and was reborn in heaven.

From then on, while experiencing prosperity in the worlds of gods and humans, ninety-one aeons ago from now, when Vipassī Buddha was dwelling in the Khema Deer Park depending on the city of Bandhumatī, he passed away from the deva world and was reborn in a poor Brahmin family.

At that time, Vipassī Buddha preached the Dhamma once every seven years, and there was a great commotion. Deities throughout the whole of Jambudīpa proclaimed, "The Teacher will preach the Dhamma!" The Brahmin heard that news.

That Brahmin had only one lower garment to wear. Likewise, the Brahmin woman had only one. As for the upper garment for wrapping around, there was only one for both of them. Therefore, he was known throughout the city as "Ekasaṭaka Brahmin." When there was a meeting for some business of the Brahmins, he would leave the Brahmin woman at home and go himself. When there was a meeting of Brahmin women, he would stay at home and the Brahmin woman would go, wearing that garment.

On the day of the great commotion for hearing the Dhamma, the Brahmin asked the Brahmin woman, "Lady, will you listen to the Dhamma during the night or during the day?" The Brahmin woman said, "We womenfolk are unable to listen to the Dhamma at night; I will listen only during the day." So, leaving the Brahmin at home and wearing that garment, she went during the day with other female lay devotees to the Teacher...
130:
The Brahmin woman, having paid homage to the Blessed One and sat in a suitable place, listened to the Dhamma and returned together with the other female lay devotees. Then the Brahmin, leaving the Brahmin woman at home and wrapping himself in that single garment, went to the monastery.

At that time, the Teacher was seated upon the decorated Dhamma-seat in the midst of the assembly. Holding a magnificent fan, he preached the Dhamma as if bringing down the celestial Ganges, or as if churning the great ocean using Mount Sineru as a churning stick. As the Brahmin sat at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, in the very first watch of the night, fivefold rapture (pīti) arose, pervading his entire body. He folded the garment he was wearing and thought, "I shall offer this to the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala)." At that moment, stinginess (macchariya), which points out a thousand faults, arose within him. He thought, "There is only this one garment for both the Brahmin woman and me; there is no other wrap. It is impossible to go outside without a cloak." Thus, he became unwilling to give in every way.

Then, when the first watch had passed and the middle watch arrived, rapture arose in the same manner. The Brahmin thought as before and remained unwilling to give. When the middle watch had passed and the last watch arrived, rapture arose once again. He decided, "Let there be life or death, I shall face the consequences later," and folding the garment, he placed it at the feet of the Teacher. Then, bending his left arm and striking his right arm against it three times, he shouted three times, "I have won! I have won!"

At that time, King Bandhuma was listening to the Dhamma while sitting behind a curtain at the back of the Dhamma-seat. To a king, the sound "I have won" is unpleasant. He sent a man, saying, "Go and ask him why he says this." When the man went and questioned him, the Brahmin replied, "Others, mounting elephants and the like, and wielding swords and shields, conquer enemy armies; such victory is not extraordinary. But I, as if breaking the head of a rogue bull following behind with a club and making it flee, have crushed the heart of stinginess and offered my cloak to the Possessor of Ten Powers. I have conquered that stinginess."

The man returned and reported the matter to the King. The King said, "Friends, we did not know what was worthy of the Possessor of Ten Powers; only the Brahmin knew," and he sent a pair of cloths. Seeing the pair of cloths, the Brahmin thought, "This King did not give me anything at first while I sat silently, but now he gives to me as I praise the virtues of the Teacher. What use is this pair of cloths to me, which I obtained by relying on the virtues of the Teacher?" and he offered that pair of cloths also to the Teacher.

The King asked, "What did the Brahmin do?" and upon hearing that he had offered that pair of cloths also to the Teacher, he sent another two pairs. The Brahmin offered those as well. The King sent another four pairs, and in this manner, he continued until he had sent thirty-two pairs of cloths. Then the Brahmin thought, "This giving is becoming like taking by increasing and increasing," and for himself...
131:
(The King) sent the pairs of cloths. The Brahmin thought, "What use is this pair of cloths to me, which arose due to the virtues of the Teacher?" and he offered that pair also to the Blessed One Vipassī. The King asked, "What did the Brahmin do?" and hearing that he had offered that pair also to the Teacher, he sent another two pairs. The Brahmin offered those two pairs as well. The King sent another four pairs, and so on, until he had sent thirty-two pairs. Then the Brahmin, thinking, "This giving is like taking by increasing," took two pairs—one for himself and one for the Brahmin woman—and offered the remaining thirty pairs to the Teacher. From then on, he became a close devotee of the Teacher.

Then one day, during the cold season, the King saw the Brahmin listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher. He gave him his own red woolen blanket (kambala) worth a hundred thousand, saying, "From today onwards, wear this blanket and listen to the Dhamma." The Brahmin thought, "What use is this blanket to me when placed upon this foul body (pūtikāya)?" and he went and made it into a canopy over the Teacher's bed inside the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). Later, early one morning, the King went to the monastery and sat in the presence of the Teacher inside the Perfumed Chamber. At that time, the six-colored Buddha-rays struck the blanket, and the blanket appeared exceedingly beautiful. The King, looking at it, recognized it and said, "Venerable Sir, this blanket is ours; we gave it to the Brahmin Ekasāṭaka." The Buddha replied, "Great King, you honored the Brahmin, and the Brahmin honored me."

The King, being inspired with faith, thought, "The Brahmin knew what was appropriate, but we did not." He then prepared all things useful to humans in groups of eight and gave the donation known as the "Gift of Eights" (Sabba-aṭṭhaka), and appointed him to the position of Chaplain (Purohita). That Chaplain, knowing that "eight of eight kinds makes sixty-four," arranged sixty-four ticket-meals (salākabhatta) and gave alms for the rest of his life. He maintained his virtue, and after passing away, he was reborn in heaven.

After passing away from that heaven, he was reborn in this auspicious aeon (Bhadda-kappa) in the house of a householder in Vārāṇasī, during the interval between the two Buddhas, Koṇāgamana and Kassapa. When he came of age and was living the life of a householder, he was walking in the forest one day to relieve his weariness. At that time, a Paccekabuddha was making a robe on the riverbank, and as the border material (anuvāta) was insufficient, he began to fold it and put it away. The householder's son, seeing this, asked, "Venerable Sir, why are you folding it and putting it away?" The border...
132:
"It is not enough," he said. "Venerable sir, please make a border with this cloth," he requested, offering his upper garment and making the aspiration: "In every place I am reborn, may I never suffer any loss."

At that time, in the house of that householder's son, while the sister was quarreling with her sister-in-law, a Paccekabuddha entered for alms. Then, the sister of the householder's son offered alms-food to the Paccekabuddha and, referring to the wife of the householder's son, made the aspiration: "May I be kept a hundred leagues away from such a fool." The wife of the householder's son, standing at the door of the house, heard these words and thought, "May this monk not eat the food offered by this sister-in-law." She took the bowl, threw away the alms-food, filled it with mud, and gave it back. Seeing this, the other (the sister) said, "You fool, abuse me or strike me first if you wish. But it is not proper to throw away food from the bowl of such a Venerable One, who has fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable eons, and give him mud instead." Then, remorseful reflection arose in the wife of the householder's son. She said, "Wait, venerable sir," threw away the mud, washed the bowl, rubbed it with scented powder, filled it with the four sweet foods (catumadhura), poured ghee the color of a lotus calyx on top, and placed the shining alms-food into the hands of the Paccekabuddha. The wife of the householder's son made the aspiration: "Just as this alms-food is radiant, so may my body be radiant." The Paccekabuddha gave a blessing and flew into the sky. Those two, husband and wife, performed meritorious deeds throughout their lives and were reborn in heaven. Passing away from there, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, the lay follower was reborn in Bārāṇasī as the son of a treasurer with a wealth of eighty crores. The other (the wife) was also reborn as the daughter of a similar treasurer.

When the householder's son reached maturity, they brought that same treasurer's daughter to him. Because of the power of that bad deed committed in a previous life which had not yet yielded its full result, as soon as she entered her husband's house, within the threshold, her entire body began to emit a foul odor like an open latrine. The treasurer's son asked, "Whose smell is this?" and hearing it was the treasurer's daughter's, he said, "Take her away," and sent her back to her family's house in the same manner she was brought. In this way, she was sent back from seven different places.

At that time, the Kassapa Buddha attained Parinibbāna. For that Buddha, they began building a stupa one league high with golden bricks worth a hundred thousand each. While the stupa was being built, the treasurer's daughter thought, "I have been rejected and sent back from seven places. What is the use of my life?"
133:
She had the ornaments she wore on her body broken down and made into a golden brick, one cubit long, one span wide, and four finger-breadths thick. Then, taking a lump of yellow orpiment (haritāla) and red realgar (manosilā), and carrying eight bunches of lotuses, she went to the site where the stupa was being built. At that moment, as a row of bricks was being laid around, one brick was missing to join the two ends. The treasurer's daughter said to the mason, "Please place this brick here." The mason replied, "Dear lady, you have come at a good time; place it yourself."

The treasurer's daughter climbed up, mixed the orpiment and realgar with oil, used that mixture as mortar to set the brick, and after making an offering with the eight bunches of lotuses on top, she paid homage and made the aspiration: "In every place I am reborn, may the scent of sandalwood waft from my body, and the scent of blue lotuses waft from my mouth." After paying homage to the stupa and circumambulating it clockwise (padakkhiṇa), she departed.

Then, at that very moment, the treasurer's son, who had first taken her to his home, remembered the treasurer's daughter. In the city, a festival had been proclaimed. The treasurer's son asked his attendants, "Friends, there was a treasurer's daughter who was brought here then; where is she?" When they said, "Lord, she is at her parents' house," he said, "Bring her here; we shall celebrate the festival." Those attendants went, paid respects to the treasurer's daughter, and stood there. When asked by her, "Brothers, why have you come?" they told her the reason.

"Brothers, I have offered the ornaments I wore to the stupa; I have no ornaments left," she said. The attendants went and told the treasurer's son. He said, "Bring her; she will receive ornaments to wear." So they brought the treasurer's daughter. As soon as she entered the house, the scent of sandalwood and blue lotuses wafted throughout the entire house.

The treasurer's son asked her, "Previously, a foul odor wafted from your body, but now the scent of sandalwood wafts from your body and the scent of blue lotuses from your mouth; why is this?" The treasurer's daughter told him of the meritorious deed she had performed from the beginning. The treasurer's son, being inspired, thought, "The Buddha's Dispensation is indeed a means of deliverance from suffering!" He had the golden stupa, one league in height, covered with a woolen robe-shroud and decorated it here and there with golden lotuses the size of chariot wheels. From those golden lotuses, jewel-tassels twelve cubits long were suspended. That treasurer's son remained in that human world for the rest of his life and was reborn in heaven. When he passed away from heaven, he was reborn in a minister's family in a place about one league from Bārāṇasī. The treasurer's daughter also passed away from the deva world and was reborn as the eldest daughter in a royal family.
134:
When the minister's son and the princess reached maturity, a festival was proclaimed in the village where the minister's son lived. The minister's son said to his mother, "Mother, give me a cloth; I will play at the festival." The mother took out a washed cloth and gave it to him. "Mother, this cloth is very coarse; give me another," he said. She took out another and gave it, but he rejected that too. Again, she took out another, and he rejected it as well.

Then the mother said to her son, "Dear son, we were born in such a house; we do not have the merit to obtain a cloth more delicate and soft than this." "Mother, if that is so, I shall go to a place where such cloth can be obtained," he replied. The mother said, "Dear son, I wish for you to obtain the kingship in the city of Bārāṇasī this very day." The minister's son paid homage to his mother and said, "Mother, I shall go." The mother said, "Go, dear son." However, in her mind, she thought, "Where will this son go? He will likely just sit here or there, or perhaps just stay in the house."

Due to the power of his merit, the minister's son left the house, went to the city of Bārāṇasī, and lay down on the ceremonial stone slab (Maṅgalasilāpaṭṭa) in the park, covering himself including his head. That day was the seventh day after the King of Bārāṇasī had passed away.

After performing the king's funeral rites, the ministers sat in the royal courtyard and consulted together, saying, "The king had only one daughter and no son. A kingdom without a king is not proper. Who should become king?" After consulting, they said to one another, "You be the king," "You be the king." The chaplain (Purohita) said, "It is not proper to search extensively; let us release the festive chariot (Phussaratha)."

The ministers harnessed four Sindh horses, white as kumuda lilies, placed the five royal regalia (Pañca-rājakakudhabhaṇḍa) and the white parasol (Setacchatta) on the chariot, released the chariot, and had musical instruments played behind it. The chariot exited through the eastern gate and headed toward the park. Some said, "The chariot is heading toward the park out of habit; let us turn it back." But the chaplain said, "Do not turn it back."

The chariot circled the young man clockwise and stood ready for him to mount. The chaplain moved aside the edge of the covering cloth and, looking at the soles of his feet, said, "Let alone this island of Jambudīpa, this man is worthy to rule even over the four great islands with their two thousand surrounding small islands." He then ordered, "Play the musical instruments again! Play the musical instruments again!" and had them played three times.

Then the young man uncovered his face, looked out, and asked, "Friends, for what purpose have you come?" "Great King, the kingship has come to you," they replied. "Where is the king?" he asked. "Sire, he has gone to the world of the gods (passed away)," they replied. "How many days has it been?" he asked. "Today...
135:
...is the seventh day," they replied. "Does the king have no son or daughter?" he asked. "Sire, there is a daughter, but no son," they replied. "I shall take up the kingship," he declared. At that very moment, the ministers had a consecration pavilion built, adorned the princess with all kinds of ornaments, brought her to the park, and performed the consecration (Abhiseka) of the young man.

Then, they offered the consecrated king a set of garments worth a thousand pieces. The king asked, "Friends, what is this for?" "Great King, it is for wearing," they replied. "Friends, is this cloth not very coarse? Is there no other more delicate cloth?" he asked. "Great King, among the garments used by humans, there is no cloth more delicate than this," they replied. "Did your king wear such as this?" he asked. "Yes, Great King," they replied. "I do not think your king was a man of great merit. Bring a golden pitcher (Suvaṇṇabhiṅgāra); we shall obtain cloth," he commanded. The ministers brought a golden pitcher. The king rose, washed his hands and rinsed his face, then taking water in his hand, he sprinkled it toward the eastern direction. At that very moment, breaking through the thick earth, eight wish-fulfilling trees (Kapparukkha) sprang up. Again, taking water, he sprinkled it in the south, west, and north directions. Thus, in all four directions, eight trees each, a total of thirty-two wish-fulfilling trees sprang up. The king put on one celestial garment and draped another over his shoulders. He then had a drum beaten throughout the kingdom of King Nanda, proclaiming, "Let no women who spin thread spin any more thread." He then had the white parasol raised, and being fully adorned and prepared, he mounted a noble elephant, entered the city, ascended the palace, and enjoyed great prosperity.

As time passed, one day the Queen, seeing the King's great prosperity, showed a compassionate expression, saying, "Oh, how pitiful!" When asked, "Queen, why is this?" she replied, "Great King, your prosperity is indeed very great. In the past, you believed in the Buddhas and performed good deeds. But now, you do not perform any wholesome deeds that would be the cause for future prosperity." "To whom shall I give? There are no virtuous ones," he said. "Great King, the island of Jambudīpa is not empty of Arahants. You just prepare the offerings; I will find the Arahants," she replied. The next day, the King had offerings prepared at the eastern gate. Early in the morning, the Queen undertook the Uposatha vows, and on the upper floor of the palace, facing the east, she prostrated herself on her breast and made an aspiration: "If there are Arahants in this direction, may they come tomorrow and accept our alms." There were no Arahants in that direction, so they gave the prepared offerings to the poor and beggars.
136:
On the following day, he prepared an offering at the southern gate and did the same. On the next day, he did the same at the western gate. On the day the offering was prepared at the northern gate, the Queen extended an invitation in the same manner. Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha, the eldest of the five hundred Paccekabuddhas who were the sons of Queen Padumavatī and were residing in the Himālayas, addressed his younger brothers: "Friends, King Nanda invites you; please accept his invitation." Having accepted, they washed their faces at Lake Anotatta the next day and, traveling through the air, descended at the northern gate. People went and informed the King, "Great King, five hundred Paccekabuddhas have arrived." The King, along with the Queen, went and paid homage, took their alms bowls, and invited the Paccekabuddhas up to the palace, where he made an offering. After the meal, the King knelt at the feet of the Sanghatthera (the eldest) Paccekabuddha, and the Queen knelt at the feet of the Sanghanavaka (the youngest) Paccekabuddha, saying: "Venerable sirs, may you not be weary for lack of the four requisites; may we not decline in merit. Please give us your word to reside here for the rest of your lives for our sake." Having secured their promise, they prepared a residence within the royal garden with five hundred leaf-huts and five hundred walkways in every detail and had them reside there.

As time passed in this way, a rebellion broke out in the King's border region. Then the King advised the Queen, saying, "I shall go to suppress the border rebellion; do not be negligent in attending to the Paccekabuddhas," and departed. Even before the King returned, the life-force of the Paccekabuddhas was exhausted. Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha, after spending the three watches of the night in meditative play (jhāna-kīḷā), at dawn, while leaning against a support plank and remaining standing, attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). In this same manner, all the remaining Paccekabuddhas also attained Parinibbāna. The next day, the Queen had the Paccekabuddhas' residence smeared with fresh cow dung, scattered flowers, lit incense, and sat waiting for the arrival of the venerable ones. Seeing that they did not come, she sent a man, saying, "Go, dear man, find out if anything is unwell with the venerable ones." That man went and opened the door of Mahāpaduma's leaf-hut. Not seeing him there, he went to the walkway and saw him standing, leaning against the support plank. He paid homage and said, "Venerable sir, it is time for the meal." How could a body that has attained Parinibbāna speak? Thinking, "He must be asleep," he went closer and touched the top of the foot with his hand. Realizing from the coldness and stiffness of the feet that he had attained Parinibbāna, he went to the second, then the third, and so on. Having realized that all the venerable ones had attained Parinibbāna, he went to the royal palace. When asked, "Dear man, where are the Paccekabuddhas?" he replied, "Your Majesty, they have attained Parinibbāna."
137: The Queen, wailing and weeping, left the city with the people and went to the place where the Paccekabuddhas had attained Parinibbāna. She had grand funeral honors performed, carried out the final rites for the Paccekabuddhas, took the relics, and enshrined them in a stupa. When King Nanda returned after suppressing the border rebellion, he asked the Queen who had come to welcome him, "My dear, were you not negligent toward the venerable Paccekabuddhas? Are the venerable ones free from illness?" "Great King, they have attained Parinibbāna," she replied. The King thought, "Even for such wise beings, death occurs; where can there be escape from death for us?" He did not enter the city but went straight into the garden, summoned his eldest son, handed over the kingship to him, and himself became an ascetic. The Queen also thought, "If the King becomes a monk, what shall I do?" and became an ascetic in that very garden. Both of them developed meditative absorption (jhāna) and, upon passing away, were reborn in the Brahma realm. While they were living in the Brahma realm, our Teacher (the Buddha) appeared in the world, set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and in due course entered the city of Rājagaha. While the Teacher was residing in Rājagaha, this Pipphali youth was conceived in the womb of the chief consort of the Brahmin Kapila in the Brahmin village of Mahātittha in the kingdom of Magadha. This Bhaddā Kāpilānī was also conceived in the womb of the chief consort of a Brahmin of the Kosiya clan in the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda. As they grew up in due course, when Pipphali youth reached twenty years of age and Bhaddā reached sixteen, his parents looked at their son and pressured him greatly, saying, "Dear son, you have reached the proper age; the family lineage must be established." The youth said, "Do not speak such words in my hearing. As long as you are alive, I will look after you. After your passing, I will renounce the world and become an ascetic." After a few days, the parents spoke again, and the youth refused in the same way. They spoke again, and he refused again. From then on, the mother spoke to him constantly. The youth thought, "I will make my mother understand," and giving a thousand nikkhas of red gold, he had goldsmiths fashion a golden statue of a woman. When the work of polishing and smoothing was finished, he had it dressed in red cloth, adorned with beautiful flowers and various ornaments, and then summoned his mother, saying, "Mother, if I find an object of such quality, I will stay at home. If not..."
138:
He said, "I will not stay at home." The wise Brahmin woman thought, "My son is meritorious; he has given gifts and made aspirations. When performing merit, he did not do so alone. Surely there must be a woman, resembling a golden statue, who performed merit together with him." She then summoned eight Brahmins, satisfied them with all sensual pleasures, placed the golden statue on a chariot, and sent them off, saying, "Go, dear ones. Wherever you see a maiden of such a nature in a family equal to ours in birth, clan, and wealth, present this very golden statue as a gift."

The Brahmins, saying, "This is indeed our task," set out. Thinking, "Where shall we go?" they decided, "The Madda kingdom is a source of precious women; let us go to the Madda kingdom." They went to the city of Sāgala in the Madda kingdom. There, they placed the golden statue at a bathing ghat and sat down to one side.

At that time, Bhaddā’s nurse, having bathed and adorned Bhaddā and seated her in a magnificent chamber, came to bathe herself. Seeing the statue, she thought, "My lady has come here." Scolding her, she said, "You ill-bred girl, why have you come here?" and raising her hand, she struck the statue on the cheek, saying, "Go quickly!" Her hand shook as if it had struck a stone. She stepped back and said, "Seeing such a firm and large neck, I thought it was my lady. This statue is not even fit to be the maid who handles my lady's garments."

Then those men surrounded the nurse and asked, "Is your lady of such an appearance?" She replied, "What is this statue worth? My lady is a hundred times, a thousand times more beautiful than this. When she sits in a twelve-cubit chamber, there is no need to light a lamp; the radiance of her body alone dispels the darkness." "If that is so, come," they said. Taking the nurse and placing the golden statue on the chariot, they stood at the door of the Brahmin of the Kosiya clan and announced their arrival.

The Brahmin welcomed them and asked, "Where have you come from?" "From the house of the Brahmin Kapila in Mahātittha village in the Magadha kingdom," they replied. "For what reason have you come?" they were asked. "For such and such a reason," they said. "It is well, dear ones. That Brahmin is equal to us in birth, clan, and wealth. I shall give the maiden," he said, and accepted the gift. Those Brahmins sent a message to the Brahmin Kapila, saying, "The maiden is found; perform what needs to be done." Hearing that message, they told the youth Pipphali, "It is said that a maiden has been found." The youth thought, "I thought they would not find one, but now they say they have. Since I have no desire for this, I will send a letter." Going to a private place...
139:
The youth Pipphali wrote a letter: "May Bhaddā obtain a household life suitable to her birth, clan, and wealth. I shall depart and become a monk. Do not be regretful later." Bhaddā also, hearing "They wish to give me to such and such a person," went to a private place and wrote a letter: "May the noble son obtain a household life suitable to his birth, clan, and wealth. I shall depart and become a monk. Do not be regretful later." The two letters met on the way. When asked, "Whose letter is this?" they said, "It is the letter sent by the youth Pipphali to Bhaddā." When asked, "Whose is this?" they said, "It is the letter sent by Bhaddā to the youth Pipphali." Having read both, they said, "Look at the behavior of these children!" and tearing them up, they threw them away in the forest. Then, writing an identical letter, they sent it to both sides. Thus, even though they were unwilling, the union of the two took place.

On that very day, the youth Pipphali took a flower garland and placed it. Bhaddā also took a flower garland and placed it. They placed those garlands in the middle of the bed. After eating their evening meal, both came together, saying, "Let us go to bed." The youth Pipphali got onto the bed from the right side. Bhaddā, having got on from the left side, said, "On whosever side the flowers wither, let it be known that a thought of lust has arisen in that person. This flower garland must not be touched." Fearing physical contact with each other, they spent the three watches of the night without falling asleep. During the day, there was not even a mere smile. They did not indulge in sensual pleasures and, as long as their parents were alive, they did not manage the estate. Only when their parents passed away did they take charge.

The wealth of the youth Pipphali was immense, amounting to eighty-seven koṭis. The gold dust discarded daily from scrubbing his body alone amounted to twelve Magadhan measures (nāḷi). There were sixty large tanks fitted with machinery. The estate spanned twelve yojanas. There were fourteen villages as large as the city of Anurādhapura, fourteen divisions of elephants, fourteen divisions of cavalry, and fourteen divisions of chariots.

One day, he mounted an adorned horse and, surrounded by a large crowd, went to the workplace. While standing at the edge of the field, he saw crows and other birds picking up and eating worms and other insects from the places turned up by the plows. He asked, "Dear ones, what are these birds eating?" "They are eating worms, lord," they replied. "To whom does the evil kamma committed by these birds belong?" he asked. "It belongs to you, lord," they replied. Then the youth Pipphali thought, "If the evil committed by these birds falls upon me, what should I do? What benefit is there for me in eighty-seven koṭis of wealth, a twelve-yojana estate, sixty tanks with machinery, and fourteen villages? I shall hand over all this wealth to Bhaddā Kāpilānီ, leave the house, and become a monk." At that moment, Bhaddā Kāpilānī was also sitting surrounded by her nurses, having spread out three measures (pattha) of sesame in the courtyard. Seeing crows eating the sesame pests...
140:
“If the demerit committed by these birds becomes mine, what benefit can eighty-seven koṭis of wealth, an estate twelve yojanas in extent, sixty tanks fitted with sluices, and fourteen villages provide for me? Having handed over all this wealth to Bhaddā Kāpilānī, I shall leave home and go forth.” Thus he reflected.

Bhaddā Kāpilānī, at that moment, had three jars of sesame seeds spread out in the courtyard. While sitting surrounded by her nurses, she saw crows eating the sesame worms and asked, “Mothers, what are these crows eating?” “Lady, they are eating sesame worms,” they replied. “To whom does the demerit belong?” she asked. “It belongs to you, lady,” they said. Then Bhaddā thought, “For me, four cubits of cloth and a measure of rice are sufficient. If the demerit committed by so many people becomes mine, I will certainly not be able to lift my head from the round of suffering even in a thousand births. As soon as my lord returns, I shall hand over everything to him and leave home to go forth.”

The young man returned, bathed, ascended the palace, and sat on a magnificent throne. Then, a meal worthy of a universal monarch (Cakkavatti) was prepared for him. After the two had eaten and the attendants had left, they sat in a secluded place.
