The young man asked Bhaddā, “Bhaddā, how much wealth did you bring when you came to this house?” “My lord, it was fifty-five thousand carts,” she said. “I hand over all that wealth to you, along with the eighty-seven koṭis of wealth in this house, the sixty tanks fitted with sluices, and all other possessions,” he said. “My lord, where will you go?” she asked. “I shall go forth,” he replied. “My lord, I too have been sitting here waiting for your arrival; I too shall go forth,” she said. To the two of them, the three planes of existence appeared like a burning leaf-hut. They sent for saffron-dyed robes and clay bowls from the market, shaved each other's hair, and saying, “Our going forth is dedicated to those who are Arahants in the world,” they placed their bowls in bags, slung them over their shoulders, and descended from the palace. Not a single slave or worker in the house noticed them.

Then, having left the Brahmin village and passing through the gate of the servants' village, the villagers recognized them by their appearance and gait. They wept, prostrated at their feet, and said, “My lords, why do you leave us helpless?” “Friends, we go forth because we see the three planes of existence like a burning leaf-hut. You should wash your own heads and live as those liberated from servitude.” They departed even as the people were weeping. While the Elder was walking ahead, he looked back and thought, “This Bhaddā Kāpilānī is a woman worth the whole of Jambudīpa, and she follows behind me. There is reason for someone to think, ‘Even though they have gone forth, they cannot part and are acting inappropriately.’ Some might become angry and towards us...”
141:
“If I were to make each of you free, it would not be finished or sufficient even in a hundred years. Therefore, wash your own heads and live as free people.” Having said this, they departed even as the people were weeping. While the Elder was walking ahead, he looked back and reflected: “This Bhaddā Kāpilānī is a woman worth the whole of Jambudīpa, and she follows behind me. It is possible that someone might think, ‘Even after going forth, these two cannot be apart; they are doing what is unsuitable.’ Or some might have a corrupt mind towards us and fill the states of woe (apāya). It is proper for me to go after leaving her.” Such a thought arose.

As the young Pipphali walked ahead, he saw a fork in the road and stood at the junction. Bhaddā also arrived, paid homage, and stood there. Then he said to her, “Bhaddā, seeing a woman like you following behind me, people might think, ‘Even after going forth, they cannot be apart,’ and with corrupt minds towards us, they will fill the states of woe. At this fork in the road, you take one path, and I will go by the other.”

“It is so, venerable sir. For those who have gone forth, women are a stain. They will see our fault, saying, ‘Even after going forth, they cannot be apart.’ You, venerable sir, take one path, and I shall take another, and we shall be apart.” Having said this, she circumambulated him three times, paid homage at four points with the five-point prostration, and raising her joined palms, which shone with the meeting of her ten fingernails, she said, “The friendship and intimacy established over a period of a hundred thousand aeons (kappas) is broken today.” She continued, “Venerable sir, you are of the right-hand nature; the right path is suitable for you. We women are of the left-hand nature; the left path is suitable for us.” Having paid homage, she set out on her path. When the two of them parted, this great earth roared and trembled as if saying, “Though I can bear the Cakkavāḷa mountains and Mount Sineru, I cannot bear your virtues.” A sound like thunder occurred in the sky, and the Cakkavāḷa mountains echoed.

The Fully Enlightened One, sitting in the Gandhakuṭī of the Veḷuvana Monastery, heard the sound of the earthquake and reflected, “On whose account does the earth tremble?” He realized, “The young Pipphali and Bhaddā Kāpilānī have gone forth for my sake, renouncing immeasurable wealth. At the place of their parting, this earthquake has occurred due to the power of the virtues of both. It is proper for me to show them favor and support.” Thinking thus, he departed from the Gandhakuṭī...”
142:
The Blessed One himself took his bowl and robes and, without inviting even a single one of the eighty great elders, traveled a distance of three gāvutas to meet [Kassapa]. Between the city of Rājagaha and the town of Nālandā, at the foot of a banyan tree named Bahuputtaka, he sat down cross-legged. When he sat there, he did not sit like an ordinary monk who wears rag-robes, but assuming the form of a Buddha, he sat emitting dense Buddha-rays of eighty cubits. At that moment, the Buddha-rays, having the dimensions of leaf-umbrellas, cartwheels, and the pinnacles of gabled houses, flickered and darted here and there, making that forest shine with a single radiance as if a thousand moons and a thousand suns had risen. The forest was as beautiful as the sky with a brilliant host of stars through the glory of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, or like a body of water with well-bloomed paduma, kumuda, white, red, and blue lotuses. The trunk of a banyan tree is usually white, its leaves green, and its fruits red. However, on that day, that hundred-branched banyan tree appeared entirely golden in color.

Venerable Mahākassapa thought, 'This noble one will be my teacher; it is for his sake that I have gone forth.' From the moment he saw him, he approached with great humility, and having bowed at three places, he said: 'Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am the disciple. Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am the disciple.' Then the Blessed One said to the Elder: 'Kassapa, if you were to show such deep respect to the great earth, even it would be unable to bear it. But for the Tathāgata, who knows the greatness of such virtues, the respect you show cannot move even a single hair of mine. Sit, Kassapa, I shall give you your inheritance.' Then the Blessed One granted him ordination through three exhortations. Having granted it, he departed from the foot of the Bahuputtaka banyan tree and proceeded on the journey with the Elder as his attendant monk. The Buddha's body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, while Mahākassapa's body was adorned with seven marks of a Great Man. Mahākassapa followed the Buddha's footsteps like a small boat towed behind a great golden ship. After the Blessed One had walked a short distance, he stepped off the path and indicated his desire to sit at the foot of a certain tree. The Elder, knowing that 'The Blessed One wishes to sit,' folded his own old double-layered rag-robe (saṅghāṭi) into four and spread it out.

Then the Blessed One sat on that robe, and stroking the robe with his hand, he said: 'Kassapa, this old rag-robe of yours is very soft.' The Elder [thought], 'The Blessed One...'
143:
Knowing that 'The Blessed One remarks on the softness of my rag-robe; he must wish to wear it,' the Elder said: 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One wear this rag-robe.' When asked, 'Kassapa, what will you wear?', he replied, 'Venerable sir, if I receive the robe worn by you, I shall wear it.' The Buddha said: 'Kassapa, will you be able to wear this worn-out rag-robe used by me? On the day I took this rag-robe, the great earth shook to its water-limit. This robe used and worn out by Buddhas cannot be worn by one of little virtue. It is fitting only for one who is capable, able to fulfill the practice, and a rag-robe wearer by nature to take it.' Having said this, he exchanged robes with the Elder.

Having thus exchanged robes, the Blessed One wore the robe previously worn by the Elder, and the Elder wore the robe of the Teacher. At that moment, even this insentient great earth shook to its water-limit, as if saying: 'Venerable sir, you have done a difficult thing; never before has a robe worn by oneself been given to a disciple; I am unable to bear your virtues.' The Elder, without pride, thinking 'Now I have received the robe used by the Buddhas; what more is there for me to do?', undertook the thirteen ascetic practices (dhuta-guṇa) in the presence of the Buddha. Remaining a worldling for seven days, at dawn on the eighth day, he attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The Teacher praised the Elder with discourses such as: 'Monks, Kassapa is like the moon; when approaching families, he draws back his body and mind, always like a newcomer, not bold in body, speech, or mind.' Later, based on this very Kassapa Saṃyutta, he placed the Elder in the pre-eminent position: 'Among my disciples who are proponents of the ascetic practices, Mahākassapa is the foremost.'

## The Story of Venerable Anuruddha

In the fifth sutta, the phrase 'Among those with the divine eye, that is, Anuruddha' means that among the monks possessing the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), Venerable Anuruddha is the foremost. His pre-eminence should be understood through his practiced mastery (vasībhāva). It is said that the Elder, except for the short time spent seeking food and eating, spent the rest of his time developing light and dwelling while observing beings with his divine eye. Thus, through his mastery practiced day and night, he became the foremost among those with the divine eye. Furthermore, because of his aspiration made for a hundred thousand aeons, he became the foremost among those with the divine eye.
144:
Regarding the aspiration made throughout those hundred thousand aeons, the successive account of the Elder Anuruddha’s past kamma is as follows: This young man, the future Anuruddha, also went along with a great crowd of people going to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma in the afternoon during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. At that time, this young man was a wealthy householder, though obscure and undistinguished. Having paid homage to the Ten-Powered One, he stood at the edge of the assembly and listened to the Dhamma discourse. The Teacher, connecting the discourse in its proper sequence, appointed a certain monk who possessed the divine eye to the foremost position in that regard.

Then the householder thought: "Great indeed is this monk, whom the Teacher himself has appointed to the foremost position among those with the divine eye. Oh, how wonderful it would be if I too, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, were to become the foremost among those with the divine eye!" Having aroused this thought, he went through the assembly and invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks for the following day. On the next day, having given a great offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, he thought, "I aspire to a great position." In that same manner, inviting them day after day, he maintained a great offering for seven days. After offering excellent robes to the Blessed One and his retinue, he said: "Venerable Sir, I do not perform this act of reverence for the sake of heavenly or human prosperity. Rather, seven days ago, you appointed a monk to the foremost position among those with the divine eye. May I too, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, become the foremost among those with the divine eye, just like that monk." Having made this aspiration, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet. The Blessed One, looking into the future and knowing that the householder's aspiration would be fulfilled, said: "Good man, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In his dispensation, you will be the one named Anuruddha, the foremost among those with the divine eye." Having said this and given the blessing after the meal, he returned to the monastery.

The householder also performed meritorious deeds without interruption as long as the Buddha lived. When the Teacher attained Parinibbāna and a golden stūpa seven yojanas high was completed, he approached the Saṅgha and asked: "Venerable sirs, what is the preliminary practice for the divine eye?" When they replied, "Lay follower, it is proper to give the gift of lamps," he said, "Very well, sirs, I shall do so." He first had a thousand lamp-stands made for a thousand lamps. After that, he had many thousands of lamp-stands made, some smaller than the first, and others even smaller than those. As for the remaining lamps, they were beyond measure.
145:
Thus, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, after a hundred thousand aeons had passed, he was reborn in a householder's family in Bārāṇasī during the time of the Buddha Kassapa. When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna and a stūpa one yojana high was completed, he had many bronze bowls made and filled them with clarified butter. Placing a lump of molasses in the center of each, he lit them and arranged them around the stūpa so that their rims touched. He had a very large bronze bowl made for himself, filled it with clarified butter, and lit a thousand wicks around its rim. Having wrapped the central peak with a piece of cloth and lit it, he carried that bronze bowl on his head and circumambulated the one-yojana stūpa throughout the entire night in worship. Thus, in that life too, having performed meritorious deeds until the end of his life, he was reborn in the deva world.

Again, during a period when no Buddhas appeared, he took rebirth in a poor family in that same city of Bārāṇasī and lived depending on the treasurer Sumana; his name was Annabhāra. That treasurer Sumana used to give great alms daily at his door to the destitute, travelers, and beggars. Then one day, a Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha entered the attainment of cessation on Mount Gandhamādana. Emerging from that attainment, he reflected, "Whom should I favor today?" Paccekabuddhas are known for their compassion toward the poor. He thought, "Today I should favor Annabhāra." Knowing that Annabhāra would soon return home from the forest, he took his bowl and robes, flew through the air from Mount Gandhamādana, and stood before Annabhāra at the village gate.

Annabhāra, seeing the Paccekabuddha holding an empty bowl, paid homage and asked, "Venerable sir, have you received any alms-food?" "Greatly meritorious donor, I shall receive some," he replied. "Venerable sir, please wait here for a moment," Annabhāra said, and hurried home to ask his wife, "Dear, is there a portion of rice set aside for me, or not?" "There is, my lord," she replied. Annabhāra went back, took the bowl from the Paccekabuddha's hand, and returned, saying, "Dear, because we did not perform meritorious deeds in previous lives, we have to long for food..."
146:
(Because of not having performed meritorious deeds in previous lives, they) had to live longing for food. "Even though we have the desire to give, we have no offerings. When we have offerings, we do not find a recipient. Today, I have seen the Venerable Uparittha Paccekabuddha, and I have my own portion of rice. Put my portion of rice into this bowl," he said to his wife.

That wise woman thought, "My husband is giving his own portion of rice; I too should be a sharer in this gift." Thinking thus, she also put her own portion of rice into the bowl of Uparittha Paccekabuddha and offered it. Annabhāra brought the bowl, placed it in the hands of the Paccekabuddha, and said, "Venerable Sir, may I be released from such a miserable livelihood as this."

"Great donor, may it be so," the Paccekabuddha said.

Annabhāra spread his upper garment in a certain place and said, "Venerable Sir, please sit here and partake of the meal." The Paccekabuddha sat there and partook of the food while contemplating the ninefold loathsomeness. When he had finished eating, Annabhāra offered water for washing the bowl. Having finished the business of the meal, the Paccekabuddha gave the following blessing:

"May all that you wish for and desire be fulfilled.
May all your intentions be perfected like the full moon on the fifteenth day."

After giving the blessing, he departed on his way. The deity guarding the parasol of Sumana the Treasurer said, "Aha! A gift, a supreme gift, well-established in Uparittha Paccekabuddha!" and uttered "Sādhu" three times. Sumana the Treasurer asked, "Do you not see me giving gifts for all this time?"

(The deity) replied, "I am not uttering Sādhu for your gift, but I utter Sādhu because I am delighted by the alms-food given by Annabhāra to Uparittha Paccekabuddha."

Sumana the Treasurer thought, "This is indeed wonderful! Although I have given gifts for so long, I have not been able to make the deity utter Sādhu. This Annabhāra, while living depending on me, has been able to make the deity utter Sādhu with just a single offering of alms-food because he found a suitable recipient. I should give him suitable wealth and make that alms-offering my own." He then had Annabhāra called and asked, "Did you give any gift to anyone today?"

"Yes, master, I gave my own portion of rice to Uparittha Paccekabuddha," he replied. "Friend, take a kahāpaṇa and give that alms-offering to me." "I cannot give it, master," he said. Even though the treasurer increased the offer up to a thousand kahāpaṇas, Annabhāra...
147:
Annabhāra said, "I will not give it even for a thousand kahāpaṇas." Sumana the Treasurer said, "Friend, very well. If you do not wish to give the alms-food, take the thousand and give me the share of merit (patti) for that alms-offering." Annabhāra replied, "I do not know whether it is proper or improper to give the share of merit. I will ask the Venerable Uparittha Paccekabuddha, and if it is proper to give, I will give it." He went and caught up with the Paccekabuddha and asked, "Venerable Sir, Sumana the Treasurer is offering me a thousand kahāpaṇas and asking for the share of merit of the alms-food given to you. Should I give it or not?"

The Paccekabuddha said, "Wise man, I will give you a simile. For example, in a village of a hundred houses, if a lamp is lit in one house and the people from the remaining houses come with their own oil and wicks and light them from that lamp, would the light of the first lamp decrease or would it remain?" "Venerable Sir, the light would become even brighter," he replied. "Wise man, in the same way, whether it is a ladle of gruel or a spoonful of rice, when one shares the merit of one's gift with others, whether with a hundred or a thousand, the merit increases according to the number of people shared with. Although you offered only one meal, when you share the merit with Sumana the Treasurer, it becomes the merit of two meals: one share for you and one share for him."

Then Annabhāra bowed to the Paccekabuddha, went to Sumana the Treasurer, and said, "Master, please take the share of merit of the alms-food." The treasurer said, "Friend, take this thousand kahāpaṇas." Annabhāra said, "I am not selling the alms-food; I am only sharing the merit out of faith." The treasurer replied, "Dear man, you share the merit out of faith; I, for my part, give this thousand to honor your virtue. Please take it." Annabhāra said, "May it be so," and accepted the thousand. The treasurer said, "Dear man, from the time you received this thousand, you no longer need to work with your own hands. Build a house on the main street and live there. Ask me for whatever you need."

Alms-food given to a Paccekabuddha who has just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) yields results on that very day. Therefore, although Sumana the Treasurer did not usually take Annabhāra with him on other days, he took him along on that day.

Due to Annabhāra's merit, the King of Bārāṇasī ignored the treasurer and looked only at Annabhāra. The treasurer asked, "Great King, why do you look at this man so intently?" The King replied, "I look because I have never seen him on other days." The treasurer said, "Great King, this man is endowed with virtue worthy of being looked at." "What virtue does he have?" the King asked. "Great King, today he gave the rice he was to eat to Uparittha Paccekabuddha and has received a thousand from my hand," he replied. "What is his name?" the King asked. "He is called Annabhāra," the treasurer replied. "He deserves to receive from my hand just as he did from yours; I too shall honor him," said the King, and he granted him a thousand kahāpaṇas. Then he ordered, "Men, find a site for this Annabhāra to live." As the king's men were clearing a site, every time they struck with a hoe, they found the necks of underground gold pots touching each other, and they reported this to the King.
148:
“Your Majesty, he is named Annabhāra,” they replied. The King said, “Since he received [merit] from your hand, he deserves to receive from my hand as well; I too shall honor him,” and gave him a thousand [pieces of wealth]. “Friends, do you know where this man lives?” he asked. “Yes, Your Majesty,” they replied. While clearing a site for a house, they saw treasure pots standing neck to neck wherever the hoes struck, and they informed the King. The King said, “In that case, go and dig.” As they dug, the treasure pots sank into the ground. They went back and informed the King again. The King said, “Dig in the name of Annabhāra.” They went and dug, saying, “Let it be in the name of Annabhāra alone.” Treasure pots emerged like mushroom buds wherever the hoes struck. They brought the wealth and piled it before the King. The King assembled his ministers and asked, “Who else in this city possesses such wealth?” “No one else, Your Majesty,” they replied. “Then let this Annabhāra be known as the Dhanaseṭṭhi (Wealthy Merchant) in this city,” he declared. On that very day, he received the ceremonial parasol of a Seṭṭhi.

From then on, he performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, and upon passing away, he was reborn in the celestial realm. After wandering through the worlds of gods and humans for a long time, at the time of our Buddha's appearance, he took rebirth in the house of Amitodana the Sakyan in the city of Kapilavatthu. On the day of his naming, they gave him the name Anuruddha. He was the younger brother of Mahānāma the Sakyan and the son of the Buddha's paternal uncle. He was extremely delicate and possessed great merit. His meals appeared only in golden bowls. One day, his mother, thinking, “I will make my son understand the word 'no' (natthi),” covered an empty golden bowl with another golden bowl and sent it to him. Along the way, deities filled it with celestial cakes. Thus, he was a man of great merit. He enjoyed luxury like a god, surrounded by adorned dancing women in three palaces suited for the three seasons.

At that time, our Bodhisatta also passed away from the Tusita heaven and took rebirth in the womb of King Suddhodana's chief queen. Growing up in due course, he lived in the household for twenty-nine years before departing on the Great Renunciation. Gradually, he realized Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). After spending seven weeks at the Bodhi tree, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana) at the Deer Park in Isipatana. While benefiting the world, he arrived at the city of Rājagaha. Hearing that “My son has arrived in Rājagaha,”
149:
hearing this, King Suddhodana, the father, sent ten ministers, each with a retinue of a thousand, saying, “Friends, go and bring my son.” They were all ordained through the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination. Being invited by the Elder Kāludāyī to travel, the Buddha departed from Rājagaha surrounded by twenty thousand monks and went to the city of Kapilavatthu. At the gathering of his kinsmen, he performed various miracles and delivered a profound Dhamma discourse, letting the multitude drink the nectar of the Deathless (Nibbāna). On the second day, taking his bowl and robes, he stood at the city gate and reflected, “What is the custom of the Omniscient Buddhas upon arriving at their ancestral city?” Realizing that “The custom is to wander for alms from house to house,” he proceeded to collect alms. Hearing that “My son is wandering for alms,” the King came to him. The Buddha preached the Dhamma to the King, who then invited him into the palace and offered great honor and hospitality. Having bestowed blessings upon his kinsmen in Kapilavatthu and ordaining Prince Rāhula, he soon departed from Kapilavatthu to travel through the Malla country and arrived at the Anupiya Mango Grove.

At that time, King Suddhodana assembled the Sakyans and said, “If my son had remained in the household life, he would have become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) endowed with the seven treasures. My grandson, Prince Rāhula, would also have traveled surrounded by a host of warriors. You also know this matter. But now my son has become a Buddha; let the warriors alone be his retinue. Each of you, give one son from each family.” When he said this, a thousand Sakyan princes ordained at once. At that time, Mahānāma was the head of the household. He approached the Sakyan Anuruddha and said, “Dear Anuruddha, now the most famous Sakyan princes are following the Blessed One and ordaining. In our family, there is no one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. Therefore, either you ordain, or I shall ordain.” Hearing these words, Anuruddha felt no delight in the household life and went forth from the home into homelessness as the seventh person [including himself]. The sequence of his ordination is as recorded in the Saṅghabhedaka-khandhaka.

Among those who went to the Anupiya Mango Grove and ordained, the Elder Bhaddiya attained Arahantship within that very rainy season. The Elder Anuruddha attained the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu). Devadatta attained the eight meditative attainments. The Elder Ānanda...
150:
Venerable Ānanda was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Venerable Bhagu and Venerable Kimila attained Arahatship at a later time. The past aspirations (abhinīhāra) of all these elders will be mentioned in their respective places in the Pali texts. As for this Venerable Anuruddha, he took a meditation subject from the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, and went to the Pācīnavaṃsamigadāya forest in the Cetiya country. While practicing the recluse's Dhamma, he contemplated seven thoughts of a great man (mahāpurisavitakka). However, he struggled with the eighth thought. The Blessed One, knowing that "Anuruddha is struggling with the eighth thought of a great man," thought, "I shall fulfill his thought." He went to that forest, sat on the prepared noble Buddha-seat, and fulfilled the eighth thought of a great man. After teaching the practice of the Great Noble Lineage (mahā-ariyavaṃsa-paṭipadā), adorned with contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation, He flew into the sky and went to the Bhesakalāvana forest.

Just as the Tathāgata had departed, the elder became a great Arahant endowed with the three knowledges (tevijjā). Reflecting on the Buddha's teaching and the Dhamma he had personally realized, he thought: "The Blessed One, knowing my mind, came and fulfilled the eighth thought of a great man for me. My heart's desire has reached its pinnacle." He then recited these verses:

"Knowing my thought, the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world,
Approached me by means of his power with a mind-made body.

Just as my thought was, he taught even further than that;
The Buddha, delighting in non-proliferation, taught the Dhamma of non-proliferation.

Having understood that Dhamma, I dwelt delighting in the Dispensation;
I have attained the three knowledges and fulfilled the Buddha's Dispensation."

Later, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, He placed the elder in the foremost position (etadagga), declaring: "Anuruddha is the foremost among those of my disciples who possess the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu)."

## The Story of Elder Bhaddiya

In the sixth sutta, 'uccākulikānaṃ' means those born in high-class families. 'Bhaddiya' was the Sakyan king who went forth together with Venerable Anuruddha. 'Kāḷigodhāya putto' means that the princess was called 'Kāḷi' because she was dark-complexioned, and 'Godhā' was her name. Therefore, she was called 'Kāḷigodhā'.
151:
It is said that he was the son of that queen. Why was this Elder declared the foremost among those of high birth? Is it because there were none of higher birth than him? Indeed, there were none. His mother was the eldest in age among the Sakyan princesses, and he himself had renounced the kingship that had come to him in the Sakyan clan to become a monk. For this reason, he was called the foremost among those of high birth. Furthermore, by the power of his past aspirations, he was born into royal families and ruled as a king for five hundred consecutive births. For this reason also, he was called the foremost among those of high birth.

Regarding his question, the chronological account is as follows: In the past, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was born into a family of great wealth and, as previously mentioned, went to listen to the Dhamma. On that day, seeing the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among monks of high birth, he thought, "In the future, may I also become the foremost among monks of high birth in the Dispensation of a Buddha." He then invited the Tathāgata and offered a great donation for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. He made an aspiration at the Buddha's feet, saying, "Venerable Sir, by the merit of this gift, I do not desire any other prosperity; I only wish to be the foremost among monks of high birth in the Dispensation of a future Buddha."

The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that the aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied: "This deed of yours will be successful. At the end of one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. You will be the foremost among monks of high birth in his Dispensation." Having given the prophecy and the blessing after the meal, the Buddha returned to the monastery. Having received that prophecy, he asked about the deeds that lead to being born in a high family. He performed many kinds of meritorious deeds throughout his life, such as making seats for preaching Dhamma, spreading covers over them, offering fans for Dhamma-preachers, attending to the needs of Dhamma-preachers, and offering lamp oil in the Uposatha halls. After passing away from that life, he wandered through the worlds of gods and humans. In the interval between the time of Kassapa Buddha and our Blessed One, he was born into a householder's family in Bārāṇasī.

At that time, many Paccekabuddhas came from Mount Gandhamādana and resided in a suitable place on the banks of the Ganges in Bārāṇasī to partake of their alms-food. That householder's son, seeing those Paccekabuddhas always taking their meals in that place...
152:
Knowing [that the Paccekabuddhas were about to eat], he spread out eight stone slabs and served the Paccekabuddhas for the rest of his life. After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for the interval between two Buddhas, he was reborn into a kshatriya family in the city of Kapilavatthu during the time of this Buddha. On the day of his naming ceremony, they named him Prince Bhaddiya. When he came of age, following the same manner described in the Anuruddha Sutta below, he became one of the six princes and, while the Blessed One was staying in the Anupiya Mango Grove, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher and attained Arahatship. Later, while the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery, he declared, "Among my disciples who are of high birth, the Elder Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷigodhā, is the foremost," thus placing him in the position of Etadagga.

## The Story of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya

In the seventh sutta, "mañjussarānaṃ" means those with sweet voices. "Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya" means one who is short in stature and named Bhaddiya. Regarding the background of this Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, this is the chronological account: This future elder was also reborn into a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. As mentioned before, he went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. At that time, seeing the Teacher appoint a monk with a sweet voice to the position of Etadagga, he thought, "Oh, may I also become the foremost among the monks with sweet voices in the dispensation of a future Buddha, just like this monk." Having made this wish, he invited the Teacher and gave a great offering to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha for seven days.

"Venerable Sir, by the merit of this gift, I do not desire any other prosperity; I only wish to become the foremost among the monks with sweet voices in the dispensation of a future Buddha." Saying this, he prostrated at the feet of the Teacher. The Blessed One, looking into the future and seeing that the wish would be fulfilled, prophesied, "This deed of yours will be accomplished. One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In his dispensation, you will be the foremost among the monks with sweet voices." Having said this, he returned to the monastery.

Having received that prophecy, he performed wholesome deeds for the rest of his life. After passing away from that life, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of Vipassī Buddha, he became a cuckoo named "Cittapatta." While living in the Khema Deer Park, one day he went to the Himalayan mountains and, while returning with a sweet mango in his beak, he saw the Teacher surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks and thought: "On other days, I have seen the Tathāgata empty-handed, but today I have this ripe mango..."
153:
"...which I brought for my young ones. I will find and give them another mango, but it is proper to offer this one to the Dasabala (Vipassī Buddha)." Thinking thus, he descended from the sky and flew down. The Teacher, knowing the cuckoo's mind, looked at his attendant, the Elder Asoka. The elder took out the alms-bowl and placed it in the Teacher's hand, and the cuckoo placed the ripe mango into the Blessed One's bowl. The Teacher sat right there and consumed the mango. The cuckoo, with a heart full of faith, repeatedly contemplated the virtues of the Dasabala, paid homage, and returned to its nest, spending seven days in the bliss of rapture. Although this was the only wholesome deed performed in that existence, because of that deed, his voice became sweet and melodious.

During the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, when efforts were being made to build a stupa, they consulted, "What size shall we make it?" Some said, "Let us make it seven yojanas in size." Then others said, "This size is too large; let us make it six yojanas." From there, they suggested reducing it to five, four, three, and two yojanas. At that time, this person (the future Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya), who was a master builder, said, "Friends, come, it is proper to build a stupa that can be easily maintained in the future." Taking a rope and measuring, he stood at a distance of one gāvuta and said, "Let each entrance be one gāvuta wide; the stupa shall be one yojana in circumference and one yojana in height." The people followed his words. Thus, he limited the size of the stupa of the Buddha, who is beyond measure. Due to that deed, in every life he was reborn, he was shorter in stature than others.

In the time of our Teacher, he was reborn into a wealthy family in Sāvatthī and was named "Bhaddiya." When he came of age, he went to the Jetavana Monastery where the Teacher was staying, listened to the Dhamma, and having gained faith, he went forth. Taking a meditation subject from the Teacher and practicing Vipassanā, he attained Arahatship. Later, the Teacher, sitting in the midst of the noble Saṅgha, appointed the Venerable Bhaddiya to the foremost position among the monks with sweet voices.

## The Story of the Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja

In the eighth sutta, "sīhanādikānaṃ" means among those who utter a brave voice (roar the lion's roar). It is said that on the day the Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja attained Arahatship, he took the key and went from monastery to monastery, from cell to cell, roaring a lion's roar: "If anyone has doubts regarding the Path or the Fruit, let him ask me!" Even standing before the Buddha, he uttered the brave words: "Venerable Sir, my task in this dispensation is completed." Therefore, he became the foremost among those who roar the lion's roar. This is the chronological account regarding that elder's background. To elaborate: the future Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was a king of lions at the foot of Mount Citta during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. The Blessed One, surveying the world at dawn, saw the lion's potential to attain the Path and Fruit. After wandering for alms in Haṃsavatī and finishing his meal, the Buddha entered the lion's cave while the lion was out hunting and sat there in the air in cross-legged posture, entering the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). When the lion returned with food, he stood at the cave entrance and saw the one sitting inside the cave..."
154:
"Venerable Sir, the task to be done by me in this Dispensation has reached its completion." Thus he uttered a bold word like a lion's roar. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who utter a lion's roar.

Regarding the matter of this Elder's questions, the sequential account is as follows: This future Elder was reborn as a lion at the foot of a mountain during the time of Buddha Padumuttara. When the Blessed One surveyed the world at dawn, He saw the special cause for this lion to attain the Path and Fruit. After wandering for alms in the city of Haṃsavatī and finishing His meal, the Blessed One entered the lion's cave while the lion was away seeking food. He sat cross-legged in the air and entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). When the lion returned with food, he stood at the cave entrance and saw the Blessed One, the Possessor of Ten Powers, sitting inside the cave. He thought, "There is no other being capable of coming and sitting in my place. This man is truly great, sitting cross-legged inside the cave. His bodily radiance also spreads all around. I have never seen such a wonder before. This man must be the foremost among those worthy of offerings in this world. I, too, should pay him honor and respect according to my strength and ability." Thinking thus, he brought various flowers from water and land, and spread a floral seat from the ground up to the level of the cross-legged seat. He remained standing throughout the night, paying homage before the Blessed One. The next day, he removed the old flowers and spread the seat again with fresh flowers.

In this manner, for seven days, he prepared the floral seat, generating powerful joy and rapture (pīti-somanassa), and kept watch at the cave entrance. On the seventh day, the Blessed One emerged from the attainment of cessation and stood at the cave entrance. The lion king also circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right, paid homage at the four directions, and then stood aside. The Blessed One reflected, "This much merit will be a strong support (upanissaya) for this lion to attain the Path and Fruit," and then flew into the air and returned to the monastery.

That lion, being distressed by the separation from the Buddha, passed away and took rebirth in a wealthy family (mahāsāla) in the city of Haṃsavatī. When he came of age, one day he went to the monastery with the city dwellers. While listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Blessed One appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those who utter a lion's roar. Following the same method as before, he performed great alms-giving for seven days and made a wish for that position. The Blessed One, seeing that his wish would be fulfilled, gave him the prophecy. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, and after passing away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realms...
155:
...and while wandering between the celestial and human realms, he was reborn in a wealthy Brahmin family in the city of Rājagaha during the time of our Buddha's appearance. By name, he was Bharadvāja. When he reached maturity, he learned the three Vedas and wandered about teaching mantras to five hundred young students. Because of his position as a leader, he himself would receive the alms-food of all people at invited places. It is said that this Bharadvāja had a somewhat greedy nature. Together with those students, he would wander about seeking only gruel, rice, and snacks, asking, "Where is there gruel? Where is there rice?" Because he wandered about cherishing only alms-food wherever he went, he became well-known as "Piṇḍola Bharadvāja."

One day, when the Blessed One arrived at Rājagaha, Piṇḍola Bharadvāja heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and ordained. Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship. As soon as he attained Arahantship, he took a key and went from monastery to monastery, from precinct to precinct, wandering about and uttering a bold word like a lion's roar: "If anyone has doubts regarding the Path or the Fruit, let him ask me!" One day, the Elder Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, using his psychic power, took a sandalwood bowl the color of a hibiscus flower, which had been hung in the air by a merchant of Rājagaha using a series of bamboos. Surrounded by a great crowd of people shouting "Sādhu," he came to the monastery and placed it in the hand of the Tathāgata. Although the Blessed One already knew, He asked, "Bharadvāja, from where did you get this bowl?" The Elder explained how he had obtained it. The Blessed One rebuked him in many ways, saying, "You have shown such superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) to the great crowd; you have done what should not be done." He then prescribed a training rule: "Monks, psychic powers which are superhuman states should not be shown to laypeople. Whoever should show them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

Later, a discussion arose among the community of monks: "The Elder Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, who has a bold voice like a lion's roar, said in the midst of the Sangha on the day he attained Arahantship, 'If anyone has doubts regarding the Path or the Fruit, let him ask me.' Even in the presence of the Buddhas, he declared his attainment of Arahantship, while other disciples remained silent. By the very fact of having a bold lion's roar, he inspired faith in the great crowd, flew into the air, and took the sandalwood bowl." The monks combined these three qualities and reported them to the Blessed One. Buddhas, indeed, rebuke those who deserve rebuke and praise those who deserve praise. Therefore, in this instance, taking only the Elder's praiseworthy quality, the Blessed One said, "Monks, it is because of the development of three faculties..."
156:
Because of having frequently developed the faculties, the monk Bhāradvāja declared final knowledge: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.' Which three? They are the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. Monks, because these three faculties have been developed and frequently practiced, the monk Bhāradvāja declared final knowledge: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.' The Blessed One praised that Elder and placed him in the foremost position among the monks who roar the lion's roar.

## Story of the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta

In the ninth story, the Story of the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, 'Puṇṇa' is his name, and he is called 'Mantāṇiputta' because he is the son of the Brahmin lady Mantāṇī. Regarding the matter of his question, this is the sequential account: This future Elder Puṇṇa, long before the appearance of the Padumuttara Buddha, was born into a wealthy Brahmin family in the city of Haṃsavatī. On the day of his naming, they named him Gotama. When the youth Gotama reached maturity, he learned the three Vedas and became proficient in all arts. While wandering accompanied by five hundred youths, he reflected on the three Vedas and, not seeing the Dhamma of liberation, he thought: 'These three Vedas are like the trunk of a banana tree, smooth on the outside but without essence inside; wandering while holding onto these Vedas is like pounding husks. What benefit is there for me in these Vedas?' Thus, he renounced to become an ascetic, developed the Divine Abodes (Brahma-vihāras), and thinking, 'With undiminished jhāna, I shall be reborn in the Brahma realm,' he went to the foot of a mountain with the five hundred youths and became an ascetic. That ascetic Gotama had eighteen thousand followers. Having attained the five supernormal powers and the eight attainments, he taught the preliminary practice of kasiṇas to his disciples as well. All those disciples, abiding by the teacher's advice, also attained the five supernormal powers and the eight attainments.

After a long time had passed and the ascetic Gotama had grown old, the Padumuttara Buddha, having first attained supreme enlightenment and set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, resided near the city of Haṃsavatī accompanied by one hundred thousand monks. One day at dawn, while surveying the world, the Buddha saw the ascetic Gotama's...
157:
...supportive conditions for his retinue to attain the fruit of Arahantship, and also the fact that the ascetic Gotama would make an aspiration, saying, 'May I be the foremost among the monks who are Dhamma preachers in the dispensation of a future Buddha.' Having seen this, the Buddha performed his morning bodily ablutions early, took his own bowl and robes, and went in an unrecognised form while the ascetic Gotama's disciples had gone to the forest to search for roots and various fruits. He stood at the door of the leaf-roofed hut of the ascetic Gotama. Although the ascetic Gotama did not know that a Buddha had appeared, seeing the Ten-Powered One from afar, he thought: 'This man appears as one liberated from the world; one endowed with such a physical build and marks, if he stays in the household life, becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch, and if he renounces, becomes an Omniscient Buddha who has opened the roof of defilements.' Knowing this, he paid homage to the Ten-Powered One as soon as he saw him and invited him, saying, 'Come here, Blessed One,' and having prepared a seat for the Buddha, he offered it. The Tathāgata sat down, preaching the Dhamma to the ascetic.

At that time, those ascetics, thinking, 'We will offer the most excellent forest roots and fruits to our teacher and then eat the remainder,' were returning when they saw the Ten-Powered One sitting on a high seat and their teacher sitting on a low seat. They thought: 'Look, we have wandered thinking, "There is no one superior to our teacher in this world." But now we see a person sitting on a high seat while making our teacher sit on a low seat; this man must indeed be a great person.' Thus thinking, they came carrying their baskets of fruit. The ascetic Gotama, fearing that 'These disciples might pay homage to me in the presence of the Ten-Powered One,' said from afar: 'Dear ones, do not pay homage to me; the foremost person in the world with its devas, the person worthy of homage from all, is sitting here; pay homage to him.' The ascetics, thinking, 'The teacher would not speak without knowing,' all paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata. 'Dear ones, we have no other food suitable to be given to the Ten-Powered One; let us offer these forest roots and fruits,' he said, and placed the most excellent fruits into the Buddha's bowl. The Teacher partook of the forest roots and fruits. Thereafter, the ascetic also ate together with his disciples. After the Teacher had finished his meal, he thought: 'Let the two chief disciples come, bringing one hundred thousand monks.' At that moment, the chief disciple, the Elder Mahādevala, reflected, 'Where has the Blessed One gone?' and knowing that the Buddha was expecting their arrival, he brought one hundred thousand monks, went to the Buddha, paid homage, and stood there.

The ascetic Gotama said to his disciples: 'Dear ones, we have no other offerings; the monks of the Saṅgha are standing in hardship. Let us prepare flower seats for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha; bring flowers that grow in water and flowers that grow on land.' Those disciples, at that very moment, brought flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain by psychic power and arranged the seats as described in the story of the Elder Sāriputta. The entering into the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and the holding of the parasol, etc., should also be understood according to the method already mentioned. On the seventh day, the Padumuttara Buddha, having arisen from the attainment of cessation, addressed the surrounding ascetics...
158:
Reflecting, "Where has the Teacher gone?" and realizing, "The Teacher is expecting our arrival," he took a hundred thousand monks, went to the Teacher's presence, paid homage, and stood there respectfully.

The ascetic Gotama said to his disciples, "Friends, we have no other offerings; the Sangha of monks is staying here with difficulty. Let us prepare a flower-seat for the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. Bring flowers that grow in water and on land." At that very moment, they brought flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain by psychic power and arranged the seats in the same manner as described in the story of the Elder Sāriputta. The entering into the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and the holding of the parasol should all be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

On the seventh day, the Teacher emerged from the attainment of cessation and, seeing the ascetics standing around him, addressed the disciple who had attained the pre-eminent rank (etadagga) in preaching the Dhamma: "Monk, this group of ascetics has made a great offering. Preach a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) regarding this flower-seat to these ascetics." Accepting the Teacher's command, that monk reviewed the Three Piṭakas and preached the discourse of appreciation. At the conclusion of that monk's sermon, the Teacher himself preached the Dhamma, emitting a voice like that of Mahābrahmā. At the conclusion of the sermon, except for the ascetic Gotama, the remaining eighteen thousand matted-hair ascetics attained Arahatship.

However, the ascetic Gotama, being unable to penetrate the Four Noble Truths in that existence, asked the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, who is this monk who preached the Dhamma first? What is his name in your Dispensation?" "Gotama, this monk is the foremost among those who preach the Dhamma in my Dispensation," the Buddha replied. "Venerable Sir, by the merit of this service performed for seven days, may I also, like this monk, become the foremost among those who preach the Dhamma in the Dispensation of a future Buddha," he made this wish and prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet.

The Teacher, looking into the future and knowing that the ascetic's wish would be fulfilled without obstacle, prophesied, "At the end of a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. You will be the foremost among those who preach the Dhamma in his Dispensation." Then, he addressed those ascetics who had attained Arahatship, saying, "Come, monks (Etha bhikkhavo)." Immediately, the hair and beards of all the ascetics disappeared, and they appeared wearing psychic robes and carrying bowls...
159:
Those monks appeared like elders of sixty years' standing. The Teacher, taking the Sangha of monks, went to the monastery. The ascetic Gotama also served the Buddha Padumuttara for the rest of his life, performing wholesome deeds to the best of his ability. After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was born into a wealthy brahmin family in the brahmin village of Doṇavatthu, not far from the city of Kapilavatthu, during the time of our Blessed One. On the day of his naming ceremony, they named him the youth Puṇṇa (Puṇṇa-māṇava). After the Teacher attained Supreme Enlightenment and set the Noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, he eventually arrived and stayed near the city of Rājagaha. At that time, the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña went to Kapilavatthu and ordained his nephew, the youth Puṇṇa. On the following day, the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña went to the presence of the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala), paid homage to the Blessed One, asked for permission, and went to the vicinity of Lake Chaddanta to reside. The Elder Puṇṇa, the son of the brahmin woman Mantāṇī, did not yet follow his uncle, the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña, to the Teacher's presence, thinking, "I will go to the presence of the Possessor of Ten Powers only after reaching the goal of a monk's duty." He remained in Kapilavatthu and, practicing with wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra), attained Arahatship before long. There were also five hundred clansmen who ordained in his presence. Since the Elder himself was a master of the ten subjects of discourse (dasa kathāvatthu), he also exhorted those five hundred disciples with the ten subjects of discourse. All those disciples, abiding by his exhortation, attained Arahatship.

Knowing that they had reached the goal of their monk's duty, those monks approached their preceptor and said, "Venerable Sir, our duty is completed; we have also mastered the ten great subjects of discourse. It is now time for us to see the Possessor of Ten Powers." Hearing their words, the Elder thought, "The Teacher knows that I am a master of the ten subjects of discourse. When I preach the Dhamma, I do so without omitting the ten subjects of discourse. If I go, all these monks will follow me in a crowd. To go and see the Possessor of Ten Powers while mingling with a crowd (gaṇasaṅgaṇikā) is not appropriate for me. Let these monks go and see him first." Then he said to those monks, "Friends, you go ahead and see the Tathāgata. Pay homage to the feet of the Possessor of Ten Powers on my behalf. I will follow by the same path you have taken."

All those elders were residents of the birthplace of the Possessor of Ten Powers, Kapilavatthu. All were those whose taints were exhausted (khīṇāsava), and all were masters of the ten subjects of discourse. Without violating the exhortation of their preceptor...
160:
As those monks traveled by stages, having crossed a journey of sixty leagues, they arrived at the Veḷuvana Great Monastery in Rājagaha, paid homage at the feet of the Buddha, and sat down in a suitable place. Now, it is the custom of the Blessed Buddhas to exchange pleasantries with visiting monks. Accordingly, the Blessed Buddha engaged in sweet conversation of welcome with those monks, saying, "Monks, are you keeping well?" and so forth. Then He asked, "Monks, from where have you come?" When they replied, "From our birthplace, Kapilavatthu," the Buddha asked, "Monks, who is the monk in your birthplace who is so highly esteemed by his fellow practitioners, being himself of few desires and a speaker to other monks on having few desires—one who has attained the ten subjects of discourse?" They informed Him, "Venerable Sir, it is the Venerable Puṇṇa, the son of Mantāṇī." Upon hearing this, the Venerable Sāriputta desired to see that Elder.

Thereafter, the Teacher went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī. Having heard that the Buddha had arrived there, the Elder Puṇṇa went and met the Tathāgata right inside the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. After listening to the Dhamma, the Elder paid homage to the Buddha and, for the sake of seclusion, went to the Andhavana forest and sat at the foot of a certain tree for his day-abiding. The Venerable Sāriputta, having heard of his departure, followed him, keeping him in sight. Having noted the opportunity, he approached the foot of that tree, exchanged pleasantries with the Elder, and inquired about the sequence of the seven purifications, beginning with the purification of virtue. The Elder answered every question asked by the Venerable Sāriputta. Both Elders rejoiced in each other's well-spoken words. Later, while seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, the Teacher appointed the Elder Puṇṇa to the foremost position among the speakers of Dhamma.

## The Story of the Elder Mahākaccāna

In the tenth sutta, "saṅkhittena bhāsitassa" means of the Dhamma spoken in brief. "Vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajantānaṃ" means among those who analyze the meaning by expanding upon that teaching in detail. It is said that while others can fulfill the Tathāgata's brief words either by way of meaning or by way of phrasing, this Elder can fulfill them by way of both. Therefore, he is called "foremost." His past aspiration was also of such a nature.
161:
This is the sequential account of the Elder Kaccāna's past deeds. This future Elder Mahākaccāna, it is said, was born into a wealthy householder family during the time of the Padumuttara Buddha. Having reached maturity, he went to the monastery one day in the manner already described. While standing at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position among those who analyze in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Teacher himself. He thought, "Great indeed is this monk whom the Teacher praises so! It would be well if I too were to become such a monk in the dispensation of a future Buddha." He invited the Teacher and, in the manner already described, gave a great offering for seven days. Then he made an aspiration, prostrating at the Teacher's feet: "Venerable Sir, by the fruit of this honor, I do not crave any other prosperity. But in the future, in the dispensation of a Buddha, may I obtain that same position like the monk whom you appointed to that rank seven days from today." The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that this clansman's aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied: "O clansman, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In his dispensation, you will be the foremost among those who analyze in detail the meaning of what is spoken in brief." Having given the blessing of appreciation, the Teacher departed.

That clansman performed meritorious deeds for the rest of his life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was reborn in a family in Bārāṇasī. When the Teacher passed into Parinibbāna, he went to the site where a golden stupa was being built and made an offering of a golden brick worth a hundred thousand, making this aspiration: "Blessed One, wherever I am reborn, may my body have a complexion like the color of gold." Thereafter, having performed meritorious deeds for the rest of his life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans during the interval between two Buddhas. At the time of our Buddha's appearance, he was reborn in the house of the royal chaplain in the city of Ujjeni. On the day of his naming, his parents thought, "Our son has a body with a golden complexion; he has come bringing his own name," and so they named him Young Kañcana. As he grew up, he learned the three Vedas and, upon his father's death, received the position of royal chaplain. By his clan, he was known as Kaccāna. King Caṇḍapajjota assembled his ministers and said, "Friends, a Buddha has appeared in the world. Go, dear ones, you who are capable of bringing that Buddha, and bring Him here." They replied, "Great King, there is no one else capable of bringing the Buddha; only our teacher, the brahmin Kaccāna, is capable. Please send him." The King summoned the brahmin Kaccāna and said, "Friend, go to the Buddha." Kaccāna replied, "Great King, if I may have the opportunity to go and become a monk, I shall go." The King said, "Friend, do as you wish, but just bring the Buddha back." The brahmin Kaccāna, thinking, "For one going to the Buddha, there is no need for a large retinue," went with a group of seven others, himself being the eighth. At that time, the Buddha taught the Dhamma to the brahmin Kaccāna. At the end of the discourse, he, along with the seven others, attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights.
162:
## 

“Only the Brahmin named Kaccāna, our teacher, is capable of inviting the Blessed One; please send him,” the ministers requested. The King summoned the Brahmin Kaccāna and said, “Dear friend, go to the presence of the Blessed One.” He replied, “Great King, I shall go if I am allowed to ordain.” The King said, “Dear friend, do whatever you wish, but bring the Blessed One here.” The Brahmin Kaccāna thought, “For one going to the presence of the Buddhas, there is no need for a large retinue,” and he set out with seven others, making eight in total. Then the Teacher taught him the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, he, along with his seven companions, attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The Teacher stretched out His hand and said, “Come, bhikkhus!” At that very moment, their hair and beards disappeared, and they appeared like elders of sixty years’ standing, carrying miraculous bowls and robes.

When Venerable Kaccāna had reached the summit of his monkly duties, he did not remain silent; like Venerable Kāḷudāyī, he praised the journey to Ujjeni to encourage the Teacher to go. The Teacher, hearing the Elder’s words, understood, “Kaccāna desires my journey to his birthplace.” Buddhas do not go to unsuitable places unless there is a specific reason. Therefore, He said to the Elder, “Bhikkhu, you go yourself; even when you go, the King will be inspired with faith.” The Elder thought, “Buddhas do not speak twice,” and after paying homage to the Tathāgata, he set out for Ujjeni with the seven monks who had come with him. On the way, they reached a market town named Telapanāḷi and wandered for alms there.

In that town, there were two daughters of merchant families. One was born into a ruined family and lived in poverty, depending on a nurse after her parents passed away. However, her physical form was perfect, and her hair was exceptionally longer than that of other women. In that same town, another daughter from a wealthy merchant family had thin hair. Previously, she had sent a messenger to the poor girl, saying, “I will give a hundred or a thousand [pieces of money],” but she had been unable to obtain the hair.

On that day, the poor merchant’s daughter saw Venerable Mahākaccāna, surrounded by seven monks, approaching with an empty bowl. She thought, “This monk of brahmin lineage, with a complexion like gold, comes with a bowl as clean as if it had just been washed, and I have no other wealth. That merchant’s daughter once sent for my hair. Now, with the wealth obtained from this hair, I can give a gift to the Elder.” She sent her nurse to invite the monks and had them sit inside the house. While the monks were seated, she entered her room and had the nurse cut her hair...
163:
“Mother, give this hair to that merchant’s daughter and bring whatever she gives; we shall offer alms-food to the venerable ones,” she said. The nurse wiped away her tears with the back of her hand and, holding her heart in grief with one hand, concealed the hair from the presence of the Elders and went to the wealthy merchant’s daughter.

Even if a commodity is valuable, it is often disregarded if the owner brings it for sale themselves. Therefore, the wealthy merchant’s daughter thought, “Previously, I could not obtain this hair even for much wealth; but now that it is cut, she will not get the original price.” She said to the nurse, “Previously, I could not obtain the hair from your mistress even for much wealth; but lifeless hair scattered about in an ordinary place is worth only eight kahāpaṇas.” She gave only eight kahāpaṇas. The nurse brought the coins and gave them to the merchant’s daughter. The merchant’s daughter prepared alms-food worth one kahāpaṇa for each portion and had it offered to the Elders. The Elder, reflecting and seeing the girl’s supporting conditions (upanissaya), asked, “Where is the merchant’s daughter?” “Venerable sir, she is in the inner room,” they replied. “Call her,” he said. Out of respect for the Elders, she came at the first word, paid homage to the Elders, and developed strong faith. Because alms-food placed in a good field of merit yields results in this very life, as soon as she paid homage to the Elders, her hair returned to its original state. The Elders, having accepted the alms-food, flew into the air while the merchant’s daughter was watching and descended in the Kañcana Garden.

The gardener, seeing the Elder, went to the King and said, “Great King, my master, the chaplain Kaccāna, has ordained and arrived at the garden.” King Candappajjota went to the garden, paid homage to the Elder who had finished his meal with the fivefold prostration, and sitting to one side, asked, “Venerable sir, where is the Blessed One?” “Great King, the Teacher did not come himself but sent me,” he replied. “Venerable sir, where did you receive alms today?” he asked again. The Elder, in accordance with the King’s question, told the whole story of the difficult deed performed by the merchant’s daughter. The King prepared a dwelling for the Elder, invited him, and then returned to the palace. He summoned the merchant’s daughter and established her in the position of Chief Queen. For this woman, the attainment of fame and retinue occurred in this very life.
164:
From that time on, the King paid great honor and respect to the Elder. Having gained faith in the Elder's Dhamma discourse, the multitude of people went forth into the monkhood in the presence of the Elder. From then on, the entire city was radiant with the color of saffron robes and was filled with the breeze caused by the monks' wearing of robes and other activities. That Queen also conceived and, after ten months, gave birth to a son. On the day of the naming ceremony, they named him Prince Gopāla, taking the name of his grandfather, the wealthy merchant. That Queen became known as Queen Gopālamātā (Gopāla's mother) because of her son's name. The Queen, having great faith in the Elder, obtained the King's consent and built a monastery for the Elder in the garden named Kañcanavana. After the Elder had inspired faith in the city of Ujjeni, he returned to the presence of the Teacher. Later, while the Teacher was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, based on the circumstances surrounding the arising of these three discourses—the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta, the Kaccāna-peyyāla, and the Pārāyana Sutta—he placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who can analyze in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief.

## 14. Etadagga Chapter

## (14) 2. Second Etadagga Chapter

## The Story of Venerable Cūḷapanthaka

198-200. In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'manomayaṃ' refers to that which is created by the mind. In the context of the teaching "He approached through power with a mind-made body," the body created by the mind is called the mind-made body (manomayakāya). Also, in the context of the teaching "He is reborn in a certain mind-made body," the body produced by the mind is called the mind-made body. In this instance, it is that very body produced by the mind that is intended. In that regard, when other monks produce a mind-made body, they can produce only three or four, not many. Furthermore, they produce them as identical forms performing a single type of action. Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, however, could create a thousand monks with a single reflection. He did not make even two of them identical, nor did he have them performing only one type of action; he could make them perform various different actions. Therefore, he is the foremost among those who create mind-made bodies.
165: Elder Cūḷapanthaka is also the foremost among those skilled in cetovivaṭṭa (mastery of mind-evolution/concentration), while Elder Mahāpanthaka is said to be the foremost among those skilled in saññāvivaṭṭa (mastery of perception-evolution/insight). Among these two elders, Elder Cūḷapanthaka is called 'cetovivaṭṭakusala' because he attained the four jhānas of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), while Elder Mahāpanthaka is called 'saññāvivaṭṭakusala' because he attained the four jhānas of the formless sphere (arūpāvacara). Elder Cūḷapanthaka is known as cetovivaṭṭakusala due to his skill in concentration (samādhi), while Elder Mahāpanthaka is known as saññāvivaṭṭakusala due to his skill in insight (vipassanā). Between these two, one is skilled in the characteristics of concentration, and the other is skilled in the characteristics of insight. Likewise, one is deeply immersed in concentration, and the other is deeply immersed in insight. One is skilled in condensing the factors of absorption, and the other is skilled in condensing the objects of meditation. Similarly, one is skilled in determining the factors of absorption, and the other is skilled in determining the objects of meditation; thus should the connection be understood here.Furthermore, Elder Cūḷapanthaka is called cetovivaṭṭakusala because, having attained the fine-material sphere jhānas, he emerged from the jhāna factors and reached Arahantship. Elder Mahāpanthaka is called saññāvivaṭṭakusala because, having attained the formless sphere jhānas, he emerged from the jhāna factors and reached Arahantship. Both were named 'Panthaka' because they were born on the road. Among them, the firstborn was named Mahāpanthaka, and the later-born was named Cūḷapanthaka.Regarding the past deeds of both these elders, the sequential account is as follows: Long ago, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, two brothers who were householders living in the city of Haṃsavatī, being endowed with faith and devotion, went regularly to the presence of the Teacher to listen to the Dhamma. One day, the younger brother saw the Teacher placing a monk, who was endowed with two qualities, in the foremost position, saying, "This monk is the foremost in my dispensation among those who create mind-made bodies and those skilled in cetovivaṭṭa." He thought, "This monk is truly great; being a single person, he can fulfill two qualities and move about. It would be good if I too, in the future, could be one who fulfills two qualities in the dispensation of a Buddha." He invited the Teacher as in the previous method, gave a great offering (mahādāna) for seven days, and said, "Venerable Sir, seven days ago, You placed a certain monk in the foremost position for the qualities of manomaya and cetovivaṭṭakusala, saying 'This monk is the foremost in my dispensation.' May I also, by the fruit of this meritorious deed, be one who fulfills two qualities like that monk." Thus, he made an aspiration.
166:
The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that the householder's aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, prophesied: "At the end of one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. That Buddha will appoint you to these two positions." Having given this prophecy and expressed appreciation, he departed. The elder brother of that householder also, one day seeing the Teacher appointing a monk skilled in the transformation of perception to a pre-eminent position (etadagga), performed a great deed of merit and made an aspiration. The Teacher also gave him a prophecy.

Both of these individuals performed meritorious deeds while the Teacher was still alive. When the Teacher attained Parinibbāna, they made offerings of gold at the shrine of his relics. After passing away from there, they were reborn in the celestial realm. While they were wandering through the realms of gods and men, one hundred thousand aeons passed. Among them, the meritorious deeds performed by Mahāpanthaka in the interval need not be mentioned. Cūḷapanthaka, however, went forth as a monk during the dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa and practiced the white kasiṇa (odāta-kasiṇa) for twenty thousand years, and was subsequently reborn in the celestial city. Then, our Teacher attained supreme enlightenment, set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and resided at the Veḷuvana Monastery near the city of Rājagaha.

At this point, it is appropriate to stop and relate the story of the birth of these two brothers. In the city of Rājagaha, it is said that the daughter of a wealthy merchant's family (Dhanaseṭṭhi) had an affair with her own slave. Thinking, "Others might come to know of this deed of mine," she said: "It is no longer possible for us to live in this place. If my parents find out about this fault, they will tear me to pieces. Let us go and live in another region." Taking her personal jewelry and wealth, she left through the main gate, saying, "Let us go and live in a place where others will not know us," and they both departed.

While they were living in a certain place, she conceived a child due to their cohabitation. When the pregnancy reached maturity, she consulted with her husband: "My pregnancy has reached maturity. Giving birth in a place devoid of relatives and friends will only bring suffering to both of us. Let us go to my family home." He delayed the days, saying, "We shall go today, we shall go tomorrow." She thought: "This fool does not dare to go because of the greatness of his own fault. Parents are indeed solely seekers of one's welfare. Whether he goes or not, I should go." While the man was away from the house, she packed the household goods, informed the neighbors that she was going to her family home, and set out on the journey.
167:
Then, when that man returned home and did not find her, he inquired of the neighbors. Hearing that she had "gone to her family home," he followed her in haste and caught up with her on the way. For her, the birth occurred right there on the road. The man asked, "My dear, what is this?" She replied, "Lord, a son has been born." He asked, "What shall we do now?" She said, "The purpose for which we were going to the family home has been fulfilled on the way. What is the use of going there? Let us turn back." Both being of one mind, they turned back. Because the boy was born on the road (pantha), they named him Panthaka. Not long after, she conceived another child. The entire story should be understood in detail as before. Because that child was also born on the road, they named the first-born Mahāpanthaka and the later-born Cūḷapanthaka.

Taking both children, they went back to their own place of residence. While living there, the young Mahāpanthaka heard other children calling out "Uncle, Great Uncle, Grandfather, Grandmother," and he asked his mother: "Mother, other children speak of 'Grandfather and Grandmother.' Do we have no relatives?" She replied, "Yes, dear, you have no relatives here. But in the city of Rājagaha, there is a wealthy merchant named Dhanaseṭṭhi who is your grandfather. There you have many relatives." He asked again, "Mother, why do we not go there?" The woman did not tell her son the reason for her not going, but when the sons spoke of it again and again, she said to her husband: "These children are troubling me greatly. Will our parents eat our flesh if they see us? Come, let us show the children their grandfather's family." He said, "I will not be able to face them, but I will take you there." She said, "Very well, lord, by some means or other, it is proper that the children should see their grandfather's family." So the two of them took the children and, in due course, reached Rājagaha. Staying at a rest house by the city gate, the mother of the children sent word to her parents that she had arrived with the two children.

When the parents heard that news, they said: "For beings wandering in saṃsāra, there is no one who has not been a son or a daughter. But they have committed a great offense against us. It is not possible for them to stand within our sight. Let them take this much wealth and go to a comfortable place to live their lives. But send the children here." The merchant's daughter took the wealth sent by her parents and handed the children over to the messengers who had arrived...
168: (The grandfather) gave those riches and sent the boys with the messengers who had come. The boys grew up in their grandfather's house. Of the two boys, Cūḷapanthaka was very young. Mahāpanthaka, however, used to go with his grandfather to listen to the Dhamma of the Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala). Constantly hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, the desire to ordain arose in Mahāpanthaka. He said to his grandfather, "Grandfather, if you would permit me, I would like to ordain." The grandfather replied, "What are you saying, dear? For me and for the whole world, your ordination is better than that of others. If you are able, dear, then ordain." Having agreed, he took him to the Teacher. The Teacher asked, "Great Merchant, have you obtained the boy?" "Yes, Bhante, this boy is my grandson; he says he wishes to ordain in your presence," he replied. The Teacher commanded a monk who went for alms, "Ordain this boy." That elder taught him the meditation on the five skin-parts (tacapañcaka kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him. After learning much of the Buddha's word, the novice Mahāpanthaka received higher ordination (upasampadā) upon reaching twenty years of age. Having become a bhikkhu, through wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra), he attained the four formless jhānas. Emerging from the factors of jhāna, he attained Arahantship. Thus, he became the foremost among those skilled in the transformation of perception (saññā-vivaṭṭa). Spending his time in the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition, he thought, "Could I give this bliss to Cūḷapanthaka?" Then he went to the merchant grandfather and said, "Great Merchant, if you agree, I would like to ordain Cūḷapanthaka." "Bhante, please ordain him," the merchant replied. The elder ordained the boy Cūḷapanthaka and established him in the ten precepts. The novice Cūḷapanthaka stayed with his elder brother. He tried to learn this verse: "As a fragrant Kokanada lotus blooms in the morning with its scent unfaded, see the radiant Aṅgīrasa, shining like the sun in the sky." He would learn it, but as he learned each subsequent word, the previous one would vanish. While he was striving to learn this verse, four months passed. Then Mahāpanthaka said to him, "Cūḷapanthaka, you are unfit for this Dispensation. In four months, you cannot even learn a single verse. As for the duties of a monk, you..."
169: "...how will you bring it to completion? Get out of here!" (the elder brother said). Expelled by the elder, Cūḷapanthaka stood weeping at the edge of the monastery. At that time, the Teacher was staying in Jīvaka's Mango Grove near Rājagaha. Then Jīvaka sent a man, saying, "Invite the Teacher along with five hundred monks." At that time, the Venerable Mahāpanthaka was the meal-allocator (bhattuddesaka). When requested, "Bhante, please accept the meal for five hundred monks," he replied, "I accept for all except Cūḷapanthaka." Hearing this, Cūḷapanthaka became even more distressed. The Teacher, seeing Cūḷapanthaka's exhaustion, thought, "When I have gone, Cūḷapanthaka will understand (the Four Noble Truths)." He went and showed himself nearby and asked, "Panthaka, why are you weeping?" "Bhante, my elder brother is expelling me," he replied.
