"Panthaka, your brother does not possess the knowledge of the inclinations and latent tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) of other individuals. You are one who is to be tamed by a Buddha (buddha-veneyya)," the Teacher said. Miraculously creating a clean piece of cloth, He gave it to him and said, "Panthaka, take this piece of cloth and meditate while reciting 'Rajoharaṇaṃ, rajoharaṇaṃ' (Removal of dust, removal of dust)." Cūḷapanthaka sat down, rubbing the cloth with his hands and reciting "Rajoharaṇaṃ, rajoharaṇaṃ." As he rubbed it, the fibers of the cloth became soiled. Rubbing it further, it became as dirty as a cloth used to wipe a cooking pot. Reaching the maturity of his knowledge, he contemplated the rise and fall (khaya-vaya) in that cloth, thinking, "This piece of cloth is naturally white and pure, but because of my physical body (upādinnaka-rūpa), it has become soiled. My mind is also of such a nature." Developing concentration and using the four jhānas of the fine-material sphere as a basis, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Having attained the mind-made jhāna (manomaya-jhāna), he became capable of becoming many from one, and one from many. Through the path of Arahantship itself, the Three Pitakas and the six higher knowledges (abhiññā) came to him. The next morning, the Teacher went with four hundred and ninety-nine monks and sat in Jīvaka's house. Cūḷapanthaka, however, did not go because his meal had not been accepted. When Jīvaka prepared to offer the rice gruel, the Teacher covered the bowl with his hand. "Bhante, why do you not accept the offering?" he asked. "Jīvaka, there is still one monk in the monastery..."
170:
"Jīvaka," (the Buddha said). That Jīvaka sent a man, saying, "Go, friend, and bring the venerable one sitting in the monastery." Even before that man arrived, Elder Cūḷapanthaka created a thousand monks. He made no two monks alike in appearance, and even their monastic duties, such as arranging robes, were made to be different from one another. Seeing the many monks in the monastery, the man returned to Jīvaka and said, "Sir, the Saṅgha of monks in the monastery is very numerous; I do not know which venerable one is to be invited." Jīvaka asked the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, what is the name of the monk sitting in the monastery?" "Jīvaka, his name is Cūḷapanthaka," he replied. "Go, friend, ask 'Which one is named Cūḷapanthaka?' and bring him," (Jīvaka) said. The man went to the monastery and asked, "Venerable Sir, which one is named Cūḷapanthaka?" All thousand monks said, "I am Cūḷapanthaka, I am Cūḷapanthaka." The man returned to Jīvaka again and said, "All the thousand or so monks are saying 'I am Cūḷapanthaka, I am Cūḷapanthaka'; I do not know that 'such and such a person is to be invited'." Jīvaka, having penetrated the Four Truths and knowing by way of inference that "This is a monk with psychic powers," said, "Friend, say to the very first monk who spoke, 'The Buddha invites you, Venerable Sir,' and take hold of the corner of his robe." The man went to the monastery and did so, and immediately the thousand or so monks vanished. He took the Elder and went. At that moment, the Buddha accepted the rice gruel.

When the Dasabala (the Buddha), having finished his meal, returned to the monastery, a discussion arose in the Dhamma Hall: "How wonderful and great are the Buddhas! They could make a monk, who was unable to learn even a single verse for four months, possess such great psychic power." The Buddha, knowing the thoughts of those monks, came and sat on the prepared seat and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?" "Venerable Sir, it is no other talk; Cūḷapanthaka has received a great benefit from you, and we are only speaking of your virtues," they replied. "Monks, it is not surprising that he has now received the supramundane inheritance by following my advice; in the past, when his wisdom was not yet mature, he also received a mundane inheritance by following my advice," he said. The monks requested, "Venerable Sir, when was that?" and the Buddha brought forth the past story to show them.

Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a wise and clever treasurer named Cūḷakaseṭṭhi...
171:
(Cūḷakaseṭṭhi) knew all omens. One day, while going to serve the king, he saw a dead mouse on the road. Considering the constellation at that moment, he said, "A young man with the eye of wisdom could take this mouse, support a wife, and engage in business."

A certain poor young man heard the treasurer's words and thought, "This treasurer would not speak without knowing." He took the dead mouse, gave it to a shop for cat food, and received a small coin (kākaṇika). With that money, he bought molasses, took a pot of drinking water, and seeing flower-gatherers coming from the forest, gave them small pieces of molasses and offered them water with a ladle. Those flower-gatherers each gave him a handful of flowers. With those flowers as capital, the next day he again took molasses and a pot of drinking water and went to the flower garden. That day, the flower-gatherers gave him half-plucked flower bushes and left. Before long, he obtained eight kahāpaṇas by this means.

Later, on a day of heavy wind and rain, he went to a neglected garden, gathered the fallen wood into a pile, and while sitting there, received sixteen kahāpaṇas from the royal potter. When he had twenty-four kahāpaṇas, he thought, "I have this plan," and placed a large water pot at a place not far from the city gate, serving five hundred grass-cutters with drinking water. Those grass-cutters said, "Friend, you are very helpful to us; what can we do for you?" He replied, "Please help me when a matter of importance arises for me." Moving here and there, he made friends with land-traders and sea-traders.

A land-trader told him, "Tomorrow, a horse dealer will come to this city with five hundred horses." Hearing this, he gave a signal to the grass-cutters and had each of them bring two bundles of grass. Then, when the horses entered the city, he sat with a pile of a thousand bundles of grass at the city gate. The horse dealer, unable to find grass for the horses in the whole city, bought those grasses from him for a thousand (kahāpaṇas).

After a few days, his sea-trader friend informed him, "A large ship has arrived at the port." He thought, "I have this plan..."
172:
Taking a hired carriage for temporary use, fully equipped with all attendants for eight kahāpaṇas, he went to the port. He gave a ring to the ship's captain as a deposit and had a curtained area set up in a nearby place. Sitting there, he commanded his men, "When the foreign merchants arrive, inform me through the third messenger." Hearing that "the ship has arrived," about a hundred merchants from Bārāṇasī came, thinking, "We shall take the goods." The sailors told them, "You cannot get the goods; a great merchant has already given a deposit at such-and-such a place." Hearing this, those merchants came to him. The attendants waiting at his feet informed him of the merchants' arrival through the third messenger, according to the previously given signal. Those hundred or so merchants each gave one thousand to become shareholders in the ship with him, and then each gave another thousand to have him relinquish his share, thus making all the goods their own property. That man, taking two hundred thousand, returned to Bārāṇasī. Thinking, "I should be one who knows gratitude," he took one hundred thousand and went to Cūḷaseṭṭhi.

Then Cūḷaseṭṭhi asked him, "Dear son, what work did you do to obtain this wealth?" He replied, "I obtained it within only four months by following the advice you gave." Hearing his words, the Treasurer thought, "It is no longer proper to keep such a youth as a subordinate of others," and gave him his daughter who had reached marriageable age, making him the master of all his wealth. That noble son, upon the death of the Treasurer, took the position of Treasurer in that city and remained there for the rest of his life, passing away according to his kamma. The Teacher, having told these two stories and connecting the relevance, spoke this verse upon reaching Buddhahood:

"With even a small capital, a wise and discerning person,
Can build himself up,
Just as a wise man blows a small fire to make it grow."

In this way, the Teacher showed this matter to the monks assembled in the Dhamma Hall. This is the sequential account starting from the past aspirations of the two Great Disciples. Later, while the Teacher was seated on the Dhamma throne surrounded by the assembly of Noble Ones, he placed Elder Cūḷapanthaka in the foremost position among those who create mind-made bodies and those skilled in the evolution of consciousness, and Elder Mahāpanthaka among those skilled in the evolution of perception.
173:
## The Story of Elder Subhūti

In the third sutta, 'araṇavihārīnaṃ' means among those who dwell without defilements. Defilements such as lust (rāga) are called 'raṇa'; because of the absence of those defilements, dwelling without defilements is called 'araṇavihāra'. Those who have such a dwelling are called 'araṇavihārī'. Among those who dwell without defilements, Elder Subhūti is the foremost. Although it is true that other Arahants also dwell without defilements, the Elder received this title because of his manner of preaching the Dhamma. When other monks preach the Dhamma, they might speak praise or blame with reference to individuals, but when the Elder preaches the Dhamma, he preaches without departing from the method taught by the Teacher; therefore, he became the foremost among those who dwell without defilements.

In the fourth sutta, 'dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ' means among those worthy of noble offerings. In this regard, although it is true that other Arahants are also the most worthy recipients of offerings, the Elder, when going for alms, enters the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (metta-jhāna) at every house. Emerging from the attainment, he accepts the alms, reflecting, "By doing this, there will be great fruit for the donors of alms." Therefore, he is called the foremost among those worthy of offerings. Furthermore, his physical form was very perfect; it shone exceedingly like a decorated archway or a beautiful painted cloth. Therefore, he is called 'Subhūti'.

Regarding the past deeds of that Elder, the sequential account is as follows: This future Elder Subhūti was born into a wealthy Brahmin family in the city of Haṃsavatī even before Padumuttara Buddha appeared in the world, and was named 'Nanda Māṇava'. When Nanda reached the proper age, he studied the three Vedas, but seeing no essence in those Vedas, he went forth as an ascetic at the foot of a mountain together with his retinue of forty-four thousand youths. He attained the five higher powers (abhiññā) and the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti), and he also made his disciples attainers of jhāna.

At that time, Padumuttara Buddha appeared in the world and was residing near the city of Haṃsavatī. One day at dawn, while surveying the world, He saw the potential for the attainment of Arahatship by Nanda the ascetic's matted-hair disciples, and Nanda the ascetic's aspiration for a specific foremost position of a disciple endowed with two qualities. Early in the morning, after attending to His physical needs, He took His bowl and robes during the forenoon and went to Nanda the ascetic's hermitage, following the same manner described in the story of Elder Sāriputta.
174:
In that hermitage, the offering of various fruits, the arranging of flower-seats, and the attainment of the cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) should be understood in the manner already described.

When the Teacher arose from the attainment of cessation, he commanded a disciple endowed with two qualities—the quality of living without defilements (araṇavihārī) and the quality of being worthy of the highest offerings (dakkhiṇeyya)—saying, "Give the words of appreciation (anumodanā) for the flower-seats to the group of ascetics." That disciple, standing in his own domain and reflecting on the Tipiṭaka, gave the words of appreciation. At the end of that monk's discourse, the Teacher himself taught the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, all forty-four thousand ascetics attained Arahantship. However, the ascetic Nanda, being focused on the manner of the monk who gave the appreciation, was unable to direct his knowledge according to the sequence of the Teacher's discourse. The Teacher stretched out his hand to the remaining monks, saying, "Come, monks (Etha, bhikkhave)." All of them became like elders of sixty years' standing, their hair and beards disappearing, and bearing supernatural requisites.

The ascetic Nanda, having paid homage to the Teacher and standing before him, asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the name of this monk in your Dispensation who gave the appreciation for the flower-seats to the group of ascetics?" "This monk is one who has reached the foremost position (etadagga) in the quality of living without defilements and the quality of being worthy of the highest offerings," he replied. "Venerable Sir, by this meritorious deed performed for seven days, I do not aspire to any other prosperity. In the future, in the Dispensation of a Buddha, may I be one endowed with these two qualities like this elder," he made his aspiration. The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacles, gave the prophecy and departed. The ascetic Nanda also listened to the Dhamma in the presence of the Ten-Powered One from time to time and, with his jhānas undiminished, was reborn in the Brahma realm. This was his good deed. The deeds in the intervening period are not mentioned.

After passing through a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in the house of the merchant Sumana in the city of Sāvatthī, and they named him Subhūti. Later, our Teacher appeared in the world and resided near the city of Rājagaha. At that time, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika took goods produced in Sāvatthī and went to the house of his friend, the merchant of Rājagaha. Upon learning that the Teacher had appeared, he approached the Teacher residing in the Sītavana forest and, upon his first sight, [attained] the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala)...
175:
Established in the fruit of Stream-entry, he requested the Teacher to come to Sāvatthī. Along the forty-five league journey, he spent one hundred thousand [coins] per league to have monasteries built. In Sāvatthī, he purchased the garden land of Prince Jeta, measuring eight karīsas, by covering it with crores of coins, and there he built and offered a monastery for the Blessed One. On the day of the monastery's dedication ceremony, this householder Subhūti went along with the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and, while listening to the Dhamma, gained faith and went forth. After becoming fully ordained, he mastered the two Matikas, requested a meditation subject, and while practicing the recluse's Dhamma in the forest, he developed insight (vipassanā) and, using loving-kindness jhāna (mettā-jhāna) as a basis, attained Arahantship. When teaching the Dhamma, he would teach in the manner already mentioned (with loving-kindness), and when going for alms, he would emerge from loving-kindness jhāna and accept alms in the manner already mentioned. Then, the Teacher, based on these two reasons, placed him in the foremost position among monks who live without defilements and those who are worthy of offerings.

## The Story of the Elder Khadiravaniya Revata
The fifth [category], "āraññakānaṃ," means "among those who dwell in the forest." Khadiravaniya Revata was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta). He did not live in the forest like other elders who, while living in the forest, select a suitable forest, suitable water, and suitable alms-resort. Without regarding such suitability, he resided in the Khadiravana (Acacia Forest), which was uneven with gravel and stones. Therefore, he is called the foremost among forest-dwellers.

The sequential account of his past aspiration is as follows: It is said that in the past, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was born in the city of Haṃsavatī and lived by working with boats at the Payāgapatiṭṭhāna ferry on the Great Ganges River. At that time, the Teacher, wandering for alms accompanied by a hundred thousand monks, arrived at the Payāgapatiṭṭhāna ferry. Seeing the Ten-Powered One, he thought, "I do not have the opportunity to see the Buddha all the time; this is the moment for me to accumulate good deeds." He had boats lashed together to form a raft, had cloth canopies erected above, hung garlands of perfumes and flowers, and spread exquisite floor coverings below, and then ferried the Teacher and his followers to the other shore.
176:
At that time, the Blessed One appointed a forest-dwelling monk to a foremost position (etadagga). Seeing that elder, the boatman thought, "It would be fitting if I too could become the foremost among forest-dwellers in the dispensation of a future Buddha." He invited the Blessed One, offered a great alms-giving (mahādāna) for seven days, and prostrating at the feet of the Blessed One, he made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, just like that monk whom you have appointed to the foremost position, may I also become the foremost among forest-dwellers in the dispensation of a future Buddha." Seeing that there would be no obstacles, the Blessed One prophesied, "In the future, in the dispensation of Gotama Buddha, you will become the foremost among forest-dwellers," and then departed. No other deeds are mentioned in the interval.

Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in the womb of the Brahmin lady Sārī in the Brahmin village of Nālaka in the kingdom of Magadha during the time of our Blessed One's appearance. He was born as the youngest son among three brothers and three sisters, and they named him Revata. Then his parents thought, "The Sakyaputtiya monks take our grown-up children and ordain them. Let us bind our son Revata with the bond of marriage while he is still young." They brought a girl from a similar clan, made Revata pay respects to her grandmother, and said, "Dear daughter, may you live long and become as old as your grandmother." Hearing the parents' words, Revata thought, "This girl is still young, in her first stage of life. Does it mean that this girl's appearance will become like my grandmother's? I will ask their intention first." He then asked, "What are you saying?" They replied, "Dear boy, we are saying may this girl reach old age like your grandmother." He asked, "Will this girl's appearance become like this?" They replied, "Dear boy, what are you saying? Even those with great merit become like this."

He thought, "This appearance will indeed become like this, with wrinkled skin, grey hair, and broken teeth. Why should I take delight in such an appearance? I will go the way my elder brothers have gone." Then, pretending to play, he said to boys of his own age, "Friends, come, let us play a race," and went outside. Although his parents said, "Dear boy, do not go outside on your wedding day," he continued to pretend to play with the boys, and when his turn to run came, he went a little distance and delayed...
177:
...and returned. When the second turn came, he went faster than the first time and returned. When the third turn came, knowing "This is my time (to escape)," he ran straight ahead and went to the forest where the monks who wear rag-robes (paṃsukūla) resided. Having paid respects to the elders, he requested ordination. They said, "Good man, we do not know whose son you are. You have come dressed in finery; who would dare to ordain you?" That youth Revata raised both arms and wailed loudly, "They are robbing me! They are robbing me!" Monks gathered from here and there and asked, "Good man, there is no one here who would take your clothes or ornaments. Yet you say 'They are robbing me.' What are you referring to?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, I am not referring to my clothes and ornaments. Indeed, the robbery of my three types of prosperity (human, divine, and Nibbāna) is taking place. I am referring to that." He then said, "Do not ordain me just yet. Do you know my elder brother?" They asked, "What is your brother's name?" He replied, "In lay life, his name was Upatissa, but now they say he is known as Sāriputta." The monks said, "Friends, if that is so, this clansman is our younger brother. Our eldest brother, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), previously told us: 'All our relatives are of wrong view. If anyone comes saying they are our relative, ordain them by any means.' This person is the elder's own younger brother; ordain him." They taught him the meditation on the five parts ending in skin (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him. Later, when he reached twenty years of age, they gave him higher ordination and directed him in meditation.

The elder took the meditation subject and entered the aforementioned Khadira forest (Acacia forest) not far from his teachers and preceptors to practice the Dhamma of a recluse. He strove with the thought, "I will not see the Blessed One or my elder brother until I reach Arahantship." Three months passed. Being a youth of a delicate family, his mind shrank because he had to eat coarse food, and his meditation had not yet reached liberation. After the three months, having completed the rainy season retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he continued to practice the Dhamma of a recluse in that same forest. As he practiced, his mind became one-pointed. He developed insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship.
178:
Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I have heard that my younger brother Revata has ordained. Whether he is finding delight [in the Dispensation] or not, I shall go and see him." The Blessed One, knowing that the Elder Revata was established in insight meditation (vipassanā), refused twice. On the third request, knowing that he had attained Arahatship, the Buddha said: "Dear Sāriputta, I too will go. Inform the monks."

The Elder assembled the community of monks and announced to all: "Friends, the Blessed One wishes to go on a journey. Let those who wish to follow come along." When the Blessed One went on a journey, the monks who remained behind were few. Most monks wished to go, thinking: "We shall behold the golden-hued body of the Blessed One and listen to his sweet Dhamma talks." Thus, the Blessed One set out, surrounded by a large retinue of monks, with the intention: "I shall see Revata."

Then, at a certain place, the Venerable Ānanda reached a crossroads and asked the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, there are two paths here. Which path should the Saṅgha take?" The Buddha asked: "Ānanda, which path is straight?" "Venerable Sir, the straight path is thirty yojanas long, but it is a path through an uninhabited wilderness. The circuitous path is sixty yojanas long, but it is safe and well-provisioned with alms-food," he replied. The Buddha then asked: "Ānanda, is Sīvali with us?" "Yes, Venerable Sir, he is with us," he replied. "If so, let the Saṅgha take the straight path. We shall test the merit of Sīvali," the Buddha declared.

Surrounded by the retinue of monks, the Blessed One took the forest path to test the merit of the Elder Sīvali. From the point they entered the path, the host of deities created a city at every yojana and prepared monasteries for the Saṅgha led by the Buddha to reside. The deities, acting like workers sent by a king, brought gruel, food, and other offerings, asking: "Where is the Venerable Sīvali? Where is the Venerable Sīvali?" The Elder had those offerings accepted and went to the Blessed One. The Blessed One partook of them together with the community of monks.

In this manner, the Blessed One enjoyed the offerings and traveled one yojana each day. After crossing the thirty-yojana difficult journey, he reached the dwelling place of the Elder Revata in the Khadiravana (Acacia Forest). The Elder, knowing that the Blessed One was arriving, used his psychic powers to create monasteries at his dwelling place sufficient for the Saṅgha led by the Buddha, as well as a Gandhakuṭi for the Blessed One, and places for night and day rest. For the Blessed One...
179:
The Elder Revata, knowing that the Blessed One was arriving, used his psychic powers to create monasteries at his dwelling place sufficient for the Saṅgha led by the Buddha, as well as a Gandhakuṭi for the Blessed One, and places for night and day rest. He then went to welcome the Blessed One. The Blessed One entered the monastery via a path that had been decorated and prepared. When the Tathāgata had entered the Gandhakuṭi, the monks also entered their assigned dwellings according to seniority. The deities, thinking, "Now is not the time for food, it is the time for drinks," brought eight kinds of pānaka (syrups/drinks). The Blessed One drank the pānaka together with the Saṅgha. In this manner, while the Tathāgata was enjoying the offerings, half a month (fifteen days) passed.

Then, some dissatisfied monks, while sitting in a certain place, started a conversation: "The Blessed One, saying 'He is the younger brother of my Chief Disciple,' has come to see such a monk who is busy with new construction (navakamma). Near this monastery, what could the Great Jetavana Monastery or Veḷuvana Monastery and others possibly do [to compare]? This monk is only a performer of such new construction; what kind of monk's duty (samana-dhamma) could he possibly be practicing?" Then the Blessed One thought: "If I stay here for a long time, this place will become crowded. Forest-dwelling monks desire solitude. It will be an uncomfortable dwelling for Revata." Thus, he went to the Elder Revata's daytime resting place. The Elder was sitting alone on a stone slab, leaning against a backrest board at the end of the cloister walk. Seeing the Blessed One coming from afar, he went to welcome and pay homage to him.

Then the Blessed One asked him: "Revata, this is a place of wild beasts. When you hear the sounds of fierce elephants, horses, and so on, what do you do?" "Venerable Sir, when I hear the sounds of those creatures, only delight in the forest (araññarati) arises in me," he replied. In that place, the Blessed One spoke to the Elder Revata in five hundred verses on the benefits of living in the forest. The next day, after wandering for alms in a nearby place, he sent the Elder Revata back. Then, for those monks who had spoken ill of the Elder, the Buddha caused them to forget their walking sticks, sandals, oil tubes, and umbrellas. When those monks returned for their requisites, although they went by the same path they had come, they could not recognize the place. This was because, while they had first come by a decorated and prepared path, that day they had to go by a rough path, resulting in them having to squat or crawl on their knees in various places. Treading through bushes, trees, and thorns, they reached the place where they had stayed, and only then did they recognize their umbrellas, sandals, walking sticks, and oil tubes hanging on various acacia stumps. At that time, those monks...
180:
Knowing that "this monk is one of great power (iddhimā)," they took their requisites and came, saying, "Such is the honor and respect prepared for the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala)." While the laywoman Visākhā was sitting in her house, she asked the monks who arrived first, "Venerable sirs, is the dwelling place of Venerable Revata pleasant?" The monks replied, "Laywoman, that dwelling is pleasant; it is comparable to the Nandana and Cittalatā gardens." Then she asked the monks who arrived last of all, "Venerable sirs, is the dwelling place of Venerable Revata pleasant?" They replied, "Laywoman, do not ask. That place is not even fit to speak of. It is an acacia forest (khadiravana), uneven with gravel and stones. That monk lives there."

Visākhā, having heard the words of the monks who arrived first and those who arrived last, wondered, "Which monks' words are true?" In the evening, she took perfumes and flowers, went to attend upon the One of Ten Powers, and after paying homage, sat in a suitable place and asked the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, some venerable ones praise Venerable Revata's dwelling place, while others disparage it. What is the reason for this, Venerable sir?" The Blessed One said, "Visākhā, whether it be delightful or not, the place where the minds of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) find delight, that very place is called delightful." He then spoke this verse:

"Whether in a village or in a forest, in a valley or on a plain,
Wherever Arahants dwell, that land is delightful."

Later, while the Blessed One was sitting in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones at the Jetavana Monastery, He placed the elder in the foremost position among the monks who are forest-dwellers (āraññaka).

## The Story of Elder Kaṅkhā-Revata

In the sixth sutta, 'jhāyīnaṃ' refers to those who have attained jhāna and delight in jhāna. It is said that the elder entered many meditative attainments (samāpatti), being only slightly less than those entered by the One of Ten Powers. Therefore, he became the foremost among those who practice jhāna. He is called 'Kaṅkhā-Revata' because of his state of having doubts (kaṅkhā). 'Kaṅkhā' means 'kukkucca' (scrupulousness); the meaning is one who is scrupulous. If one asks, "Are there no other monks who are scrupulous?" Yes, there are. However, this elder developed scrupulousness even regarding things that were allowable (kappiya). Because of that, his scrupulous nature became very well-known, and thus he became known by the name 'Kaṅkhā-Revata'.

Regarding the question of his past, this is the chronological account: It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he went to the monastery with a great crowd as in the previous accounts. Standing at the edge of the assembly, he saw the Buddha placing a monk in the foremost position among those who delight in jhāna, and he thought, "It would be good if I too could reach such a status in the future." At the end of the discourse, he invited the Blessed One and, as in the previous accounts, performed great offerings for seven days. He then addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, because of this meritorious deed, I do not aspire for any other wealth. Just as you have placed that monk in the foremost position among those who practice jhāna on the seventh day from today, may I also become the foremost among those who practice jhāna in the Dispensation of a future Buddha." Padumuttara Buddha, looking into the future and seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, said: "In the future, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In the Dispensation of that Buddha..."
181:
While listening to the Dhamma, that man saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position among those who delight in meditative absorption (jhāna). Thinking, "It would be good if I too could become such a person in the future," he invited the Teacher at the end of the teaching. Following the previous method, he performed a great offering for seven days and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, by this meritorious deed, I do not aspire for any other prosperity. Just as you appointed a monk seven days ago to the foremost position among those who practice jhāna, may I also become the foremost among those who practice jhāna in the dispensation of a future Buddha."

The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that the wish would be fulfilled, prophesied: "At the end of a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In his dispensation, you will be the foremost among those who practice jhāna." Having said this, he departed. That man performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn into a wealthy family in the city of Sāvatthī. One evening, he went to the monastery along with a great crowd of people going to hear the Dhamma. Standing at the edge of the assembly, he heard the Dhamma talk of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala), gained faith, and was ordained, attaining full admission (upasampadā).

Having requested a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and performing the preliminary work for jhāna, he attained jhāna. Using that very jhāna as a basis, he attained the fruit of Arahantship. Except for a few meditative attainments (samāpatti) that only the One of Ten Powers can enter, that Elder entered many attainments and became one who had mastery over the jhānas day and night. Later, the Teacher, based on this quality, appointed him to the foremost position among those who practice jhāna. Because he used to have scruples (kukkucca) even regarding allowable things, saying, "Friends, molasses is not allowable; mung beans are not allowable," he became known as "Kankhārevata" (Revata the Doubter) due to the state of his doubt (kankhā), which is called kukkucca.

## The Story of Elder Soṇakoḷivisa
The seventh [category], "āraddhavīriyānaṃ," means among those who have exerted effort, those with perfected energy. In the name "Soṇo Koḷiviso," "Soṇa" is the name of the Elder, and "Koḷivisa" is his clan name (gotta). Alternatively, it means "Koṭivessa," signifying a son of a merchant family (vessa) who has reached the pinnacle (koṭi) of wealth. While other monks had to increase their energy, this Elder only had to relax his energy. Therefore, he became the foremost among those who have exerted energy.
182: Regarding the matter of the Elder Soṇa Koḷivisa, the sequential account is as follows: In the past, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, this future Elder was born into a merchant family and was named Siriwaḍḍha. When he came of age, he went to the monastery as in the previous manner, and while standing at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those of energetic effort. He thought, 'It would be good if I too could become such a person in the future.' At the end of the discourse, he invited the Buddha, gave a great donation for seven days, and made an aspiration in the same manner as previously mentioned. The Teacher, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, gave him a prophecy as in the previous manner and returned to the monastery. That merchant Siriwaḍḍha performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and after a hundred thousand aeons had passed, during this Bhadda-kappa, after Kassapa Buddha had attained Parinibbāna and before our Buddha had appeared, he was conceived in a respectable family in Vārāṇasī. He used to play in the Ganges River with his companions. At that time, a Paccekabuddha with worn-out robes, thinking, 'I will spend the rains retreat by building a leaf-hut on the banks of the Ganges near Vārāṇasī,' was gathering sticks and creepers brought down by the current. This youth went with his companions, paid respectful homage, and asked, 'Venerable Sir, what are you doing?' The Paccekabuddha replied, 'Youth, the rains retreat is approaching, and it is proper for monks to have a place to stay.' He said, 'Venerable Sir, please be patient and wait for just this one day; tomorrow I will prepare a place for you to stay.' The Paccekabuddha, intending to favor the youth, consented. Knowing his consent, the youth left, and on the next day, after preparing offerings and honors, he stood watching for the Paccekabuddha's arrival. The Paccekabuddha, reflecting on where he should go for alms that day, knew and went to the door of that youth's house. Seeing the Paccekabuddha, the youth was filled with great devotion and affection; he took the bowl, offered alms-food, and obtained a promise, saying, 'Venerable Sir, please come only to my house door throughout this rains retreat.' After the Paccekabuddha had finished his meal and departed, the youth went with his companions and, in a single day, built and offered a leaf-hut, a walkway, and places for the night and day for the Paccekabuddha. When that Paccekabuddha entered the leaf-hut, on the floor smeared with fresh cow dung, thinking, 'May mud not cling to his feet,' he spread his own garment and a red rug worth a hundred thousand as a floor covering. Seeing the radiance of the Paccekabuddha's body match the color of the rug, he was greatly inspired and said: 'Just as the color of this rug shines most beautifully from the moment you stepped on it, so too, wherever I am born, may the color of my hands and feet be like the color of the Bandhujīvaka flower, and may my touch be like that of a cotton tuft beaten a hundred times...'
183:
Seeing the youth, he was filled with love and devotion for the Paccekabuddha; he took the bowl, offered alms, and obtained a promise, saying, 'Venerable Sir, please come only to my house door throughout this rains retreat.' After the Paccekabuddha had finished his meal and departed, he went with his companions and, in a single day, built and offered a leaf-hut, a walkway, and places for the night and day for the Paccekabuddha to reside.

When that Paccekabuddha entered the leaf-hut, on the floor smeared with fresh cow dung, keeping in mind, 'May mud not cling to his feet,' he spread his own red rug garment worth a hundred thousand as a floor covering. Seeing the radiance of the Paccekabuddha's body match the color of the rug, he was greatly inspired and made an aspiration, saying: 'Venerable Sir, just as the color of this rug shines most beautifully from the moment you stepped on it, so too, in every life I am born, may the color of my hands and feet be like the color of the Bandhujīvaka flower, and may I have a touch as soft as a cotton layer beaten a hundred times.' That youth served the Paccekabuddha for three months, and at the time of the Pavāraṇā at the end of the rains, he offered the three robes. The Paccekabuddha, with his bowl and robes complete, departed for Mount Gandhamādana.

That young man, after wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was conceived in the house of a deputy treasurer in the city of Kāḷacampā during the time of our Buddha. From the time of his conception, thousands of gifts and presents arrived at the treasurer's house. On the day of his birth, the entire city performed honors and offerings simultaneously. Later, on the day of his naming, his parents named him 'Soṇa Kumāra' (Prince Soṇa), saying, 'Our son has come bringing his own name; his body's complexion is as if poured with liquid red gold.'

Then, they had sixty nurses surround him and let him grow up in comfort like a celestial youth. The preparation of food for that youth was as follows: They plowed an area of about sixty karīsas and cultivated it using three types of water. Into the irrigation channels entering the fields, they poured thousands of jars of milk and scented water. When the ears of the Shali rice were at the milk-producing stage, to prevent animals like parrots from eating them and to keep the rice husks delicate, they drove stakes at the boundaries and at intervals, placed sticks on top, covered them with mats, surrounded them with curtains, and kept guard all around. When the crop was ready, they smeared the granary with four kinds of perfumes and scented it from above with the finest fragrances. Thousands of men went down into the field, cut the ears of Shali rice from the stalks, made them into handfuls, tied them with ropes, and dried them. Then, they spread perfumes on the lower floor of the granary and spread the ears of Shali rice on top. Thus, spreading them layer by layer, they filled the granary and closed the door. For three years...
184: They close the granary door; they open it only when three years have passed. When it is opened, the entire city becomes fragrant. When the Sāli rice is pounded, drunkards buy the husks, and minor attendants receive the broken rice. They select the Sāli rice grains struck by the pestle. They put those grains in a golden basket, filter them many times, and then put them once into boiling pure essence and take them out; the two ends of that rice look very much like jasmine flowers. They put that food in a golden bowl, place it on top of a silver tray filled with boiling milk-rice with little water, and place it before the merchant's son. After the merchant's son eats just enough to sustain himself, he rinses his mouth with scented water and washes his hands and feet. Then they bring various mouth-freshening perfumes to the young Soṇa, whose hands and feet have been washed. They spread a rug decorated with noble figures where he treads. The palms and soles of the young Soṇa are red like the color of Bandhujīvaka flowers and soft like the touch of cotton beaten a hundred times; on his soles, hair grew in the shape of jeweled earrings circling to the right. If he got angry with someone, he would say, 'Know this, I will step on the ground.' When he came of age, they built three palaces suitable for the three seasons for him and provided dancers to serve him. He lived like a celestial being, enjoying great wealth. Then, when our Teacher attained omniscience and preached the noble Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, while residing near Rājagaha, King Bimbisāra of Magadha summoned him to see the hair on his soles and sent him to the Teacher along with eighty thousand villagers. Having heard the Dhamma, Soṇa gained faith and requested ordination from the Teacher. Then the Buddha asked, 'Have you been permitted by your parents?' and learning that he was not yet permitted, He refused, saying, 'Soṇa, Tathāgatas do not ordain a son without parental permission.' The young Soṇa accepted the Buddha's words with respect, went to his parents to get permission, returned to the Teacher, and was ordained under a certain monk. This is just a summary here; the detailed procedure of his ordination should be known as it appears in the Vinaya Mahāvagga. While Soṇa lived in Rājagaha after receiving the lower and higher ordinations, many relatives and friends brought offerings and honors, and they spoke of the merit of his physical beauty. Other people also came to see him. Then Elder Soṇa thought, 'Many people are coming to me; how will I be able to perform the work of meditation or insight? I will take a meditation subject from the Teacher and go to Sītavana cemetery to practice the Dhamma of a recluse...'
185:
People spoke of the excellence of the youth Soṇa’s beauty, and others also came to see him. Then the Elder thought: "Many people come to me; how will I be able to perform the work of a meditation subject or insight? It would be good if I were to request a meditation subject from the Teacher and go to the Sītavana cemetery to practice the Dhamma of a recluse. There, people will not come, being repulsed by the fact that it is a cemetery. In this way, my task as a monk will reach its completion." Having thus reflected, he requested a meditation subject from the Teacher and went to the Sītavana forest to begin practicing the Dhamma of a recluse.

The Elder thought: "My body is extremely delicate. It is not possible to reach happiness through ease alone; it is proper to practice the Dhamma of a recluse even by exhausting the body." Then, undertaking only the postures of standing and walking, he put forth effort. Blisters arose and burst on the edges of the delicate soles of the Elder's feet, and the walking path became covered in a mass of blood. When he could no longer walk with his feet, he strove by moving along the walking path on his knees and hands. Although he put forth such strenuous effort, he was unable to achieve even a glimmer of light. He thought: "If there were others with energetic effort, they would be just like me. Yet, even though I strive in this way, I am unable to give rise to the Path or Fruition. Surely, I am not one who understands quickly (ugghaṭitaññū), nor one who understands through expansion (vipaṭitaññū), nor one who needs guidance (neyya); I must be one for whom the word is the maximum (padaparama). What is the use of my life as a monk? I shall return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds."

At that time, the Teacher, knowing the Elder's thought, went there in the evening surrounded by a company of monks. Seeing the walking path stained with blood, He exhorted the Elder with the simile of the lute (vīṇā). Having taught him a meditation subject for the purpose of balancing effort and tranquility, He departed for Gijjhakūṭa Mountain. The Elder Soṇa, having received the exhortation in the presence of the Ten-Powered One, soon established himself in Arahantship. Later, while the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma at Jetavana Monastery surrounded by a company of monks, He placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who possess energetic effort.

## Soṇakuṭikaṇṇattheravatthu

In the eighth sutta, regarding the term "kalyāṇavākkaraṇānaṃ," vākkaraṇa means the act of speaking; the meaning is "of those who have sweet speech." This Elder, together with the Ten-Powered One in the same Fragrant Chamber...
186:
He preached the Dhamma to the Blessed One with a sweet voice. Then the Teacher gave him his approval (Sādhu). Because of that, he became the foremost among those of good utterance. Soṇa was his name, but because he wore an ear-ornament worth a crore (koṭi), he was called Koṭikaṇṇa, meaning 'one with an ornament worth a crore'.

In the matter of his past aspiration, this is the sequential account: This future Elder Soṇa, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, went to the monastery with the people as in the previous manner. Standing at the edge of the assembly while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a monk to the foremost position among those of good utterance. He thought, 'It would be good if I too were to become the foremost among those of good utterance in the dispensation of a future Buddha.' He then invited the Ten-Powered One, gave a great offering for seven days, and made a wish: 'Venerable Sir, seven days ago you appointed a certain monk to the foremost position among those of good utterance. May I also, by the fruit of this meritorious deed, become such a person in the dispensation of a future Buddha.' Seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, the Teacher prophesied, 'In the future, in the dispensation of Gotama Buddha, you will be the foremost among those of good utterance,' and then departed.

That man performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. Before the appearance of our Ten-Powered One, he passed away from the deva world and took rebirth in the womb of a lay follower named Kāḷī of Kuraraghara. When her pregnancy was mature, she went to her family home in the city of Rājagaha.

At that time, our Teacher attained omniscience and turned the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana. At the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, deities from the ten-thousand-fold world system gathered. There, a Yakkha named Sātāgira, who was one of the twenty-eight Yakkha generals, heard the Dhamma of the Ten-Powered One, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), and thought: 'I wonder if this sweet Dhamma has been heard by my friend Hemavata or not?' Looking through the assembly of devas and not seeing him, he thought, 'Surely my friend does not know of the appearance of the Triple Gem. I shall go and speak of the virtues of the Ten-Powered One and inform him of the Dhamma that has been realized.' Thus, together with his retinue, he set out toward Hemavata through the sky above Rājagaha.
187:
The Yakkha Hemavata also saw the three-thousand-league Himavanta blooming with flowers out of season and thought, 'I shall play in the Himavanta with my friend Sātāgira.' He then set out with his retinue through the sky above Rājagaha. The leading forces of both Sātāgira and Hemavata met in the sky above the house of the lay follower Kāḷī. They asked each other, 'Whose retinue are you?' and replied, 'We are Sātāgira’s retinue,' and 'We are Hemavata’s retinue.' Being joyful, they went and informed their respective Yakkha generals. Those two generals also met in the sky above the lay follower’s house at that very moment.

General Sātāgira asked Hemavata, 'Friend, where are you going?' 'Friend, I am coming to you.' 'For what reason?' 'Seeing the Himavanta in bloom, I came to play there with you.' Then Hemavata asked, 'Friend, where are you going?' 'Friend, I am coming to you.' 'For what reason? Do you know why the Himavanta is in bloom?' 'Friend, I do not know.'

'Prince Siddhattha, the son of King Suddhodana, having shaken the ten-thousand-fold world system and realized Omniscient Knowledge, has turned the peerless and noble Wheel of Dhamma in the midst of the devas from the ten-thousand-fold world system. Do you not know that the Wheel has been turned?' 'Friend, I do not know.' 'You only know that flowers are blooming in this part of the Himavanta, but friend, today the entire ten-thousand-fold world system has become like a single mass of garlands to honor that Great Man.' 'Let the flowers be; have you seen that Teacher with your own eyes to your heart's content?' 'Yes, friend, I have seen the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and drunk the nectar of the Deathless (Amata). Friend, I have come to you because I want you to know this Deathless Dhamma as well.'

While those two generals were conversing, the lay follower Kāḷī, who had risen from her auspicious bed and was sitting, heard their conversation and took note of the sound. She reflected, 'This sound is from above, not below; it is spoken by non-humans, not humans.' She sat there with attentive ears and a concentrated mind. Then—

'Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha (said the Yakkha Sātāgira),
The divine night has arrived;
The Teacher of perfect name,
Come, let us see Gotama.'
188:
When Sātāgiri the Yakkha had spoken thus—

"O friend, is the mind of that Exalted One, who is endowed with supreme qualities, well-established toward all beings?
O friend, is the intention of that Exalted One under his own control regarding both the pleasant and the unpleasant?" (Thus Hemavata the Yakkha asked.)

In this way, Hemavata the Yakkha inquired about the Teacher's bodily conduct, livelihood, and mental conduct. Sātāgiri the Yakkha answered every question asked. Thus, at the conclusion of the Hemavata Sutta, which described the physical appearance and virtues of the Teacher, Hemavata the Yakkha directed his wisdom according to the sequence of the Dhamma teaching of his friend Sātāgiri and was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.

At that time, Kālī the lay follower, while the Dhamma was being preached to another, though she had never seen the Tathāgata before, developed faith through hearing. Just like one eating food served and prepared by another, she was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. Among all women, Kālī the lay follower was the very first to become a Stream-enterer and was the most senior of all. Simultaneously with her becoming a Stream-enterer, she gave birth that very night. On the day of naming the newborn son, she named him Soṇa. After staying at her parents' house as long as she wished, Kālī the lay follower went to her husband's house.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana was residing on Mount Upavatta, depending on that city. The lay follower attended to the Elder. The Elder went regularly to her house. The youth Soṇa also became well-acquainted with the Elder, moving about in his presence regularly. Later, that youth went forth as a novice in the presence of the Elder. The Elder, wishing to grant him higher ordination, searched for a quorum for three years before ordaining him. After becoming a monk, Soṇa requested and received a meditation subject, developed insight, and attained Arahatship. Having learned the Sutta Nipāta in the presence of the Elder himself, and having completed the rainy season retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he wished to see the Teacher and asked permission from his preceptor.

The Elder said, "Soṇa, when you go, the Teacher will have you stay in the same Fragrant Chamber and will urge you to preach the Dhamma; you shall preach the Dhamma. The Teacher, being pleased with your Dhamma talk, will grant you a boon. When you accept the boon, take such and such boons, and in my name, pay homage at the feet of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala)." Having received permission from his preceptor, the Elder Soṇa went to the house of his mother, the lay follower, and informed her. She also...
189:
"Excellent, dear son! When you go to see the Ten-Powered One, take this woolen rug, and having made it a floor covering in the Fragrant Chamber where the Teacher resides, spread it out." Thus she offered the woolen rug. The Venerable Soṇa took the rug, put his lodgings in order, and in due course went to the place where the Teacher resided. Approaching while the Ten-Powered One was seated on the Buddha-seat, he paid homage and stood at a respectful distance. The Teacher exchanged pleasantries with him and addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, arrange a lodging for this monk." The Venerable Ānanda, knowing the Teacher's intention, spread the floor covering even within the Fragrant Chamber itself.

Then the Blessed One, having spent much of the night in the open air, entered the Fragrant Chamber. The Venerable Soṇa also, having spent much of the night in the open air, entered the monastery. In the last watch of the night, the Teacher took the lion's posture, and rising at dawn, he sat down. Knowing that "By this time, Soṇa's physical fatigue will have subsided," he urged the Venerable Soṇa: "Monk, let the Dhamma occur to you to speak." The Venerable Soṇa, with a sweet voice and without losing even a single syllable, recited the discourses of the Aṭṭhakavagga. At the conclusion of the talk, the Blessed One gave his approval (Sādhukāra), saying: "Monk, you have well-grasped the Dhamma. The teaching as it was when I preached it and as it is today are identical; there is nothing deficient or redundant." Thus he expressed his appreciation.

The Venerable Soṇa, reflecting that "This is the right opportunity," paid homage to the Ten-Powered One according to his preceptor's instructions and requested all the boons, starting with the permission for higher ordination by a group of five with a Vinaya expert as the fifth member. The Teacher granted them. Again, the Elder paid homage according to his mother's instructions and said, "Venerable Sir, this woolen rug was sent by the lay follower to be used as a floor covering in the Fragrant Chamber where you reside." Having offered the rug, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Teacher, performed the circumambulation, and departed. This is a summary of the matter. The full details, starting from the Elder's going forth, can be known as they appear in the Udāna.

Thus, the Elder, having received the eight boons from the Teacher, went to his preceptor, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, and reported the whole event. The next morning, he went to the door of his mother's house and stood for alms. The lay follower, hearing that "My son is standing at the door," came out quickly, paid homage, and took the bowl from his hand...
190:
Taking the bowl from the hand of Elder Soṇa, she invited him to sit inside the house and offered him food. Then, at the conclusion of the meal, she asked the Elder, "Dear son, did you see the Blessed One, the Possessor of Ten Powers?" "Yes, laywoman, I did," he replied. "Dear son, did you pay homage to the Buddha on my behalf?" she asked. "Yes, I did. And that woolen blanket you offered was spread as a floor covering in the place where the Tathāgata resides," he said. "Dear son, is it true that you preached a sermon to the Buddha, and that the Buddha also expressed his approval by saying 'Sādhu' to you?" she asked again. "Laywoman, how do you know this?" he asked. "Dear son, the deity residing in my house told me on the day the Blessed One, the Possessor of Ten Powers, gave you his approval: 'The deities throughout the entire ten thousand world-systems are shouting Sādhu.' Dear son, I also aspire for you to preach that same sermon to me, just as you preached it to the Buddhas," she requested. The Elder accepted his mother's request. Knowing his acceptance, the laywoman had a pavilion built at the gate and had him preach the sermon to her in the same manner he had preached to the Buddha. Thus, this story originated here. Later, the Buddha, while seated in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones, placed Elder Soṇa in the foremost position (Etadagga) among those who speak beautifully.

## The Story of Elder Sīvali

In the ninth discourse, with the words "Lābhīnaṃ yadidaṃ Sīvali," the Buddha showed that, excluding the Tathāgata, Elder Sīvali is the foremost among the monks who receive gains. The following is the chronological account of his past deeds: This future Elder Sīvali, during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, went to the monastery as mentioned before and, while standing at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, saw the Buddha placing a monk in the foremost position among those who receive gains. He thought, "It would be good if I too could become such a person in the future." He then invited the Possessor of Ten Powers and, after giving a great alms-offering for seven days in the same manner as before, made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, by this meritorious deed, I do not desire any other prosperity. In the future, under the dispensation of a Buddha, may I also be the foremost among those who receive gains, just like the monk whom you have now placed in this foremost position." Seeing that there would be no obstacles, the Buddha prophesied, "This aspiration of yours will be fulfilled in the future under the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama," and then departed.

That young man, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was reborn in a village not far from the city of Bandhumatī during the time of the Buddha Vipassī. At that time, the citizens of Bandhumatī, having consulted with the King...
191:
...were giving alms to the Buddha Vipassī. One day, while all of them were collectively giving alms, they looked to see what was missing from their offerings and did not see any honey or curd (thickened like molasses). Thinking, "We will fetch it from somewhere," they stationed a man on the road leading from the countryside into the city.

At that time, this young man (the future Elder Sīvali) was coming from his village carrying a pot of curd as thick as molasses, thinking, "I will bring some item [to sell]." While on his way to the city, he washed his face and, looking for a pleasant spot to wash his hands and feet before entering, he saw a honeycomb on a branch, about the size of a plow head and free of flies. Thinking, "This has appeared due to my merit," he took it and entered the city. The man stationed by the citizens saw him and asked, "O man, for whom are you bringing this honey and curd?" "Sir, it is for no one; I have brought this to sell," he replied. "In that case, O man, take this one kahāpaṇa (coin) and give me that honey and curd," the man said.

The young man thought, "This honey and curd are not worth much, yet this man is offering a large amount at once; I should investigate this." Then he said to him, "I cannot give it for one kahāpaṇa." "If so, take two and give it," the man said. "I will not give it for two either," he replied. In this manner, as the price was increased further and further, it reached one thousand kahāpaṇas. The young man thought, "It is not right to hold out for too much, but let me first ask about his purpose." Then he asked him, "This honey and curd are not worth much, so why are you offering so many coins to take them?"

"Friend, here in this city of Bandhumatī, the citizens are competing with the King to give alms to the Buddha Vipassī, the Possessor of Ten Powers. Not seeing these two items in their collection of offerings, they are searching for them. If they do not get these two, the citizens will be defeated. Therefore, I am buying them for a thousand kahāpaṇas," the man explained. "Is such an offering suitable only for the citizens, or is it not suitable for others to give?" the young man asked. "It is not forbidden for anyone to give," the man replied. "Is there anyone among the citizens' offerings who gives a thousand kahāpaṇas in a single day?" he asked. "Friend, there is no such person," the man answered. "Do you know that these two items, honey and curd, are worth a thousand kahāpaṇas?" he asked. "Yes, I know," the man said. "If so, go and tell the citizens: 'A man will not sell these two items for a price; he wishes to offer them with his own hands. Therefore, do not worry about these two things.' And you, be a witness to my being the chief in this offering," the young man said.

That villager, using a small amount of money (about a māsaka) that he had brought for provisions, bought five kinds of spices (pañcakatu) and ground them into powder. After draining the whey from the curd, he squeezed the honeycomb, mixed it with the spice powder, and prepared it by placing it in a lotus leaf.
192:
The man took the honey-cake and sat down at a place not far from the Buddha. Observing his turn amidst the offerings being brought by the multitude, and knowing the opportunity, he approached the Buddha and said, "Venerable Sir, this is the gift of a poor man. Out of compassion for me, please accept this." Out of compassion for him, the Buddha accepted the offering in the stone bowl presented by the Four Great Kings. He then made a resolution so that even when distributed to six million eight hundred thousand monks, it would not be exhausted.

Having performed the act of paying homage to the Buddha after the meal, that clansman stood at a suitable place and said, "Venerable Sir, today I have seen the Buddha. The people of Bandhumatī are bringing offerings to you. By the result of this meritorious deed, may I be one who attains supreme gain and retinue in every life I am reborn." The Buddha said, "Clansman, may it be as you wish," and after performing the thanksgiving for the meal for him and the townspeople, He departed.

That clansman, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in the time of our Buddha, he was conceived in the womb of Princess Suppavāsā. From the time of conception, hundreds of gifts arrived day and night, and Princess Suppavāsā attained great prosperity. Then, to test her merit, they had her touch a basket of seeds with her hand; from each single seed, a hundred or a thousand stalks emerged. From a field of only one karīsa, fifty or sixty carts of grain were produced. At the time of filling the granary, they had her touch the granary door with her hand; due to the princess's merit, wherever people took grain from, it would be filled again. Even from a full pot of rice, saying "This is the princess's merit," when they gave to anyone, the rice would not be exhausted as long as she did not rise from her seat. While the child was still in the womb, seven years passed.

When the pregnancy matured, she experienced severe pain for seven days. She called her husband and, thinking "I wish to give an offering while I am still alive before I die," she sent him to the Buddha. "Go, inform the Buddha of this situation and invite Him. Whatever the Buddha says, note it well and come back to tell me." The prince went and reported her message to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "May Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, be happy. May she, being healthy and free from disease, give birth to a healthy son." Hearing this, the prince paid homage to the Blessed One and set out toward his home. Even before he arrived, Princess Suppavāsā...
194:
Later, the Blessed One went to Sāvatthī. Venerable Sīvali paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, I will test my merit; please give me five hundred monks." The Blessed One said, "Sīvali, take them." Taking the five hundred monks, he set out towards the Himalayas and traveled through a forest path. A deity residing in a banyan tree, who was the first to see him, provided offerings for seven days. Thus, he—

First saw the banyan tree, second the Paṇḍava mountain,
Third the Aciravatī river, and fourth the Vara ocean.

Fifth he saw the Himalayas, sixth he reached the Chaddanta lake,
Seventh he reached the Gandhamādana mountain, and eighth he reached Venerable Revata.

In all these places, they provided offerings for seven days each. On the Gandhamādana mountain, however, a deity king named Nāgadatta provided milk-rice on one of the seven days and ghee-rice on another. The assembly of monks asked, "Friend, we do not see any cows being milked for this deity king, nor do we see any churning of curds. Deity king, from where does this come to you?" The deity king replied, "Venerable sirs, this is the result of offering milk-rice by tickets (salāka-bhatta) during the time of Kassapa Buddha." Later, the Blessed One, taking the occasion of the welcoming by Venerable Revata who lived in the Khadiravana forest, appointed the Elder [Sīvali] to the foremost position among those in His dispensation who receive the greatest gains and followers.

## The Story of Venerable Vakkali
In the tenth discourse, "saddhādhimuttānaṃ" refers to those who are resolved through faith; it shows that Venerable Vakkali is the foremost among monks with strong faith. While the faith of others needs to be increased, the Elder's faith had to be decreased (to balance it with wisdom). Therefore, he is called the foremost among those resolved through faith. Vakkali was his name.

The sequential account of his past deeds is as follows: This future Venerable Vakkali, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, went to the monastery as previously described and, while standing at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, saw the Blessed One appoint a monk to the foremost position among those resolved through faith. He thought, "May I also become such a person in the future." As previously described, he invited the Blessed One, gave great offerings for seven days, paid homage to the Buddha, and said, "Venerable Sir, by this meritorious deed, may I, like the monk whom you have appointed to the foremost position among those resolved through faith..."
195:
...become the foremost among those resolved through faith in the dispensation of a future Buddha." He made this aspiration. The Blessed One, seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, gave the prophecy and departed.

He too, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, took rebirth in a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Blessed One; they named him Vakkali. When he reached maturity, he learned the three Vedas. Seeing the Blessed One wandering in Sāvatthī surrounded by the assembly of monks, he looked at the perfection of the Buddha's physical body and, being insatiable in viewing that physical perfection, he wandered along with the Blessed One. He would go to the monastery with the Blessed One as He went, and remain standing there just to gaze at the perfection of His body. When the Buddha sat in the Dhamma hall and preached, he would stand directly in front of the Blessed One and listen to the Dhamma. This young Vakkali gained faith and, thinking, "If I live in the midst of a house, I will not get to see the Blessed One constantly," he requested ordination and became a monk in the presence of the Blessed One.

From then on, except for the time of taking meals, he spent the rest of his time standing in a place where he could see the Blessed One, abandoning wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and only gazing at the Blessed One. The Blessed One, awaiting the maturation of Vakkali's wisdom, said nothing for a long time while the Elder wandered about merely for the sake of seeing His form. Knowing, "Now his wisdom has reached maturity; it is possible to make him realize the truth," He said: "Vakkali, what is the use to you of seeing this foul body? Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me. He who sees me sees the Dhamma. For, Vakkali, seeing the Dhamma, one sees me; seeing me, one sees the Dhamma."

Even though the Blessed One gave such an admonition, the Elder could not leave the sight of the Blessed One to go elsewhere. Then the Blessed One thought, "This monk will not realize the truth without gaining a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega)." As the time for the rains retreat approached, He went to Rājagaha and, on the day of entering the retreat, dismissed the Elder, saying, "Go away, Vakkali." The words of Buddhas are to be obeyed; therefore, the Elder, unable to remain in opposition to the Blessed One and not daring to come before the Blessed One for three months, thought, "What can be done now? I have been dismissed by the Tathāgata; I no longer get to see Him in person. What is the use of my life?" and he climbed the precipice of the Gijjhakūṭa mountain. The Blessed One, knowing his state of distress, thought, "This monk, [receiving] comfort from me..."
196:
“If this monk does not receive relief from me, his strong sufficing condition (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit will be destroyed,” the Buddha thought, and so he emitted a radiance to manifest himself. From the moment he saw the Blessed One, the great dart of grief was removed from the Venerable Vakkali. Like bringing a flood of water into a dry lake, the Blessed One, in order to arouse strong joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa) in Venerable Vakkali, spoke this verse from the Dhammapada:

“The monk who is full of joy,
And has faith in the Buddha’s teaching,
Will reach the peaceful state,
The bliss of the stilling of formations.”

He then stretched out his hand to Venerable Vakkali, saying, “Come, Vakkali.” The Elder thought, “I have seen the One of Ten Powers, and I have even received the invitation ‘Come’.” Arousing intense joy, and not even knowing how he was moving, he leaped into the air toward the presence of the One of Ten Powers. While standing on the mountain, reflecting on the verse spoken by the Blessed One, he suppressed his joy while still in the air, attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and descended while paying homage to the Blessed One. Later, while seated in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones, the Blessed One placed the Elder in the foremost position among those liberated by faith (saddhādhimutta).

## Description of the Second Chapter.

## 14. Etadagga Chapter

## (14) 3. Third Etadagga Chapter

In the first sutta of the third chapter, “sikkhākāmānaṃ” means among those who, desiring the three trainings, practice them with devotion. By the word “Rāhulo”, he indicates his own son, Venerable Rāhula. It is said that from the day of his ordination, the Elder, upon rising early in the morning, would take a handful of sand and toss it up, wishing, “Oh, may I receive today from the Blessed One and my teachers and preceptors as much advice and instruction as there are these grains of sand.” Therefore, he became the foremost among those who desire training.

In the second sutta, “saddhāpabbajitānaṃ” means among those who went forth out of faith. “Raṭṭhapāla” refers to one born in a family capable of protecting the country or capable of restoring a broken country...
197:
...Raṭṭhapāla is so named because he was born into a family capable of protecting the country or capable of sustaining a ruined country. Having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One and gained faith, he fasted for fourteen meals and obtained permission from his parents to go forth before ordaining. Therefore, he became the foremost among those who went forth out of faith.

## The Story of the Elders Rāhula and Raṭṭhapāla

Regarding the past deeds of both these Elders, the sequential account is as follows: It is said that both of them were born into wealthy householder (gahapati-mahāsāla) families in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the past Buddha Padumuttara. Their names or clans during their youth are not mentioned. Having reached maturity and established themselves in the household life, after the passing of their respective fathers, both householders summoned their respective treasurers. Seeing the immeasurable wealth, they thought, “Our grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and others were unable to take this vast mass of wealth with them. We should now take this wealth by some means (i.e., by giving it away).” Both of them then began to give great alms to the destitute, the poor, travelers, and others in four locations. One householder would ask each person who came to his alms-hall what they liked among gruel, snacks, and so on, and gave them exactly that. For that reason, he became known by the name “Āgatapāka”. The other, without asking, would fill whatever vessel was brought to him. For that reason, he became known as “Anaggapāka” (one who cooks and offers without limit), meaning one whose cooking is immeasurable.

Both householders, early one morning, went outside the village to wash their faces. At that time, two powerful ascetics from the Himalayas arrived through the air for alms and descended not far from those two friends. Thinking, “May they not see us,” they stood to one side. Both householders, having prepared the requisites such as the ascetics’ gourds and vessels, approached and paid homage to the ascetics who were intending to enter the village for alms. Then the ascetics asked, “At what time did you arrive, O meritorious ones?” They replied, “Just now, venerable sirs.”

They took the gourds from the ascetics’ hands, invited them to their homes, offered alms-food, and at the conclusion of the meal, obtained a promise for regular alms. Among those two ascetics, one was of a hot physical temperament. By his psychic power, he would split the waters of the great ocean and go to the abode of the Naga King Pathavindhara to spend the day (resting). Having enjoyed a suitable climate and returned, when giving the blessing (anumodanā) at the house of the householder who served him, he used to say, “May it be like the Pathavindhara Naga abode.” Then one day, the serving householder said, “Venerable sir, when you give the blessing...”
198:
Having spoken thus, they took the gourd-vessels from the hands of those ascetics and led them to their own homes. At the conclusion of the meal, they received a promise from the ascetics to come regularly for alms.

Among those two ascetics, one was of a physical nature that suffered from heat. By his own psychic power, he would part the waters of the great ocean, go to the mansion of the Naga King Pathavindhara, and sit there for his day-abiding. Having enjoyed the suitable climate and returned, while performing the blessing for the meal in the house of his supporter, the householder, he would say, "May it be like the mansion of the Naga King Pathavindhara." Then one day, the supporting householder asked him, "Venerable sir, when you perform the blessing, you say, 'May it be like the mansion of the Naga King Pathavindhara.' We do not know the meaning of this. Venerable sir, what is meant by this?" "Yes, householder, I mean, 'May your prosperity be like the prosperity of the Naga King Pathavindhara.'" From then on, the householder fixed his mind on the mansion of the Naga King Pathavindhara.

The other ascetic went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm and performed his day-abiding in the empty Serisaka mansion. While coming and going, he saw the prosperity of Sakka, the king of devas, and when performing the blessing for his supporting householder, he would say, "May it be like the mansion of Sakka." Then that householder also asked him, just as the other companion had asked that ascetic. Upon hearing the ascetic's words, he fixed his mind on the mansion of Sakka. Both of them were reborn in the very places they had desired.

The one reborn in the Pathavindhara mansion became the Naga King named Pathavindhara. At the moment of his rebirth, seeing his own Naga form, he became remorseful, thinking, "Alas, the ascetic who frequented my house spoke the praises of a place that is truly unpleasant! This is a place where one moves about by crawling on one's belly. Surely that ascetic did not know of any other place." At that very moment, Naga dancers, fully adorned and prepared, began to play the five kinds of musical instruments in all directions for that Naga King. At that same instant, he discarded that Naga form and assumed the appearance of a young man. For half a month, the Four Great Kings go to wait upon Sakka. Therefore, he too went with the Naga King Virūpakkha to wait upon Sakka. Sakka, seeing him coming from afar, recognized him. Then, when he had come near and stood there, Sakka asked, "Friend, where were you reborn?" "Great King, do not ask; I was reborn in the Naga realm, a place of crawling on the belly. You, however, obtained a good friend." "Friend, do not [think] 'I was reborn in an unsuitable place'..."
199:
(Sakka thought:) "Do not think, 'I have been reborn in the Naga realm, which is an unsuitable place.' The Buddha Padumuttara has appeared in the world. Having performed an extraordinary deed of merit for that Buddha, aspire for this very place (Tāvatiṃsa); then we shall both live happily." The Naga King agreed, saying, "So be it, O King." He went and invited the Buddha Padumuttara, and together with his Naga retinue, he prepared offerings and honors for seven nights in his Naga mansion.

The next day at dawn, the Teacher addressed his attendant, the Elder Sumana: "Sumana, today the Tathāgata will go a long distance for alms. Let not the worldling monks follow; let only those who are bearers of the Three Piṭakas, possessors of the analytical insights, and endowed with the six higher powers follow." Hearing the Teacher's words, the Elder informed all the monks. One hundred thousand monks ascended into the sky along with the Teacher. When the Naga King Pathavindhara came with his Naga retinue to welcome the Teacher, he surrounded the Teacher and observed the community of monks as they approached, treading upon the jewel-colored waves on the surface of the ocean. He looked first at the Teacher, and finally at the youngest of the Saṅgha, the Teacher's son, a novice named Uparevata. He felt great joy and emotion, thinking, "Such psychic power and majesty in the rest of the disciples is not surprising, but such psychic power and majesty in this very young boy novice is indeed most wonderful!"

Then, while the Buddha was seated in that Naga mansion and the remaining monks sat down in order, the seat of the novice Uparevata happened to be directly in front of the Teacher. Whether giving gruel or giving solid food, the Naga King would look once at the Buddha and once at the novice Uparevata. It is said that on the body of that novice, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man were visible, just as on the body of the Teacher. Then the Naga King thought, "This novice appears just like the Buddhas; how is he related?" He asked a certain monk sitting nearby, "Venerable sir, how is this novice related to the Buddha?"
