"Great King, he is his son," the monk replied. The Naga King thought, "This monk is indeed great; he has obtained the status of being the son of such a glorious Tathāgata. His body also appears, in part, like the body of the Buddhas. It would be well if I too could become such a person in the future." Having given a great gift for seven days, he made an aspiration: "Venerable sir, by the power of this extraordinary deed of merit, may I, like this Uparevata, become the son of a Buddha in the future."
200:
The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacle, gave the prophecy: "In the future, you will be the son of Gotama Buddha," and then departed.

When a half-month (fifteen days) had passed, the Naga King Pathavindhara again went with the Naga King Virūpakkha to wait upon Sakka. Then Sakka asked the Naga King who was standing nearby: "Friend, do you desire this celestial realm?" He replied, "Great King, I do not desire it." "What fault do you see?" he asked. He replied, "Great King, there is no fault. However, I have seen the novice Uparevata, the son of the Blessed One. From the time I saw that novice, my mind has not inclined toward anything else. I have made a wish: 'In the future, may I be such a son of a Buddha.' Great King, you too should make a wish. Let us not be separated in whatever life we are born into," he said.

Sakka accepted the Naga King's words. Seeing a monk of great power, he reflected, "From what family did this clansman come forth to ordain?" He realized, "This is the son of a family capable of restoring a ruined kingdom; he fasted for fourteen days to obtain his parents' permission to ordain, and then he went forth." Although he knew, he asked the Blessed One as if he did not know. After performing a great offering for seven days, he made a wish: "Venerable Sir, by the result of this meritorious deed, may I, like this clansman, become the foremost of those who go forth out of faith in the dispensation of a future Buddha." The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacle, gave the prophecy: "Great King, in the future, you will be the foremost of those who go forth out of faith in the dispensation of Gotama Buddha," and then departed. Sakka also returned to his own celestial city.

Both of them, passing away from their respective places of rebirth and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, passed many thousands of aeons. Counting back ninety-two aeons from this present Bhadda-kappa, a Buddha named Phussa appeared in the world. His father was a king named Mahinda. There were also three younger brothers born of a different mother. Every day, the King, being extremely possessive, thinking, "The Buddha is mine alone, the Dhamma is mine, the Sangha is mine," personally and constantly provided food to the Blessed One.

Then one day, there was a rebellion in the border region of that King. He called his sons and said, "Dear sons, the border region is in revolt. Either you or I must go. If I go, you must serve the Blessed One in this manner." The three sons said simultaneously, "Father, there is no need for you to go..."
201:
"...We shall suppress the thieves." Having paid homage to their father, they went to the border, suppressed the thieves, and returned as victors of the battle. On the way, they consulted with the ministers who attended them: "Friends, as soon as we arrive, our father will grant us a boon. What boon should we take?" The ministers said, "Princes, after your father passes away, there is no luxury that will be difficult to obtain. Take only the boon of the privilege to serve and look after your elder brother, Phussa Buddha." The princes said, "What you say is excellent." Being of one mind, they went and saw their father. Then the father, being pleased with his sons, granted them a boon. The princes requested the boon: "We wish to have the privilege of serving and looking after the Tathāgata for three months." The King said, "It is not possible to give this; take another boon." They pleaded, "Father, we have no need for any other boon. If you wish to give, please grant us only this boon." As the sons pleaded repeatedly, the King, thinking, "I cannot refuse since I have already promised," said, "Dear sons, I grant you the boon. However, Buddhas are difficult to approach, as they wander alone like lion kings. Be diligent and heedful while serving the Blessed One."

The princes thought, "It is proper for us to serve the Tathāgata in a fitting manner." Being of one mind, they undertook the ten precepts and became pure, free from the taints of defilements. They appointed three men to take responsibility at the Buddha's alms-hall. Among them, one was the collector of taxes and grains, one was the measurer of offerings, and one was the manager of offerings. Among them, the collector of taxes and grains became King Bimbisāra in this present life. The measurer became the lay follower Visākha. The manager became the Elder Raṭṭhapāla. That person, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life in that existence, was reborn in the celestial realm. This Elder Rāhula was the eldest son of King Kikī of Kāsi during the time of Kassapa Buddha, and they named him Prince Pathavindhara. That prince had seven sisters. Those sisters had seven precincts built for the Blessed One. Prince Pathavindhara obtained the position of sub-king. He said to his sisters, "Give me one of the precincts you have built." They replied, "Brother, you are in the position of sub-king; it is you who should give to us. You should build another precinct." Hearing his sisters' words, he had five hundred monasteries built. Some also say five hundred precincts. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life in that existence, he was reborn in the celestial realm. In the time of our present Buddha, Prince Pathavindhara became our...
202:
He took conception in the womb of the chief queen of our Bodhisatta. His friend was also born in the house of the merchant Raṭṭhapāla in the market town of Thullakoṭṭhita in the Kuru country.

Then, our Blessed One, having realized the Four Noble Truths and set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, arrived at Kapilavatthu in due course and ordained Prince Rāhula. The procedure for Prince Rāhula's ordination is already mentioned in the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi. To the ordained Rāhula, the Teacher preached the Rāhulovāda Sutta by way of constant admonition. Rāhula also used to rise early, take up a handful of sand, and say, "May I receive today from the presence of the Blessed One and from my teachers and preceptors as much admonition as there is sand in this handful."

A discussion arose among the community of monks: "The novice Rāhula is indeed easy to admonish; he is a son worthy of his father." The Teacher, knowing the thoughts of the monks, thought, "When I go there, a Dhamma teaching will increase, and the virtues of Rāhula will become manifest." He went to the Dhamma hall, sat on the Buddha's seat, and addressed the monks: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, we are discussing the novice Rāhula's quality of being easy to admonish." The Teacher, remaining on that subject, brought forth the Miga Jātaka to illustrate Rāhula's virtues and said:

"O sister, the deer who sleeps in three postures, who has many wiles,
Who has eight hooves, and drinks water at midnight,
Breathing on the ground with only one nostril,
My nephew deer can escape (the hunter) by six means."

Then, during his time as a seven-year-old novice, the Teacher preached the Ambalaṭṭhika-rāhulovāda Sutta, saying, "Lest Rāhula, being young and fond of play, should tell a deliberate lie." During his time as an eighteen-year-old novice, while following the Blessed One for alms, Rāhula looked at the perfection of the Blessed One's physical form and his own, and began to have thoughts connected with sensual desire. To him, the Teacher preached the Mahārāhulovāda Suttanta in the manner beginning with, "Whatever form, Rāhula..." The Rāhulovāda Sutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya and the Rāhulovāda Sutta in the Aṅguttara Nikāya are merely the Elder's practice of insight (vipassanā). Then, the Teacher, knowing the maturity of his knowledge, preached the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta while sitting in the Andhavana forest during the time when Rāhula was a monk of no seniority (avassika). At the end of the discourse, the Elder Rāhula attained Arahantship together with a hundred thousand crores of deities.
203:
The number of deities who became Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners was beyond counting. Later, the Teacher, sitting in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, placed the Elder in the foremost position among those in this Dispensation who are desirous of training (sikkhākāmānaṃ).

When the Teacher was wandering on tour in the Kuru country and arrived at the market town called Thullakoṭṭhita, a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, gained faith. Having asked permission from his parents, he approached the Blessed One and, by the Teacher's command, was ordained in the presence of a certain Elder. From the day of Raṭṭhapāla's ordination, the merchant householder, seeing monks passing by the door of his house, would revile and scold them, saying, "What business do you have at this house? I had only one son, and you have taken him away; what will you do now?"

The Teacher, after staying in Thullakoṭṭhita for half a month, returned to Sāvatthī. There, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, reflecting wisely and performing his duties, developed insight and attained Arahantship. Having asked permission from the Teacher, he went to Thullakoṭṭhita to see his parents. While wandering for alms from house to house in that town, he received stale and putrid barley bread at his father's house and consumed it as if it were ambrosia. Invited by his father, he accepted and, on the second day, after eating the almsfood at his father's house, he established the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) toward the adorned women. While still standing, he preached the Dhamma and then, like an arrow released from a bowstring, he flew into the air and went to King Koravya's Migacīra garden. Sitting on the auspicious stone slab, he preached the Dhamma adorned with the four kinds of loss (pārijuñña) to the King who had come to see him. Wandering on tour in due course, he returned to the presence of the Teacher. Thus did this story arise. Later, the Teacher, sitting in the midst of the Noble group, placed the Elder Raṭṭhapāla in the foremost position among those clansmen in this Dispensation who have ordained through faith (saddhāpabbajitānaṃ).

## The Story of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna
In the third sutta, with the words "pathamam salākam gaṇhantānaṃ," it is shown that the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna is the foremost among the monks who take the first ticket (lot). It is said that on the day the Teacher was invited by the laywoman Mahāsubhaddā and was going to the city of Ugga, the Elder thought, "Today the Teacher will go to a distant village for alms; let not the worldlings (puthujjana) take the ticket..."
204:
## 
When it was said, "Let only the five hundred Arahants take the voting tickets," Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna uttered a brave word like a lion's roar and took the ticket first. On the day invited by Cūḷasubhaddā, when the Blessed One was traveling to Sāketa, he also took the ticket first among the five hundred monks. Likewise, when the Buddha was traveling to the Sunāparanta country, it was the same. For these reasons, the Elder became the foremost (etadagga) among those who first receive the voting tickets. Kuṇḍadhāna was indeed the name of that Elder.

Regarding the past deeds of this Elder, the sequential account is as follows: This future Elder was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Following the aforementioned manner, while listening to the Dhamma at the monastery, he saw the Teacher appoint a monk to the foremost position among those who first receive the voting tickets. He performed great meritorious deeds for the Buddhas and aspired to that position. The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacles, gave him the prophecy. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was reborn as a terrestrial deity (bhummadeva).

It is the nature of long-lived Buddhas that they do not hold the Uposatha every fortnight. For instance, the Buddha Vipassī held the Uposatha only once every six years. However, the Buddha Kassapa recited the Pātimokkha once every six months. At the time of reciting the Pātimokkha, two monks who were friends living in different regions set out, thinking, "We shall perform the Uposatha."

This terrestrial deity thought, "The friendship between these two monks is very firm. If there were someone to cause a rift, would it break or not?" Watching for an opportunity, he followed them closely.

Then, one Elder handed his bowl and robes to the other and went to a place with water to clean himself. Having washed his hands and feet, he emerged from near a thicket. The terrestrial deity, following right behind that Elder, manifested in the form of an extremely beautiful woman, shaking her hair as if re-tying it, wiping dust from her back, and adjusting her lower garment. She emerged from the thicket following the Elder's footsteps.

The companion Elder, who was waiting nearby, saw this and became distressed, thinking, "My friendship with this monk, which has lasted for a long time, is now destroyed. If I had known such a thing would happen, I would not have been intimate with this monk for so long." As the other monk approached, he said, "Here, friend, take your bowl and robes. I do not wish to travel the same path with a wicked companion like you." Upon hearing those words...
205:
The heart of that conscientious monk felt as if it were pierced by a sharp spear. Then he said to the other monk, "Friend, why do you speak like this? For all this time, I am not aware of committing even an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Yet today you call me 'wicked'; what did you see?" "What is the use of what others saw? Did you not just emerge from the same place with a woman adorned in such a manner?" the other Elder replied. "Friend, there is no such thing with me; I did not see such a woman," he said. Although he spoke thus up to three times, the other Elder did not believe his words. Taking only what he had seen as the truth, he refused to travel the same path with that monk and went to the Teacher by another route. The other monk also went to the Teacher by a different route.

Later, when the community of monks was entering the Uposatha hall, that Elder saw the other monk in the hall and said, "In this Uposatha hall, there is a wicked monk of such a name; I cannot perform the Uposatha with him," and he went outside and stood there. The terrestrial deity thought, "I have committed a grave wrong," and in the guise of an old lay devotee (upāsaka), went to the Elder and asked, "Venerable sir, why are you standing in this place?" "Layman, a wicked monk has entered this Uposatha hall; because I do not wish to perform the Uposatha with him, I have come out to stand here," he replied. "Venerable sir, do not hold such a view; this monk is of pure virtue. The woman you saw was actually me. I did that deed because I wanted to test whether the friendship of these Elders was firm or not, and to observe who was conscientious and who was not," he explained. "Good man, who are you?" the Elder asked. "Venerable sir, I am a terrestrial deity," he replied. While speaking, the deity stood by his divine power, prostrated at the Elder's feet, and entreated him, "Venerable sir, please forgive me. The Elder (the accused) is not aware of this fault. Please perform the Uposatha," and he led the Elder into the Uposatha hall. That Elder performed the Uposatha in the same place only that once; however, in terms of friendly intimacy, he never stayed in the same place with that monk again. The karma of this Elder is not mentioned further, but the accused Elder, practicing insight meditation (vipassanā) stage by stage, attained Arahantship.

Due to the consequence of that evil deed, the terrestrial deity was not released from the states of deprivation (apāya) for the entire interval between two Buddhas. Even if he occasionally reached the human state, any fault committed by someone else would fall upon him alone. He was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Blessed One. They named him the youth Kuṇḍadhāna. When he came of age, he learned the three Vedas, and in his old age, having heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, he gained faith and ordained as a monk. From the day Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna received higher ordination, an adorned woman appeared to enter the village when he entered, leave when he left, enter the monastery when he entered, and stand when he stood. Thus, she appeared to follow him constantly. The Elder himself did not see the woman. However, due to the consequence of the evil deed he had done in the past, others saw that woman. Women offering rice gruel (yāgu) in the village would mock him, saying, "Venerable sir, let this bowl of gruel be for you, and let this bowl of gruel be for this woman who is your companion." The Elder suffered great distress. When he went to the monastery, the novices also...
206:
During the time of the Blessed One, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī. They named the youth Dhānamāṇava. When he reached maturity, he learned the three Vedas. In his old age, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Teacher, he gained faith and was ordained. From the day of his higher ordination, a woman, beautifully adorned and prepared, appeared to enter the village whenever he entered, and leave whenever he left. When he entered the monastery, she entered; when he stood, she stood. Thus, she was clearly seen constantly following him. The Elder himself did not see her, but due to the result of his past evil kamma, she was visible to others.

Women giving rice-gruel alms in the village would mock him, saying, "Venerable sir, this portion of gruel is for you, and this portion is for our friend here." The Elder suffered great distress. Even when he returned to the monastery, novices and young monks would surround him and mock him, saying, "Elder Dhāna has become unvirtuous." For that reason, he became known as Kuṇḍadhāna Thera. Unable to endure the mockery they made, he became agitated and said, "You are the unvirtuous ones! Your preceptors are unvirtuous! Your teachers are unvirtuous!"

Then they reported him to the Blessed One, saying, "Kuṇḍadhāna is speaking such harsh words to the young novices." The Blessed One had him summoned and asked, "Monk, is it true?" When he replied, "It is true, Blessed One," the Buddha asked, "Why do you speak thus?" He replied, "Venerable sir, I speak thus because I cannot endure the constant harassment." The Buddha said, "You have not yet been able to exhaust the evil kamma you committed in the past until this day. Monk, do not speak such harsh words again," and he uttered these verses:

"Speak not harshly to anyone; those thus addressed might answer you back.
Indeed, contentious speech is painful; retribution might touch you.
If you can make yourself as still as a broken gong,
then you have reached Nibbāna; no contention is found in you." (Dhammapada 133-134)

People also told King Kosala about the Elder wandering with a woman. The King sent men saying, "Go, friends, and investigate." He himself, with a small retinue, went to the Elder's dwelling and stood watching from a suitable place. At that moment, the Elder was sitting and sewing, and that woman appeared to be standing not far from him.
207:
When King Kosala saw the woman, he thought, "There must be some reason for this," and went toward where she stood. As the King approached, she seemed to enter the leaf-hut where Kuṇḍadhāna Thera resided. The King also entered the hut along with her, but after searching everywhere and not seeing her, he concluded, "This is not a real woman; it is merely a result of the Elder's unwholesome kamma." Although he had initially approached the Elder without paying respects, once he realized the situation was not as it seemed, he returned, paid homage to the Elder, and sat in a suitable place. He asked, "Venerable sir, do you suffer any hardship regarding alms-food?" The Elder replied, "It is well, Great King."

"Venerable sir, how could I have known (your past kamma)? Who could have faith in you while you wander with such a woman who causes defilement? From this day forth, there is no need for you to go anywhere. I will support you with the four requisites. Do not be negligent in wise reflection." Thus, he arranged to provide alms-food regularly. Having received the King's support and due to the suitability of the food, the Elder attained a concentrated mind, developed insight, and reached the fruit of Arahantship. From the moment he became an Arahant, that woman disappeared.

While Mahāsubhaddā was living among a family of wrong views in the city of Ugga, she thought, "May the Blessed One have compassion on me." She undertook the Uposatha precepts, and being free from the scent of defilements, she stood on the upper terrace of the palace and made an act of truth: "May these jasmine flowers not stay on the way, but become a canopy over the head of the Ten-Powered One. By this sign of the flower canopy, may the Ten-Powered One accept my alms-food tomorrow along with five hundred monks." Then she threw eight handfuls of jasmine flowers. The flowers flew and remained as a canopy over the Blessed One's head while he was preaching the Dhamma. When the Blessed One saw the jasmine canopy, he mentally accepted Subhaddā's invitation for alms. The next day at dawn, he said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, today we shall go for alms to a distant place. Do not give the voting tickets to worldlings; give them only to the Noble Ones."

Venerable Ānanda announced to the monks, "Friends, today the Blessed One will go for alms to a distant place. Let the worldlings not take them; let only the Noble Ones take the voting tickets." Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna was the very first to stretch out his hand, saying, "Friend, bring the ticket." Venerable Ānanda thought, "The Blessed One does not have the tickets given to such monks; he has them given only to the Noble Ones." He then went and reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Give the ticket to the monk who asks for it." Venerable Ānanda thought, "If I am to give the ticket to Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna..."
208:
"If it were inappropriate, the Teacher would surely forbid it; there must be some special reason," he thought, and went forth to give the voting ticket to Kuṇḍadhāna. Even before Venerable Ānanda arrived, the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna had entered the fourth jhāna, the basis for supernormal knowledge, and standing in the air by psychic power, he stretched out his hand and took the ticket, saying, "Bring it, friend Ānanda; the Teacher knows me. The Teacher does not forbid a monk like me from taking the first ticket." Based on this incident, the Teacher appointed that Elder to the foremost position among those who receive the first voting ticket in this Dispensation.

## Story of the Elder Vangīsa
In the fourth sutta, "paṭibhānavantānaṃ" indicates that the Elder Vangīsa is the foremost among those possessed of ready wit (the ability to compose verses). Whenever this Elder approached the Ten-Powered One, from the moment he came into sight, he would approach while praising the Teacher's virtues with hundreds and thousands of verses, comparing him to the moon, the sun, the sky, the great ocean, a noble elephant, and the king of lions. Therefore, he became the foremost among those with ready wit.

Regarding the matter of his attainment, the sequential account is as follows: This future Elder, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, was reborn into a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Following the previous manner, he went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma and saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position among those with ready wit. He performed acts of merit for the Teacher and made an aspiration: "May I also become the foremost among those with ready wit in the future." Having received the prophecy from the Teacher, he performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In the time of this Buddha, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī. They named him Vangīsa. When he reached maturity, he studied the three Vedas. Pleasing his teacher, he learned the art called "Chavasīsamanta" (the corpse-head mantra), by which he could know, "This being is reborn in such-and-such a realm," by tapping a skull with his fingernail.

The Brahmins, realizing, "This man is the means of our livelihood," seated the young Vangīsa in a covered carriage and traveled through villages, market towns, and royal capitals. Stopping at city gates or market gates and seeing a crowd gathered, they would say, "Whoever sees Vangīsa gains wealth, or gains fame, or goes to heaven." Hearing these words, many people, wishing to see him, gave gifts.
209:
Kings and great ministers of kings went to those Brahmins and asked, "What is the teacher's special knowledge?" They replied, "Do you not know? In the whole of Jambudīpa, there is no other wise man like our teacher. He can take the skulls of those who died even more than three years ago, tap them with his fingernail, and know, 'This being is reborn in such-and-such a category.'" Vangīsa, in order to dispel the doubts of the people, would summon various people and tell them their own destinations. Relying on that skill, he received hundreds and thousands of pieces of wealth from the hands of the people.

The Brahmins took the young Vangīsa and wandered as they pleased, eventually returning to Sāvatthī. Standing not far from the Jetavana Monastery, Vangīsa thought, "They say the ascetic Gotama is wise. It is not right for me to always wander about following only the words of these Brahmins; I should also go to the presence of the wise." He said to the Brahmins, "You go on; I will go to see the ascetic Gotama without a large crowd." They said, "Vangīsa, do not desire to see the ascetic Gotama. For whoever sees him, he converts them with his magic." Vangīsa, disregarding their words, went to the presence of the Teacher, exchanged pleasant greetings, and sat to one side.

Then the Teacher asked him, "Vangīsa, do you know any art?" "Yes, Master Gotama, I know an art called Chavasīsamanta." "What does that mantra do?" "Even for those who died more than three years ago, by reciting that mantra and tapping the skull with my fingernail, I know the place of rebirth." The Teacher showed him a skull of one reborn in hell, one of one reborn among humans, one of one reborn among devas, and one of one who had attained Parinibbāna.

Vangīsa tapped the first skull and said, "Master Gotama, this being has gone to hell." "Excellent, excellent, Vangīsa! You have seen well. Where has this being gone?" the Buddha asked. "To the human world, Master Gotama." "Where has this being gone?" "To the deva world, Master Gotama," he said, stating the destination of all three. However, when he tapped the skull of the one who had attained Parinibbāna with his fingernail, he saw neither the end nor the beginning. Then the Teacher asked, "Vangīsa, can you not know?" "Master Gotama, wait a moment; let me examine it," he said, turning it over again and again. How could he know the destination of an Arahant through an art outside the Dispensation? Then, sweat poured from Vangīsa's forehead. He stood silent in shame. Then the Teacher...
210:
The Blessed One said, "Vangīsa, are you tired?" "Yes, Gotama, I am very tired. I am unable to know the destination of this being. If you know it, please tell me," he replied. "Vangīsa, I know that, and I also know that which is far superior to this art," the Blessed One said, and he spoke these two verses from the Dhammapada:

"He who knows in every way the passing away and the rebirth of beings; him, who is unattached, well-gone, and enlightened, I call a Brahmin.

He whose destination is unknown to gods, gandhabbas, and humans; him, who has destroyed the taints and is an Arahant, I call a Brahmin."

Then Vangīsa said, "Gotama, there is no loss for one who exchanges art for art. I shall give you the mantra that I know; you, in turn, give me this mantra (the art of knowing the destination)." The Blessed One replied, "Vangīsa, we do not give by exchanging mantras; we give just as it is." "Very well, Gotama, please give me the mantra," Vangīsa said, and showing respect, he sat down with his hands joined in reverence. The Blessed One asked, "Vangīsa, in your tradition, is there no such thing as a probationary period (parivāsa), such as providing material goods or serving the teacher, for those who learn a valuable mantra or any art?" "Gotama, there is," he replied. "Know then that our mantra requires no such probation," the Blessed One said.

Brahmins are never satiated with mantras and arts; therefore, Vangīsa said to the Blessed One, "Gotama, I will do as you say." The Blessed One said, "Vangīsa, when we give this mantra, we give it only to one who has the same appearance (the appearance of a monk) as us." Vangīsa, thinking, "I must learn this mantra even if I have to do something first," said to his retinue of Brahmins, "Do not worry about me becoming a monk. Once I have learned this mantra, I will be the foremost in the entire Jambudīpa. When that happens, it will be beneficial for you as well." Thus, for the sake of the mantra, he ordained in the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Wait a while for the preliminary practice of the mantra," and taught him the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra). That wise man, while reciting the thirty-two parts of the body, contemplated the nature of rise and fall (impermanence) therein, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained the fruit of Arahantship.

When Vangīsa attained Arahantship, the Brahmins thought, "What is the news of Vangīsa? Let us go and see." They went to him and asked, "O Vangīsa, have you finished learning the art from the ascetic Gotama?" "Yes, I have learned it," he replied. At that...
211:
...the Brahmins said, "Come then, let us go." Venerable Vangīsa replied, "You go; my business of going with you is finished." "We told you from the beginning that the ascetic Gotama entices those who come to see him with his magic. Now you have fallen under the power of the ascetic Gotama; what can we do with you anymore?" they said, and departed by the same way they had come. Whenever Venerable Vangīsa went to see the Buddha (the Possessor of Ten Powers), he would go while composing a verse of praise. Therefore, the Blessed One, while seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, appointed him to the foremost position among those of ready wit (paṭibhānavantānaṃ).

## The Story of Venerable Upasena Vangantaputta

In the fifth sutta, "samantapāsādikānaṃ" means among those who are inspiring (pleasing) in every way. Upasena was the name of that Elder. Because he was the son of the Brahmin Vanganta, he was called Vangantaputta. This Elder was not only inspiring himself, but his retinue was also inspiring. Thus, by virtue of the name acquired through his retinue, he became known as the foremost among those who are inspiring in all respects.

The sequential account of this Elder's aspiration is as follows: He too was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, he went to the presence of the Teacher as in the previous accounts. While listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appoint a monk to the foremost position among those who are inspiring in all respects. He performed great works of merit for the Teacher and aspired to that specific position. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in the womb of the Brahmin lady Sārī in the village of Nālaka during the time of this Buddha. They named him the youth Upasena.

When he reached maturity, he learned the three Vedas. After hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha (the Possessor of Ten Powers), he gained faith and ordained. After being ordained for one year (vassa), he thought, "I shall increase the Noble lineage," and he ordained a young man of good family and gave him full ordination. When that Elder had completed his second vassa and his student had completed his first vassa, he thought, "The Blessed One will be pleased upon seeing me," and he came to see the Blessed One, bringing his co-resident student (saddhivihārika) with him. The Blessed One, after the Elder had paid homage and sat in a suitable place, asked, "Monk, how many years (vassa) have you been ordained?" "Bhante, I have two years," he replied. "And how many years has this monk been ordained?" the Blessed One asked. "Bhante, he has one year," he replied. "How is this monk related to you?" the Blessed One asked. "Bhante, he is my co-resident student," he replied. Then the Blessed One said to Venerable Upasena, "Too quickly..."
212:
The Buddha said, "O foolish man, you have turned back to the abundance of followers (and requisites)," and rebuked him in many ways. Having received the rebuke from the Buddha, the Elder paid homage to the Buddha and thought, "With this very mouth, as glorious as the full moon, which has rebuked me, I shall cause the Buddha to give praise, relying on my retinue." On that very day, he went to a certain place, practiced Vipassana, and before long attained Arahantship.

After attaining Arahantship, because the Elder had gone forth from a noble family and was a renowned Dhamma preacher on earth, many young men of good family, being inspired by his Dhamma talks, left their friends, ministers, and relatives to ordain under him. He told them, "I am a forest-dweller; if you are able to be forest-dwellers, then ordain." He taught them the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutanga), and when they replied, "Venerable sir, we are able," he ordained them. They undertook those various ascetic practices according to their strength. When the Elder reached ten years of seniority (vassa), having mastered the Vinaya, he gave full ordination to all of them. Thus, about five hundred monks who had received full ordination became his retinue.

At that time, while the Buddha was staying at Jetavana Monastery, he informed the Saṅgha of monks, "Monks, I wish to go into solitary retreat for half a month," and stayed alone. The Saṅgha of monks made an agreement: "Whichever monk approaches to see the Buddha must be made to confess a pācittiya offense." Then, Elder Upasena, thinking, "I will see the Buddha," went to Jetavana with his retinue, approached the Buddha, paid homage, and sat at a suitable place. To start a conversation, the Buddha addressed one of the Elder's co-residents, "Monk, do you like these rag-robes (pāṃsukūla)?"

"Venerable sir, I do not like rag-robes," he replied, and then, out of respect for his preceptor (upajjhāya), he declared his status as a rag-robe wearer. At this point, the Buddha gave praise to the Elder, saying, "Excellent, excellent, Upasena!" and spoke of his virtues in many ways. This is a summary here; in detail, this story appears in the Vinaya Pali (Pārājika 565). Later, while sitting in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones, the Buddha placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who are inspiring in all respects (samantapāsādika) in this Dispensation.

The Story of Elder Dabba Mallaputta. 214. In the sixth sutta, "senāsanapaññāpakānaṃ" means among those monks who assign lodgings. Let me speak of this. When Elder Dabba assigned lodgings, there was no unpleasant compound or uncleaned dwelling in the eighteen great monasteries.
213:
## The Story of the Elder Dabba Mallaputta

In the sixth sutta, 'senāsanapaññāpakānaṃ' means among those who assign lodgings. It is said that when the Elder was assigning lodgings, in the eighteen great monasteries, there was no unswept courtyard, no unprepared dwelling, no uncleaned couch or bench, and no unprovided drinking water or water for use. Therefore, he became the foremost among those who assign lodgings. His name was Dabba. Because he was born into the Malla royal family, he was known as Dabba Mallaputta.

Regarding his past deeds, this is the chronological account: In the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was born into a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī. When he came of age, he went to the monastery as previously mentioned and, while listening to the Dhamma, saw the Teacher placing a monk in the foremost position among those who assign lodgings. Having performed a meritorious act, he aspired to that position and received a prophecy from the Teacher. After performing meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he went forth when the Dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa was declining. At that time, he and six others, making seven monks in total, were of one mind. Seeing other monks acting disrespectfully toward the Dispensation, they consulted together, "What shall we do here? Let us practice the recluse's Dhamma in a suitable place and make an end of suffering." They constructed a ladder, climbed to the top of a high mountain, and said, "Let those who know the strength of their own minds throw down the ladder. Let those who have attachment to life go down. Do not be full of regret later." With one mind, they all threw down the ladder. Admonishing each other, "Friends, be diligent," they sat in places that pleased their minds and began to practice the recluse's Dhamma.

Among those seven monks, one Elder attained Arahatship on the fifth day. Thinking, "My task as a monk is finished; what shall I do here?" he brought almsfood from the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) by psychic power and said, "Friends, enjoy this almsfood. Let the task of going for alms be my responsibility; you just perform your own work of the recluse's Dhamma." [The others replied,] "Friends, when we were throwing down the ladder, did we say, 'Whichever monk first realizes the Dhamma, let him bring almsfood; the rest will eat what he brings and practice the recluse's Dhamma'?" "No, friends." "You have attained the extraordinary Dhamma because of your past causes. We too, if we are able, will make an end to the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). You may go."
214:
"Go your way," he said. The Elder, who was an Arahant, being unable to convince those six monks, partook of his alms-food in a pleasant place and departed. Another Elder attained the fruit of Anāgāmi (Non-Returner) on the seventh day, and after passing away from that state as a monk, was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma realm.

The remaining five Elders, after passing away from that state, wandered through the celestial and human realms for the interval between two Buddhas, and were reborn into various families during the time of this Buddha's appearance. One was born into a family in the city of Takkasilā in the Gandhāra kingdom. One was born in the womb of a female wanderer (paribbājikā) in the Pabbateyya kingdom. One was born in the house of a householder in the city of Suppāraka in the Bāhiya kingdom. One was born in the house of a householder in the city of Rājagaha. This Venerable Dabba, however, was conceived in the house of a Malla king in the city of Anupiya in the Malla kingdom. When his mother was about to give birth, she passed away; they took her deceased body to the cemetery, placed it on a funeral pyre, and set it on fire. Due to the heat of the fire, the layers of her abdomen split in two. By the power of his own merit, the child sprang out and fell onto a heap of dabba grass (or a wooden post). They took the child and gave him to his grandmother. When she named him, she gave him the name "Dabba" because he had gained his life after falling onto the heap of dabba grass.

When Prince Dabba reached the age of seven, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, was wandering through the Malla kingdom and arrived at the market town of Anupiya, staying in the Anupiya Mango Grove. Upon seeing the Teacher, Prince Dabba felt devotion just by the sight of him and, desiring to ordain, asked his grandmother for permission, saying, "I will ordain in the presence of the Ten-Powered One." She said, "Very well, dear," and taking Prince Dabba, went to the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, please ordain this prince." The Teacher gave a sign to a certain monk, saying, "Monk, ordain this boy."

Hearing the Teacher's words, that Elder, while ordaining Prince Dabba, taught him the meditation on the five parts ending in skin (tacapañcaka kammaṭṭhāna). Being one who had fulfilled his past merits and made a firm resolution, the boy established himself in the fruit of Sotāpatti (Stream-entry) even as the first lock of hair was being shaved. He established himself in the fruit of Sakadāgāmi (Once-returner) as the second lock was being shaved, and in the fruit of Anāgāmi as the third. The completion of shaving all his hair and the realization of the fruit of Arahatship occurred simultaneously, neither before nor after the other.

The Teacher, after staying in the Malla kingdom as long as he pleased, went to Rājagaha and took up residence in the Veḷuvana Monastery. There, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having gone into seclusion and reflected on the completion of his task as a monk, thought of dedicating himself to performing duties for the Saṅgha.
215:
Having reflected on the completion of his task as a monk, Venerable Dabba desired to dedicate himself to performing the major and minor duties of the Saṅgha, thinking, "What if I were to assign lodgings (senāsana) and designate meals (bhatta) for the Saṅgha?" He approached the Teacher and informed him of his thought. The Teacher, having given him his approval (Sādhu), accepted him as the assigner of lodgings and the designator of meals. Then, the Teacher, considering that "this Dabba, though young, is established in a great position," granted him full ordination (upasampadā) even at the age of seven.

From the time he was ordained, Venerable Dabba Mallaputta assigned lodgings and accepted and designated meals for all the monks residing around Rājagaha. His reputation as an assigner of lodgings became well-known in all directions: "It is said that Dabba Mallaputta assigns lodgings for monks of similar inclination in the same place; he assigns lodgings even in distant places. He even leads those who are unable to go by means of his psychic power."

Then, whether at the proper time or not, monks would say, "Friend, assign us a lodging in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove," or "Assign us one in the Maddakucchi Deer Park," and they would go, observing the psychic power of Venerable Dabba. He, too, would create a mind-made body through psychic power, and for each Elder, he would create a monk resembling himself. With a glowing finger, he would walk ahead of them and, after saying, "This is the couch, this is the stool," and so on, and arranging the lodging, he would return to his own dwelling. This is just a summary here; the detailed account appears in the Vinaya Pali. Based on this circumstance, the Teacher, while sitting in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha at a later time, placed Venerable Dabba Mallaputta in the foremost position (etadagga) among those who assign lodgings.

## The Story of the Elder Pilindavaccha
By the seventh phrase, "devatānaṃ piyamanāpānaṃ" (dear and pleasing to the deities), it is shown that the Elder Pilindavaccha is the foremost among those who are dear and pleasing to the deities. It is said that before the appearance of a Buddha, he was a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) who established the masses in the five precepts and made them destined for heaven. Most of the deities reborn in the six sensual heavens, having received his advice, looked at their own prosperity in their respective places of rebirth and wondered, "Depending on whom did we obtain this heavenly prosperity?"
216:
When the deities reflected, they saw this Elder and, thinking, "Because of this Elder, we have now obtained celestial bliss," they constantly paid homage to him, evening and morning. Therefore, that Elder attained the foremost position (Etadagga) among those who are beloved and dear to the deities. Pilinda was his name, and Vaccha was his clan. Combining both, he is called the Elder Pilindavaccha.

The sequential account regarding this Elder's matter is as follows: This future Elder was born into a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma teaching in the same manner as previously mentioned, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those beloved and dear to the deities. Aspiring for that position, he performed meritorious deeds throughout his life. After wandering through the realms of deities and humans, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha. They named him Pilindavaccha. Later, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, he gained faith, went forth, and was ordained. Developing insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship.

When this Elder spoke with either laypeople or monks, he always addressed them with the term "outcast" (vasala), saying, "Hey, outcast, come here," "Hey, outcast, go," "Hey, outcast, bring it," or "Hey, outcasts." Because of this, the monks approached the Tathāgata and asked, "Venerable Sir, are not those who are Noble Ones free from harsh speech?" The Buddha replied, "Monks, for Noble Ones, there is no such thing as harsh speech spoken with the intent to disparage others. However, it may occur due to a habit (vāsanā) practiced in previous lives." They asked again, "Venerable Sir, the Elder Pilindavaccha always says 'outcast, outcast' when speaking with laypeople or monks. What is the reason for this, Blessed One?" "Monks, this way of speaking by my son is not a habit formed in this life. In the past, for five hundred lives, he was born into a Brahmin family that was accustomed to using the word 'outcast.' He speaks thus only because of a long-standing habit, not with the intent of being harsh. Even if the speech of Noble Ones appears harsh, it is pure because the intention is not harsh; there is not even a slight trace of demerit in such speech." Having said this, he uttered this verse in the Dhammapada:

"One should speak truthful, instructive speech that is not harsh, by which one would not offend anyone. Him I call a Brahmin."

Then one day, while the Elder was entering Rājagaha for alms, he saw a man entering the city carrying a bowl filled with long peppers (pippalī). He asked, "Hey, outcast, what is in your bowl?" The man thought, "This ascetic is speaking harsh words to me so early in the morning; I should give him a fitting reply."
217:
"Venerable Sir, there are mouse droppings in my bowl," he replied. "Outcast, let it be so," the Elder said. When the man moved out of the Elder's sight, all his long peppers turned into mouse droppings. He thought, "These long peppers look like mouse droppings; are they real or not?" Wanting to investigate, he squeezed them with his hand. Upon realizing they were indeed mouse droppings, he became deeply distressed. He wondered, "Is it only the peppers in this bowl that have become like this, or those on the cart as well?" He went and looked, and seeing that all the long peppers were the same, he pressed his hand to his chest and thought, "This is not the work of anyone else; it must be the work of the monk I met early this morning. Surely there must be a way. I will find out the reason by inquiring where that monk went." He asked about the path the Elder had taken and followed him.

Then a man saw him walking along, extremely angry, and asked, "Friend, you are walking along very angrily; for what reason are you going?" He told the man what had happened. Hearing his words, the man said, "Friend, do not worry. It must be my master, the Elder Pilindavaccha. You should fill this same bowl and go stand before the Elder. When he asks, 'Outcast, what is this?', reply, 'Venerable Sir, they are long peppers.' The Elder will say, 'Outcast, let it be so.' Then all the long peppers will return to their original state." He did as instructed, and all the long peppers returned to their original condition. This is the extent of this story. Later, the Blessed One, taking the reason for his being beloved by deities as the basis, appointed the Elder to the foremost position among those beloved and dear to the deities.

## The Story of the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya

In the eighth sutta, "khippābhiññānaṃ" indicates that the Elder Dārucīriya is the foremost among those who possess swift realization. This Elder attained Arahantship at the very end of a brief Dhamma teaching; there was no need for preliminary tasks for the paths and fruits. Therefore, he is called the foremost among those with swift realization. Because he was born in the Bāhiya country, he was named Bāhiya. Later, because he wore bark-cloth, he was named Dārucīriya.

The sequential account regarding this Elder's past deeds is as follows. To speak in detail: this future Dārucīriya was also born into a family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those with swift realization. Having performed extraordinary meritorious deeds and aspiring for that position, he performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of deities and humans. During the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha...
218:
The sequential account regarding the matter of the Elder Dārucīriya is as follows: This future Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya was born into a family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Dhamma teaching of the Buddha, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those of quick intuition (khippābhiññā). He performed an extraordinary act of merit and made a resolution for that same position. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, he wandered through the celestial and human realms. During the time when the Dispensation of Kassapa Buddha was declining, he practiced the Dhamma of a recluse together with the monks mentioned above. Being possessed of perfect virtue, he passed away and was reborn in the celestial realm.

Having resided in the celestial realm for the interval between two Buddhas, he was reborn into a family in the Bāhiya country during the time of this current Buddha. Upon reaching adulthood, while living as a householder, he thought, "I shall engage in trade," and boarded a ship bound for Suvaṇṇabhūmi. Before the ship could reach its intended destination, it was wrecked in the middle of the ocean, and many people became food for fish and turtles. This Bāhiya, however, grabbed a piece of wood and managed to reach the port of Suppāraka on the seventh day. Upon reaching the human settlement, he thought, "It is not proper to approach people in a naked state." He then took some moss (sevala) from a large pond nearby, wrapped it around his body, and entered for alms carrying a potsherd that was lying in a certain place.

When people saw him, they thought, "If there are Arahants in the world, they must be like this person. Does this venerable one not wear clothes because of his exalted state, or would he take them if given?" Wishing to test him, they brought various kinds of clothes from different directions. He thought, "If I had not come in this appearance, these people would not have faith in me. It is proper to do something to deceive these people and make a living." Thus, he did not accept the clothes. The people, becoming even more devoted, offered him great honor and hospitality. After finishing his meal, he went to a nearby shrine (devakula). The people followed him and prepared the shrine for him. He thought, "These people have such faith and offer such honor just because I am wearing moss. It is proper for me to live as one who is even more superior to them." He then took light wooden planks, planed them, fastened them together with bark fibers to make a garment, and lived his life wearing that.
219:
At that time, among the seven monks who practiced the Dhamma during the time of Kassapa Buddha, one monk was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma realm. Immediately after being reborn, that Brahma looked at his own Brahma-attainment and, reflecting on where he had come from, saw the place on the mountain peak where the seven monks had practiced the Dhamma. Reflecting on the rebirth places of the remaining six monks, he knew that one had attained Parinibbāna and the other five were reborn in the sensuous-sphere celestial realms. Thus, he would occasionally reflect on those five persons.

Now, reflecting with the thought, "Where are they?", he saw Bāhiya Dārucīriya living by deception near the port of Suppāraka to make a living. Then he thought, "This foolish man is indeed ruined. Previously, while practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, due to his extremely exalted state, he did not even consume the alms-food brought by Arahants. But now, for the sake of his stomach, he wanders about deceiving the world by claiming to be an Arahant when he is not. He also does not know that the Buddha has appeared. I shall go and stir him with a sense of urgency (saṃvega) and let him know that the Buddha has appeared." At that very moment, he descended from the Brahma realm to the port of Suppāraka and appeared before Bāhiya at the end of the first watch of the night.

Bāhiya, seeing the radiance at his dwelling place, came out and stood there. Looking at the Great Brahma, he raised his joined palms and asked, "Who are you?" The Brahma replied, "I am your former companion. Having attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), I was reborn in the Brahma realm. The eldest among us attained Arahatship and passed into Parinibbāna. You five were reborn in the celestial realm. Seeing you living here by deception, I have come to admonish you." He then spoke these words: "Bāhiya, you are not an Arahant, nor have you entered the path to Arahatship. You do not even possess that kind of practice by which you could become an Arahant or enter the path to Arahatship." Then, he informed him of the Buddha's appearance and his residence in Sāvatthī, saying, "Go to the Teacher's presence," and after sending him off, he returned to the Brahma realm.

Bāhiya Dārucīriya, stirred by the Great Brahma, thought, "I shall seek the path to liberation." He traveled the distance of one hundred and twenty leagues in a single night and reached the Teacher while he was entering the village for alms. Prostrating at the Teacher's feet, he pleaded three times, "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma; let the Sugata teach me the Dhamma." The Teacher, knowing that "By this time, Bāhiya's wisdom has reached maturity," admonished him with this advice: "Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: 'In the seen, there will be only the seen.'"

At the end of the teaching, while still standing on the road, Bāhiya directed his insight according to the teaching and attained Arahatship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Having reached the completion of his task as a monk, he requested ordination from the Teacher. As he did not have a complete set of bowl and robes, he went to search for them and picked up pieces of cloth from a rubbish heap. At that time, a spirit (yakkhinī) who had a grudge against him from a past life possessed the body of a young cow and gored Bāhiya, causing his death. When the Teacher came out of Sāvatthī, he saw Bāhiya lying on the rubbish heap on the road and said, "Monks, take Bāhiya's body." He had the body carried away, performed the funeral rites, and had a stupa (cetiya) built at the crossroads. Afterwards, a discussion arose in the midst of the Saṅgha, "The Buddha has..."
220:
The Blessed One gave him the instruction. At the conclusion of the teaching, while still standing in the middle of the street, Bāhiya directed his insight in accordance with the teaching and attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

Knowing that his task as a monk had reached its completion, he requested ordination from the Blessed One. As he did not yet have a complete set of bowl and robes, while searching for them, he was collecting pieces of cloth from a rubbish heap. At that time, a non-human being (amanussa) who had been a rival in a past life possessed the body of a young cow and caused Bāhiya to meet his end. While departing from Sāvatthī, the Teacher saw Bāhiya fallen on the rubbish heap in the middle of the street and said, "Bhikkhus, take the body of Bāhiya Dārucīriya." He had the body carried out, performed the funeral rites, and had a stupa built at the crossroads.

Afterward, a discussion arose among the Saṅgha: "The Blessed One had the funeral rites for Bāhiya performed together with the community of monks, and had a stupa built after taking the relics. What path did he realize? Was he a novice or a monk?" Such thoughts arose. The Teacher, taking that incident as the basis, declared, "Bhikkhus, Bāhiya was wise," and further developing the Dhamma teaching, he revealed Bāhiya's attainment of Parinibbāna. Again, a discussion arose among the Saṅgha: "The Teacher did not preach much Dhamma to Bāhiya, yet he says he attained Arahantship. How can this be?" The Teacher said, "Whether the Dhamma is little or much is not the point; it is like medicine for one who has swallowed poison," and he spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:

"Even if there be a thousand verses composed of meaningless words,
Better is a single word of a verse, hearing which one is calmed."

At the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings drank the nectar of the Deathless (Nibbāna). This story of the Elder Bāhiya is not told in detail here as it appears in the Udāna. Later, while seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, the Teacher placed Elder Bāhiya in the foremost position (etadagga) among those of quick realization (khippābhiññā).

## The Story of Elder Kumārakassapa
In the ninth [position], "cittakathikānaṃ" means among those who preach the Dhamma in a multifaceted and beautiful manner. It is said that when the Elder preached the Dhamma even to one or two people, he would teach in an understandable way, adorning it with many similes and reasons. Therefore, he became the foremost among those who are skilled speakers.
221:
Regarding the matter of Elder Kumārakassapa, this is the chronological account. This future Kumārakassapa was conceived in a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Dhamma from the Buddha. Seeing the Teacher place a certain monk in the foremost position among skilled speakers, he performed great meritorious deeds and aspired to that position. After wandering through the realms of gods and humans, during the time when the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha was nearing its end, he became one of seven monks who practiced the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) on a mountain top. Passing away from that life with his virtue intact, he was reborn in the celestial realm and enjoyed prosperity for the interval between two Buddhas. In the time of our Teacher, he was conceived in the womb of a young woman of good family in the city of Rājagaha.

That woman had initially pleaded with her parents for permission to ordain, but not receiving it, she went to her husband's home and became pregnant. Unaware of her pregnancy, she served her husband, and when she received his permission, she ordained among the bhikkhunīs. When the signs of pregnancy became visible, the bhikkhunīs questioned Devadatta, who said, "She is not a true recluse." When they asked the Blessed One, the Teacher assigned the responsibility to Elder Upāli. The Elder summoned the families living in Sāvatthī and the laywoman Visākhā to investigate, and he concluded, "The pregnancy was obtained before she ordained; her ordination is faultless and pure." The Blessed One also gave his approval to the Elder, saying, "The legal issue (adhikaraṇa) has been well-decided."

That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image. King Pasenadi of Kosala took the child and had him raised, naming him Kassapa. Later, the King had him adorned and brought him to the Teacher to be ordained as a novice. Because he was ordained while still a youth (kumāra), when the Blessed One would say, "Call Kassapa," or "Give this fruit or food to Kassapa," and people asked, "To which Kassapa?", the Blessed One would usually say, "To Kumārakassapa." Because he received his name in this way, even when he grew up, he was still called Kumārakassapa. Furthermore, because he was the foster son of the King, he was also known as Kumārakassapa.

From the time of his ordination, he practiced Vipassanā and studied the word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana). At that time, a Mahābrahmā who had practiced the Dhamma of a recluse together with him on the mountain top during the time of Kassapa Buddha, and who had attained the fruit of Anāgāmi and been reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm, looked back and saw Kumārakassapa. Thinking, "My friend is struggling in Vipassanā; I will go and show him the method of Vipassanā and provide the means for attaining the paths and fruits," he remained in the Brahma realm and [posed] fifteen...
222:
The Great Brahma, having formulated the questions, appeared at the end of the night in the Andhavana forest where the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa was residing. Seeing the light, the Elder asked, "Who is there?" The Brahma replied, "In the past, I practiced the Dhamma of a recluse together with you, attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala), and was reborn as a Brahma in the Suddhāvāsa realm." When asked, "For what reason have you come?" the Great Brahma, to explain the reason for his arrival, told him those questions and said, "You should learn these questions and, at dawn, approach the Blessed One and ask him. Apart from the Blessed One, there is no one else capable of answering these questions." Having said this, he returned to the Brahma realm.

The Elder also approached the Blessed One the following day, paid homage, and asked the questions exactly as the Great Brahma had instructed. The Blessed One answered the questions, leading the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa to the fruit of Arahantship. Having learned the answers as the Blessed One had explained, the Elder went to the Andhavana forest, practiced insight meditation (Vipassanā), and attained Arahantship. From then on, when preaching the Dhamma to the fourfold assembly, he preached only eloquent and profound discourses, adorned with many similes and logical reasons. Later, on account of the Pāyāsi Sutta, which was preached to King Pāyāsi and adorned with fifteen questions, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position among those who are eloquent speakers (cittakathika) in this Dispensation.

## The Story of the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita
In the tenth discourse, the term "paṭisambhidāpattānaṃ" indicates that the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita is the foremost among those who have attained the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). This Elder, because of his mastery and proficiency in his own analytical insights, would only ask questions related to the analytical insights whether he was approaching and questioning the famous Great Disciples or approaching and questioning the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala). Due to this practiced mastery, he became the foremost among those who have attained the analytical insights.

The chronological account regarding his questioning is as follows: This future Elder was born into a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Blessed One's Dhamma discourse, he saw the Blessed One place a certain monk in the foremost position among those who had attained the analytical insights. He performed a great act of merit and aspired for that position. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha's era, he was born in Sāvatthī...
223:
The future Mahākoṭṭhita was born into a brahmin family. They named the boy Koṭṭhita. When he reached maturity, he learned the three Vedas. One day, having heard the Buddha's Dhamma discourse, he gained faith and ordained as a monk. From the time he attained monkhood, while practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Having always mastered the analytical insights, whenever he asked questions, he did so only regarding the analytical insights. Later, the Blessed One, based on the Mahāvedalla Sutta, placed him in the foremost position among those who have attained the analytical insights.

## Story of the Elder Ānanda

219-223. Regarding the words "bahussutānaṃ" (among the learned) and so forth in the first sutta of the fourth chapter, there are other elders who are also learned, mindful, wise, energetic, and attendants. However, when this Venerable Ānanda learned the words of the Buddha, he did so by standing in the position of a treasurer of the scriptures (pariyatti) in the Dispensation of the Ten-Powered One. Therefore, he became the foremost among the learned (bahussuta). The mindfulness of this elder in learning and retaining the words of the Buddha was particularly stronger than that of other elders; therefore, he became the foremost among the mindful (satimanta). This venerable one alone, while remaining in a single posture, could learn sixty thousand words and understand all the words exactly as taught by the Teacher; therefore, he became the foremost among the wise (gatimanta). The energy of this venerable one in learning, reciting, and retaining the words of the Buddha, as well as his energy in serving the Teacher, was incomparable to others; therefore, he became the foremost among the energetic (dhitimanta). In serving the Tathāgata, he did not serve in the same manner as other attendant monks; for other monks did not serve the Tathāgata for a long time, nor did they serve by understanding the mind of the Buddhas. This elder, however, from the day he received the position of attendant, was possessed of applied energy and served by understanding the mind of the Tathāgata. Therefore, he became the foremost among the attendants (upaṭṭhāka).
224:
Regarding the matter of the Venerable Ānanda, this is the chronological account. One hundred thousand aeons ago from this present age, a Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in the world. His royal city was named Haṃsavatī. His father was King Nanda, and his mother was Queen Sumedhā. The Bodhisatta was named Prince Uttara.

On the very day his son was born, the Bodhisatta made the Great Renunciation, became a monk, and through the practice of meditation, gradually attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). After uttering the solemn exclamation "Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ," he spent seven days at the seat of enlightenment (Bodhi-pallaṅka). Thinking, "I shall set my foot upon the earth," he extended his foot. At that moment, the earth split open, and a lotus of the size previously mentioned emerged from below. Because of that lotus, the Blessed One became known as "Padumuttara." He had two chief male disciples, Devala and Sujāta, and two chief female disciples, Amitā and Asamā. His attendant was named Sumana. The Blessed One Padumuttara, while showing favor to his father, resided in the capital city of Haṃsavatī, surrounded by a hundred thousand monks.

Now, his younger brother was named Prince Sumana. The Great King, his father, granted Prince Sumana a revenue-yielding village located one hundred and twenty leagues away from the city of Haṃsavatī. The prince would occasionally come to visit his father and the Teacher. Then one day, a disturbance broke out in the border region, and Prince Sumana sent word to the King. The King sent a reply, saying, "Why did I station you there?" The prince suppressed the bandits and sent word back to the King, saying, "Great King, the countryside is now peaceful." The King was delighted and said, "Let my son come quickly."

The prince had about a thousand ministers. Along the way, he consulted with them, saying, "If my father is pleased and grants me a boon, what should I choose?" Some ministers said, "Take elephants, horses, territories, or the seven treasures." Others, however, said, "You are the sons of a sovereign who rules the land; wealth is not difficult for you to obtain. Even if you obtain it, you must eventually leave all this behind. Only merit can be taken with you. Therefore, when the King grants a boon, choose the boon of being allowed to serve the Blessed One Padumuttara for three months."

The prince said, "You are my good friends (kalyāṇa-mitta). Although I did not have such a thought, you have inspired it in me. I shall do as you say." He went and paid homage to his father. The King embraced him, kissed him on the head, and said, "Dear son, I grant you a boon." The prince then requested, "Great King, I wish to serve the Blessed One with the four requisites for three months to make my life fruitful. Great King, please grant me this boon." The King replied, "Dear son, I cannot grant that. Choose another boon." The prince said, "Great King, those who are kings..."
225:
...there are no two words (broken promises). Please grant me only this boon. I have no use for any other." The King said, "Dear son, the mind of the Buddhas is difficult to know. If the Blessed One does not wish it, even if I grant it, what will happen?" The prince replied, "Very well, Great King, I shall find out the Blessed One's mind," and went to the monastery.

At that time, the Blessed One had finished his meal and entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). Prince Sumana went to the monks who were gathered in the assembly hall. The monks asked him, "Prince, why have you come?" He replied, "I have come to see the Blessed One. Please show me the Blessed One." They said, "Prince, we do not get the opportunity to see the Teacher at any moment we desire." He asked, "Venerable sirs, who then gets to see him whenever they wish?" They answered, "Prince, the Elder named Sumana does." He asked, "Venerable sirs, where is that Elder?" Having asked for the Elder's location, he went there, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, I wish to see the Blessed One. Please show me the Blessed One."

While the prince was watching, the Elder entered into the meditative absorption of the water-kasina (āpo-kasiṇa-jhāna), resolved that the great earth be water, dived into the earth, and appeared right in the Blessed One's Fragrant Chamber. Then the Blessed One asked him, "Sumana, why have you come?" He replied, "Bhante, Prince Sumana has come to see the Blessed One." The Buddha said, "In that case, monk, prepare a seat." Again, while the prince was watching, the Elder took the Buddha's seat, dived into the Fragrant Chamber, appeared outside the precinct, and prepared the seat in the precinct. Seeing these two miraculous acts, Prince Sumana thought, "This monk is indeed very great!"

The Blessed One also came out of the Fragrant Chamber and sat on the prepared seat. The prince paid homage to the Blessed One and engaged in pleasant conversation. When the Buddha asked, "Prince, when did you arrive?" he replied, "Bhante, while you were entering the Fragrant Chamber, the monks told me, 'We do not get to see the Blessed One whenever we wish,' and sent me to the Elder. The Elder, however, showed you to me with just a single word. Bhante, I think this Elder is very beloved (intimate) in your Dispensation." The Buddha said, "Yes, Prince, this monk is beloved in my Dispensation." The prince asked, "Bhante, by doing what does one become beloved in the Dispensation of the Buddhas?" The Buddha replied, "Prince, it is by giving gifts, undertaking the precepts, and observing the Uposatha." The prince said, "Bhante, I also wish to be beloved in the Dispensation like this Elder. Please accept my alms-food for tomorrow." The Blessed One accepted.
226:
The Blessed One accepted the invitation by remaining silent. The Prince went to his residence, prepared a grand offering throughout the night, and for seven days, he donated 'Khandhāvāra-bhatta' (alms-food provided in a camp). 

On the seventh day, he paid homage to the Buddha and said, "Venerable Sir, I have received permission from my father to attend to you for the three months of the rainy season; please accept my invitation to reside for the Vassa for those three months." The Blessed One, considering whether there would be benefit in going there and seeing that there would be, said, "Prince, the Tathāgatas delight in secluded dwellings (suññāgāra)."

The Prince replied, "I understand, Blessed One; I understand, Sugata," and added, "Venerable Sir, I shall go ahead and build a monastery. When I send word, please come with a hundred thousand monks." Having obtained the Buddha's promise, he went to his father and said, "Great King, the Blessed One has given me his word. When I send word, please allow the Blessed One to come." After paying homage to his father, he departed and built a monastery at every yojana along the journey of one hundred and twenty yojanas.

Upon reaching his city and searching for a site to build the monastery, he saw the garden of a householder named Sobhana. He purchased it for one hundred thousand coins and spent another one hundred thousand to construct the monastery. There, he built a Gandhakuṭi for the Blessed One, and for the other monks, he built huts, caves, and pavilions for their use during the day and night. He completed the surrounding walls and the gatehouse, then sent word to his father: "My task is finished; please invite the Blessed One to come."

The King, after offering alms-food to the Blessed One, said, "Blessed One, Prince Sumana's task is complete; he awaits your arrival." The Blessed One, surrounded by a hundred thousand monks, journeyed while staying at the monasteries located at every yojana. Hearing that the Buddha was arriving, the Prince went out for one yojana to welcome him, honoring him with scents and flowers, and led him to the monastery. He then formally offered the monastery, saying:
"This Sobhana garden, purchased for one hundred thousand,
Built for one hundred thousand,
May the Great Sage accept it."
Thus, he handed over and donated the monastery.

On the day of entering the Vassa, after making offerings, the Prince called his wife, children, and ministers and said, "The Buddha has come to us from afar. Indeed, the Buddhas prioritize the Dhamma; they do not prioritize material offerings (āmisa)..."
227:
...they are not those who look for material offerings. "Therefore, during these three months of the rainy season, I will wear only two garments, observe the ten precepts, and reside right here in this monastery. You all should continue to give alms to the hundred thousand Arahants in this same manner for the three months."

While residing near the dwelling of Elder Sumana, the Prince observed all the major and minor duties the Elder performed for the Blessed One. He thought, "This Elder Sumana is exceedingly beloved in this position of attendant. It is fitting that I too should aspire to this specific office." As the Pavāraṇā day approached, he entered the village, gave a great alms-offering for seven days, and on the seventh day, placed sets of the triple robes at the feet of the hundred thousand monks. Paying homage to the Blessed One, he said, "Venerable Sir, this merit I have performed, starting from the Khandhāvāra alms-offering for seven days, is not done out of a desire for the prosperity of Sakka, nor for the prosperity of Māra or Brahmā. Rather, it is done solely out of a desire to become an attendant to a Buddha. Therefore, may I also become the attendant of a future Buddha, just like Elder Sumana." He then prostrated himself with the fivefold touching (pañcapatiṭṭhita). The Blessed One, seeing that there would be no obstacles for the Prince, delivered the prophecy and then departed. Hearing that prophecy, the Prince thought, "The Buddhas do not speak double words," and from the second day onwards, he acted as if he were following the Buddha Gotama, carrying his bowl and robes.

In that Buddha's era, he gave alms for a hundred thousand years and was reborn in heaven. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he offered his upper garment to an Elder walking for alms so that the Elder could receive the bowl. He was reborn in heaven again, and after passing away from there, he became the King of Benares. While in his noble palace, he saw eight Paccekabuddhas arriving through the air from Mount Gandhamādana. He invited them, offered them food, and built eight leaf-roofed huts for them in his royal garden. He prepared eight jeweled couches and gem-studded bowl-rests in his palace for them to sit on and attended to them for ten thousand years. These are the well-known accounts.

Having given alms for a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven along with our Bodhisatta. After passing away from there, he was born in the palace of Amitodana the Sakyan. At that time, because he was born bringing joy and delight to all his relatives, they named him "Ānanda." In due course, when the Buddha, having renounced the world and attained Supreme Enlightenment, first returned to Kapilavatthu, and then departed from there, Ānanda left along with princes such as Bhaddiya to join the Buddha's retinue and was ordained. Not long after, hearing the Dhamma from Elder Puṇṇa, the son of the brahmin lady Mantāṇī, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. The time when the Venerable Ānanda was ordained and established in the fruit of Stream-entry was during the first twenty years of the Buddha's enlightenment, when he was constantly...
228:
## 

Then, when the Blessed One departed (from Kapilavatthu), while the princes were ordaining to serve as his retinue, (Venerable Ānanda) departed along with princes such as Bhaddiya and others. Having ordained in the presence of the Blessed One, before long, he heard a Dhamma discourse from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta and was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala).

At that time, during the first twenty years of the Blessed One's enlightenment, there were attendants who were not permanent. Sometimes the Venerable Nāgasamāla would take the bowl and robes and attend to him; sometimes the Venerable Nāgita, sometimes the Venerable Upavāna, sometimes the Venerable Sunakkhatta, sometimes the novice Cunda, sometimes the Venerable Sāgata, sometimes the Venerable Rādha, and sometimes the Venerable Meghiya (would take turns to attend). Among those elders, once the Blessed One was traveling on a long journey with the Venerable Nāgasamāla and reached a fork in the road. Then the elder stepped off the path and said, "Venerable Sir, I will go by this path." Then the Blessed One said, "Come, monk, let us go by this path."
