The elder said, "Venerable Sir, please take your bowl and robes; I will go by this path," and he prepared to place the bowl and robes on the ground. Then the Blessed One said, "Bring them, monk," and taking the bowl and robes, he proceeded. The monk Nāgasamāla, who went by the other path, was attacked by robbers who took his bowl and robes and also split his head. Thinking, "Now only the Blessed One is my refuge, no one else," the Venerable Nāgasamāla, with blood flowing, came to the presence of the Blessed One. When asked, "Monk, what is this?", he reported the whole matter. Then the Blessed One consoled him, saying, "Monk, do not worry; it was for this very reason that I forbade you."

On another occasion, the Blessed One went to the village of Jantugāma in the Pācīnavaṃsa Deer Park together with the Venerable Meghiya. There, after wandering for alms in Jantugāma, the Venerable Meghiya saw a delightful mango grove by the riverbank and said, "Venerable Sir, please take your bowl and robes; I will practice the ascetic Dhamma in that mango grove." Although forbidden three times by the Blessed One, he went there, but being overwhelmed and oppressed by unwholesome thoughts, he returned and reported the matter. The Blessed One also said to him, "I forbade you because I foresaw that these unwholesome thoughts would overwhelm you," and then proceeded in stages to Sāvatthī. There, while seated on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the Gandhakuṭi precinct, surrounded by the community of monks, he addressed the monks: "Monks, I am now old. When it is said, 'Let us go by this path,' some monks go by another path; some drop my bowl and robes on the ground. (I need) a permanent attendant monk for me..."
229:
Elder Meghiya, having been repeatedly overwhelmed and oppressed by unwholesome thoughts, returned and reported the matter. The Blessed One said, "It was because I foresaw that these unwholesome thoughts would overwhelm and oppress you that I forbade you," and in due course, he traveled to Sāvatthī. While seated on the noble Buddha-seat prepared within the precinct of the Gandhakuṭī in Sāvatthī, surrounded by the community of monks, he addressed the monks: "Monks, I am now old. Some monks, when told 'Let us go by this path,' go by another path. Some monks drop my bowl and robes on the ground. Seek out a monk who will be my permanent attendant." A sense of spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose among the monks.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said, "Venerable Sir, desiring only You, I have fulfilled the perfections for an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) plus a hundred thousand aeons. Is it not fitting for one of great wisdom like myself to be the attendant? I will serve You." The Blessed One declined, saying, "Enough, Sāriputta! The direction in which you reside is not empty because of your presence. Your instruction is like the instruction of the Buddhas. Therefore, I have no need of you for the duties of an attendant." In this same manner, the eighty great disciples, beginning with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, rose and made the request, but the Blessed One declined them all.

The Venerable Ānanda, however, remained seated in silence. Then the monks said to him, "Friend Ānanda, the community of monks is requesting the position of attendant; you should also request it." Ānanda replied, "Friends, what kind of position is it that is obtained by requesting? Does the Teacher not see me? If the Teacher is pleased, he will say, 'Let Ānanda attend on me.'" Then the Blessed One said, "Monks, Ānanda does not need to be urged by others; he will know by himself and will attend on me." Then the monks said again, "Rise, friend Ānanda, rise! Request the position of attendant to the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala)." The Elder rose and requested eight boons: four refusals and four requests.

The four refusals were: "Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will not give me the fine robes he himself receives; if he will not give me the fine alms-food; if he will not allow me to stay in the same Gandhakuṭī; and if he will not take me along when he goes to an invitation—only then will I serve the Blessed One." When asked, "Ānanda, what disadvantage do you see in this?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, if I were to receive these things, there would be those who say, 'Ānanda enjoys the fine robes and alms-food received by the One of Ten Powers; he stays in the same Gandhakuṭī and goes to invitations together with him. It is for the sake of such gains that he serves the Tathāgata. What burden is there in serving like this?'" These were the four refusals.

The four requests were: "Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will go to an invitation accepted by me; if I may be allowed to bring the audience who have come from other countries and provinces to see the Blessed One into his presence at the very moment they arrive; if I may be allowed to approach the Blessed One at the very moment doubt arises in me; and if the Blessed One will repeat to me the Dhamma he has taught in my absence—only then will I serve the Blessed One." When asked, "What benefit do you see in this?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, in this world, there are sons of good family endowed with faith who [ask] the Blessed One for the opportunity..."
230:
“I will serve the Blessed One in this way,” he said. When asked, “Ānanda, what benefit do you see in this?” he replied: “Venerable Sir, in this world, faithful sons of good family, unable to find an opportunity with the Blessed One, say to me: ‘Venerable Ānanda, tomorrow please accept alms at our house together with the Blessed One.’ If the Blessed One does not go there, I will not have the opportunity to show the assembly [the Buddha] at the moment they desire, nor to dispel their doubts. There will be those who criticize, saying: ‘Why does Ānanda serve the One of Ten Powers? The Blessed One does not even grant him this much favor.’ Furthermore, in the absence of the Blessed One, people will ask me: ‘Friend Ānanda, where was this verse, this sutta, this Jātaka taught?’ If I cannot answer that question, there will be critics saying: ‘Friend, do you not even know this much? Why do you wander for a long time following the Blessed One like a shadow?’ Therefore, I desire the re-preaching of the Dhamma that was taught in my absence.” Thus he requested these four boons. The Blessed One granted them to him.

Having taken these eight boons, he became the permanent attendant. For the sake of this very position, he reached the fruit of the perfections (pāramīs) fulfilled for a hundred thousand aeons. From the day he received the position of attendant, the Elder Ānanda served the One of Ten Powers with two kinds of water (cold and hot), three kinds of tooth-sticks (short, medium, and long), by massaging the hands and feet, massaging the back, and sweeping the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). Thinking, “At such a time, it is proper for the Teacher to receive such a thing; at such a time, it is proper to do such a task,” he was one who served closely during the day. At night, holding a large torch, he circled the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber nine times throughout the night. This was Ānanda’s thought: “If sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) should overcome me, I would not be able to respond when the One of Ten Powers calls.” Therefore, he did not let the torch leave his hand all night. This is the brief account. Later, while the Teacher was staying at the Jetavana Monastery, he praised the virtues of the Treasurer of the Dhamma, Elder Ānanda, in many ways, and appointed the Elder to the foremost (etadagga) position among the monks who are learned (bahussuta), mindful (satimanta), of good course (gatimanta), resolute (dhitimanta), and attendants (upaṭṭhāka) in this Dispensation.

## The Story of Elder Uruvela Kassapa

In the second sutta, “mahāparisānaṃ” means that Uruvela Kassapa is the foremost among those with large followings. While other elders may have a large following at certain times, for this venerable one, together with his two brothers...
231:
...at other times their following may be small. For this venerable one, however, together with his two brothers, there was a constant following of one thousand ascetics. If each of them ordained one person, there would be two thousand ascetics; if each ordained two, there would be three thousand. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those with large followings. His clan name was Kassapa. Because he went forth in the Uruvela forest, he was known as Uruvela Kassapa.

The following is the chronological account of his past deeds: In the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn in a family of good standing in the city of Haṃsavatī. Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those with large followings. He thought, “It would be good if I too could become such a monk in the future.” He then offered a great gift (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for seven days, presented them with sets of three robes (ticīvara), and after paying homage to the Teacher, made an aspiration to attain the foremost position among those with large followings. Seeing that there would be no obstacles, the Teacher prophesied: “In the future, in the Dispensation of Gotama Buddha, you will be the foremost among those with large followings,” and then departed.

That son of good family performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. Ninety-two aeons ago from this present age, he was reborn as the younger step-brother of Phussa Buddha. His father was King Mahinda. He had two other younger brothers. Thus, the three brothers attained various positions. As mentioned below, they quelled a rebellion in the border regions and, receiving a boon from their father the King, they chose the boon: “We will serve the One of Ten Powers for the three months of the rains retreat.” Then it occurred to those three brothers: “It is proper for us who are serving the One of Ten Powers to perform suitable deeds.” Therefore, they appointed one minister to the position of revenue collector, one minister to manage the income and expenditure, and one minister to the position of serving the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. They themselves undertook the ten precepts and observed the training rules for the three months of the rains retreat. As mentioned below, those three ministers became King Bimbisāra, the lay devotee Visākha, and the young man Raṭṭhapāla during the time of our Buddha.

Those princes, at the end of the rains retreat, personally made offerings of the four requisites to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and performed meritorious deeds throughout their lives. Long before our Buddha appeared, they were born into a brahmin family and their...
232:
By virtue of their lineage, those three men also became known by the name Kassapa. When they reached maturity, they learned the three Vedas. Among those brothers, the eldest had a retinue of five hundred youths, the middle one three hundred, and the youngest two hundred. When they looked for the essence in their own scriptures, they saw only the benefits of the present life, not the benefits of the life hereafter. Then, the eldest brother went to the forest of Uruvelā with his retinue and, having gone forth as an ascetic, became known as Uruvela Kassapa. The one who went forth at a bend in the river Ganges became known as Nadī Kassapa. The one who went forth at Gayāsīsa became known as Gayā Kassapa.

While they were living there as ascetics, after many days had passed, our Bodhisatta went forth in the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana), realized Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññutañāṇa), and in due course set the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) in motion. He established the five monks (Pañcavaggiya) in the fruit of Arahantship, and having also disciplined the fifty-five friends led by the young man Yasa, he sent out the sixty Arahants for the benefit of the many, saying, "Monks, wander on a journey (cārika)." After disciplining the Bhaddavaggiya princes, he saw the special potential of Uruvela Kassapa and knew, "If I go, the three brothers together with their retinues will attain the fruit of Arahantship." Thus, alone and without a companion, he went to the dwelling place of Uruvela Kassapa. He requested to stay in the fire-shrine (aggāgāra) and, starting with the subduing of the naga in that shrine, through three thousand five hundred miracles, he disciplined Uruvela Kassapa along with his retinue and granted them ordination. Knowing that Uruvela Kassapa had been ordained, the other two brothers also came with their retinues and were ordained. All of them became "Ehi Bhikkhu" monks, possessing miraculous bowls and robes.

The Teacher took those thousand monks and went to Gayāsīsa. Sitting upon a stone slab, he considered, "What kind of Dhamma teaching is suitable for these people?" He thought, "These people have wandered about serving and worshipping fire. It is appropriate to show them the three realms of existence as being like a burning house." Thus, he preached the Ādittapariyāya Sutta. At the end of the teaching, all of them attained the fruit of Arahantship. Surrounded by them, the Teacher went to the Laṭṭhivana Garden in the city of Rājagaha, according to the promise previously given to King Bimbisāra. The King, hearing that the Buddha had arrived, approached the Teacher with one hundred and twenty thousand brahmins and householders. Having paid homage, he sat in a suitable place. The Teacher looked at the entire assembly and saw that the people were showing great respect to Uruvela Kassapa. [Thinking,] "Whether these people [know] my greatness or Kassapa's greatness..."
233:
"...or if they do not know who is greater, and being possessed of such thoughts, they are unable to receive the teaching," he signaled to the Elder, "Kassapa, cut off the thoughts of your attendants." The Elder, accepting the Teacher's word, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Teacher with the fivefold prostration, and flew into the air to the height of a palm tree. Displaying psychic powers, he declared, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am the disciple. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am the disciple." Then, descending, he paid homage at the feet of the Buddha. In this manner, for the seventh time, he flew into the air to the height of seven palm trees, and returning once more, he paid homage at the feet of the Buddha and sat in a suitable place.

At that time, the great multitude became free of doubt regarding the Teacher, [thinking,] "This person is the Great Ascetic in the world." Then the Teacher preached the Dhamma to them. At the end of the teaching, King Bimbisāra, together with one hundred and ten thousand brahmins and householders, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti). Ten thousand declared their status as lay followers (upāsaka). Those thousand monks who were the retinue of Uruvela Kassapa also thought according to their own inclination, "Our task of monkhood is completed. What shall we do by going outside?" and they continued to wander about surrounding only the Elder Uruvela Kassapa. Among those monks, if each took one pupil, there would be two thousand; if each took two, there would be three thousand. From that time on, it is appropriate to speak of how many pupils those monks had. This is the story here. Later, while the Teacher was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, he placed the Elder in the foremost position among those with large retinues.

## The Story of the Elder Kāḷudāyi

In the third sutta, "kulappasādakānaṃ" means among those who inspire faith in families. This Elder inspired faith in the palace of King Suddhodana, who had not yet seen the Buddha. Therefore, he became the foremost among those who inspire faith in families.

The chronological account of this Elder's quest is as follows: He too was born into a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Buddha Padumuttara. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher place a certain monk in the foremost position among those who inspire faith in families. Having performed acts of merit, he aspired to that position. He performed wholesome deeds throughout his life...
234:
Our Bodhisatta, while wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was conceived in his mother's womb. On that very day, [the future Kāludāyī] was conceived in the house of a minister in the city of Kapilavatthu. Because he was born on the same day as the Bodhisatta, he was placed on a white cloth wrap on that very day and taken to serve the Bodhisatta. Indeed, these seven—the Bodhi tree, Rāhula’s mother, the four great treasure pots, the state elephant, the horse Kaṇṭhaka, the minister Channa, and Kāludāyī—were born on the same day and are thus called the 'Sahajāta' (co-natals). On the day of his naming, because he was born on a day when the whole city was filled with joy, they named him 'Udāyī'. However, because his complexion was slightly dark, he became known as 'Kāludāyī'. He grew up playing as a childhood companion with the Bodhisatta.

Later, the Bodhisatta departed on the Great Renunciation, attained Omniscience in due course, set the Noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and while benefiting sentient beings, resided near Rājagaha. At that time, King Suddhodana heard that "Prince Siddhattha has attained Buddhahood and is residing at Veluvana Monastery near Rājagaha." He sent a minister along with a thousand followers, saying, "Bring my son here." That minister traveled the sixty-yojana journey and entered the monastery while the Buddha was preaching in the midst of the fourfold assembly. Thinking, "Let the King's message wait for a moment," he stood at the edge of the assembly and listened to the Teacher's Dhamma. While standing there, he attained Arahantship along with his thousand followers. Then the Teacher stretched out his hand and said, "Come, bhikkhus!" At that moment, they all became like senior elders of sixty years' standing, bearing miraculous bowls and robes. From the moment they attained Arahantship, being Noble Ones (Ariyas) who are equanimous, they did not deliver the King's message to the Buddha. The King, thinking, "The one who went does not return, nor is any news heard," sent another minister in the same manner, saying, "Come, dear son, you go." That minister also went, attained Arahantship with his followers in the same way, and remained silent. In this manner, the King sent nine ministers along with nine thousand followers. All of them accomplished their task [of liberation] and remained silent. Then the King thought, "These many people, having no affection for me, have said nothing to the Buddha about coming here. Even if others go, the Buddha..."
235:
"...they will not be able to bring him. But my son Udāyī is of the same age as the Buddha, a playmate from the days of playing in the dust, and he has affection for me." Having summoned Kāludāyī, he said, "Dear son, go with a thousand followers and bring the Buddha." Kāludāyī replied, "Great King, I will bring him if I am allowed to ordain like those who went before." The King said, "In whatever manner you do it, just let me see my son." Saying "Very well, your Majesty," he took the King's message and went to Rājagaha. Standing at the edge of the assembly during the Teacher's Dhamma talk, he listened to the Dhamma and attained Arahantship along with his followers, becoming established in the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' state. Then he thought, "It is not yet the time for the Buddha to go to his ancestral city. It will be the time when the spring season (Vasantā) arrives, when the forests are in full bloom and the earth is covered with green grass." Waiting for the right time, and knowing it had arrived, he said:

"It is neither too cold nor too hot; there is no excessive famine or hunger.
The earth is lush and green; this is the time, O Great Sage."

In this way, with sixty verses, he praised the beauty of the journey for the Buddha to travel to his ancestral city. The Teacher, reflecting, "Udāyī is praising the beauty of the journey; it is time to go to Kapilavatthu," set out on his journey with an entourage of twenty thousand monks, traveling at a leisurely pace.

Elder Udāyī, knowing the Teacher had set out, thought, "It is proper to inform the Great King, my father." He rose into the air and appeared in the King's palace. King Suddhodana, seeing the Elder, was joyful. He had him sit on a magnificent throne, filled his bowl with various delicious foods prepared for himself, and offered it. The Elder rose and showed his intention to depart. When the King said, "Dear son, please sit and eat," he replied, "Great King, I will go and eat in the presence of the Teacher." The King asked, "Dear son, where is the Teacher?" He replied, "Great King, he has set out on his journey with twenty thousand monks to see you." The King said, "Venerable sir, please eat this almsfood, and until my son reaches this city, please bring almsfood for him from this very palace." The Elder finished his meal, took the food to be brought to the Buddha, and after preaching a Dhamma talk, inspired faith in the entire royal household even before they saw the Buddha. While everyone was watching, he [tossed] the bowl
236:
The Elder Kāḷudāyī sent the alms-bowl into the sky, and he himself flew into the air, took the alms-food, and placed it in the hand of the Blessed One. The Blessed One partook of that alms-food. The Elder brought alms-food daily from the palace of King Rājagaha and offered it to the Blessed One, who was traveling a distance of sixty leagues. Thus the story should be understood. Later, the Blessed One, saying, "He has inspired confidence in the entire palace of my father, the Great King Suddhodana," placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who inspire confidence in families (kulappasādaka).

## Story of the Elder Bākula

In the fourth sutta, "appābādhānaṃ" means being free from illness. The Elder was named Bākula because he was raised in two families. 

Regarding his past deeds, this is the sequential account: It is said that in the past, more than a hundred thousand aeons and an incalculable period ago, before the appearance of the Ten-Powered Anomadassī, he was reborn in a brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he learned the three Vedas. Seeing no essence for the future life in the three Vedas, he thought, "I will seek the benefit of the hereafter," and became an ascetic at the foot of a mountain. Having attained the five supernormal powers and the eight attainments, he spent his time in the sport of jhāna. At that time, the Bodhisatta Anomadassī attained omniscience and was wandering with a retinue of noble disciples. The ascetic, hearing that "The Triple Gem has appeared," went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and at the end of the discourse, was established in the refuges; however, he was unable to give up his position as an ascetic. From time to time, he would go to see the Teacher and listen to the Dhamma.

Then, on one occasion, the Tathāgata developed an ailment of stomach wind. The ascetic, having come to see the Teacher and hearing that "The Teacher is ill," asked, "Venerable sir, what is the ailment?" When told it was "stomach wind," he thought, "This is the time for me to perform merit," and went to the foot of the mountain, gathered various medicines, and gave them to the attendant elder, saying, "Offer this medicine to the Teacher." Immediately upon using the medicine, the stomach wind was pacified. When the Teacher was comfortable and healthy, the ascetic went and said: "Venerable sir, if the Tathāgata has become comfortable through my medicine, by the result of that merit, may no illness even as much as the time it takes to milk a cow occur in my body in every life I am reborn."

This was the meritorious deed performed in that life as an ascetic. When he passed away from that life, he was reborn in the Brahma realm, and after wandering through the deva and human realms for an incalculable period...
237:
...and he prayed, "May there be no illness in my body, even for the duration of milking a cow." This was his meritorious deed in that existence. Passing away from there, he was reborn in the Brahma realm and wandered through the worlds of gods and humans for one incalculable period. During the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was reborn in a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Upon reaching maturity, he saw the Blessed One appointing a monk to the foremost position among those free from illness. He performed a special meritorious deed and aspired for that position. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, he wandered through the worlds of gods and humans and was reborn in a Brahmin family in the city of Bandhumatī, even before the appearance of the Buddha Vipassī. As in the previous manner, he became an ascetic, attained the jhānas, and lived at the foot of a mountain. The Bodhisatta Vipassī also attained omniscience and, surrounded by six million eight hundred thousand monks, stayed in the Khema Deer Park near the city of Bandhumatī, supporting his father, King Bandhuma. Then, this ascetic, knowing that the Blessed One had appeared in the world, came and listened to the Dhamma and was established in the refuges. Although he could not give up his life as an ascetic, he would occasionally come to pay respects to the Blessed One.

Once, with the exception of the Blessed One and the two chief disciples, the other monks developed a headache due to the contact of the wind from poisonous trees blooming in the Himalayas. When the ascetic came to pay respects to the Blessed One, he saw the monks lying down with their heads covered and asked, "Venerable Sirs, why is the community of monks unwell?" They replied, "Friend ascetic, the monks have an illness caused by grass pollen." The ascetic thought, "This is the time for me to perform the service (veyyāvacca) for the community of monks and increase my merit." By his own power, he collected and prepared various medicines and offered them. The illness of all the monks was pacified at that very moment. He lived out his life and was reborn in the Brahma realm. After wandering through the worlds of gods and humans for ninety-one aeons, he was reborn in a respectable family in Bārāṇasī during the time of the Buddha Kassapa. While living as a householder, he thought, "My house is very old. I will go to the edge of the forest, bring timber, and build a house." While going with carpenters, he saw a dilapidated great monastery on the way and thought, "Let my house-building wait. That house will not go with me to the hereafter. I should first do what will follow me to the hereafter." Thinking thus, he had the carpenters take the timber and built an Uposatha hall, a refectory, a fire room, a cloister, a meeting hall, a storehouse (kappiya-kuṭi), a latrine, and an infirmary at that old monastery. He also provided all kinds of medicines to be used by the community of monks. That young man performed merit throughout his life and, after wandering through the worlds of gods and humans for one Buddha-interval (buddhantara), was reborn in a merchant family in the city of Kosambī, even before the appearance of our Blessed One.
238:
Thinking, 'It is proper to do so,' he had those same carpenters take the building materials and constructed an Uposatha hall in that monastery. He also had a dining hall, a fire room, a long walkway, a steam room (jantāghara), a storehouse (kappiya-kuṭi), a latrine, and an infirmary built. He prepared and provided all kinds of medicines and requisites to be used and consumed by the Saṅgha of monks.

Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans for the interval between two Buddhas. Before the appearance of our Buddha, who is endowed with the Ten Powers, he took rebirth in the house of a merchant in the city of Kosambī. From the day of his conception, that merchant family attained the pinnacle of gain, fame, and prosperity. Then, after giving birth to the son, his mother thought: 'This child is meritorious and has performed special perfections. As long as he remains healthy and lives a long life, he will be the provider of wealth and prosperity for us.' Thinking that children who bathe in the Great Yamunā River on the day of their birth become free from disease, she sent him to be bathed. However, the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya say: 'On the fifth day, after performing the head-washing ceremony, she sent him to play in the river.'

While the nurse was letting the child play by dipping him in and out of the water in that river, a large fish saw the child and, thinking 'This is my food,' opened its mouth and approached. The nurse abandoned the child and fled, and the large fish swallowed him. Being a meritorious being, he did not suffer but felt as if he had entered a bedchamber and was sleeping. Due to the child's power, the large fish felt as if it had swallowed a hot iron plate; burning, it swam swiftly for thirty leagues and entered the net of a fisherman living in the city of Vārāṇasī. Usually, large fish die only when they are caught in a net and beaten to death, but this one died as soon as it was taken out of the net due to the child's power. Although fishermen usually cut open and sell large fish upon catching them, due to the child's influence, they did not cut this fish but carried it whole on a shoulder pole. They wandered through the city saying, 'We will sell this for a thousand coins,' but no one bought it.

In that city, there was a wealthy merchant family with a fortune of eighty crores who had no children. When the fishermen reached the door of that merchant's house and were asked, 'For how much will you give it?' they replied, 'For a thousand coins.' The household bought it for a thousand coins. Although the merchant's wife did not usually like to handle fish on other days, on that day she placed the fish on a board and cut it open herself. While fish are usually cut from the belly, she cut it from the back...
239:
Upon cutting open the fish, she saw a child with a golden complexion in its belly. Crying out, 'I have obtained a son in the fish's belly!' she took the child to her husband, the merchant. The merchant immediately had the drum beaten and, taking the child, went to the King and said, 'Your Majesty, I have found a child in the belly of a fish. What should I do?' The King said, 'This child is meritorious; he could live in a fish's belly without ailment. Raise him.'

The other family heard that a merchant family in Vārāṇasī had reportedly obtained a child from a fish's belly. They went there. When the child's original mother saw the child adorned and playing, she said, 'This child is truly delightful,' and taking him, she told the actual story. The other merchant's wife said, 'He is my son.' When asked, 'Where did you get him?' she replied, 'In the belly of a fish.' The first mother said, 'He is not your son, he is mine.' When asked, 'Where did you get him?' she replied, 'I carried him in my womb for ten months, and then a fish swallowed him while he was playing in the river.' The other replied, 'Your son must have been swallowed by another fish; I found this child in the belly of a fish.' Both went to the royal palace. The King said, 'Since this woman carried him in her womb for ten months, she cannot be said not to be his mother. And since those who catch fish do not usually remove the entrails and liver before selling, this woman who found him in the fish's belly also cannot be said not to be his mother. Therefore, let the child be the heir to both families.' From then on, both families reached the pinnacle of gain, fame, and retinue. Because the boy was raised by two families, they named him Prince Bākula.

When he reached the age of discretion, three palaces were built for him in each of the two cities, and dancers were provided. He lived for four months in each city. After staying for four months in one city, a pavilion was built on rafts, and he was placed on the rafts along with the dancers. Enjoying his wealth, he would travel to the other city after four months. The dancers living in that city, saying 'He will reach the halfway point in two months,' would go out to meet him, surround him, and bring him to their city in two months. The dancers who had come from the other city would then turn back and return to their own city. After staying in that city for four months, he would return to the other city in the same manner. Thus, enjoying his wealth, he reached the age of eighty.
240:
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having attained omniscience and set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, arrived at Kosambī while wandering in due course. The teachers of the Majjhima-bhāṇaka (Reciters of the Middle Length Discourses) say he arrived at Vārāṇasī. The merchant Bākula, hearing that the "Possessor of Ten Powers" (Dasabala) had arrived, took many flowers and scents, went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and having gained faith, ordained. This monk Bākula remained an ordinary person (puthujjana) for only seven days, and at dawn on the eighth day, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

At that time, the women who were his attendants during his lay life in the two cities came from their respective family homes, stayed at the monastery where the Elder resided, and having made robes, sent them to him. For half a month, the Elder used the robes sent by the people of Kosambī, and for half a month, the robes sent by the people of Vārāṇasī. In this manner, whatever excellent robes were available in both cities, they were brought only for the Elder.

While living as a householder for eighty years, the Elder never experienced any illness, even for as long as it takes to pick up a ball of scent with two fingers and smell it. In his eightieth year, he entered the monkhood with ease. Even after becoming a monk, the Venerable Bākula had not the slightest illness nor any deficiency in the four requisites. At the time of his final passing (parinibbāna), he preached the entire Bākula Sutta to his old friend from his lay life, the naked ascetic (Acela) Kassapa, by way of demonstrating his own physical and mental well-being, and then attained parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Thus, the circumstances arose. While the Elder was still alive, the Teacher, when appointing the Elders to their respective positions in order, placed the Elder Bākula in the foremost position among those of good health (appābādha) in this Dispensation.

## The Story of the Elder Sobhita
With the fifth phrase, "among those who recollect past lives" (pubbenivāsaṃ anussarantānaṃ), the Buddha showed that the Elder Sobhita is the foremost among those capable of recollecting the continuity of the aggregates (khandha) lived in the past. When that Elder was recollecting the continuity of the past aggregates in order, he took the method and understood the rebirth without consciousness in the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) for five hundred aeons, like showing a footprint in the sky. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who can recollect past lives.

The following is the chronological account of his past deeds: This future Elder Sobhita was also reborn in a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position among those who possess the knowledge of recollecting past lives...
241:
...seeing him placed in the foremost position, he performed an act of merit and aspired for that position. That future Elder Sobhita performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, and while wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Buddha's appearance. They named him Sobhita.

Later, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma teaching and gained faith, he ordained, developed insight (vipassanā), attained Arahantship, and became one who had mastered the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). When the Elder Sobhita was recollecting his past births in order, he saw his rebirth as long as he was in the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) without consciousness. After that, not seeing the occurrence of mental states (citta-cetasika) for five hundred aeons in between, but seeing the death (cuti) at the end, he reflected, "I see the rebirth and the death, but I do not see the occurrence of mental states in between. How can this be?" By way of logical deduction, he reached the conclusion, "I must have been in the realm of non-percipient beings." Based on this circumstance, the Teacher placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who can recollect past lives.

## The Story of the Elder Upāli
In the sixth discourse, with the words "among the bearers of the Vinaya, that is, Upāli" (vinayadharānaṃ yadidaṃ upāli), the Buddha showed that the Elder Upāli is the foremost among the monks who bear the Vinaya (Discipline). It is said that the Elder took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) directly from the Tathāgata, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. Having learned the Vinaya Piṭaka directly from the Tathāgata, he solved three cases—the Bhārukacchaka case, the Ajjuka case, and the Kumārakassapa case—by correlating them with the Buddha's omniscience. Therefore, he became famous as the foremost among the bearers of the Vinaya.

The following is the chronological account regarding his solving of questions: In the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was reborn in a family home in Haṃsavatī. One day, while listening to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position among the bearers of the Vinaya. He performed an act of merit and aspired for that position. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in a barber's house during the time of our Buddha. They named him the boy Upāli. When the boy Upāli reached maturity, he became a trusted servant who prepared the requisites for six princes. When those six princes went out to ordain while the Tathāgata was staying in the Anupiya Mango Grove, he went out with them and ordained. The procedure of his ordination is exactly as it appears in the Pali texts.

When Upāli had ordained and reached full monkhood, he requested a meditation subject from the Buddha and said, "Venerable Sir, please allow me to live in a forest monastery." The Buddha said, "Monk, for you who live in the forest, a single razor..."
242:
When that Venerable Upāli had gone forth and received higher ordination, he requested a meditation subject from the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, please allow me to live in the forest." The Teacher said, "Bhikkhu, for you living in the forest, only one duty (the duty of insight) will increase; but if you live in our presence, you will fulfill both the duty of insight (vipassanā-dhura) and the duty of study (gantha-dhura)." The Elder, accepting the Teacher's words, practiced the work of insight and before long attained Arahantship. Then the Teacher himself taught the Elder the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. Later, the Elder decided the three cases mentioned below. The Teacher, having given a "Sādhu" (well done) for each decision, based on those three decisions, appointed the Elder to the foremost position among those who are masters of the Vinaya.

## The Story of Venerable Nandaka
In the seventh sutta, "bhikkhunovādakānaṃ yadidaṃ nandako" means that this Elder, when preaching the Dhamma, led five hundred nuns to the fruit of Arahantship in a single session. Therefore, he became the foremost among those who advise nuns.

The sequential account (biography) of that Elder is as follows: In the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who advise nuns. Having performed a great meritorious deed, he aspired for that position. Having performed merit throughout his life and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he took rebirth in a noble family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, gained faith, went forth in the presence of the Teacher, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. He also became proficient in the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa). When the four assemblies gathered, he was able to preach by capturing the minds of all; thus, he became known as "Dhammakathika Nandaka". The Tathāgata also, when the five hundred Sakyan princes who had gone forth after the dispute over the water-coil (cumbaṭaka) at the bank of the Rohiṇī River became dissatisfied, took those bhikkhus to Lake Kuṇāla and preached the Kuṇāla Jātaka. Knowing their sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he preached the Four Noble Truths and established them in the fruit of Stream-entry. Later, he preached the Mahāsamaya Sutta and led them to the highest fruit, Arahantship. The former wives of those Elders said, "What shall we do now in this world?" and all being of one mind, they approached Mahāpajāpati Gotamī and requested to go forth. Those five hundred Sakyan princesses also received the going forth and the higher ordination in the presence of the Theri. In the immediately preceding life, those five hundred nuns had been the personal attendants of Venerable Nandaka when he was a prince. At that time, the Teacher said, "Let the bhikkhus advise the nuns." When Venerable Nandaka's turn arrived, knowing that those nuns had been his personal attendants in a previous life, he thought: "Seeing me sitting in the midst of this community of nuns, preaching the Dhamma by bringing forth similes and reasons, another bhikkhu who possesses the knowledge of past lives might look into this matter and think, 'Venerable Nandaka even to this day...'"
243:
Those women, being of one mind, approached Mahāpajāpati and requested to go forth. Those five hundred princesses received the going forth and the higher ordination in the presence of the Theri. In the immediately preceding life, all those nuns had been the personal attendants (harem) of Venerable Nandaka when he was a prince.

At that time, the Teacher said, "Let the bhikkhus advise the nuns." When the Elder's turn arrived, knowing that those nuns had been his personal attendants in a previous life, he thought: "Seeing me sitting in the midst of this community of nuns, preaching the Dhamma by bringing forth similes and reasons, another bhikkhu who possesses the knowledge of past lives might look into this matter and think, 'Venerable Nandaka even to this day cannot let go of his harem; this Venerable looks beautiful surrounded by his harem.'" Therefore, he did not go himself but sent another bhikkhu. However, those five hundred nuns longed only for the Elder's advice. For this reason, the Blessed One said to the Elder, "When your turn arrives, do not send another; go yourself and advise the community of nuns." The Elder, unable to refuse the Teacher's word, gave advice to the community of nuns on the fourteenth day when his turn arrived, and through the Dhamma teaching adorned with the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), he established all those nuns in the fruit of Stream-entry.

Those nuns, being delighted with the Elder's Dhamma teaching, went to the Blessed One and reported the qualities they had realized. The Blessed One, reflecting, "By whose preaching of the Dhamma will these nuns reach the higher paths and fruits?" saw that "By hearing that same Dhamma teaching of Nandaka, all these five hundred will reach Arahantship." On the next day, he sent them again to the Elder to listen to the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma on the next day, they all attained Arahantship. On that day, when those nuns came to him, the Blessed One, knowing the fruitfulness of the Dhamma teaching, said, "Yesterday, Nandaka's Dhamma teaching was like the moon on the fourteenth day; today, it is like the moon on the fifteenth day." Having given a "Sādhu" to the Elder and making that very event the occasion, he appointed the Elder to the foremost position among those who advise nuns.
244:
## The Story of the Elder Nanda

In the eighth sutta, with the phrase 'indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ,' the Buddha shows that the Elder Nanda is the foremost among those who guard the doors of the six sense faculties. Indeed, although there are no disciples of the Buddha who do not guard their sense doors, the Elder Nanda, whenever he wished to look in any of the ten directions, would not look without first delimiting that direction through the power of the fourfold clear comprehension. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who guard the sense doors.

The account of his past aspiration is as follows: This future Elder Nanda, in the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, was reborn in a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī. Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those who guard the sense doors. He performed a great meritorious act and aspired to that position. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in the womb of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī in the city of Kapilavatthu. On the day of his naming ceremony, because he was born bringing joy and delight to the assembly of kinsmen, they named him Prince Nanda.

The Great Being, having attained Omniscience, having turned the noble Wheel of Dhamma, and performing acts of favor for the world, went from Rājagaha to the city of Kapilavatthu. Upon the very first meeting, he established his father, King Suddhodana, in the fruit of Stream-entry. On the following day, he went to his father's palace, gave admonition to the mother of Rāhula, and preached the Dhamma to the remaining people. On the next day, while the ceremonies for Prince Nanda's consecration, house-warming, and marriage were taking place, the Buddha went to that palace, made the prince hold his alms-bowl, and set out toward the monastery to ordain him. The consecration ceremony did not affect Prince Nanda as much as the words of Janapadakalyāṇī. When he was departing while holding the bowl, Janapadakalyāṇī, who was in the upper part of the magnificent palace, opened the lion-window and uttered these words: 'Come back quickly, my lord.' Hearing this, and wishing to look back due to the power of sensual desire rooted in the household life, he was unable to take the object of his desire as he pleased because of his respect for the Buddha; thus, he felt distress in his heart. Then, while he was thinking, 'He will stop at this place, he will stop at that place,' the Buddha led him to the monastery and ordained him. Even after being ordained, being unable to refuse, he remained silent. From the day of his ordination, he remembered only the words spoken by Janapadakalyāṇī. At that time, she seemed as if she were standing nearby. Whenever that Elder, oppressed by discontent, wished to go a little elsewhere, as soon as he passed a thicket or a pillar, it was as if the Buddha were standing in front of him. Then, like a chicken feather thrown into a fire, he would turn back and enter only his own dwelling place.
245:
That Janapadakalyāṇī seemed as if she were standing in a place not far from the Elder Nanda. That Elder Nanda, being oppressed by discontent (anabhirati), went to another small place; in going thus, just by passing a thicket or a tree, it was as if the Buddha were standing in front of him. Then, the Elder Nanda, like a chicken feather thrown into a fire, turned back again and entered only his own dwelling place.

The Buddha thought: 'Nanda is living very heedlessly; he is unable to subside his discontent. It is proper to bring peace to this Nanda's mind.' Then he said to the Elder Nanda: 'Nanda, come, let us go on a journey to the celestial realm.' The Elder Nanda asked: 'Venerable Sir, how can I go to the celestial realm, a place to be reached only by those with psychic powers?' The Buddha said: 'You just arouse the thought of going; you will go and see.' By the power of the Buddha's majesty, that Elder Nanda went to the celestial realm together with the Tathāgata. Looking at the Vejayanta Palace, the residence of Sakka, the king of gods, he saw five hundred nymphs.

The Buddha, seeing the Elder Nanda looking at those nymphs by the power of the sign of beauty (subhanimitta), asked: 'Nanda, are these nymphs more pleasing, or is Janapadakalyāṇီ more pleasing?' He replied: 'Venerable Sir, compared to these nymphs, Janapadakalyāṇī appears like a female monkey with her ears and nose cut off.' The Buddha said: 'Nanda, such nymphs as these are not difficult to obtain for those who practice the ascetic life.' He said: 'Venerable Sir, if the Buddha will be the guarantor for me to obtain those nymphs, I will practice the ascetic life.' The Buddha said: 'Nanda, practice the ascetic life with confidence. If you should pass away while still subject to rebirth, I shall be the guarantor for your obtaining those nymphs.' Thus, the Buddha, having wandered through the celestial realm as he pleased, returned to the Jetavana monastery.

From then on, the Elder Nanda practiced the ascetic life day and night for the sake of the nymphs. The Buddha commanded the monks: 'You all wander about in Nanda's dwelling place, saying here and there: "It is said that a certain monk, making the Buddha his guarantor, is practicing the ascetic life for the sake of nymphs."' Accepting the Buddha's words, they wandered about saying within the Elder's hearing: 'It is said that the Venerable Nanda is a hireling; it is said that the Venerable Nanda is a bought one. He lives the holy life for the sake of nymphs. It is said that the Buddha is his guarantor for obtaining five hundred dove-footed nymphs.' When the Elder Nanda heard those words, he aroused reflection, thinking: 'These monks are not speaking of anyone else; they are speaking with reference to me. My behavior is improper.' He then developed insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship. At the very moment he attained Arahantship...
246:
A deity informed the Blessed One of this matter, and the Blessed One himself already knew it. On the following day, the Elder Nanda approached the Blessed One and said: "Venerable Sir, I release the Blessed One from the promise made to me for the attainment of five hundred pink-footed nymphs." Thus, this story arose. Later, while the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery, he appointed the Elder to the foremost position among those who guard the doors of the sense faculties.

## The Story of Mahākappina Thera

In the ninth sutta, "bhikkhuovādakānaṃ" indicates that the Elder Mahākappina is the foremost among those who exhort the monks. Indeed, this Elder, while delivering a single Dhamma discourse, caused a thousand monks to attain Arahantship. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who exhort the monks.

Regarding the matter of his past deeds, this is the chronological account: This future Elder was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. Later, while listening to the Dhamma discourse of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appoint a monk to the foremost position among those who exhort the monks. Having performed meritorious deeds, he aspired to that position. Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in a good family in the city of Bārāṇasī during the time of the Buddha Kassapa. He became the leader of a group of a thousand men and had a great monastery built, adorned with a thousand rooms. All those people performed wholesome deeds throughout their lives and, with the lay devotee Kappina as their leader, were reborn in the celestial realm along with their wives and children. For the interval between two Buddhas, they wandered through the realms of gods and humans.

Then, even before our Buddha appeared, this Kappina took rebirth in the royal house in the city of Kukkuṭavatī in the border region. The remaining men were reborn in the families of ministers in that same city. Among them, Prince Kappina ascended the throne after his father passed away and became known as King Mahākappina. The woman who had been his wife when they performed meritorious deeds in a previous life was reborn into a royal family of equal status and became the chief queen of King Mahākappina. Because her complexion was like the color of the anojā flower, her name was Queen Anojā. King Mahākappina was also a lover of knowledge. Having risen early in the morning, he [went out] to the four directions...
247:
He sent swift messengers through the four gates, instructing them: "Wherever you see those who are very learned and possessors of great knowledge, return from that place and inform me."

At that time, our Teacher, the Buddha, had appeared in the world and was residing near Sāvatthī. During that period, merchants living in the city of Sāvatthī took goods produced in Sāvatthī, went to that city [Kukkutavatī], stored their goods, and thinking, "We shall see the King," took gifts and went to the gate of the royal palace. Hearing that "The King has gone to the park," they went to the park and, standing at the gate, informed the gatekeeper. Then, it was reported to the King, and the King had the merchants summoned. While they stood paying homage with the gifts they had brought, the King asked, "Friends, where have you come from?" "Your Majesty, we have come from Sāvatthī," they replied. "Is your country prosperous? Is the King righteous?" he asked. "Yes, Your Majesty, it is prosperous, and the King is righteous," they replied. "Is there any special news in your region?" he asked again. "Your Majesty, there is, but it is not proper to speak of it with unwashed mouths," they said. The King had water provided from a golden pitcher. The merchants washed their mouths, and facing the direction of the Buddha, they raised their joined palms and said, "Your Majesty, the Buddha-gem has appeared in our country." As soon as the King heard the word "Buddha," joy pervaded his entire body. Then he asked, "Friends, did you say 'Buddha'?" "Your Majesty, we said 'Buddha'," they replied. Having made them say it three times, he thought, "The word 'Buddha' is immeasurable; it is impossible to set a limit to it." Being thus inspired by that word, he gave them a hundred thousand coins and asked again, "Is there any other news?" "Your Majesty, the Dhamma-gem has appeared," they replied. Upon hearing that, he took their confirmation three times in the same manner, gave another hundred thousand coins, and asked once more, "Is there any other news?" "Your Majesty, the Saṅgha-gem has appeared," they replied. Hearing that as well, he took their confirmation in the same manner, gave another hundred thousand coins, and having written the details of the gift on a tablet, he sent them, saying, "Friends, go to the presence of the Chief Queen." When the merchants had left, he asked his ministers, "Ministers, the Buddha has appeared in the world; what will you do?" "Your Majesty, what do you wish to do?" they asked. "I shall ordain," he declared. "We also shall ordain," they replied. All of them, without regard for their homes or wealth, departed on the very horses they had ridden there.
248:
The merchants went to Queen Anojā and showed her the letter. Having read the letter, the Queen asked, "Dear friends, the King has granted you many kahāpaṇas; what service have you performed?" They replied, "O Queen, we have brought pleasant news." "Dear friends, can you let us hear it as well?" she asked. "O Queen, we can; however, it is not proper to speak with unpurified mouths," they replied. Queen Anojā then had water brought in a golden pitcher. The merchants washed their mouths and reported the news in the same manner they had reported it to the King. Upon hearing this, the Queen was filled with joy and, following the King's example, made them affirm each phrase three times. For each affirmation, she gave three hundred thousand, totaling nine hundred thousand kahāpaṇas. In total, the merchants received one million two hundred thousand kahāpaṇas. Then she asked the merchants, "Dear friends, where is the King?" They replied, "O Queen, he has departed, saying he will ordain." "In that case, dear friends, you may go," she said, dismissing the merchants. She then summoned the wives of the ministers who had gone with the King and asked, "Dear ladies, do you know where your husbands have gone?" They replied, "Noble Lady, we know; they have gone with the King to play in the park." "Dear ladies, it is true they went, but having gone to that park and heard that 'The Buddha has arisen, the Dhamma has arisen, the Saṅgha has arisen,' they have gone saying, 'We will ordain in the presence of the Blessed One.' What will you do?" she asked. They asked, "Noble Lady, what do you yourself wish to do?" She replied, "I shall ordain; I do not wish to keep on the tip of my tongue the vomit spat out by those kings." "If that is so, we too shall ordain," they said, and all the women had their chariots harnessed and set out.

King Mahākappina, together with a thousand ministers, reached the bank of the Ganges. At that time, the Ganges was overflowing with water. Seeing the river, he thought, "This Ganges is overflowing and teeming with fierce fish. There are no servants or men with us who could make a boat or a raft for us. The virtues of the Blessed One are spread from the Avīci hell below to the highest plane of existence (Bhavagga) above. If this Teacher is truly the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), may the tops of these horses' hooves not get wet." With this act of truth, they made the horses gallop over the surface of the water. Not even the top of a single horse's hoof got wet; they reached the other bank as if traveling on a royal highway. Further on, they reached another great river. "What is the name of this second river?" he asked. "O King, it is named Nīlavāhinī; it is about half a yojana in depth and width," they replied. In that river, there was no other act of truth; only by that same act of truth concerning the Buddha...
249:
By that same act of truth, they crossed that river (the Nīlavāhinī), which was half a yojana wide. Then, reaching the third great river named Candabhāgā, they crossed it as well by that same act of truth.

The Teacher, too, having arisen from the attainment of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) at dawn that day, surveyed the world and saw, "Today, King Mahākappina, having renounced a kingdom of three hundred yojanas, is coming with a retinue of a thousand ministers to ordain in my presence." Thinking, "It is proper for me to go and welcome them," he attended to his physical needs early in the morning. Surrounded by the community of monks, he wandered for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, having returned from the alms round, he himself took his bowl and robes, flew into the air, and arrived at a great banyan tree (Mahānigrodha) on the bank of the Candabhāgā river, opposite the landing place where they would emerge. Sitting there cross-legged and establishing mindfulness before him, he emitted the six-colored Buddha-rays. As the King and his ministers emerged from that landing place, they saw the Buddha-rays darting here and there. Beholding the face of the Blessed One, which was as beautiful as the full moon, they reached a conclusion just by the sight: "This is surely the Teacher for whose sake we set out to ordain." From the very spot they saw him, they approached, bowing in homage, and paid respects to the Teacher.

King Mahākappina, holding the Teacher's ankles, paid homage and sat down in a suitable place together with the thousand ministers. The Teacher delivered a Dhamma discourse to them. At the conclusion of the teaching, all of them were established in the Fruit of Arahantship and requested ordination from the Teacher. The Teacher, knowing, "These people have given gifts of robes in the past and thus have come bringing their own bowls and robes," stretched out his golden-hued hand and said, "Come, monks (Ehi Bhikkhavo), the Dhamma is well-expounded; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering." That very call became the novice ordination and higher ordination for those venerable ones. They surrounded the Teacher like elder monks of sixty years' standing.

Queen Anojā, too, having reached the bank of the Ganges with a retinue of a thousand chariots, did not see any boat or raft brought for the King. With her own wisdom, she thought, "The King must have gone by making an act of truth. Indeed, that Teacher did not appear for the benefit of the King and ministers alone. If that Teacher is truly the Perfectly Enlightened One, may our chariots not sink in the water." So thinking, she made the chariots gallop over the surface of the water. Not even the rims of the chariot wheels got wet. She crossed the second and third rivers by that same act of truth concerning the Buddha. As they were emerging from the river, at the foot of the banyan tree...
250:
(The Queen) saw the Blessed One. The Blessed One also thought, "If these women see their own husbands, lustful desire will arise and create an obstacle to the Paths and Fruits, and they will not be able to listen to the Dhamma." Thus, he made it so they could not see each other. All those women came up from the landing place, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down. The Blessed One delivered a Dhamma discourse to them. At the end of the discourse, all the women were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and then saw each other again. The Blessed One thought, "Let the Theri Uppalavaṇṇā come." The Theri came, ordained all the women, and took them to the nunnery. The Blessed One, taking a thousand monks, traveled through the air to the Jetavana monastery.

Then, the Elder Mahākappina, knowing that his task as a monk had reached its completion, became free from concern and spent his time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). Whether in the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling, he frequently uttered the inspired exclamation: "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!" The monks started a conversation: "Elder Kappina is uttering this exclamation because he remembers the happiness of kingship." They reported this to the Tathāgata. The Blessed One said, "My son is uttering this exclamation because of the bliss of the Path and the bliss of the Fruit," and spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:

"One who drinks the Dhamma lives happily with a serene mind;
The wise person always delights in the Dhamma revealed by the Noble Ones."

Then one day, the Blessed One called the thousand disciple monks of that Elder and asked, "Monks, does your teacher preach the Dhamma to you?" (The monks) replied, "Venerable Sir, he does not. He lives without exertion, devoted only to dwelling in the happiness of the present life; he does not give even a word of advice to anyone." The Blessed One had the Elder summoned and asked, "Kappina, is it true that you do not give even a word of advice to your disciples?" "It is true, Blessed One," he replied. "Brahmin, do not do so. From today onwards, preach the Dhamma to your disciples." The Elder accepted the Blessed One's words with great respect, saying, "Very well, Venerable Sir." In a single session, he preached the Dhamma to the thousand monks and led them all to the Fruit of Arahatship. Later, while the Blessed One was seated in the midst of the Saṅgha and assigning the Elders to their respective positions, he placed the Elder Mahākappina in the foremost position among those who give exhortation to monks (Bhikkhu-ovādaka).
251:
## The Story of the Elder Sāgata
In the tenth discourse, "tejodhātu-kusalānaṃ" means that among those who are skilled in entering the fire element, the Elder Sāgata is the foremost. This Elder, through the attainment of the fire element, exhausted the power of the Ambatittha Naga with his own power and made that Naga free from poisonous pride. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those skilled in the fire element.

The following is the sequential account of his past deeds: This future Elder was reborn in a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, he saw the Blessed One appoint a monk to the foremost position among those skilled in the fire element. He performed a great meritorious deed and aspired to that position. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha. They named him the youth Sāgata. Later, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, he gained faith, became a monk, and developed the eight meditative attainments, reaching mastery (vasībhāva) in them.

Then one day, while the Blessed One was wandering on a journey, he arrived near the city of Kosambī. At that time, at a river landing, many visiting travelers had become enemies of an old former boatman and had beaten and killed him. With a mind full of resentment, he made a wish and was reborn at that very landing as a Naga king of great power. Because of his resentment, he would cause rain out of season and not allow rain during the proper season, so the crops did not flourish well. The people of the entire country performed annual offerings to appease that danger and built a house for him to live in. The Blessed One also crossed at that same landing and, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, went there thinking, "I will stay the night in that very place."

Then the Elder Sāgata, hearing that "there is a fierce Naga king here," thought, "I should tame this Naga king, make him free from poisonous pride, and prepare a place for the Blessed One to stay." He entered the Naga king's dwelling and sat down cross-legged. The Naga became angry and thought, "Who is this shaveling that has entered my dwelling and is sitting here?" and emitted smoke. The Elder emitted even more smoke. The Naga blazed with fire; the Elder also blazed with even greater fire and exhausted the Naga's power. That Naga thought, "How great...
252: "...this monk truly is!" and prostrating at the Elder's feet, he said, "Venerable Sir, I go to you for refuge." "There is no need to take refuge in me; take refuge in the Ten-Powered Blessed One," the Elder replied. The Naga king agreed, saying "Very well," and became a follower who took refuge in the Blessed One. From then on, he did not harm anyone, and he caused the rain to fall properly, so the crops were fully abundant. The people of Kosambī heard that "the Venerable Sāgata has tamed the Naga who lives at the Mango Landing (Ambatittha)," and while waiting for the Blessed One's arrival, they prepared great offerings for the Ten-Powered Blessed One. After making great offerings to the Blessed One, on the advice of the group of six monks (Chabbaggiya), they prepared clear liquor the color of a pigeon's foot in every house. The next day, when the Elder Sāgata was walking for alms, they offered a little in every house. Since it was a time before the training rule had been prescribed, the Elder, being requested by the people, in every house...
253:
Elder Sāgata drank [the alcohol] little by little and, having gone to a place not far away, lost mindfulness due to the lack of food and fell down in a place where rubbish was discarded. When the Blessed One was departing after finishing His meal, He saw the Elder and had him brought [to the monastery]. Upon returning to the monastery, He rebuked him and prescribed a training rule. On the following day, Elder Sāgata regained mindfulness and, hearing about what he had done, confessed his fault and asked the Blessed One for forgiveness. Having developed a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he cultivated insight (vipassanā) and attained the fruit of Arahatship. Thus, this story arose in the Vinaya. This story should be understood in detail as it appears in the Vinaya Pali. Later, while the Blessed One was staying at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, as He was appointing the Elders to their respective positions in order, He placed Elder Sāgata in the foremost position among those skilled in the fire element (tejodhātu).

## The Story of Elder Rādha
With the eleventh term, 'paṭibhāneyyakānaṃ', the Blessed One shows that Elder Rādha is the foremost among the monks who are the cause of the manifestation of the Buddha's Dhamma teachings. Based on the Elder's manifestation of wisdom and his convincing faith, new and fresh Dhamma teachings appear to the Blessed One. Therefore, the Elder became known as the foremost among those who inspire the manifestation of the Dhamma.

The sequential account of his case is as follows: This future Elder Rādha was also born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Buddha Padumuttara. Later, while listening to the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching, he saw the Blessed One appointing a monk to the foremost position among those who inspire the manifestation of the Dhamma. He performed a meritorious deed and aspired to that position. Having served the Tathāgata for the rest of his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in a Brahmin family in the city of Rājagaha during the time of this Buddha's appearance and was named 'Youth Rādha'.

When he grew old, he was not respected by his children and wife. Thinking, 'I will spend my time by ordaining,' he went to the monastery and requested the Elders for ordination. No one wished to ordain him, saying, 'He is a worn-out old Brahmin.' Then one day, the Brahmin went to the Blessed One, performed his duties, and sat in a suitable place. The Blessed One, seeing the perfection of his supporting conditions (upanissaya) for attaining the Paths and Fruits, and wishing to initiate a Dhamma conversation, asked, 'Brahmin, do your children and wife look after you?' He replied, 'Venerable Gotama, how could they look after me? They have driven me out, saying I am old.'

When the Blessed One asked, 'Brahmin, is it not suitable for you to ordain?', he replied, 'Venerable Gotama, who will ordain me? No one wishes to ordain me because I am very old.' The Blessed One gave permission to Elder Sāriputta to ordain the Brahmin. The Elder, placing the Blessed One's words on his head, ordained the Brahmin Rādha. Thinking, 'The Blessed One had this Brahmin ordained with respect; it is not proper for me to look after him without respect,' he took Elder Rādha and went to a village monastery. In that monastery, as Elder Rādha was a newly ordained monk and gains were scarce, the Elder gave him his own lodging. He also gave his own choice alms-food to Elder Rādha and went for alms-round himself. Having obtained suitable lodging and food, Elder Rādha [took] a meditation subject from Elder Sāriputta...
254:
'They have driven me out, saying I am old,' he replied. When asked, 'Brahmin, is it not suitable for you to ordain?', he replied, 'Venerable Gotama, who will ordain me? No one wishes to because of my old age.' The Blessed One gave permission to Elder Sāriputta to ordain the Brahmin. The Elder, placing the Blessed One's words on his head, ordained the Brahmin Rādha and thought, 'The Blessed One had this Brahmin ordained with respect; it is not proper for me to look after him disrespectfully.' He took Elder Rādha and went to a village monastery. In that village monastery, as Elder Rādha was a newly ordained monk and gains were difficult, the Elder gave him his own lodging. He also gave his own choice alms-food to Elder Rādha and went for alms-round himself. Having obtained suitable lodging and food, Elder Rādha took a meditation subject from Elder Sāriputta and soon attained the fruit of Arahatship.

Then the Elder took Elder Rādha and came to see the Blessed One. The Blessed One, though knowing, asked, 'Sāriputta, how is your resident pupil whom I gave you? Is he not dissatisfied with the Dispensation?' He replied, 'Venerable Sir, a monk who is very delighted in the Dispensation should be like this Elder Rādha.' Then, a conversation arose in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding Elder Sāriputta: 'Elder Sāriputta is one who knows the favors done to him and requites them (kataññū katavedī).' Hearing this, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, it is not surprising that Sāriputta is grateful and requites favors now; in the past, even when he was born in a life with rootless rebirth (ahetuka-paṭisandhi), he was indeed grateful and requited favors.' The monks asked, 'Venerable Sir, at what time did this happen?'

Monks, in the past, at the foot of a mountain, about five hundred carpenters entered a great forest, cut timber and other materials, built a large raft, and floated it down the river. At that time, a noble elephant, while grabbing a branch with its trunk in an uneven place, could not withstand the force of the branch breaking and stepped on a sharp tree stump with its foot. The stump pierced its foot, and it suffered intense pain. Unable to move forward, the elephant lay down right there. After a few days, seeing the carpenters passing near him, the elephant thought, 'Depending on these people, I shall find relief for my life,' and followed behind them. When the carpenters turned around and saw the elephant, they fled in fear. The elephant, knowing they were fleeing, stood still; only when they stopped did he follow again.

The head carpenter thought, 'This elephant follows us when we stand and stands still when we flee; there must be a reason for this.' All the carpenters [went] to various trees...
255:
The carpenters climbed up the trees and sat waiting for the arrival of that noble elephant. That noble elephant came to the carpenters, showed them his foot, and lay down on his side. Then, the thought occurred to the carpenters: "Friends, this elephant has come because he is ill, not for any other reason." They went near the elephant and saw a splinter stuck in his foot. Saying, "This is the reason why this elephant has come," they made an incision at the edge of the splinter with a sharp adze, tied it firmly with a rope, and pulled it out. Then, they squeezed the wound to remove the pus and blood, washed it with astringent water, and applied a medicine they knew. Before long, they made the elephant healthy and comfortable.

When the noble elephant recovered from his illness, he thought: "These carpenters have been of great help to me; I have regained my life because of them. I should be one who is grateful and appreciative towards these carpenters." He then went to his dwelling place and brought back a white Gandha elephant calf. When the carpenters saw the calf, they were extremely delighted, saying, "Our elephant has even brought his son!"

The noble elephant thought: "If I stay here, they will not know the reason for my coming, wondering 'Why has he come?'" and so he departed from where he stood. The elephant calf followed closely behind his father. Knowing that the calf was following him, the noble elephant gave a vocal signal for him to turn back. Hearing his father's command, the calf turned back and went to the carpenters. Although the carpenters knew, "This noble elephant must have come to give us this calf," they sent him away, saying, "We have no work for you to do here; go back to your father."

The noble elephant sent the calf back to the carpenters again, even though the calf had returned to him three times. From then on, the carpenters kept the elephant calf with them and looked after him. At mealtime, each person gave him a handful of rice, and the calf received as much food as he desired until he was full. That elephant calf would carry the timber and materials that were cut inside the forest by the carpenters and pile them up in the courtyard. In this way, he performed other helpful tasks as well.

The Teacher (the Buddha) brought forth this account to illustrate the grateful nature of the Elder Sāriputta in the past. At that time, the Elder Sāriputta was the great elephant, and the monk who had given up his effort, mentioned in the occasion of the discourse, was the elephant calf. Upon reaching the Saṃyutta Nikāya, in the entire Rādha Saṃyutta, and also in the Dhammapada...
256:
"One should associate with a wise person who points out faults and reproves, as if he were one who reveals a hidden treasure. It is better, and never worse, for one who associates with such a wise person." (Dhammapada, 76).

This verse is known as the Dhamma teaching of the Elder Rādha. Later, when the Teacher was placing the Elders in their respective foremost positions in order, He placed the Elder Rādha in the foremost position among those with quick wit (paṭibhāna).

## The Story of the Elder Mogharāja

In the twelfth sutta, the phrase "lūkhacīvaradharānaṃ" indicates that the Elder Mogharāja is the foremost among those who wear coarse robes. This Elder wore rag-robes (paṃsukūla) characterized by three types of coarseness: coarseness of the cloth, coarseness of the thread used for sewing, and coarseness of the dye. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who wear coarse robes.

The chronological account of his question-task is as follows: This future Elder also took rebirth in a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher placing a certain monk in the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes. He performed an act of merit and aspired for that position. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. Long before the appearance of Kassapa Buddha, he took rebirth in the house of a minister in the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana. When he reached maturity, he served King Kaṭṭhavāhana and obtained the position of a minister.

At that time, Kassapa Buddha appeared in the world. King Kaṭṭhavāhana heard that "A Buddha has appeared in the world," and calling the minister, he said: "Dear friend, I hear that a Buddha has appeared in the world. It is not possible for both of us to leave this border city empty at the same time. You go first to the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), and having confirmed the appearance of the Buddha, bring the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) to this city." He sent him along with a thousand men. In due course, the minister went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma discourse, gained faith, and ordained right there. He practiced the recluse's Dhamma for twenty thousand years. All the men who went with him, however, turned back and returned to the king.

This Elder, having fulfilled his virtue, passed away and wandered through the realms of devas and humans for one Buddha-interval (buddhantara). Long before the appearance of our Ten-Powered One...
257:
