He took conception in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named the youth Mogharāja. King Kaṭṭhavāhana, having performed extraordinary meritorious deeds under the Blessed One Kassapa, wandered through the realms of devas and humans for one buddhantara with his retinue. Before the appearance of our Blessed One, he took conception in the house of the royal chaplain in Sāvatthī and was named the youth Bāvarī. Later, that youth Bāvarī mastered the three Vedas and lived teaching the arts to sixteen thousand young brahmins. Then, during the reign of King Pasenadi of Kosala, upon the death of his father, he was given the position of royal chaplain. At that time, this youth Mogharāja also studied the arts under the brahmin Bāvarī.

Then one day, the brahmin Bāvarī went into seclusion and, while looking for the essence in the arts he had mastered, he did not see any essence for the hereafter. Thinking, 'I shall go forth as an ascetic and seek the essence for the hereafter,' he approached King Kosala and asked permission to go forth. Having been granted permission by the king, he departed to go forth, surrounded by sixteen thousand young brahmins. King Kosala also sent a minister along with him, giving him a thousand coins, saying, 'In the place where the teacher goes forth, arrange a dwelling place for him.' While searching for a pleasant place to live, the brahmin Bāvarī moved away from the Middle Country and had a dwelling place built for himself on the banks of the Godhāvarī River, in the border region between the territories of King Assaka and King Muḷaka.

Then a man went to see the matted-hair ascetics and, with their permission, built a dwelling for himself on the land belonging to them. Seeing what that man had done, another hundred families built a hundred houses. All of them gathered and said, 'We are living on the land belonging to the venerable ones; there is no reason to live here for free. We shall give you something so that you may live in comfort.' Thus, each person offered one coin...
258:
...and placed it at the dwelling place of the brahmin Bāvarī. All the coins brought there amounted to about one hundred thousand. The brahmin Bāvarī asked, 'For what purpose have these been brought?' They replied, 'Venerable sir, it is for the sake of an offering so that you may live in comfort.' He said, 'If I had desired silver and gold, I would not have gone forth, abandoning a great mass of wealth. Take your coins and go.' They replied, 'We have already relinquished these to the venerable sir and shall not take them back. We shall bring them every year in this same manner. May the venerable sir take these and give them as alms.' The brahmin consented and bestowed them as gifts to the poor, wayfarers, and beggars. His reputation as a donor who gave repeatedly became well-known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

Then, in the village named Dunniwiṭṭha in the kingdom of Kaliṅga, the wife of a brahmin born in the lineage of the brahmin Jūjaka repeatedly urged her husband, saying, 'Bāvarī, it is said, is giving alms. Go and bring gold and silver from him.' Being thus urged by her and unable to resist, he went to Bāvarī. The brahmin Bāvarī, having finished giving alms, had entered his leaf-hut and was lying down, reflecting on his generosity, when that brahmin arrived. Upon arrival, he said, 'Brahmin, give me a gift! Brahmin, give me a gift!' Bāvarī said, 'Brahmin, you have come at the wrong time. I have already given to all the beggars who arrived; there are no coins left now.' He replied, 'Brahmin, I do not need many coins. For you who give such a great amount in alms, it is impossible to be without coins. Give me five hundred coins.' Bāvarī said, 'Brahmin, I do not have even five hundred. You will receive them when the next time for giving alms arrives.' He said, 'How can I come at your next time of giving?' Then, making a mound of sand at the door of Bāvarī’s leaf-hut, scattering red flowers all around, and moving his lips as if chanting a mantra, he said, 'May your head split into seven pieces!'

The brahmin Bāvarī thought, 'This wandering brahmin of great austerity, having taken up ascetic practices, says to me that on the seventh day my head shall split into seven pieces. And I do not have the five hundred coins to be given to this brahmin. Surely, he will kill me.' Thus, while he lay there with the shaft of sorrow pierced within him, at the end of the night, at dawn, Bāvarī’s mother, who had been reborn as a deity, appeared. Seeing her son pierced by the shaft of sorrow, she came and spoke thus:
259:
“Dear son, this brahmin knows neither the head nor the splitting of the head; you too do not know that a Buddha has arisen in the world. If you have any doubt, go to the presence of the Blessed One and ask; that Blessed One will explain this matter to you.” From the moment the Brahmin Bāvarī heard the words of the deity, he felt relieved. At dawn the next day, he called all his disciples and said, “Sons, it is said that a Buddha has arisen in the world. Go quickly and find out whether he is indeed a Buddha or not, then return and inform me. I shall go to the presence of the Blessed One. However, I am old and the danger to my life is difficult to know. Go to the presence of that Blessed One and ask questions using these signs.” Thus, he prepared and gave them the questions concerning the splitting of the head.

Then he thought, “All these youths are wise. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One and reaching the completion of their duties as monks, they might or might not return to me.” Then, he gave instructions to his nephew, the youth Ajita: “You, however, should certainly return to me. Come back and tell me of the virtues you have attained.” Then, those sixteen thousand matted-hair ascetics, making the youth Ajita their leader along with the sixteen chief disciples, set out on their journey saying, “We shall ask questions of the Blessed One.” Wherever they arrived, they were asked, “Venerables, where are you going?” They replied, “We are going to ask questions in the presence of the Ten-Powered One,” and they gathered followers from the outskirts, traveling a distance of many hundreds of leagues. The Blessed One thought, “On the day they arrive, there will be no opportunity for others; this place is suitable for this assembly.” He then went and sat upon the Back Rock (Piṭṭhipāsāṇa) at the Rock Shrine (Pāsāṇacetiya). The youth Ajita, together with his followers, ascended that Back Rock and, seeing the perfection of the Blessed One’s physical body, thought, “This man must surely be a Buddha who has removed the veil in this world.” He proceeded while mentally asking the questions sent by his teacher.

On that day, the assembly gathered at that place extended for twelve leagues. Among those sixteen chief disciples, the youth Mogharāja was stiff with pride, thinking, “I am wiser than all.” It occurred to him, “This youth Ajita is the eldest of all; it is not proper for me to ask my questions before him...”
260:
...(thinking it) improper, he felt ashamed and did not ask his question first. After Ajita had finished asking, he became the second to ask the Blessed One. The Blessed One thought, “The youth Mogharāja is stiff with pride; his wisdom has not yet reached maturity. It is proper to restrain his pride.” Thus, He said, “Wait, Mogharāja, let others ask their questions first.” Having received this rebuke from the Blessed One, the youth Mogharāja thought, “For so long, I have wandered thinking there is no one wiser than I. Buddhas do not speak without knowing. The Teacher must have seen a fault in my question,” and he remained silent. When eight people had asked their questions in succession, he could no longer restrain himself and stood up again as the ninth. The Blessed One rebuked him once more.

He remained silent again, thinking, “Now I shall not be able to even be the most junior in the Saṅgha.” He then asked his question as the fifteenth person. Then, the Blessed One, knowing that his wisdom had matured, answered the question. At the conclusion of the teaching, Mogharāja, along with his retinue of one thousand matted-hair ascetics, attained Arahantship. In this same manner, the remaining fifteen thousand matted-hair ascetics also attained Arahantship. All of them became ‘Ehi Bhikkhu’ monks, bearing miraculously created bowls and robes. The remaining people (who attained lower stages like Sotāpanna) are not mentioned. From that time on, the Elder Mogharāja wore robes characterized by three types of coarseness. Thus, the story arose in the Pārayanavagga. Later, while the Blessed One was residing at Jetavana, when He was appointing the elders to their respective positions of eminence, He placed the Elder Mogharāja in the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes in this Dispensation, saying, “Monks, among my monk disciples who wear coarse robes, Mogharāja is the foremost.”

## Commentary on the Fourth Vagga.
## The commentary on the Theragāthā, consisting of forty-one suttas, is finished.
